case_summary.text: Excise & Customs : Where assessee had deflated price of its final product and used transport firm to claim inflated freight charges, thereby, reducing assessable value, department was right in demanding duty on proper value with interest and penalty.

Customs : Deemed addition in respect of 'loading, unloading and handling charges' under rule 9(2)(b) of Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 at 1 per cent of CIF, even where actual charges are available, is ultra vires section 14; hence, said deemed addition at 1 per cent of CIF would apply only if actual charges are not ascertainable

Excise & Customs : Where department had been grossly negligent in pursuing matter and had been challenging order before various forums contrary to procedure laid down by law and had consumed 11 years and 227 days, condonation of delay could not be allowed, as assessee must have arranged his financial affairs, which need not be disturbed at such distance of time

EXCISE/ST/VAT : In case of transnational group import, loading of value by lower authority was applied uniformly without reference either to base price of each article of import or of total value of consignment in each bill of entry and appropriate proceedings for finalization of assessment was initiated by 'proper officer'; order of loading was to be set aside
Excise & Customs : Ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were not liable to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purposes

ST : Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013 providing for recovery after expiry of 30 days from date of filing of stay application before Commissioner (Appeals) was illegal; recovery can be made only if assessee has delayed decision
Excise & Customs : If it is found that assessee had deflated assessable value of its final product by inflating freight charges, demand of duty on proper value with interest and penalty is valid

GST/EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where assessee had changed its method of valuation as per rule 8 of Excise valuation Rules on advice of Department in course of audit, Adjudicating Authority, without referring to said communication could not invoke extended period of limitation and hold that assessee was guilty of suppression of relevant facts and thereby impose duty following Rule 4 Valuation

Excise & Customs : Assessee, who is benefited by exemption, is bound to discharge post-import/clearance liability during period when such Notification was in force; department cannot enforce compliance with post-import/post-clearance condition for period after rescission of exemption notification
Assessment order valid as presence of portal reference number proves digital authentication; writ dismissed for unexplained delay: HC
Imports made by assessee, himself, at another port may be regarded as identical goods for custom valuation
Dept. couldn’t recover duty during pendency of stay application if such pendency wasn’t attributable to assessee

GST/EXCISE/ST/VAT : A Notification would come into effect from date and time when it was electronically printed in gazette and mere uploading same on website would have no significance and, therefore, where Notification No. 29/2018-cus, dated 01-03-2018 was updated on 02-03-2018 and came to be published in official gazette on 06-03-2018 whereas custom duty had already been paid by assessee on 05-03-2018, enhanced amount sought to be realised from assessee on basis of aforesaid Notification was unlawful

INCOME TAX : Where assessment order was passed in case of assessee by Assessing Officer under section 153C read with section 143(3) making addition of certain amount under section 69B on 21-4-2021 for assessment year 2016-17, since assessment order was ought to be passed on 31.12.2020, thus, there was delay of 111 days, impugned order was barred by limitation
Excise & Customs : Circular trading viz. import and export of same goods many times, cannot be alleged to reject FOB value of exports when CIF value of imports was accepted each time

Excise/ST/GST : Where circular, invalidating utilization of amount available in Electronic Credit Ledger for due compliance of pre-deposit, had come into force only on 28.10.2022 and impugned appeal had been filed much before circular came into force, hence, circular would apply only prospectively, therefore, impugned order by appellate tribunal passed against appellant-department was valid

GST : Demand raised against assessee pursuant to Circular No. 34/8/2018-GST, dated 01-03-2018 and Notification No. 9/2023-CT, was to be stayed till next date of hearing in view of fact validity of both Circular and Notification was under challenge before various fora

Excise & Customs: In case of undervaluation of goods imported at Chennai port, imports of same goods made by assessee himself at Mumbai port may be regarded as 'identical/similar goods' and may be used to determine customs value of imports at Chennai

EXCISE/ST/VAT : An officer who did assessment, could only undertake reassessment under section 28(4) of Customs Act, hence, goods, cameras having been cleared for import by a Deputy Commissioner of Customs who decided that goods were exempted, Additional Director General of DRI was not proper officer to exercise power under section 28(4)

CST & VAT : Where assessee was transporting chicks within State of Kerala and Competent Authority detained same on plea that value of chicks had not been disclosed at floor rate prescribed in two circulars, since circulars would be applicable only for import of chicks into State, chicks could not be detained on question of undervaluation
Service provided after import would not enhance assessable value even if directly related to imported goods: CESTAT

Excise & Customs : In case of delay in passing of review order by Department on account of sufficient cause, instead of non-suiting Department on technical ground, it would be appropriate that dispute between parties is decided on merits by compensating assessee, for prejudice caused to it, by way of payment of costs

Excise & Customs : Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013 is non est insofar it mandates recovery during pendency of stay applications, where such applications remain pending for reasons not attributable to assessee

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Delhi High Court denied to interfere with right of ICDs or CFSs to recover penal charges from importers in accordance with tariff so fixed, where goods continued to remain in premises of ICDs or CFSs beyond "free period" during COVID pandemic lockdown period which disrupted movement of goods

IT : Expression 'even if delay in disposing of appeal is not attributable to assessee' as inserted in third proviso to section 254(2A) by virtue of Finance Act, 2008 failed to achieve its object that assesses should not misuse stay orders granted in their favour by adopting delaying tactics, same is to be struck down
Excise & Customs : Any delay in payment of duty i.e., where duty is paid much after removal of goods, assessee is liable to interest irrespective of whether assessment is provisional or final

Excise & Customs : A CHA cannot be expected to be a better expert on customs valuation than customs officer; hence, his license cannot be revoked merely because he did not advise importer/revenue to add certain expenses in value, especially when there was no evidence that he was aware that said expenses were includible
Department can't seek coercive recovery if delay in disposing of stay isn't attributable to assessee

Excise & Customs : When freight and insurance is charged separately on actual basis under debit notes which are like invoices, it cannot be said that freight and insurance charges are not being separately charged; therefore, same is deductible (not includible) in assessable value under Central Excise

Excise & Customs : Before assessment of value of goods based on transaction value of identical goods, it must be evidenced that imports of identical goods are comparable imports and assessee must be given reasonable opportunity to counter same
EXCISE/ST/VAT : Service rendered in India after import, even if directly related to imported goods, cannot justifiably enhance assessable value

Excise & Customs: Circular No. 967/1/2013-CX., dated 1-1-2013 mandating initiation of recovery proceedings 30 days after filing of an appeal, if no stay is granted by Commissioner (Appeals), cannot be applied to an assessee who has filed an application for stay, which has remained pending for reasons beyond control of assessee

Excise & Customs : Where relevant clarification suggesting manner of computation of value was issued only in October 1996, mis-declaration cannot be alleged for period prior to October 1996 and therefore, extended period of limitation cannot be invoked upto September, 1996

GST : Where assessee challenged impugned order on ground that it was in violation of Circular No. 200/12/2023-GST, dated 01.08.2023 and Circular No. 235/29/2024-GST, dated 11-10-2024 with submission that prior to 27-7-2023, tax was not leviable, since issue was not brought to notice of adjudicating authority at time of adjudication and raised first time before Court, instant writ petition was not to be entertained

Excise & Customs : Where, having defaulted in payment of duty beyond 30 days, assessee continued to use credit to pay duty despite prohibition on Cenvat use under rule 8(3A), assessee was liable to pre-deposit duty in cash with applicable interest

GST : Where petitioner-assessee filed writ application requesting respondent-department to accept all disputed taxes in light of Circular No. 238/32/2024 GST dated 15.10.2024, however aforementioned circular was not applicable to petitioner-assessee, but since, petitioner-assessee was willing to pay all disputed taxes including interest and penalty, therefore, writ application was disposed of by allowing petitioner-assessee to pay outstanding amount and respondent-department was directed to accept payment as fulfillment of tax liability.
HC directed dept. to allow ITC to assessee as per CBIC’s Circular as dept. did not deny the entitlement

GST/Excise/ST/VAT : Where assessee had cleared goods from factory gate as well as from depots and requested Excise Authorities to advise as to method to be adopted for depot sales so as to arrive at differential duty and Excise Authorities had not responded to request and thereafter Adjudicating Authority invoking extended period of limitation issued on assessee show cause notice alleging that assessable value in respect of depot sales was deliberately mis-declared by assessee with intention to evade payment of duty, if there was intention of assessee to evade excise duty, it would not have sought for a clarification from Excise Authorities as to correct method of calculating duty on depot sales or paid differential duty with method of valuation and, therefore, invoking extended period of limitation was not justifiable

Excise & Customs : Mere fact that order of appellate authority is not acceptable to department and is subject matter of an appeal/revision, cannot be a ground for not following it unless its operation is suspended by competent court
Excise & Customs : Department cannot recover dues during pendency of stay applications before appellate authorities, if such pendency is not attributable in any manner whatsoever to assessees

ST : Sl. Nos. 3, 6 and 9 of para 2 of Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX were read down so that recovery can be made pending stay application only if it remained pending for reasons attributed to assessee; further, Sl. No. 10 was read down to permit reasonable time to assessee to seek protection from appellate forum

IT : Where during pendency of appeal against assessment order passed under section 143(3), assessee filed a petition challenging constitutional validity of proviso to rule 9A, since assessee's appeal was pending before Commissioner (Appeals) on merits, interest of justice would be served by not examining presently issue of constitutional validity and legality of proviso to rule 9A

Excise & Customs : Cause of justice demands a consideration of appeal on merits rather than to shunt assessee out for some part of delay attributable to it and some part of technicalities that may otherwise operate; hence, appeal dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals) for want of pre-deposit was directed to be restored on assessee pre-depositing entire demand

Excise & Customs : Where assessee manufactured two machineries and used same within its factory for manufacturing of final products and subsequently it cleared these machineries to its job worker and for discharging duty liability on machineries calculated assessable value of machineries by availing benefit of depreciation, availing of depreciation was in consonance with law

Port Trust Act : Where on failure to lift consignment by original importers, appellant purchased same and demurrage charges was levied due to delay in taking delivery, since delay occurred due to ensuring compliance of various statutory obligations, demurrage charges to be remitted

GST : Where ITC was denied due to return mismatch and assessee contended that it occurred only by a reason of GSTR-2A of supplier having not reflected entire tax payment made by petitioner to supplier, in view of Circular F. No. CBIC-20001/2/2022-GST, dated 27-12-2022, which made a provision for delay in supplier uploading his invoices in his portal, assessment order was to be redone

INCOME TAX : Instructions/OMF dated 29-2-2016 and Circular dated 31-7-2017, relate to power of Assessing Officer to be exercised under section 220(6) in order to streamline process of grant of stay insofar as it relates to tax demand disputed before Commissioner (Appeals), however, by relying upon aforesaid Instruction/Circular, assessee cannot contend as a matter of right that under all circumstances, Department cannot recover more than 20 per cent of tax demand when first appeal is pending bef

ST : Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013 is void upto extent it provides for recovery of dues during pendency of stay applications even though such pendency is not attributable in any manner whatsoever to assessees

GST : Where respondent-department passed an order dated 13.12.2023 by which petitioner-assessee’s claims were rejected for reversing Input Tax Credit and petitioner-assessee was directed to pay outstanding tax, penalty and interest, however, in W.P.Nos. 25081 of 2023, it was acknowledged that petitioners-assesses’ delay in filing returns was due to unavoidable circumstances and ruled in favor of petitioners-assessees by allowing extended time period for availing ITC, further, section 16 was amended by which extension of period for availing ITC claims was allowed, despite previous limitations under Section 16(4), consequently,impugned order dated 13.12.2023 was quashed insofar as it relates to claim made by petitioner-assessee for ITC

INCOME TAX : Instructions/OMF dated 29-2-2016 and Circular dated 31-7-2017, relate to power of Assessing Officer to be exercised under section 220(6) in order to streamline process of grant of stay insofar as it relates to tax demand disputed before Commissioner (Appeals), however, by relying upon aforesaid Instruction/Circular, assessee cannot contend as a matter of right that under all circumstances, Department cannot recover more than 20 per cent of tax demand when first appeal is pending before first appellate authority

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section 14, read with  section 151A, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Levy of, and exemption from, customs duties - Valuation of goods for purposes of assessment - Whether when circular issued by Central Board of Excise and Customs (Board) remains in operation, revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to terms of statute - Held, yes - Whether circular issued by Board in which it was said that demurrage did not form part of assessable value of goods imported, same was binding on revenue and department could not contend otherwise - Held, yes

FACT: The respondent imported various petroleum products and crude oil into India and had cleared the same upon payment of customs duty. The customs authorities having noted that the respondent had paid demurrage charges to the shipowners under the charter party agreements through negotiating bank issued a show-cause notice to the appellant and included the bank charges and demurrage paid in the customs value of the goods and created additional demand of customs duty against the respondent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order. On second appeal, the Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal (CEGAT) allowed the appeal of the respondent on the grounds; (i) that the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) had issued a circular on 14-8-1991 under section 151A of the Customs Act in which it was said that the demurrage did not form part of the assessable value of the goods imported and the circular was binding on the revenue and the department could not contend otherwise, (ii) that the decision of the Supreme Court in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [1999] 113 ELT 358 relied upon by the revenue was not an authority for the proposition that demurrage payable on account of delay in discharging goods from a vessel was includible in the value of goods while assessing the customs duty payable thereon, and (iii) that under section 14 the assessable value of the imported goods must be the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold and the payment of demurrage was not an incident of an ordinary sale and an extraordinary expenditure, like demurrage, could not be included in the assessable value of the imported goods.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: PER RUMA PAL, J. - Although a circular is not binding on a Court or an assessee, it is not open to the revenue to raise the contention that is contrary to a binding circular by the Board. When a circular remains in operation, the revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to the terms of the statute. Despite the decision of the Supreme Court, the department cannot be permitted to take a stand contrary to the instructions issued by the Board. A show-cause notice and demand contrary to existing circulars of the Board are ab initio bad. It is not open to the revenue to advance an argument or file an appeal contrary to the circulars. [Para 10]

The provisions of section 151A are in pari materia with the provisions of section 119 of the Income-tax Act and section 37B of the Central Excise Act. The Parliament introduced section 151A by an amendment to the Customs Act in 1995 but with effect from 27-12-1985 (Act 80 of 1995), when the Supreme Court had already construed identical language in the manner indicated. It may be assumed that the Parliament had legislatively approved the construction by using the exact words so construed again in the Customs Act. There is, therefore, no reason why the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court under the two earlier Acts should not also be determinative of the construction put on the later in respect of a materially similar statutory provision. This was also not argued by the appellant (department). [Para 11]

The relevant circular dated 14-8-1991 provides, inter alia, that 'demurrage' and 'despatch' money may not form a part of assessable value. [Para 12]

The circular dated 14-8-1999 in no uncertain terms excludes demurrage from the assessable value. In the light of the judicial principles enunciated earlier, it was not open to the appellant to either issue the show-cause notice or contend otherwise. The demand based on an assessable value inclusive of demurrage could not be sustained as long as the circular remained operative and as long as the decisions on the issue remain good law. [Para 13]

12]

The circular dated 14-8-1999 in no uncertain terms excludes demurrage from the assessable value. In the light of the judicial principles enunciated earlier, it was not open to the appellant to either issue the show-cause notice or contend otherwise. The demand based on an assessable value inclusive of demurrage could not be sustained as long as the circular remained operative and as long as the decisions on the issue remain good law. [Para 13] The submission of the appellant that the respondent had not acted on the basis of the circular and, therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel did not apply is misconceived. The circulars issued by the CBDT under the Income-tax Act and the CBEC under section 37B of the Central Excise Act have been held to be binding primarily on the basis of the language of the statutory provisions buttressed by the need of the adjudicating officers to maintain uniformity in the levy of tax/duty throughout the country. [Para 14]

The stand of the appellant that the Supreme Court had taken the view that demurrage was includible in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) both in the adjudication order and before the Tribunal appears to have been abandoned in the written notes of submission. Apart from the decision of the Constitution Bench in Collector of Central Excise v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 143 ELT 19 on the binding nature of the circulars, in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) the decision was on landing charges. It did not construe the 1988 Rules. The circular on the other hand was issued on a re-examination of the issue in the light of the GATT Valuation principles as incorporated in the 1988 Rules. [Para 17]

Therefore, demurrage was wrongly included by the adjudicating officer in the assessable value contrary to the directive of the CBEC at a time when the circular had not been withdrawn. [Para 18]

PER P. VENKATARAMA REDDI, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW) : The revenue's appeal is liable to be dismissed in the light of the circular dated 14-8-1991 issued by the CBEC which is traceable to the power conferred on the Board by section 151A of the Customs Act. The purpose of this separate opinion is only to highlight certain doubts as to the correctness of the proposition laid down in the two Dhiren Chemical Industries' cases (supra) - one decided by the Constitution Bench and the other by a three Judge Bench. [Para 20]

The circulars issued by the Board under section 151A of the Customs Act or section 37B of the Central Excise Act are generally binding on the revenue. However, when there is a statutory mandate to observe and follow the orders and instructions of the Board in regard to specified matters, that mandate has to be complied with. It is not open to the adjudicating authority to deviate from those orders or instructions which the statute enjoins that it should follow. If any order is passed contrary to those instructions the order is liable to be struck down on that very ground. Extending this principle which flows from the statutory provision contained in section 151A of the Customs Act or a pari materia provision in other fiscal enactments, the Supreme Court also held that it is not open to the department to file an appeal against the order passed in conformity with the circular. To this extent one has no difficulty in understanding the rationale of the decisions of the Supreme Court leaving apart for the time being the decisions in which a somewhat different note was struck. However, one is unable to reconcile to the view that even after the highest Court settles the law on the subject, the view expressed by the Central Board on the same point of law should still hold the field until and unless it is revoked. [Para 21]

As is evident from section 151A the Board is empowered to issue orders or instructions in order to ensure uniformity in the classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty. The need to issue such instructions arises when there is a doubt or ambiguity in relation to those matters. The possibility of varying views being taken by the customs officials while administering the Act may bring about uncertainty and confusion. In order to avoid this situation, section 151A has been enacted on the same lines as section 37A of the Central Excise Act. The apparent need to issue such circulars is left when there is no authoritative pronouncement of the Court on the subject. Once the relevant issue is decided by the Court at the highest level, the very basis and substratum of the circular disappears. The law laid down by the Supreme Court will ensure uniformity in the decisions at all levels. By an express constitutional provision, the law declared by the Supreme Court is made binding on all the Courts within the territory of India (vide Article 141), Proprio vigore the law is binding on all the Tribunals and authorities. [Para 22]

HEADNOTE: Section 129B read with Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Orders of Appelalte Tribunal - Rectification application cannot be used as a medium for rearguing lost points - Valuation: Landed cost is the assessable value; so additions of freight and insurance is in order: Discounts cannot be allowed where invoice value is available

FACT: The appellants had imported two Toyota Corona 1600 DLX Sedans. They presented the manufacturer's invoice at the lime of assessment of Customs duly. The Customs authorities determined duty payable after adding freight, insurance and landing charges to the invoice price. Though the importers claimed 15% discount on the manufacturer's price, as well as exclusion of freight, insurance and landing charges, these claims were rejected by the Asstt. Collr. On appeal the Tribunal upheld the Asstt. Collr.'s valuation. Depreciation claims in respect of car accessories like stereo AC were also disallowed. After this the importers submitted applications for rectification of mistakes which, they argued, were obvious and apparent in the earlier order. Their main contention is that as value should have been fixed at place of removal (the market in Japan) insurance and transportation expenses etc., were to be deducted. Besides, the Department was bound by promissory estoppel to allow a discount of 15% in view of a Departmental circular providing for this discount.

HELD: Rectification application cannot be used for re-arguing those points which were already discussed and settled by the Tribunal. As there is no apparent misapplication of law by the Tribunal, earlier decision cannot be disturbed. "under the garb of a rectification application, it is not open to a party to avail it as a further chance of re-arguing the matter or calling upon the Tribunal to review the basis of the decision. Such a course would be beyond the scope of an application for rectification. The "mistakes" repeatedly urged by the applicants were the contentions raised in the main appeals and Tribunal has taken a particular view. It may be argued that they are debatable conclusions. But rectification applications are not intended for re-opening a decision."

Valuation: Tribunal decision that valuation is to be based on prices at the point of landing is upheld. Hence adding of freight, insurance etc. are correct. Deduction of 15% from market price on ground of promissory estoppel is not relevant because the calculation was based on the manufacturer's invoice, whereas deductions were allowed in those cases where the calculation was based on international prices (in. the absence of manufacturer's invoice). "The Tribunal has in the main order held that the prices at which the goods were delivered at the point of landing in India was relevant and not the price at which the transactions took place in Tokyo. The adding of freight, insurance and landing charges was held to be correct. The claim for discount was rejected by the Tribunal for the reasons already stated. The Assessment of the air-conditioners and other accessories were upheld on merits. As rightly urged by the JDR, no promissory estoppel would arise."

HEADNOTE: Section 49 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Storage of imported goods in warehouse pending clearance - Departmental instructions have no legal binding. Budget clearances - if documents are presented timely but office is prematurely closed, the importer has to be given advantage. Technicalities--procedural lapse in not presenting bank certificate is no ground to deny clearance

FACT: The petitioners are engaged in the business of texturising base flat yarn. Base yarn was imported by them and lodged in a warehouse owned by Central Warehousing Corporation. The petitioners filed two bills of entry for removal of the above goods on 16th February, 1983 and 28th February, 1983. Customs duty was paid as per rates applicable on 28th February 1983. All that remained to be done was to pay the warehousing charges and lift the goods from the warehouse. The petitioner's agents came to get release of the goods on 28.2.1983 but to their surprise found that the cash counter was closed at 3 PM instead of 4 PM and delivery counter at 4 PM instead of 5 PM. As duty on the subject goods was increased w.e.f. 1.3.1983 petitioners approached their Association, who registered a protest with the Customs authorities, along with the request that the goods should be treated as having been delivered on 28.2.1983, thus getting the benefits of the pre-budget rates. The Department refused this, and contended that the advancing of working hours was valid because of a circular issued in that behalf.

HELD: Official circulars are not binding on a citizen. Departmental action based on such circulars can be held valid only if legal validity and sanction of the same is proved. Mere cyclostyled instructions, as in the present case, have no legal validity and it is against the principles of equity that the petitioners should be held liable for the consequences, and to pay enhanced customs duty. "The question has now been rightly posed by Mr. Jagtiani the learned Counsel for the Petitioners as to what is the legal sanction for this circular and whether the same can be accepted as a mandate. The learned Counsel for the Respondent Mr. Sethna when questioned could not throw any light on this aspect much less could he effectively answer this very relevant question posed with the necessary consequences that nothing has been shown on this forum to accept the legal validity of this circular, namely, about the authority, the sanction and all other features which go to make out a validly legal circular. In the absence of any such material and even an ostensible explanation which is not coming forth this becomes inescapable to obviously strike down the validity of this circular having no existence in law at all."

2. Warehoused goods--withholding delivery even when a party has been physically present to pay the warehousing charges and lift the goods is a failure on the part of the official staff. Hence, it is fair and just that the consignments should be treated as having been released on 28.2.1983. "...the Petitioners were waiting to offer the warehousing charges between 3 p.m. and 4 p.m. and thereby they could have obtained delivery between 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. as usual, the Petitioners' assertion that even this was not done by the staff within that time also even though they were just awaiting their turn for which the entire blame lies with the staff is not seriously controverted. ......I have no reservation in my mind that......they would be liable to pay customs duty as was prevailing on 28th February 1983 and not enhanced customs duty that came into force on 1st March 1983. This result therefore appears to be unescapable."

3. Warehoused goods--Non-presentation of Bank Certificates is not sufficient ground to deny delivery of goods from warehouse as all other formalities had been complied with. "As rightly contended by Mr. Jagtiani the learned Counsel it is the monetary transaction which has the direct nexus to the schedule time of 4 p.m. which was advanced to 3 p.m. and it has nothing to do with the physical presentation of the discharge certificate from the bank and according to him if the moneys were offered before 4 p.m. then it becomes immaterial in so far as the presentation of the document is concerned because customs duty is admittedly paid earlier and warehousing charges are effered on the spot.......In my opinion the object as enunciated by sub-clause (b) does not embrace within its fold the presentation of the discharge certificate from any bank. In a way that would be only incidental because the main count would be about the payment of customs duty and the payment of warehousing charges."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - ITC - OGL - Appendix 10 of Import Policy 1982-83 - Import covered by OGL, as Letter of Credit established on 28.2.1983 and subsequently extended, remained in force on the date of shipment. Valuation - Undervaluation - Charge based on contemporary import of 1973 model of machine is arbitrary

FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand offset press against a letter of credit for Rs. 1,99,867.00 opened on 28.2.1983 and valid for negotiation up to 30.8.1983, subsequently extended up to 31.12.1983. The appellants claimed clearance of the machine under OGL in terms of para 7 of Appendix 10 of the Import Policy 1982-83. However, the Customs held that the goods could not be allowed clearance as changes of fundamental nature had been made in the letter of credit. The Collector ordered confiscation of the machine with an option to redeem it on payment of Rs. 65,000/-. He also ordered enhancement of its value to Rs. 2,57,162/- on the basis of contemporaneous import of identical machine of 1973 model.

HELD: ITC--OGL--Appendix 10 of Policy AM 1982-83--the letter of credit established on 28.2.1983, continued to be valid on the date of shipment--the import is covered by OGL (ratio of Appellate Tribunal decision in Tara Art Printers, New Delhi v. CC, Bombay). ".........on reference to para (7) of Appendix 10 of 1982-83 Import Policy, we find that it was not clearly spelled out that shipment after 31.3.1983 was permissible only in cases where delay in shipment was on account of longer manufacturing schedule. In our view, if the delivery period of the goods was extended beyond 31.3.1983 due to any reason they could be shipped on or before 31.12.1983 provided the contract entered into on or before 28.2.1983 continued to be in force on the date of shipment. In this case in the first instance the shipment was delayed on account of the country of origin having been erroneously shown in the Letter of Credit as West Germany instead of Sweden necessitating the extension of the Letter of Credit up to 30.8.1983. However, the shipment was delayed further since the intimation regarding the extension of the Letter of Credit was not received by the supplier. Thereafter, the Letter of Credit was amended again on 21.10.1983 to extend its validity up to 31.12.1983. Since the goods were shipped before 31.12.1983 against the Letter of Credit which was established on 28.2.1983 and continued to be valid on the date of shipment, we are of the view that they were covered by the OGL in terms of 1982-83 Import Policy."

2. Valuation--Undervaluation--the change is not sustainable as the Collector's decision to enhance the value of the machine on the basis of contemporary import of 1973 model, is ad hoc and arbitrary (ratio of Tribunal decision in Tara Art Printers New Delhi v. CC, Bombay). "We find that on the question of valuation as well there is sufficient force in the appellants contention that the Collector's decision to enhance the assessable value of the imported machine of 1974 make, on the basis of the price of a similar machine of 1973 model was arbitrary. It is seen that the adjudicating authority did not give any indication of the method employed for the computation of the assessable value of the imported second hand machine of 1974 make on the basis of the price of another second-hand machine of 1973 make. Since, in this case there was no evidence of the importers being related to the suppliers or any amount in excess of the invoice price having been remitted by the importers to the suppliers, the invoice price represented the value of the goods which was determinable under clause (a) of section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962. We find that the Tribunal had taken a similar view in the case of M/s. Tara Art Printers, New Delhi v. Collector of Customs, Bombay (supra) in which the adjudicating authority had determined the assessable value of the second hand printing machine of 1975 on the basis of the value of a second hand machine of 1974 model."

It is not in dispute that after the two communications of assessee, the assessee did make payment of the differential duty in question in respect of addition to the assessable value of goods on account of transportation, insurance, handling and delivery charges for the clearances made during the period 1-03-1994 to 30-11-1996. The payment was made during the period 6-12-1995 to 22-10-1997. [Para 22] The language and contents of the letter dated 5-10-1995, as reproduced hereinabove, leave nothing to doubt or guess that the assessee had pleaded, in unequivocal terms, with the department that duty was not payable on the additions made to the assessable value of goods towards transportation, insurance and handling/delivery charges. The contents of the letter dated 5-12-1995 further make it clear that despite the assessee having lodged the protest by the letter dated 5.10.1995, the department had been insisting for making such payment and hence the assessee put on record emphatic denial of the department's propositions; and the statement had been even to the extent that the insistence for such a payment would be unjust and against the principles of justice. [Para 23]

For their subject, contents and tenor, the said two letters dated 5-10-1995 and 5-12-1995 could only be regarded as the letters of protest. The contention urged on behalf of the department is that for being a protest as envisaged by rule 233B, the assessee ought to have followed the procedure prescribed by the rules and in the present case, such a procedure has not been followed. This contention is of no avail for the department. In the first place, this contention remains rather a matter of form than of substance. Secondly, the requirements of rule 233B cannot be construed in a narrow or hyper-technical manner and essentially, what is required is that substantively, there has to be a protest in writing. Thirdly, as shall be seen hereafter, all the requirements of rule 233B cannot even be employed in the fact situation of the present case. Fourthly and in any case, the rule is procedural in nature and cannot control the substantive provision of section 11B(1) of the Act. [Para 24]

Indisputably, no specific form of protest has been provided in the Rules. The simple and ordinary meaning of the expression 'protest' is: 'to express or record dissent or objection'. The dissent, disagreement, and objection of the assessee had been clear, emphatic, unequivocal, and unambiguous in the communications aforesaid. [Para 25]

So far the requirement of following the procedure prescribed by the Rules is concerned, the same has to be construed from the practical stand point and cannot be employed in a hyper technical manner. [Para 27]

The factors required to be taken into consideration in this case are that the payment was made during the period 6-12-1995 to 22-10-1997 whereas it related to the clearances made during the period 01-03-1994 to 30-11-1996. The assessee's letter dated 05-10-1995 was, in fact, a response to the communication dated 09-09-1995, as received from the Superintendent, Central Excise. It appears that the addition was sought to be insisted upon by the department at the later stage and hence came the protest from the assessee on 05.10.1995 which was followed by the communication dated 05-12-1995. When the department still insisted, the assessee made the payment. It is not in dispute that ultimately, the objections of the assessee were sustained. [Para 28]

In the totality of circumstances, it is very difficult to find as to how the requirements of sub-rule (4) of Rule 233B could have been fulfilled in respect of the clearances which had already been made before the department compelled the assessee to make payment of duty i.e., at least for the clearance made between 01-03-1994 to 05-12-1995. In the present case, in respect of these clearances, which had already been made before the department attempted to include the charges towards freight etc. in the assessable value of goods, Sub-rule (4) can only be held inapplicable. As regards the other period, even if it be taken to be a case of lapse on the part of the assessee, looking to the substantive provision of section 11B(1) of the Act and the ratio of the decisions above-referred, for such omission alone, substance of the matter is not lost altogether that the assessee was indeed protesting against the levy in question. [Para 29]

Rule 233B cannot be construed in a narrow or hyper-technical manner; and a substantive compliance thereof would meet with the requirements, so far the question of lodging of protest is concerned. In the ultimate analysis, in the present case, for the purpose of second proviso to section 11B(1), lodging of protest is required to be held complete by way of the aforesaid two communications dated 5-10-1995 and 5-12-1995. [para 30]

letter stating that he was paying the reassessed amount of duty under protest. Having once agreed to the assessment made by the department, the assessee cannot be permitted to challenge the said assessment or the impugned circular on the basis whereof the assessment was made. The fact that the assessee had initially agreed with the department's assessment has been concealed by the assessee which amounts to suppression of material facts. The assessee has not approached the court with clean hands and does not deserve any relief. In court's opinion, non-mentioning of any and every fact does not amount to suppression of material facts. A material fact is one that would have a bearing on the decision of the court. Even if the assessee mentioned in the writ petition about the factum of he having initially agreed with the department's assessment, decision would not have been any different. This is so because there can be no estoppel against the statute. Section 11A of the Customs Tariff Act does not countenance amendment of the First Schedule to the said Act by issuance of a mere departmental circular. The method in which the First Schedule has been sought to be amended is contrary to the method prescribed by section 11A and as such the circular cannot be sustained. Hence, the fact that the assessee initially agreed with the department's assessment is not a material fact and accordingly the department's point is rejected. [Para 34]

The second point urged by the department is that the assessee has not challenged the show cause-cum-demand notice dated 21-4-2014. In court's view, this is a point without any substance. The said show cause notice is admittedly based on the impugned circular. If the circular is quashed, the show cause notice automatically goes. [Para 35]

In view of what has been discussed above, the impugned circular is bad in law being without jurisdiction and cannot be sustained. The Circular No. 19/2013-CUS., dated 9-5-2013 is quashed and set aside. [Para 36]

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Valuation of excisable goods - Limitation - Provisional assessment not hit Cesa: S. 11A; CE Rule 9B. New points--hearing for making further submissions must be granted. Valuation--packing (special) is to be judged whether required for delivery of goods at factory gate. Jam packing not necessary for delivery at factory gate excludible. Deductions (Other)--loading and freight after clearance allowed--miscellaneous charges excludable after scrutiny--they should be done to actuals--best judgment valuation not attracted--when actuals available--Remand--matter remanded for further determination

FACT: Appellants, manufacturers of glass sheets, charged from their customers the price of the goods as well as extra charges on account of special packing, cost of transport, forwarding charges, breakage risk and miscellaneous charges. The dispute was whether the charges for the extras were includible in the assessable value of the goods. When the same issue had gone to the High Court earlier, the appellants had contended that they realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers and not from their local buyers. The High Court held that as the appellants realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers, the extra charges were in principle excludible from the assessable value, and further, ordered the department of investigate the assertion of the facts made by the appellants. While the matter was under enquiry, the department received some information that the appellants were indulging in under-valuation of their goods. The Anti-Evasion staff of the department scrutinised the documents of the appellants and came to the conclusion that the appellants had highly inflated the costs of the extra items so as to camouflage the true assessable value of the goods. On this ground, show cause notices were issued demanding differential excise duty of Rs. 1,88,84,508.57 and also a penalty of Rs. 50 lakhs was imposed on the appellants for making false and mis-leading declarations. Confiscation of the plant and machinery of the appellants in lieu of a fine was also ordered. The appellants contended that the show-cause notices issued by the department were time-barred as they were issued beyond the normal time of six months. Further, the appellants pointed out that there has been a violation of principles of natural justice as their request to make further clarifications on the matter, was not honoured by the department. The question as to which of the items of extras should be held to be excludible for determining the assessable value of the goods was also taken up in the instant case.

HELD: As the assessment of the goods had been made only on a provisional basis, with the consent of the appellants, the demands as per the show cause notices are not time-barred. The limitation applies only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessment "......the assessments had been made provisionally under Rule 9B of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 at their own request and on the strength of the provisional duty bond executed by them.......As per Rule 9B, the assessments made on provisional basis have to be finalised eventually and adjustments of duty made. Under Section 11A of the Act, the limitation starts running only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessments. The demands issued as per the show cause notices on 6.11.1984, 10.12.1984 and 43.1985 were, therefore, not time barred, even if the normal time limit of six months were to be applied."

2. In not granting the appellants their request for a personal hearing wherein they wanted to make further submissions regarding certain points, the department has violated the principles of natural justice. "The appellants........argued their case in part and asked for certain clarifications. They expressed their desire to make further submissions on receipt.......The Collector did not grant this further hearing and he proceeded to decide the matter. There has, therefore, been a denial of full opportunity of personal hearing."

case of Indian Oxygen Ltd. v. CCE. expenses incurred towards the loading of the goods within the factory are required to be included in the assessable value of the goods Since a separate break-up of these charges is not given out of the total transportation cost or delivery charges collected by the assessee from its customers, the case has necessarily to be remanded for determining the charges collected towards loading and handling of the goods within the factory for the purpose of charging duty thereon and I order accordingly." Limitation--Transportation charges collected through separate bills were not declared in the price lists. There was therefore, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Longer time limit is therefore available to the Department "As regards the limitation it is admitted by the appellants, as already set out above, that they were collecting charges through separate bills and therefore, there was no declaration of these charges in the price list because the prices declared were ex-works. Apparently, therefore, there was a wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts calling for invoking a larger period of 5 years for demanding the differential duty. The show cause notice was, therefore, well within the time. As regards the point.....that the law regarding includibility of loading charges within the factory was clarified only in the year 1988 by the Supreme Court in the Indian Oxygen case it maybe mentioned that the appellants have not taken this plea in their appeal memo or in the course of arguments by the learned advocate. Such a plea in my view is too vague a plea for the purpose of determining the question of limitation of the show cause notice unless the appellants came positively with definite judgments of the legal position which prevented them from showing such charges in the price list..... I direct the Assistant Collector to redetermine the differential duty after the appellants herein have furnished the break-up of the so-called delivery charges incurred towards the loading etc of the goods within the factory of the appellants which alone would be includible the assessable value of the goods. --I observe that admittedly the charges in question were not declared in the price list Furthermore, undisputably the law relating to the determination of the assessable value in the central excise cases required filing of the price list and supplying the relevant information to enable the officers to Judge the correctness of the declaration and assess the value according to law. Hence irrespective of the appellants' own views complete information was required to be supplied to the Department voluntarily--(whether as apart of the price list or a remark or as an enclosure or covering memo). The Department was also required to be vigilant and expected to call for full particulars at the earliest. However, non-supply of the information normally required for assessment amounted to suppression of relevant facts Hence the extended period was available to the Department and the show cause notice was not time barred Once this was the position, the Assistant Collector was required to re-determine the differential duty after the appellants furnished the required break-up. Hence I agree with the learned Technical Member that the matter was required to be remanded for re-determining the correct duty liability."

HEADNOTE: Rule 3 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1963 – Determination of the method of valuation - Valuation - Invoice value may not be accepted for computing duty if satisfactory explanation for substantial price difference between comparable goods is missing-Value may preferably be computed under Rule 3 and 4 if comparable goods are avail able-Assessment made by adopting even a less preferable criteria is maintainable if the assessee is not put to disadvantage - Assessable value--Landing charges form a part of assessable value

FACT: The appellants imported certain second-hand machines. The Customs authorities did not accept the invoice price on the plea that similar machines had been imported by the same assessee at a much higher price while the time gap between the two imports was not much. The goods were valued under Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules keeping in view appreciation of prices depreciation insurance, freight and landing charges. Collector (Appeals) upheld the order except that he allowed depreciation @ 10% as against 6-1/4% allowed by the lower authorities.

HELD: 1. Valuation--Invoice value may not be accepted for computing duty if comparable goods are purchased at substantially higher price. "The appellants explanation for increase in the price is that the demand for second hand machinery had gone up and the suppliers therefore raised the prices in case of latter import No evidence in support of this plea has been produced either before the lower authorities or before us. In the absence of any such evidence and the apparently large price differential in the prices of two sets of machines, the imports of which were made in the span of about nine months time, we held that the lower authorities were justified in not accepting low price as reflected in the invoice for the goods".

2. Valuation--Computation of value should preferable be under Rule 3 and 4 if comparable goods are available at different prices. "We would like to observe that in the instant case, the value of comparable goods was available and the correct rule that should have been applied by the lower authorities should have been Rule 3 of the Custom Valuation rules 1963 read with Rule 4 of the said rule. We find that the value of comparable goods imported by the appellants was acceptable to the authorities and as such there was no need for the officers to traverse beyond these rules to Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules."

3. Valuation--Assessee has no grievance if a criterion, less preferable than other available ones, is adopted if it does not put him to disadvantage. "In any case, we find that the appellants had not suffered any disadvantage on this account and probably the value fixed now in terms of the Appellate Collector's order is lower than what might have been fixed in case Rule 3 read with Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules 1963 had been resorted to. We, therefore, find no reason to accede the appellants plea for accepting the invoice value for purpose of assessment."

4. Assessable value includes landing charges. "The inclusion of landing charges in the assessable value is maintainable in law seeing that the expenditure incurred for landing would become an integral component of their intrinsic value and accordingly "the price at which such or like goods are for delivery at the time and place of importation"."

in course of the hearing of appeal to effect that section 43B has overriding effect over section 145A and had not followed order of a co-ordinate Bench of the Delhi Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2005] 92 ITD 120 and (iii) it had completely overlooked the fact that the assessee's claim for deduction of the customs duty under section 43B for subsequent years had been accepted by the Assessing Officer himself. HELD: Earlier in the course of hearing of the appeal the assessee was directed to explain the entries of customs duty payment in the profit and loss account and balance-sheet. In response to the same, the assessee filed a supplemen-tary paper-book on 21-2-2007 explaining the entries made regarding the closing stock to show that the customs duty had been included therein, and had also explained in details as to how the provisions of section 145A introduced with effect from 1-4-1999 would have no effect in view of the overriding provisions of section 43B. These submissions had been briefly adverted to in the order of the Tribunal. One of the paragraph of the order of the Tribunal showed that the contention of the assessee that since inception, that is, from the assessment year 1994-95 till the assessment year 2006-07 the assessee had been following the inclusive method of accounting for customs duty payment while valuing the stock and that was accepted by the Tribunal. Further, the Tribunal had even stated in this paragraph that this claim of the assessee was not contradicted even in the assessment order. In the same paragraph, the Tribunal had also made an observation that in the year under appeal, the customs duty formed part of the closing stock, though the duty was not debited to the profit and loss account and had also referred to the fact that the duty was separately claimed as deduction in the return of income. In one other paragraph, the Tribunal had accepted the assessee's claim in principle and had observed that it was supported by the Special Bench's order of the Tribunal in Indian Communication Network (P.) Ltd. v. IAC [1994] 49 ITD 56 (Delhi), which was approved by the Supreme Court in Berger Paints India Ltd. v. CIT [2004] 266 ITR 99/ 135 Taxman 586. However, the observations made in the said paragraph showed that the Tribunal had considered that the customs duty was not included in the valuation of the closing stock. This observation was at variance with and contradictory to its earlier finding to the effect that the duty had been included in the closing stock as per the consistent accounting practice adopted by the assessee which was accepted in the assessment. It was only in view of the latter contradictory finding that the Tribunal thought it necessary to restore the matter to the Assessing Officer with the direction to examine the applicability of section 145A to the assessee's case. Even if it was assumed for the sake of argument that the case would have had to be restored to the Assessing Officer to be processed with reference to section 145 A notwithstanding the earlier finding of the Tribunal that the customs duty was included in the valuation of the closing stock, the fact that the assessee's argument was based on the order of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra) was not considered by the Tribunal showed that there was a mistake apparent from the record in light of decision of Supreme Court in Honda Siel Power Products Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 165 Taxman 307. [Para 8]

In Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra), it was held that section 43B has overriding effect over section 145A. This decision was referred to by the Tribunal in its order while summarizing the contentions of the department but unfortu-nately it omitted to deal with this decision and considered its applicability while taking a decision to remit the matter to the Assessing Officer with a direction to examine the applicability of section 145A. This omission had caused prejudice to the assessee in the sense that it had given rise to further proceedings before the Assessing Officer involving further delay in finalising the assessment proceedings, when the legal position already stood con-cluded by the binding order of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra). The other mistake committed by the Tribunal to the prejudice of the assessee was its omission to refer to the assessee's plea that in the subsequent years, the Assessing Officer had accepted the assessee's claim under section 43B and assessments had been completed accordingly. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Valuation: Invoice value - goods contracted for import at certain price have to be assessed ad valorem at that (invoice) price

FACT: Parle Products Pvt. Ltd., imported two lots of machines from Italy. Dispute arose between them and the Customs Authorities as to the C.I.F. value of the machines for calculating duty, because the Italian firm who sold the machines had revised the prices during the period when import formalities were being dispensed with, but they finally agreed to the original price fixed by them. The Department's contention being that the enhanced price was the acceptable C.I.F. value, they claimed that the goods were under-invoiced and fines of Rs. 21,000 and 16,000 were imposed in lieu of confiscation. The fines were paid under protest, but later reduced to Rs. 5000 and Rs. 3000, after the importers went up in appeal. The revision applications filed by them were rejected and subsequently they filed the present writ petitions.

HELD: Invoice value to be taken as the C.I.F. value for calculating duty since that was the original price quoted by the manufacturer, and the price at which the machines were finally bought by the petitioners. "In my view, therefore, the department was wholly wrong in rejecting the invoice value of these two machines imported by the petitioner and, therefore, there is no justification for demanding any additional duty on the basis of the value as suggested by the department."

2. Invoice price being the actual price of the imported items, there is no violation of the provisions of Import and Export (Control) Act, 1947 or of the Import (Control) Order No. 17, as claimed by the Department, and additional customs duty and fines are therefore not maintainable, (ratio of earlier judgment). "In fact the department's attention was drawn to a case of this High Court in the Union of India and Ors. vs. Glaxo Laboratories (India) Ltd., reported in 1984 (17) E.L.T. 284 (Bombay) in which it is expressly stated that the department ought to have taken the actual price as shown in the invoice and they could not have taken into account the import value for the purpose of debiting the licence. However, the department would not follow the said judgment. In my view, the department's action in this behalf is expressly contrary to the law as laid down by this Court in the said judgment. Therefore, on that count also the department has clearly defaulted."

FACT: Facts

Assessee's appeal along with stay application was pending before High Court.

Pending stay application, Department initiated recovery proceedings in pursuance of CESTAT order in favour of revenue.

Such action was taken in accordance with Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013.

Assessee argued that CBEC had no power to issue such Circular and, in any event, Sl. Nos. 3, 6, 9, 10 and 11 of para 2 of Circular were invalid.

Issue Involved

Whether recovery proceedings were valid in law ?

HELD: A. Board has power to instructions such as those issued in impugned Circular :

Power under Customs Act comes from section 151A : Insofar as section 151A of the Customs Act is concerned, it is worded widely and includes power of the Board to issue instructions, orders and directions for the purpose of uniformity in classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty thereon or for the implementation of any other provisions of the Act or any other law for the time being in force insofar as they relate to any prohibition, restriction or procedure for import or exports of goods. The power of the Board, therefore, to issue any orders, instructions, or directions for the implementation of the provisions of the Act if the Board considers it necessary and expedient to do so cannot be questioned. Recovery of customs duty with or without interest and penalty would certainly arise out of the provisions made in the Customs Act, 1962 and the Rules made thereunder. For example, section 142 of the Customs Act pertains to recovery of sums to the Government. The Customs (Attachment of Property of Defaulters for Recovery of Government Dues) Rules, 1995 provides for the procedure for such recoveries. In that view of the matter, power of the Board to issue such instructions for recovery of customs duty would flow from section 151A of the Customs Act, 1962. [Para 11]

Section 37B of Excise Act does not directly empower issuance of such Circular : Section 37B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, however, is not so widely worded. It empowers the Board, if it considers necessary and expedient to do so for the purpose of uniformity in classification of excisable goods or with respect to levy of duty of excise on such goods, to issue orders, instructions and directions to the Central Excise Officers as deemed fit. The powers of the Board, therefore, can be exercised for the purpose of uniformity in classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty of excise on such goods. When read in conjunction, both the elements touching the powers of the Board would have a bearing on the question of classification of the goods or with the levy of duty of excise on such goods. It is highly questionable whether recovery of excise duty along with interest and penalty can form part of matter of any instructions the Board may issue in exercise of powers under section 37B of the Central Excise Act. However, this issue was not examined in view of provisions of rule 31 of Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 12]

Dy. CIT [2020] 113 taxmann.com 246/181 ITD 185 (Kolkata - Trib.), which have held that the amendment to section 50C brought into the Act by Finance Act, 2018 with effect from 1-4-2019 was to apply retrospectively with effect from 1-4-2003, when the section 50C was brought into statute. The section 56(2)(vii) being pari-materia to section 50C, and the said Circular No. 8/2018 also amending the provisions of section 56, will be applicable to the case of the assessee also and will accordingly the benefit of the said amendment will apply retrospectively in the case of the assessee also and the difference of Rs. 15.14 lakhs between the actual consideration paid and the FMV being less than 10 per cent will have to be ignored for applying the provisions of section 56(2)(vii) in the case of the assessee. Therefore, in the given facts of the case, the view of the Commissioner is not supported by any judicial authority and therefore his action in holding the assessment order passed in this case to be erroneous as well as prejudicial to the interest of the revenue is merely a change of opinion and the same is not sustainable and the same is quashed. HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, read with rules 4 and 9 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988, rule 10 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and Article 14 of the Constitution of India - Valuation of Imported Goods - Transaction Value - General - Period prior to October 2007 - Vide Notification dated 5-7-1990, customs valuation rules provided that loading, unloading and handling charges will be added to value at 1 per cent of CIF (FOB value plus freight plus insurance) irrespective of actual charges - Assessee claimed that actual charges in its case were merely Rs. 69.98 paisa but customs department added a fictional sum of Rs. 15,214.69 in value at 1 per cent of CIF value, which was arbitrary, irrational and unconstitutional - HELD : Scheme of valuation under section 14 (prior to its substitution in 2007) and valuation rules of 1988 is to take into consideration actual price of goods, except where some charges are unascertainable, in which case only, deemed additions are made - Additions in respect of cost of transport and insurance under rule 9(2) read with proviso thereto are made on actual basis and percentage-based fictional additions are made only if actual charges are unascertainable - Addition in respect of 'loading, unloading and handling charges' under rule 9(2)(b) read with proviso (ii) thereto at 1 per cent of CIF, even in those cases where actual cost paid on such an account is available and ascertainable, is ultra vires section 14 and is also arbitrary and violative of Article 14 - Therefore, proviso (ii) to rule 9(2) was read down to mean that deemed addition at 1 per cent of CIF would apply only when actual charges are not ascertainable [Paras 21 to 36] [In favour of assessee]Customs : Deemed addition in respect of 'loading, unloading and handling charges' under rule 9(2)(b) of Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 at 1 per cent of CIF, even where actual charges are available, is ultra vires section 14; hence, said deemed addition at 1 per cent of CIF would apply only if actual charges are not ascertainable

FACT: The assessees challenged constitutional validity of proviso (ii) of rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 inserted by Notification No. 39/90, dated 5-7-1990.

The assessee claimed that the actual loading, unloading and handling charges amounted to Rs. 69.98 paisa as per the tariff of the International Airport Authority of India, Madras (now Chennai). However, the Customs Authorities, on the basis of the impugned notification added a sum of Rs. 15,214.69 paisa at 1 per cent of CIF value.

The assessee argued that such a notional fixation of the handling charges with the addition of 1 per cent of CIF value, irrespective of the nature of goods, size of the cargo, was in total disregard to total handling charges, even when such actual handling charges could be ascertained. Same was irrational, arbitrary and ultra vires.

The department argued that it was found impossible to ascertain the actual amounts incurred towards loading, unloading and handling charges while making the assessment as they varied depending upon the quantities and place of import. Finding this difficulty in actual practice and in order to achieve certainty, one per cent of the CIF value was fixed to be included in the assessable value. It was argued that once this uniformity is achieved with the aforesaid provisions, merely because some would be getting the benefit while others would suffer certain detriment, is no reason for invalidating the provision when many others would be getting the benefit thereof as well. The percentage had been fixed by the rule making authority after taken into consideration the overall picture.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(23) of the Customs Act, 1962 - Import - Import-takes place when goods enter the land mast

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Valuation; Assessable value has to include unloading charges also, not merely port charges: but any bonus earned for quick unloading should be deducted

FACT: These are ten appeals which relate to the same respondent and involve common facts and issues; hence a combined order. The respondents are manufacturers of fertilizers and imported rock phosphate and sulphur in bulk quantities came to India on chartered ship. The goods were purchased on the high seas and unloading on the Indian coast was the responsibility of the respondents. For this they maintained their own wharf, unloading equipment and staff at Vishakhapatnam. 1.4% by way of landing charges stood already added to the price of the goods. The Assistant Collector held that this 1.4% did not include stevedoring charges which he added separately and recalculated the value at varying rates from Rs. 5.86 to Rs. 9.42 per MT. In appeal the Appellate Collr. set aside the Asst. Collr.'s orders and held that the 1.4% already added as landing charges were the same as unloading charges. The Department is now in appeal against the Appellate Collector's orders.

HELD: Place of importation has to be the land mass of India where goods are unloaded from the ship. Section 2(23). "Place of importation in section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, should take the similar meaning as place of removal of the imported goods, that is, the port gate. Delivery to the importer is effected only here."

2. Port landing charges comprise only wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds; any unloading charges incurred have to be included in the value for assessment in addition to the port landing charges. Section-14. "The 1.4% Port landing charge already added to the respondents, value comprised wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds and not unloading charges from ship to berth. The unloading charges have therefore to be computed and added too."

3. For calculating the unloading charges and despatch money earned because of unloading of chartered vessel before stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs, but if any money is paid as penalty for delayed unloading of the ships the same should be added.

".........despatch money earned because of unloading of the chartered vessel before the stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs. Conversely if the appellants have paid any penalty for delayed unloading of the ship the same should be added to the costs."

HEADNOTE: Section 119 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Central Board of Direct Taxes - Instructions issued by CBDT to subordinate authorities - Whether assessee was right in contending that circular dated 4-10-1969 would be applicable in its case since it was effective during relevant previous year and ITO was wrong in following circular dated 5-12-1974 which was issued while assessment proceedings were pending - Held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of production and distribution of cine pictures. During the previous year ended 18-10-1971, it had purchased the distributorship rights of six pictures. While making the assessments, the ITO followed the CBDT circular, dated 5-12-1974 and held that the cost of two pictures could be allowed as deduction in full against the income of the year and the cost of remaining four pictures was to be allowed only partially. The assessee contained that during the relevant previous year CBDT circular, dated 4-10-1969 was effective and that the ITO was bound to follow it. The AAC, however, upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal :

HELD: The circulars, instructions and directions of the Board are biding on the income-tax authorities as provided in section 119 but a circular is not law, and the assessee is not bound by it. If such circulars, directions or instructions are to the prejudice of the assessee, he may claim the benefit which was available to him under the provisions of law. However, the assessee cannot claim to be assessed in accordance with the old circular which stood modified by the Board’s subsequent circular when the assessment proceedings are pending particularly when the Board’s instruction clearly showed such an intention on the part of the Board.

The Board had specifically directed that all pending assessments may be completed in accordance with 1974 circular. Since the ITO was bound by the Board’s circular in terms of section 119, he was bound to follow the 1974 circular only.
