It was argued that once this uniformity is achieved with the aforesaid provisions, merely because some would be getting the benefit while others would suffer certain detriment, is no reason for invalidating the provision when many others would be getting the benefit thereof as well. The percentage had been fixed by the rule making authority after taken into consideration the overall picture.

HELD: I. Old section 14 v. New section 14 amended from October 2007 : A reading of the unamended section 14 would show that the earlier/old principle was to find the valuation of goods 'by reference to their value'. It introduced a deeming/fictional provision by stipulating that the value of the goods would be the price at which such or like goods are 'ordinarily sold, or offered for sale'. Under the new provision, however, the valuation is based on the transaction price namely, the price 'actually paid or payable for the goods'. Even when the old provision provided the formula of the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale, at that time also if the goods in question were sold for a particular price, that could be taken into consideration for arriving at the valuation of goods. The very expression 'ordinarily sold, or offered for sale' would indicate that the price at which these goods are actually sold would be the price at which they are ordinarily sold or offered for sale. Of course, under the old provision, under certain circumstances, the authorities could discard the price mentioned in the invoice. However, that is only when it is found that the price mentioned in the invoice is not the reflection of the price at which these are ordinarily sold or offered for sale. To put it otherwise, the reason for discarding the price mentioned in the invoice could be only when the said price appeared to be suppressed one. In such a case, the authorities could say that generally such goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale at a different price and take that price into consideration for the purpose of levying the duty. It could, however, be done only if there was evidence to show that ordinarily the price at which these goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale is higher than the price mentioned in the invoice. In fact, this fundamental concept is retained even now while introducing the concept of 'transaction value' under the amended provision. More importantly, the rules viz. Valuation Rules, 1988 had incorporated this very principle of 'transaction value' even under the old provision. No doubt, as per this provision existing today generally the price mentioned is to be accepted as it is the transaction value. However, this very provision stipulates the circumstances under which that price can be discarded. In any case, having regard to the question with which we are concerned in the present appeals, such a change in the provision may not have much effect. [Para 21]

The underlying principle contained in amended sub-section (1) of section 14 is to consider transaction value of the goods imported or exported for the purpose of customs duty. Transaction value is stated to be a price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India for delivery at the time and place of importation. Therefore, it is the price which is actually paid or payable for delivery at the time and place of importation, which is to be treated as transaction value. However, this sub-section (1) further makes it clear that the price actually paid or payable for the goods will not be treated as transaction value where the buyer and the seller are related with each other. In such cases, there can be a presumption that the actual price which is paid or payable for such goods is not the true reflection of the value of the goods. This section also provides that normal price would be the sole consideration for the sale. However, this may be subject to such other conditions which can be specified in the form of Rules made in this behalf. [Para 22]

As per the first proviso of the amended section 14(1), in the transaction value of the imported goods, certain charges are to be added which are in the form of amount paid or payable for costs and services including commissions and brokerage, engineering, design work, royalties and licence fees, costs of transportation to the place of importation, insurance, loading, unloading and handling charges to the extent and in the manner which can be prescribed in the Rules. Sub-section (2) of section 14, which remains the same, is an overriding provision which empowers the Board to fix tariff values for any class of imported goods or export goods under certain circumstances. [Para 23]

In contrast, in the unamended section 14, sub-section (1A) stipulated that the price referred to in sub-section (1) in respect of imported goods shall be determined in accordance with Rules made in this behalf. Therefore, Rules can be made in determining the price. However, these Rules have to be subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), the underline principle whereof, as stated above, is to taken into consideration actual price of the goods unless it is impermissible because of certain circumstances stipulated therein. [Para 24]

II. Scheme of Valuation Rules of 1988

HEADNOTE: Section  56,  read with sections  50C  and  263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income from other sources  -  Chargeable as  (Revision) - Assessment year  2016-17  - Assessee, an individual engaged in business of manufacturing, export and sales against Form-H of electrical wiring accessories, filed return processed under section 143(1) - Case was reopened under section 147 on ground that assessee purchased an immovable property for consideration significantly lower than circle rate - Assessee held 1/3rd share in property - On assessee’s request disputing circle rate vis-à-vis FMV, Assessing Officer referred matter to DVO, who determined FMV at ?5.16 crores; assessee’s 1/3rd share came to ?1.72 crores, leaving a difference of ?15.14 lakhs, being less than 10 per cent of consideration - Assessing Officer, after considering assessee’s response, applied amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 (treated as retrospective), and accepted that variation below 10 per cent between sale consideration and DVO-determined value was to be ignored, thereby accepting returned income - Principal Commissioner invoked section 263 (including Explanation 2) to revise assessment, holding that Circular No. 8/2018 applied prospectively and that difference between stamp duty value and sale consideration should have been added to assessee’s income - Whether since view of Principal Commissioner was not supported by any judicial authority, his action in treating assessment order as erroneous and prejudicial to interest of revenue was merely a change of opinion and unsustainable - Held, yes [Para 9.3] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, an individual engaged in the business of manufacturing, export and sales against Form-H of electrical wiring accessories, filed a return declaring income of about Rs. 33.64 lakhs for assessment year 2016-17, which was processed under section 143(1).

■

The case was reopened under section 147 on the ground that an immovable property was purchased for consideration significantly lower than the circle rate, thereby attracting the provision of section 56(2) (viib). The total consideration for the property was about Rs. 4.71 crores against circle rate of about Rs. 9.01 crores; the assessee held a 1/3rd share with consideration of about Rs. 1.57 crores (about Rs. 1.54 crores paid by cheque and about Rs. 2.92 lakhs as TDS). On the assessee’s request disputing circle rate vis-à-vis FMV, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to the DVO, who in his valuation report, ascertained the FMV of the said property at Rs. 5.16 crores, accounting for 1/3rd share of the assessee, the FMV was arrived at Rs. 1.72 crores.

■

The Assessing Officer issued notice calling for explanation on applicability of section 56(2)(viib) and considered the assessee’s response, applied the amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 (treated as retrospective), and accepted that a variation below 10 per cent between the sale consideration and the DVO-determined value should be ignored, thereby accepting the returned income. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment at total income of Rs. 33.64 lakhs as declared by the assessee.

■

The Principal Commissioner invoked section 263, holding that Circular No. 8/2018 applied prospectively from assessment year 2019-20, and thus the Assessing Officer erred in not adding the difference of Rs.15.14 lakh.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The Assessing Officer noted that the difference of the FMV as determined by the DVO and the amount paid by the assessee was Rs. 15.14 lakhs (Rs. 1.72 crores - Rs. 1.57 crores) and the said difference between the actual consideration and FMV as determined by the DVO was less than 10 per cent. The Assessing Officer thereafter, considering the amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 in line with pronouncements of various Courts and Tribunals, which held that when the margin between the actual consideration and the value ascertained by Departmental valuer was less than 10 per cent, noted that the said difference is liable to be ignored, for the purpose of Assessment. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer accepted the total income as declared by the assessee. [Para 9]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of Goods for Customs - ITC - OGL - Import permissible if firm contract covered by period of currency of OGL - Contract revised after OGL withdrawn is not valid - Valuation - Undervaluation charge cannot hold without evidence and specially when price declared is fair - Cus. Act: section 14

FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand offset printing machine and claimed clearance under OGL (Import Policy 1982-83), declaring an assessable value of Rs. 4,96,306. The goods arrived during import policy period 1983-84 when they ceased to be covered by OGL. The appellants claimed benefit of condition 7 of Appx. 10 of Policy Book for AM 1982-83, according to which, if an importer had entered into a firm contract before 28.2.1983 but the goods could not be shipped before 31.3.1983 on account of the longer delivery period involved, the shipment may be allowed up to 31.3.1984. The Additional Collector of Customs denied them this benefit on the ground that although the original contract was dated 14.10.1982 and a letter of credit was opened on 9.12.1982, there had been a change of contract subsequently reducing the price of the machine and the latter contract, which is a firm contract, was entered into only in the 1983-84 policy period when the machine was withdrawn from the OGL List, and therefore the import was unauthorised. He confiscated the machine, fixed its value at Rs. 5,62,984 on the basis of contemporary import of such a machine by some other party, and imposed a fine of Rs. 1,25,000 in lieu of confiscation.

HELD: The appellants are not entitled to the benefit of condition 7, Appx. 10 of Import Policy 1982-83 as the machine was not imported under the original contract dated 14.10.1982, but under a subsequent contract reducing the price of the machine, and this contract is to be treated as a "firm contract". The import is therefore unauthorised as it was effected during 1983-84 policy period when the subject goods were not covered by OGL. "Here, though one contract was entered into before 28.2.1983, the subject import is not the one made pursuant to that contract but was under a new contract entered into somewhere in January-February 1984 as is evident from the letter dated 3.2.1984 from the supplier as also by issuance of afresh invoice dated 29.3.1984. ...Even assuming that because the same machine is brought and the same is in relation to the contract entered into on 14.10.1982, then also the contract entered into at that time could not be taken as a firm contract, as subsequently, there has been an alteration in the most essential ingredient in a contract of sale, namely the purchase price and if that could be done, the contract initially entered into could not be taken as a firm contract. Here however is a clear case of substitution of the original contract by a new contract of purchase at the reduced price."

2. Valuation--Enhancement of assessable value not sustainable in the absence of clear data before the department and when there is evidence on record to show that the declared value is fair and reasonable. "With no clear date available before the department that the value as assessed is not proper, and when the other evidence on record indicates the value to be fair and reasonable the finding of the adjudicating authority that the subject goods have been under-valued, cannot be endorsed and as such, the said portion of the order of the authority below cannot be sustained and has to be set aside."

3. Redemption fine reduced to Rs. 1,00,000/-. "The appellants are the actual users of the machine, and they had intended and attempted to bring the same during the policy period 1982-83 but could not do so for the reasons given. In that view of the matter, and with the allegations of undervaluation as not proved, there appears some scope of showing some leniency in relation to quantum of redemption fine. In that view of the matter the fine in lieu of confiscation is reduced to Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One lac only)."

S.C. Coutinho 1981 ELT 414 the Bombay High Court held that under section 15(1) of the Customs Act, 1962 the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force and under section 68 of the same Act, it shall be the date on which the goods were actually removed from the warehouse. Following the aforesaid decision in the instant case the assessee was not entitled to deduction at the revised rates. However, in view of the order of the Tribunal in the case of Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd. v. ITO [1986] 18 ITD 64 (Bom.) (TM) the customs duty payable by the assessee would have to be added to the value of the bonded goods shown in the stock-in-trade. The net result, as held by the Commissioner (Appeals), would be that the assessee’ s income would have to be increased by the amount of the customs duty of Rs. 22,56,273. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld on this issue.

the question was as to whether the original account given by the foreign party was to be believed or the subsequent account given by it reversing the said entry was to be believed and that the ITO should have probed that matter a little more in detail instead of relying on the first letter, however, since the assessee had not satisfactory explained the credit note and there was failure to account for it in the account books, the addition was to be upheld.

On application under section 256(2) : HELD: There is no controversy about the principle that the opening stock cannot be valued in a manner different from the valuation of the closing stock. Both have to be valued on the basis of the same principle. The opening stock for the year under reference was loaded with the value of the proportionate costs of customs duty, freight and handling charges. The closing stock did not have such an addition made to it. In order to bring the two on the same level, it was necessary to disturb the valuation either of the opening stock or of the closing stock. The Tribunal preferred to disturb the closing stock by valuing it on the same principle according to which the opening stock was valued. The assessee suggested that the customs duty, freight and handling charges should have been deducted from the opening stock, to bring the principle of its valuation in accord with the principle which had been adopted for valuing the closing stock. The adoption of this procedure would have hardly brought about any change in the results and would not have adversely affected the interest of the revenue. It would, on the other hand, have given to the assessee the benefit of avoiding the inconvenience and difficulty of splitting up the charges in question and allocating the same in proper proportions to the numerous components and materials. This would have regularised the assessee's balance-sheets in all the subsequent years. The insistence of the department in disturbing the closing stock instead of the opening stock and the approval to this practice given by the Tribunal did give rise to question of law which could appropriately be referred to the High Court. However, that question did not arise from out of the order of the Tribunal, who never considered the merits or demerits of the alternative procedure of disturbing instead the opening stock on the same basis, on which the closing stock was valued. The suggestion made before the Tribunal by the assessee was to deduct the sum of custom duty, freight etc. from the purchases. There was no suggestion to make a suitable deduction from out of the value of the opening stock, as now suggested. The Tribunal had not applied its mind to the suggestion of a deduction from the opening stock and had said nothing about this in its order. Thus, the question as to whether the Tribunal was justified in law in holding that on no account the opening stock could be revalued to make it consistent with the system adopted for valuation of closing stock, could not be said to arise out of the order of the Tribunal.

Further, the assessee agreed that the opening stock included customs duty and incidental charges. There was, therefore, sufficient material for the Tribunal to hold that the closing stock might necessarily be valued likewise. Thus, the question as to whether there was any material on which the Tribunal could hold that the closing stock might necessarily include the customs duties and incidental charges was not a question which the Tribunal could refer to the High Court.

So far as question regarding credit note was concerned the Tribunal came to its conclusion after assessing the evidence before it. It was competent to determine the sufficiency of the evidence before it. The inference drawn by the Tribunal from the evidence on record was a finding of fact and its refusal to make a reference, as desired by the assessee, called for no interference.

Under those circumstances, there was no merit in the instant petition which, accordingly, was to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Notional value (Customs) cannot be added to invoice value on flimsy grounds

FACT: The respondents had imported certain plant and machinery. In terms of an agreement the respondents' Collaborators were selecting the machinery. There were no specific charges for this service. Payment made to the Collaborators in lumpsum was for the transfer of technical knowledge. Construing this payment as buyer's commission, the Asstt. Collector held that in terms of Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules, a loading of 21/2% service charges was required to be added to the invoice value of the third party suppliers. On appeal, the Collector (Appeals) set aside the above order on the grounds that in view of the machineries having been supplied by a third party, in the absence of any specific provision in the Collaboration agreement for the payment of service charges, the payment made to the Collaborators is not to be included in the assessable value of the goods. Hence this Revenue appeal.

HELD: Department's application suffers from infirmities--Collector had given the authorisation for filing the appeal without expressing any opinion about the legality or propriety of the order as specified under section 129A--Specific grounds of appeal not raised by the Department. "On going through the records we find that neither authorisation given by the Collector is in the proper Order nor appeal filed by the Department is in proper form. Section 129-A(2) specifies that before giving authorisation to file an appeal Collector should express about the illegality or impropriety of the order against which the appeal is to be filed and direct the proper Officer to appeal on his behalf to the Appellate Tribunal against such order. In this authorisation the Collector simply authorises the Assistant Collector to file an appeal without expressing any opinion about the legality or otherwise of the order and, as such, there is no proper authorisation for filing the appeal. We find that presentation of appeal also is not in the proper form since neither department has filed any grounds of appeal nor it is clear on which points department is seeking relief in the absence of grounds of appeal. Form No. CA-3 should be accompanied with statement of facts and grounds of appeal but we find that appeal form is accompanied with number of pages in the form of commentary consisting of comments on the impugned order without raising specific grounds. The appeal filed by the department is liable to be dismissed on these preliminary grounds."

2. Valuation--Department's' allegation of undervaluation is not supported by any evidence--in the absence of specific allocation, notional value cannot be added to the invoice value on account of buying commission or handling charges-Collector's order upheld. "The burden lies on the department to prove undervaluation. The department ought to make out a case for undervaluation with sufficient evidence and to prove that value shown in the invoice was not the real value. There is no evidence to show that similar goods were sold at higher price or that the collaborators acted as agents to the foreign Suppliers in getting commission or due to their services resulted in reduction of value. Further payment made to the collaborators for transfer of technical know-how and such lumpsum payment was made to their services where it is not possible for that reason to allocate the charges to individual consignments imported through them, no notional value can be added to the invoice value on account of buying commission or handling charges as it was rightly dealt with in the impugned order. We do not find any infirmity in the impugned order."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Second-hand machines falling in different age groups are not comparable. Value to be determined for each type

FACT: The appellants imported second-hand printing machines and declared their value as Rs. 2,81,193. It was noticed in the docks that in addition to the declared machines, one additional two-colour offset printing machine had been imported. This was attributed by the appellants to mistake on the part of supplier. The Department did not accept the declared value and charged the importer with under-valuation and evasion of duty. The value was determined by the Addl. Collector as Rs. 6,65,000 on the basis of value of similar machines imported by M/s. D.S. Sawant & Sons and the price list issued by M/s. Jackal International Co., a well known supplier of second-hand machines.

HELD: It is not legal to compare the price of imported second-hand machines falling in different age groups (ratio of earlier Tribunal decisions). Provision of Section 14(1)(a) of the C.A. 1962 can hardly be of any help in determining the valuation. The value should be determined on the basis of unit price of each type of machine as indicated in the supplier's invoice. "......the order passed by the Additional Collector determining the price of the imported second-hand Solna 225. Two Colour offset printing machines, on the basis of the import price of a similar machine imported by another importer and the price of the 'Guilltone 45' Polar 115 Electromat on the basis of the price list issued by another supplier of second-hand machinery is not sustainable. In our view the assessable value of the imported goods comprising of two second-hand "Solna 225--Two Colour offset printing machines" and one old "Guilltone 45' Polar 15 Electromat" machine was determinable on the basis of the unit price of each type of machine as indicated in the supplier's invoice. Since the case records do not contain the invoice and the Chartered Engineer's certificate, we remand the case to the Assistant Collector for determining the assessable value of the machines and the consequential relief to the appellants if any."

HEADNOTE: Sections 14  1515(3)(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 - Conversion of assessable value from foreign currency into Indian rupees

FACT: The appellants filed this appeal because they had to pay a higher amount of customs duty on goods imported by them as the customs authorities converted the freight amount shown in the invoice in foreign currency to Indian rupees though they had already paid the freight in Indian rupees

HELD: Assessable value of imported goods was rightly converted from foreign currency into Indian rupees as per Sec. 15(3)(a) of the Customs Act. "At the relevant time provisions of section 15(3)(a) of the Act stipulated how the value of the imported goods was to be converted from foreign currency into Indian rupees. The appellants have not disputed the fact that the rate of exchange for conversion of dollars into rupees adopted by the Custom House in their case was different from that notified by the Government. Their contention is that they had paid the freight amount in Indian rupees and that amount alone could be added to the value of the goods. In the face of a clear legal position in this behalf, we see no merit in this contention of the appellants."

2. Any special agreement between the Government of India and any international financial institution cannot override the provisions of the Customs Act. "... any special agreement between the Government of India and any foreign Government/financial institution (I.D.A. in the present case) cannot override the provisions of Customs Act. We have no hesitation, therefore, in upholding the finding of the Appellate Collector on this ground."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Discounts--World Catalogue Price less 15% discount, falling which manufacturer's net price to wholesale dealers; failing both, invoice price without discount/depreciation if not used before shipment. Ocean freight, marine insurance, and landing charges are part of delivery price,  are includible (CUS. Act, 1962--S. 14). Addl. Duty (CVD) is customs duty and not excise duty (Customs Tariff Act, 1975, S. 3). Classification--Air-conditioner is an optional accessory and is assessable separately U/H 84.12 CTA, even if invoice shows composite price

FACT: The appellant imported a new Toyota starlet car and claimed 15% discount on the invoiced price for the purpose of computing customs duty. This was rejected. Appeal also failed. Before the Tribunal, assessable value of the said car has been disputed.

HELD: 1. Assessable Value--Assessable value of an imported car is world-car-catalogue Price less 15% failing which manufacturer's Net price to whole-sale dealer's failing both invoice price. "We order that the same basis should be followed in the case of the present appellant also and his car re-assessed on the basis of the World Car Catalogue Price of the same model less 15% discount. ......In case the World Car Catalogue Price is not available with the Customs House, the Customs may ascertain the manufacturer's net price to wholesale dealers in the course of international trade in any other manner. If this course is also not feasible, the assessment may be maintained at the appellant's invoice price. There is no question of granting the 15% discount on the individual export passenger's invoice price.''

2. Assessable Value--Ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges are part of delivery price at the place of importation, hence form a part of assessable value. "Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 requires that valuation should be done on the basis of the price for delivery of the goods at the place of importation. The imported goods have to be valued according to this provision. Seeking analogy of a different enactment which deals with locally manufactured goods is a totally mis-conceived exercise. No imported goods can be delivered at the port of importation in India without incurring the ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges. These charges have, therefore, been correctly added to the basic price of the car."

3, Assessable Value--No depreciation admissible if the car has not been used abroad. "Depreciation is given if the car is possessed and used abroad. Here, the appellant purchased a brand new car and loaded it for shipment to India. He did not use the car abroad. No depreciation as asked for is permissible."

4. Additional duty--Additional duty is also customs duty and not excise duty. "Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 separately specifies the rates for basic customs duty and additional customs duty both of which are to be charged on the imported goods. The additional customs duty is also very much a duty of customs. Just because its rate generally happens to be equivalent to the excise duty chargeable on the like goods manufactured in India, it does not cease to be a customs duty."

5. Air-conditioner fitted in a car, not being an essential components, is separately assessable even if invoice shows composite price for the car and the Air-Conditioner. "An Air-Conditioner is not an essential component of the car. It is not even a standard part of the car. It is an optional accessory and is supplied to only those purchasers of cars who asked for it. The department has, therefore, correctly assessed the Air-Conditioner separately under Head 84.12 of the Tariff."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs

HELD: Valuation (Customs) - Second hand machine without spares - Misdeclaration--Proof--Onus--The onus of proving misdeclaration regarding price shown in the B/E is on the Deptt., and this onus can be discharged only on the basis of facts and not mere suspicion--Loading of invoice price on the basis of guidelines issued by the Board, and by rejecting the Chartered Engineer's Certificate not sustainable particularly in the absence of any contemporaneous import of similar goods.

In this case, bond says nothing about any interest and hence, on this ground alone, no interest is payable - Even otherwise, there was no provision for charge of interest in case of provisional assessment, before amendment in section 18 from 13-7-2006 - Since in this case, period involved and date of order final assessment was prior to 13-7-2006, no interest could be charged [Paras 20 to 26] [In favour of assessee] Section 3(1), read with section 3A, of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996 - Charge/levy - Additional Duty of Customs/CVD - Period June 1998 to August 1998 - Department sought inclusion of anti-dumping duty in 'value' for purpose of charge of additional duty of customs - Assessee argued that only any sum chargeable 'as an addition to, and in same manner as', a duty of customs, can be added and same would refer only to surcharges and not an independent levy like anti-dumping duty - HELD : Words 'as an addition to' (along with 'in same manner') are different from 'in addition to' and therefore, same would refer to 'surcharges' only and not to independent duty like anti-dumping duty - Anti-dumping duty apart from being a separate levy from a levy of customs duty is also levied in a completely different manner from that of customs duty - Further, after 2002, sections 3(2) and 3A(2) have been amended so as to expressly exclude Anti-dumping duty from 'value' - Hence, anti-dumping would not form part of 'value' for charge of additional duty of customs [Paras 32 to 36] [In favour of assessee]

Section 112, read with section 111, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Penalty - Smuggling/illegal Import - On failure to fulfil export obligation, department made demanded duties on duty-free imports along with penalty - Assessee challenged penalties - HELD : Assessee had not diverted goods meant for export to domestic tariff area - Market considerations made it difficult, if not impossible, for assessee to fulfil its export obligations - Therefore, penalty imposed ought to be set aside [Para 37] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of pig iron.

During the period June 1998 to August 1998, the assessee imported Low Ash Metallurgical (LAM) Coke under seven Bills of Entry, against four advance licenses without payment of —

basic customs duty (BCD) levied under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962,

special customs duty (SCD) levied under section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996,

special additional duty (SAD) levied under section 3A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and

anti-dumping duty (ADD) levied under section 9A of Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

The department sought to deny exemptions on failure to fulfil export obligation.

Pending final adjudication of notice by the Commissioner, the assessee duly paid the entire duty payable towards BCD, SAD and SCD after considering partial exports already made. The assessee did not make any payment towards ADD.

The department confirmed duty demands along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent as per bond.

Tribunal enhanced ADD as per revised notification but reduced interest to 15 per cent.

The assessee challenged Anti-dumping duty, interest and penalty and other computations.

Assessee's Arguments

Basic customs duty and the special customs duty as well as special additional duty was payable by the assessee.

However, anti-dumping duty was not payable at all, as assessee was exempt under Notification No. 69 of 2000.

Notification No. 30 of 1997 did not stipulate that in the event of default, interest would become payable; hence, interest was not payable.

Since assessment was provisional, there was no provision for collection of interest for the period in dispute as section 18 was amended to include such a provision only prospectively with effect from 2006.

In any case, Anti-dumping duty could not be added for purposes of computing customs duty, special customs duty and special additional duty.

Also no penalty is imposable inasmuch as nothing contumacious was done by the assessee and the export obligation could not be fulfilled only because of bona fide commercial impossibility.

Since appeal before Tribunal was filed by assessee, he could not be worse off in an appeal filed only by the assessee herein to CESTAT and that on the assumption that the assessee was liable to pay anti-dumping duty, they should only pay the said duty at the lower rate prescribed by the Commissioner as revenue had not appealed to the Tribunal against the Commissioner's order.

Revenue's Arguments

The exemption contained in Anti-dumping duty Notification 69 of 2000 was only prospective and, hence Anti-dumping duty had to be paid for the relevant period.

Interest was payable as Notification No. 30 of 1997 independently levied a charge of interest.

Order of Tribunal was correct in law.

(DSD&M) meant for filtering blood are classifiable under Tariff Item 84212900 as 'Filtering or purifying machinery'.

Assessee challenged said circular and consequent classification as invalid.

HELD: It is not in dispute that originally the goods in question, being Dialysers were classified under CTH 90189031. The impugned circular has sought to change such classification by bringing Dialysers under CTH 84212900. [Para 26] Chapter 90 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'optical, photographic, cinematographic, measuring, checking, precision, medical or surgical instruments and apparatus; parts and accessories thereof.' Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to 'instruments and appliances used in medical, surgical, dental or veterinary sciences including scientigraphic apparatus, other electro-medical apparatus and sight-testing instruments. CTH 90189031 specifically pertains to renal dialysis equipment (artificial kidneys, kidney machines and dialysers). [Para 27]

Chapter 84 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'nuclear reactors, boilers, machinery and medical appliances; parts thereof.' Heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to 'centrifuges, including centrifugal dryers; filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus, for liquids or gases.' CTH 84212900 talks of 'filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus for gases.' [Para 28]

Thus, CTH 90189031 specifically provides for dialysers whereas CTH 84212900 provides for generic description of articles. Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to medical instruments whereas heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to goods which are generally used for industrial purposes and do not appear to have any medical use. Hence, the natural classification of dialysers should be under CTH 90189031 as it was prior to issuance of the impugned circular. When a specific tariff heading for classification is available, the goods concerned cannot be classified under a generic tariff heading. A heading with a more specific description of the goods in question shall be preferred to and prevail over a heading with a more general description. Just as a special law in a particular field would prevail over a general law that may be operational in that field, a heading with a more specific description would prevail over a heading with a more general description. In this connection, rule 3(a) of the General Rules for interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act makes it very clear that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description.

If the department intends to classify the goods in question under a heading which is different from the heading under which an assessee classifies such goods, the burden of proof is on the department which has to be discharged by adducing proper evidence. In the instant case, the onus was on the department to justify the change of classification sought to be made by the impugned circular, which onus has not been discharged by the department. Thus, it is evident that the impugned circular is blatantly contrary to the said rule and is thus, not sustainable. [Para 29]

Section 11A of the Customs Tariff Act empowers the Central Government to amend the First Schedule to the said Act. Such amendment may be carried out by notification in the Official Gazette and such notification must be placed before both the Houses of the Parliament for their approval. It is trite law that where a statute empowers an authority to do a certain thing in a certain way that thing must be done only in that way or not at all. All other methods of exercising such power are forbidden. [Para 30]

In the present case, the department sought to amend the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act by issuing the impugned circular. This falls foul of section 11A of the said Act and on this ground also the impugned circular must be set aside. [Para 31]

A circular cannot take away the effect of a notification statutorily issued. [Para 32]

The impugned circular at best contains executive instructions. It is not issued under any statute and has no force of law. It cannot override the statute. Any notice, circular, guidelines etc. which are contrary to statutory laws cannot be enforced. [Para 33]

The department claims that on 6-4-2015 the assessee agreed with the decision of the department and recorded so in writing. It was only two days later, i.e., on 8-4-2015 that the assessee wrote a letter stating that he was paying the reassessed amount of duty under protest. Having once agreed to the assessment made by the department, the assessee cannot be permitted to challenge the said assessment or the impugned circular on the basis whereof the assessment was made. The fact that the assessee had initially agreed with the department's assessment has been concealed by the assessee which amounts to suppression of material facts. The assessee has not approached the court with clean hands and does not deserve any relief.

"Since the car was one year old there was no reason restricting for only two quarters as it was rightly argued on behalf of the appellant. Once depreciation is permissible it should be given to fully ear since the car was imported after one year from the date of purchase. The Tribunal has been consistently held that 15% trade discount is permissible even in the case of individual who has purchased and brought into India following the earlier decisions, we hold that the appellant is entitled to 15% trade discount. Section 14 of the Customs Act provides for the Customs Tariff Act where a duty of customs is chargeable on any goods by reference to their value, the value of such goods shall be deemed to an price at which such or like goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale, for delivery at the time and place of importation. Such price shall be calculated with reference to rate of exchange as in force on the date on which the bill of entry is presented. Hence the Department was justified in including the freight charges. Since the actual freight charges are available the Department was not correct in adding the notional value in the absence of evidence brought on record to show that special concession was granted to the appellants. Accordingly we hold that the car is to be re-assessed after allowing trade discount at 15% and depreciation for 4 quarters and further the actual freight charges incurred by the appellant is to be added to the CIF value in arriving at the assessable value. "The aforesaid provisions of the Act, therefore, clearly show that after the imported goods are discharged from the vessel at the wharf the importer cannot immediately take delivery thereof. The imported goods remain in the custody of the Port Trust Authorities till they are, inter alia, cleared for home consumption. This being the position the goods cannot be cleared and delivery taken without their being valued and assessed and, thereafter, duty being paid. Section 14 of the Act provides that the value of the goods shall be deemed to be the price of the goods for the delivery at the time and place of importation in the course of international trade. The value has to be determined with relation to the time when physical delivery to the importer can take place. Physical delivery can take place only after the bill of entry, inter alia, for home consumption is filed and it is the value at that point of time which would be relevant. It is evident that there normally will be some lapse of time between the time when the shipper discharges the goods and the time when the bill of entry is filed. The landing charges, which are imposed at or after the time of the discharge of the goods and prior to the clearance being granted under Section 47 of the Act, necessarily have to be an element which have to be taken into account in determining the value thereof for the purpose of assessing the customs duty which would be chargeable" (Para 14)
