Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Depreciation - Car (used) - 1993 model car imported in 1996 and bill of entry filed on 31.8.1996 - Car was cleared by Customs on 28.3.2005 - Depreciation for post importation period i.e. from 31.8.96 to 28.3.2005 is not permissible for determining assessable value as value at the time of import/filing of bill of entry is to be adopted - Appeal dismissed with liberty to file suit for damages against Customs (Paras 3,4, 7  9)

III. Section 11A, read with section 33A of the Central Excise Act, 1944, article 226 of the Constitution of India, section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Adjudication of demand - Assessee challenged an adjudication order on ground that : (a) it was passed almost 9 months after conclusion of hearing i.e., beyond period of 15 days/1 month specified in circular dated 5-8-2003, (b) it did not consider various submissions/evidences put forth by assessee - Department argued that impugned order was correct and even otherwise, in view of alternative remedy of appeal, writ was not maintainable - HELD : Submissions and evidences put forth by assessee were not considered, which can only be attributed to delay in passing order and, thus, delay had caused prejudice to assessee - Since impugned order was contrary to already laid down parameters of law, assessee could not be relegated to alternate remedy by way of appeal - Hence, matter was remanded back for fresh hearing and passing of order [Paras 5 to 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable Value-Customs - freight charges - addition to C.I. Value in case of import by air prior to 1987 - as per instructions of the Board contained in Appraising Manual sea freight for similar goods should be ascertained and added - case remanded

Rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 as amended - Landing Charges - Validity - Proviso (ii) - Assessable value - Section 14 of Customs Act, 1962 - provisions requiring addition of landing /handling charges at adhoc rate of 1% of CIF value even where actual charges are known - neither hit by arbitrariness nor repugnant to Section 14(1) of Customs Act, 1962 - validity of the provisions upheld - writ petition dismissed

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 -Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Second hand machinery - assessable value arrived at by taking value of new machine minus depreciation as per Board's circular - upheld - transaction value rejected - appeal dismissed (Para 7)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable Value - Second hand diesel engine - higher assessable value determined by Collector set aside as (i) the basis adopted was different from that disclosed in show cause notice, (ii) it was based on value of new engine of 2200 cc while engines under import were of 1800 cc, (iii) adhoc depreciation @ 30% was given without any basis, and (iv) it was based on price in Singapore as stated by appellants during hearing while import was from UAE - assessable value as determined by Collector in an earlier case of import of such engines to be adopted after adding Rs. 2000/- for gear box. (Paras 8, 9, 10  11)

Pre-deposit - Section 129E of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Section 14 ibid - Transaction value - Limitation - Demand - Section 28 ibid - enhancement of assessable value of non-branded goods based on value of branded goods and on one year old import, not permissible - demand notice issued after six months, time barred as assessments were final - a prima-facie case for complete waiver of pre-deposit of duty and penalty. (Paras 4  5)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962-Rule 9 (2)of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - Freight and Insurance charges -goods imported by air - invoice shows freight and insurance charges separately - 20% of FOB value as per invoice in terms of Rule 9 (2) and not actual freight and insurances charges, should have been added to FOB price in invoice - appeal allowed (Para 3)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, read with section 3 of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Valuation of Imported Goods - Tariff Value - Assessee filed bill of entries for import of RBD Palmolein oil on 3-8-2001 and 4-8-2001 - Department demanded duty on said product based on Tariff Value, as revised by Notification dated 3-8-2001 - Assessee argued that owing to 4-8-2001 and 5-8-2001 being holidays, notification was offered for sale on 6-8-2001 and therefore, same would come into effect only from 6-8-2001 - HELD : Impugned Notification dated 3-8-2001 was notified in official gazette to public only on 6-8-2001, hence, duty becomes payable only from date it is notified in official gazette - Hence, impugned demand was quashed [Paras 4  5] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Notification fixing/revising tariff values would come into force when it is notified to public i.e., offered for sale to public; hence, when Notification dated 3-8-2001 was offered for sale on 6-8-2001, it would come into force on 6-8-2001

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Barging charges - incurred from anchorage to customs notified area of unloading where landing occurs are transport cost - includible apart from 1% landing charges at place of import - If already included in CIF value, not to be added separately.(Paras 10  11)

"......We fully agree with the submissions of the appellant that the appellate authority travelled beyond his jurisdiction inasmuch as the said price list was not proposed to be made the basis for enhancement of value at any stage, by the department. This was not the case even before the Assistant Collector. The appellant, as such, were definitely deprived of opportunity to rebut the said price list. We also note that the said price list is of post-contract and post-invoicing period. Whereas the invoice is dated 26.11.90, the price list is dated 3.12.90. The prices might have been increased vide the price list dated 3.12.90. The prices of the said list cannot be made the basis for the assessment of goods invoices earlier. The department has not filed any Appeal or Cross-objections against the rejection of the invoices of M/s Sujata Digital." (Para 7)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 5 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - Comparable goods - enhancement of value on the basis of imports made after 11 months not justified - reliance on Chief Commissioner's standing order without finding out price of contemporaneous imports of comparable goods, not sustainable - case remanded (Para 3)

Assessable Value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Second hand machinery - depreciation method for determining assessable value to be adopted in absence of transaction value as new machines were purchased abroad and imported after use for some period and as basis for declared value estimated by chartered engineer not disclosed - rate of depreciation adopted as per Board's circular dt. 19.11.87 held to be reasonable

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - enhanced on basis of import through another port - enhancement set aside as it was based on mere inquiry and no evidence was disclosed to appellants (Para 5)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation - Customs - contemporaneous imports of the integrated circuits as reflected in the bill of entries filed by the order importers, acceptable - rejection of such evidence by the department on the supposed ground of their review - not justified - unsigned fax quotations, unreliable

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Contemporary imports - Transaction value - bill of entry is dt. 17.12.1999 - loading of value on the basis of bill of entry dt. 25.8.1998 is not justified as the same is not contemporary import - no reasons for rejection of declared value given - transaction value to be accepted - appeal allowed (Paras 6  9)

"....The second plea raised in support of the appellant is that the Assistant Collector as well as Collector (Appeals) erred in taking value of new machinery at the time of shipment and that the correct base value to be taken from which depreciation is to be calculated would be the price of the new machine at the time of their manufacture. This is totally valid plea which should have been followed at the time of assessment. It is stated by the Learned Counsel at this stage in response to a query from the bench that they would obtain from their suppliers the prices for the new machines in 1982-83 when the machines were purchased by the latter for their use. It may be seen whether such a price corresponds to the price of new machine certified by the Chartered Engineer and whether it also corresponds to the value arrived at from the prices shown for new machines in 1987-88 by working back by allowing appropriate deductions to arrive at the 1982-83 prices. With this direction, we set aside the impugned order and remand the matter for denovo decision for determining the correct assessable value afresh following the aforesaid procedure." (Para 5)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - Populated PCB - Transaction value - To be accepted in absence of any evidence either of contemporaneous imports of identical goods at higher price or of transaction value not being correct - It can not be rejected on the basis of market inquiry showing higher retail sale price and Deptt.'s expert's opinion - Appeal rejected (Para 5)

Section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 - Limitation - extended time limit not invokable as appellants were under bonafide belief that charges collected for certain post manufacturing activities by a separate debit note were not to be included in assessable value and Deptt. was aware of such collections - appeal allowed (Paras 45)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 5 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - loading of value of imported goods on the basis of unsustainable admission and value of contemporaneous imports which took place after 6 months after the present import not sustainable when quantity imported is also different - Value of branded goods imported by the same appellant cannot be adopted for the goods in question - Appeal allowed (Para 3)

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Assessable value - value of goods cannot be enhanced on the basis of an invoice which is more than 6-1/2 months old as the same cannot be considered contemporaneous in nature -Revenue appeal rejected. (Para 7)

Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Demand of Duties not levied or short levied - Board's circular - Effective date - circular is effective from date on which it is communicated to assessee or instructions based on it are issued - Revenue's appeal dismissed (Para 4)

Limitation - Demand -Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962- extended period is invokable as appellants did not disclose the fact of not including transport cost of daughter vessel in assessable value (Para 8)

facts.text:
The respondent imported various petroleum products and crude oil into India and had cleared the same upon payment of customs duty. The customs authorities having noted that the respondent had paid demurrage charges to the shipowners under the charter party agreements through negotiating bank issued a show-cause notice to the appellant and included the bank charges and demurrage paid in the customs value of the goods and created additional demand of customs duty against the respondent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order. On second appeal, the Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal (CEGAT) allowed the appeal of the respondent on the grounds; (i) that the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) had issued a circular on 14-8-1991 under section 151A of the Customs Act in which it was said that the demurrage did not form part of the assessable value of the goods imported and the circular was binding on the revenue and the department could not contend otherwise, (ii) that the decision of the Supreme Court in Garden Silk Mills Ltd. v. Union of India [1999] 113 ELT 358 relied upon by the revenue was not an authority for the proposition that demurrage payable on account of delay in discharging goods from a vessel was includible in the value of goods while assessing the customs duty payable thereon, and (iii) that under section 14 the assessable value of the imported goods must be the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold and the payment of demurrage was not an incident of an ordinary sale and an extraordinary expenditure, like demurrage, could not be included in the assessable value of the imported goods.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The appellants had imported two Toyota Corona 1600 DLX Sedans. They presented the manufacturer's invoice at the lime of assessment of Customs duly. The Customs authorities determined duty payable after adding freight, insurance and landing charges to the invoice price. Though the importers claimed 15% discount on the manufacturer's price, as well as exclusion of freight, insurance and landing charges, these claims were rejected by the Asstt. Collr. On appeal the Tribunal upheld the Asstt. Collr.'s valuation. Depreciation claims in respect of car accessories like stereo AC were also disallowed. After this the importers submitted applications for rectification of mistakes which, they argued, were obvious and apparent in the earlier order. Their main contention is that as value should have been fixed at place of removal (the market in Japan) insurance and transportation expenses etc., were to be deducted. Besides, the Department was bound by promissory estoppel to allow a discount of 15% in view of a Departmental circular providing for this discount.

The assessee claimed that the wharfage charge, which is a statutory port due was eligible for deductions from value of custom house agent services for calculating its taxable value. In the impugned order, the Commissioner (Appeals) had not granted the benefit of deduction on the ground that as per the Board’s Circular F. No. B/43/1/97-TRU, dated 6-6-1997, the assessee was allowed to treat 15 per cent lump-sum receipts as value of taxable services and pay service tax on this 15 per cent only. According to him if said deduction was allowed, the residual payment could not be treated as lump-sum payment and service tax liability would have to be discharged on total receipts minus deductions and not on 15 per cent of total receipts minus deductions. On the issue of time bar, he had noted that the assessee was regularly furnishing returns, which were assessed and finalized by the Department and, therefore, the larger period could not be invoked. However, for another part of the period, he had noted that once self-assessment procedure was adopted, the liability of calculating and discharging duty was of the assessee alone and no knowledge on the part of the Department could be presumed and for that period, the charge of concealment resulting in short payment of duty became sustainable.

On appeal :

The assessees challenged constitutional validity of proviso (ii) of rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 inserted by Notification No. 39/90, dated 5-7-1990.

The assessee claimed that the actual loading, unloading and handling charges amounted to Rs. 69.98 paisa as per the tariff of the International Airport Authority of India, Madras (now Chennai). However, the Customs Authorities, on the basis of the impugned notification added a sum of Rs. 15,214.69 paisa at 1 per cent of CIF value.

The assessee argued that such a notional fixation of the handling charges with the addition of 1 per cent of CIF value, irrespective of the nature of goods, size of the cargo, was in total disregard to total handling charges, even when such actual handling charges could be ascertained. Same was irrational, arbitrary and ultra vires.

The department argued that it was found impossible to ascertain the actual amounts incurred towards loading, unloading and handling charges while making the assessment as they varied depending upon the quantities and place of import. Finding this difficulty in actual practice and in order to achieve certainty, one per cent of the CIF value was fixed to be included in the assessable value. It was argued that once this uniformity is achieved with the aforesaid provisions, merely because some would be getting the benefit while others would suffer certain detriment, is no reason for invalidating the provision when many others would be getting the benefit thereof as well. The percentage had been fixed by the rule making authority after taken into consideration the overall picture.

The respondent-assessee was engaged in the business of construction. She constructed a complex during the assessment years 1993-94 to 1996-97. On completion of project in the assessment year 1996-97, the assessee, after taking into consideration the profits offered in the assessment years 1993-94 and 1994-95, offered the balance profit for taxation in the assessment year 1996-97. The Assessing Officer rejected the books of account maintained by the assessee and referred the matter to the departmental valuation cell. The valuation cell determined the value of the property at a much higher amount as against the declared value. The Assessing Officer, after making adjustments to the valuation report, completed assessment under section 143(3) by making addition. Appeal against the said order was rejected by the appellate authority. On further appeal, the assessee contended that since the department had decided by virtue of the Board circular not to make detailed scrutinies for the assessment year 1996-97 if the income declared was more than 30 per cent of the income declared in 1995-96, the assessment itself was bad. The Tribunal accepted the contention and allowed the appeal. In the instant appeal, the appellant submitted that the instructions in the circular were not binding on the Tribunal or the Court nor were available for execution to any judicial authority.

Appellants, manufacturers of glass sheets, charged from their customers the price of the goods as well as extra charges on account of special packing, cost of transport, forwarding charges, breakage risk and miscellaneous charges. The dispute was whether the charges for the extras were includible in the assessable value of the goods. When the same issue had gone to the High Court earlier, the appellants had contended that they realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers and not from their local buyers. The High Court held that as the appellants realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers, the extra charges were in principle excludible from the assessable value, and further, ordered the department of investigate the assertion of the facts made by the appellants. While the matter was under enquiry, the department received some information that the appellants were indulging in under-valuation of their goods. The Anti-Evasion staff of the department scrutinised the documents of the appellants and came to the conclusion that the appellants had highly inflated the costs of the extra items so as to camouflage the true assessable value of the goods. On this ground, show cause notices were issued demanding differential excise duty of Rs. 1,88,84,508.57 and also a penalty of Rs. 50 lakhs was imposed on the appellants for making false and mis-leading declarations. Confiscation of the plant and machinery of the appellants in lieu of a fine was also ordered. The appellants contended that the show-cause notices issued by the department were time-barred as they were issued beyond the normal time of six months. Further, the appellants pointed out that there has been a violation of principles of natural justice as their request to make further clarifications on the matter, was not honoured by the department. The question as to which of the items of extras should be held to be excludible for determining the assessable value of the goods was also taken up in the instant case.

The point for decision in the appeal is whether rule 9 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 prescribes the inclusion of demurrage charges in the assessable value. The appellants have sought waiver of pre-deposit of Customs duty demanded from them on the demurrage charges incurred by them.

The appellants imported a second-hand 1976 model, 4 colour, off-set printing machine and a second-hand 1983 model paper folding machine, both of German make, from the U.K. The declared value of these machines was £ 49,000 and £ 3000.00 respectively. Certificates from Chartered Engineers in support of the transactional value were furnished. However, since the current prices of the machines indicated in the certificates were much lower than the current price indicated by the local agents of the manufacturers of these machines and also because the prices quoted for the year of manufacture were found to be wrong, the Asstt. Collector rejected the certificates. There was a difference of Rs. 10,03,400 between the declared value and the assessable value arrived at by the Department. Alleging deliberate undervaluation with an intention to evade duty, the Asstt. Collector of Customs held both the machines liable to confiscation under section 111(m) of the Customs Act, 1962. The off-set printing machine was held to be liable to confiscation under section 111(d) as well as it was older than 7 years, which was in violation of the provisions of AM 1988-91 Import Policy. Aggrieved by the aforementioned order, the appellants have come in appeal.

The appellants had imported a consignment of 'Dielectric Heater Components of Heat Training Systems, and claimed its clearance under OGL Item No. 476, appendix 6, list 8, part I of the Import & Export Policy 1985-88. However the Addl. Collr. held that for ITC purposes, the goods were classifiable under Sl. No. 462(a) of appendix 3A. He also did not accept the invoice price and ordered enhancement of the assessable value from Rs. 5,15,696/- to Rs. 10,71,721.70 under section 14(1)(h) of the Customs Act. He confiscated the imported goods with an option to redeem on payment of fine of Rs. 10,00,000 and also imposed penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 under section 112(a) of Customs Act. In their appeal to the Tribunal, the appellants sought permission for filing certain additional evidence and a similar request was received from the Department. The appellants also stated that they were denied the opportunity of cross-examination of the two officials whose advice was taken into account and that they were not confronted with the telex relied upon for upward revision of the value which has figured only in the adjudication order.

The question for consideration was whether, in arriving at the assessable value of excisable goods, the amount of duty to be deducted should be the effective rate of duty or without taking into account the relevant exemption notifications. The appellants contended that the former amount was deductible while the departmental authorities stated that only the latter amount was deductible. It was argued by the department that the appellants had paid concessional rate of duty while clearing goods but subsequent verification of their invoices showed that they had recovered the full amount of duty payable. The Appellate Collector had held that the show-cause notices were not time-barred, as contended by the appellants, as there had been suppression of material which meant that the extended five years' time-limit was applicable. The question of filing cross objection also came up.

The appellants imported certain second-hand machines. The Customs authorities did not accept the invoice price on the plea that similar machines had been imported by the same assessee at a much higher price while the time gap between the two imports was not much. The goods were valued under Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules keeping in view appreciation of prices depreciation insurance, freight and landing charges. Collector (Appeals) upheld the order except that he allowed depreciation @ 10% as against 6-1/4% allowed by the lower authorities.

All the 11 appellants in this case imported wood by a vessel from Trinidad through a dealer in Hongkong and declared a value of US $ 321 per cbm. The Customs authorities, however, enhanced the assessable value to US $ 420 per cbm. on the basis of a telex message sent by the Charterers to the Master of the vessel that the approximate value of the wood carried in the ship was US $ 420 per cbm. The appellants question the basis of this valuation and also the correctness of the Deptt. relying on the telex as sole evidence for determining the assessable value without following the procedure for valuation laid down under Sec. 14 of the Customs Act.

The appellants manufacture weighing machines which are sold from their depots in different regions at varying prices. On the appellants quoting the price at Calcutta as the assessable value, the Excise Dept. charged them with mis-declaration as the sale prices at various depots were higher. The Department also claimed that the duty had not been paid on some of the machines removed from the factory. The appellants were asked to furnish the details of their pricing pattern, and when this was not forthcoming a show cause notice was issued demanding payment of duty based on the highest sale price; payment of duty short levied, and also a penalty.

The appellants contended that the Calcutta price represented the true assessable value and that the difference in prices at their depots was due to post clearance deductible expenses like insurance, freight and handling charges; that the show cause notice was time barred as it was served 6 months after the date of issue; that the earlier acceptance of the Department of certain contract prices should not be revoked; that a comprehensive check of the documents would prove that duty had been paid on all the machines removed.

The Department conceded that the case should be remanded and a verification made of the appellants' contention regarding removals, but claimed an extended time limit for the show cause notice on the ground of mis-declaration.

The assessee had provided in its accounts import duty on newsprint imported by it at Rs. 825 per metric ton. for the period from 1981 to 1985. The Assessing Officer noticed that the Supreme Court in its judgment dated 6-12-1984 had allowed the Government to recover only Rs. 550 per metric ton. He added the amount of difference between provision made for customs duty and the amount actually payable by the assessee as per the judgment of the Supreme Court. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the judgment of the Supreme Court did not have the effect of cancelling the levy and deleted the addition for the assessment year 1985-86. The Assessing Officer again included the said amount in the assessee’s income for the assessment year under consideration because the Government had issued a notification on 19-12-1985 and abolished the auxiliary duty and fixed the import duty at Rs. 550 per MT. The Assessing Officer also noticed that the CBEC had also issued a circular dated 10-2-1986 intimating that the effective rate of customs duty would be Rs. 550 only from 1-3-1981 to 18-12-1985, and this notification had the effect of cancelling the auxiliary duty. Since the above notification and circular issued by the CBEC fell within the relevant assessment year, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer for this year.

On second appeal :

The value of leather tanning machinery imported by the appellants was assessed by the lower authorities on the basis of ruling prices as per the price lists in force on the date of opening of letter of credit. The appellants argued that even though the prices of the machinery had more than doubled, the foreign suppliers had agreed to adhere to the old prices quoted in the proforma invoices. The (departmental authorities, however, were of the view that the concept of value under Section 14 was a deemed value and not necessarily the invoice value of a particular importer.

The question involved in the instant appeal is as to whether ship demurrage charges paid by the assessee-importer on the import of the goods were to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for purpose of levy of customs duty.

In the assessment year 1993-94, the assessee-company had claimed deduction under section 43B on account of customs duty of Rs. 39,39,096 paid in advance during the financial year 1992-93 on bonding of imported raw materials. The claim was allowed by the Assessing Officer. Subsequently, it was found that since the value of the closing stock did not include the amount of customs duty paid in advance and, thus, did not increase the profit to that extent, the allowance of deduction under section 43B was not in order. According to the petitioner, the Assessing Officer had made enquiries regarding the closing stock valuation relating to excise duty and customs duty which also included the said amount of Rs. 39,39,096 and after considering the same he disallowed Rs. 99,10,108 and also made an addition of Rs. 11 lakhs. On appeal against the said order, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s appeal excepting for one item and the said order was also given effect to by the Assessing Officer on 21-1-1997. However, the department issued notice under section 148 for reassessment of the assessee’s income for the assessment year 1993-94.

On writ :

The departmental authorities appealed against the order of the Collector (Appeals) allowing the respondents deduction of freight charges in the determination of the assessable value of the goods. They contended that Notification No. 120/75-CE is a parallel mode of determination of the assessable value of excisable goods to Section 4(a).

The appellants imported 15000 pcs. of Miniature Ball Bearings from Singapore and gave the invoice price as CIF 3000 Singapore Dollars i.e. Rs. 17,128.20. The Customs Department at Amritsar did not have the price for the goods and so requested Delhi Customs for the same. On getting the information from Delhi Customs, the Department issued a show cause notice to the party for adopting that rate for valuation i.e. 9.25 per piece However, the Asstt. Collector directed the duty to be paid on Rs. 18.40 per piece i.e. on total value of Rs. 21,76,000/- without giving any further show cause notice to the appellants. This rate of 18.40 per piece was obtained from the Central Warehousing Corporation. The appellants contended that the assessable value was to be based on the declared invoice prices unless the department could prove it incorrect. The department wanted the case to be remanded so that the party was given a proper opportunity of being heard on the evidence.

The respondents manufacture 'Electrical Stampings and Laminations' falling under T. 1.28A. In the price lists filed the respondents shoved ex-factory prices and packing charges separately. The Asstt. Collr. held that the goods in question are normally delivered after packing, as such packing charges are includible in the assessable value. On remand by the Appellate Collr., the Asstt. Collr. after reconsideration held that as there were substantial sales in loose condition, he dropped further proceedings for inclusion of packing charges in assessable value. Based on this the respondents filed a consolidated refund claim for the period January 1976 to Sept., 1980. The Asstt. Collector without going into the quantum of refund claim, once again examined the merits and concluded that the packing charges are includible in the assessable value and rejected the refund claim. The question for decision is whether it is open to another Asstt. Collr. of the same geographical jurisdiction to take note of the fact the earlier order was issued without reference to the amended provision of law and reject the refund claim on the plea that the order of the first Asstt. Collector was wrong.

Two demands were raised by the Department on the ground that costs on account of consultancy charges, erection and service charges, though recovered by the respondents from their customers through separate invoices, were not included in the assessable value of machinery sold by them. The first demand related to costs of drawing, designing and technical specifications recovered under the head 'consultancy charges' and the second demand was for installation and service charges for machinery at the customer's premises. The respondents pleaded that the demands were time barred but the Department contended that since there was suppression of the fact of two separate invoices, the extended time limit of five years was applicable.
The issue under dispute was whether overtime charges paid to customs officers should be included in the assessable value of fertilizers imported by the appellant.

The appellants claimed benefit of exemption under Notfn. No. 176/77-CE at 18.6.1977 no the ground that distillation plant manufactured by them fell under TI/68 and that the value of their clearances remained within the stipulated limit. The Department initiated proceedings on the allegations that the value of clearances had exceeded the stipulated limit. The appellants repudiated the charge contending that supervision and erection charges, packing charges, conversion charges and value of 'bought out' parts had to be excluded from the assessable value of the goods. Moreover they claimed that the demand issued beyond the period of six months from the date when duty was payable was barred by time.

All these 153 appeals raise a common set of points, viz., (1) whether notional landing charges are includible for computing the assessable value of imported goods; (2) whether customs and auxiliary duties are includible in the aggregate value of the goods for purpose of levy of addl. duty (CVD) of customs, and (3) whether packing charges are excludible from the assessable value in terms of Notfn. 184/76-Cus.

Facts

The assessee imported certain materials during the years 2005-2006, 2006-2007, 2007-2008 and it paid the Customs Duty at the prevailing rates and in terms of the provisional assessment. The Bills of Entry were pending for 3 to 5 years.

The assessee argued that the assessments were finalized during the year December 2010 to January 2011 under special drive carried out as per instructions of the Joint Secretary, Central Board of Excise and Customs, whereunder an order was passed on 13th October, 2010 nominating an Officer. However, the nominated officer did not comply with the principles of natural justice and confirmed the assessment.

The assessee filed writ petition aggrieved by the letters of demand which according to the assessee threaten to recover the sums coercively.

The department argued that all the contentions as are raised in the present petition can be raised, considered and decided therein in appeal; therefore, the writ petition be not entertained and dismissed.

The assessee had imported certain components in relation to which the customs authorities levied duty in the first instance by loading the invoice value by 20 per cent. The assessee disputed the consequent demand, but paid the additional duty under protest. The Collector of Customs later passed another order on 30-10-1980 by which he enhanced the invoice value by loading it at 100 per cent for the purpose of levy of customs duty. That was subsequently reduced in appeal to 50 per cent by order dated 30-8-1983. In view of this pending demand, the assessee claimed deduction of certain amount as additional duty payable on the import. The ITO disallowed the same on the ground that the assessee had not made any provision in the accounts. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the liability was one which had become crystallised during the year of account and was, therefore, liable to be allowed as business expenditure though no provision had been made in the accounts. The Tribunal affirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) .

On application under section 256(2) :

Respondents collect deposits from prospective purchasers and pay interest thereon at varying rates. The Department calculated notional interest on these deposits and added the same to the assessable value. The respondents pleaded that the deposits were taken to secure the transportation expenses incurred in the event the purchasers did not retire the documents from the company. Collector (Appeals) disallowed the addition made to the assessable value. Hence this appeal and stay application by revenue.

The appellant opted to adopt the invoice value of the imported goods and agreed to loading of 20 per cent as per the circular of the Special Valuation Branch, and went on periodically paying 20 per cent loaded value under the impression that the assessment was provisional. His application for refund was rejected as time barred on the ground that he had not specifically requested for treating the assessment as provisional.

The assessee was engaged in providing customs house agent's service. It recovered CMC charges from it's clients, which were levied by the computer centre for filing the bill of entry and shipping bills electronically. The revenue included above charges in assessable value of the CHA service provided by the assessees, and invoking extended period of limitation confirmed demand on the assessee. The assessee submitted that the demand was time-barred as the CMC charges were separately reimbursed by it's customer, it was under bona fide belief that same was not includable in its assessable value.

The appellants manufacture aerated waters and sell their products to various wholesale dealers from whom they recover an additional Rs. 5/- per crate as hire charges on account of delay in return of empties and Rs. 3/- per crate as compensation for not lifting the agreed quantity. Having intercepted a truck belonging to another company, carrying aerated water bottles, issued by the appellants the Collector confiscated the goods, denied the benefit of Notfn. 175/86-CE on the ground that the appellants' clearances were to be clubbed with those of the other company and raised a demand of Rs. 4,02,754/- holding that the compensation amount of Rs. 3/- per crate, a proportionate part of the Rs. 5/- levied as container hire and 80 paise per crate towards transportation charges are includible in the assessable value. He also imposed a penalty.

By virtue of a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the High Court, company 'S' amalgamated with the assessee-company. The said company paid customs duty and claimed deduction under section 43B while including the same in the purchase price and thereafter in the closing stock. The assessee added back the same in the return of income as disallowable under section 43B. When the matter reached the Tribunal, the assessee filed a cross-objection and took the additional ground that the customs duty included in the closing stock of the amalgamating company be excluded because it was not taxable income as per the Supreme Court's decision in Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. CIT [1990] 186 ITR 278/53 Taxman 92. The assessee filed application for condonation of delay in filing the cross-objection submitting that the cross-objection was filed on the basis of the decision of the Supreme Court which was delivered on 4-9-1990 as the said decision was not available when the assessee filed the return and when the appeal was filed or when the appeal was decided by the Commissioner (Appeals). The Tribunal rejected assessee's application on the ground that same was filed after delay of more than a year and no sufficient cause had been made out explaining the delay.

On reference :

Price lists submitted by the appellants had not included in the assessable value the cost of secondary special packing and delivery charges recovered from customers. The Department then raised a demand for differential duty on the ground that the aforesaid costs should have been included. The appellant company pointed out that the question of correct assessable value had already been decided by the High Court of Allahabad which had upheld the contentions of the appellant company. The Department, according to them, was now estopped from raising the plea of including the packing and delivery charges in the value. This was in accordance with the principle of constructive res judicata enunciated in Explanation IV to Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code. The Department asserted that there can be no plea of res judicata in taxation matters and that constructive res judicata was not applicable to decisions given in writ petitions under Articles 226 or 32 of the Constitution. They contended that the concept of res judicata applied to issues directly raised while in the present case the issue before the High Court was whether the price charged by the appellants' customer companies or the price charged by the appellants from their customer companies would form the basis of assessable value. It was also argued that copies of the price lists had not been supplied with the writ petition and, therefore, the High Court's order holding that the price charged by the appellant company would be the wholesale cash price, inclusive of packing and delivery charges, was not correct. Further, the question before the High Court was only regarding assessments for a past period.

The assessing officer found that the appellants had mis-declared the value of a machine and spare parts imported by them on comparison of the prices of the machine in the technical literature-cum-price-list supplied by the appellants and the prices declared in the bill of entry and accordingly demanded duty on the enhanced value of the goods. The appellants argued that the price list was not valid for assessment purposes and that they had evidence of a contemporaneous import by a Delhi company of similar goods for the same price declared. The authorities contended that the foreign supplier had agreed to allow a reduction in prices charged to the appellants on recommendation of the Delhi party as evidenced by a letter addressed by the Delhi party to the foreign supplier,

The petitioners imported high density Polyethelene moulding powder (HDPE) and sought exemption of duty and additional duty on the value of packages containing the said goods under Notification 184/76--Cus. dt. 2.8.1976. The said benefit was proposed to be availed of by reducing the invoice value of the 'goods' to the extent of value of the 'packages' containing them. If the latter was already included in the assessable value of the former and by ignoring the same if it had been shown separately in the Bill of entry. The Customs authorities had already rejected a similar claim of another petitioner on the grounds that the said notification exempted the packages only independently of the goods in order to avoid double incidence of duty. In view of the department's stand the above importer and several other similarly placed parties filed petitions in the court. The opinion of the hon'ble judge that the said notification only exempted packages from being separately charged to duty and did not provide for deducting the value of the packages from the value of goods imported, being at variance with another judgment, the matter was referred to Division Bench. The department pleaded that the packages and packing material themselves constitute goods and were liable to duty separately but for the notification under reference and that the cost of packing cannot be deducted from the assessable value of the principal goods only because it is or can be shown separately in the Bill of entry. On the other hand the petitioners argued that the only way of giving effect to the notification was to assess the value of the packages and exclude it from the invoice value of the goods which ordinarily includes the former.

Misdeclaration of the value of Glacier Brand Bearings imported by the appellants was alleged by the customs authorities who held that the goods were liable for confiscation. The appellants contended that the price mentioned in the invoices should be accepted as the proper price and that the burden of proving misdeclaration was on the department. The value of goods for the purpose of assessment, according to them, would be the deemed value as provided for in Sec. 14(1)(a) even if the invoice price is proved to be the true price as agreed to between the parties concerned. Refuting the department's contention that special nett prices for India, mentioned in a letter from a recognised and reputed supplier of the subject parts, were the actual prices, the appellants contended that the subject goods were dead stock which the exporters were prepared to sell at a particular price which was the normal international price.

A letter of credit opened by the appellants with respect to an Offset Press imported by them was subsequently amended due to certain shipping difficulties. The goods were covered by the OGL under the Import Policy for 1982-83 at the time of opening of the letter of credit, but the Customs authorities held that the amendment amounted to a new letter of credit which meant that the goods were not covered by the OGL and were, therefore, liable to confiscation. Under-valuation of the goods was also alleged. The appellants argued that the subsequent amendment did not vitiate the basic validity of the letter of credit. They submitted that the method adopted by the Collector for valuing the goods with reference to import of a similar machine by other printers was ad hoc and without any basis. They maintained that the value declared in the Bill of Entry was the correct assessable value, and the customs authorities had not discharged the burden of proving under-valuation.

The respondents had requested provisional assessment while their claim for deduction of post-manufacturing expenses was being considered. This was denied to them and a demand raised for nearly Rs. 2-1/2 lakhs. The respondents claimed this demand to be barred by limitation, which claim was upheld by the Collr. (Appeals). The Deptt., in this appeal, charged the respondents with suppression of facts with intent to evade duty. The respondents denied this allegation which they pointed out was not even contained in the show cause notice. They submitted that the delay was due only to Asstt. Collr.'s failure to pass orders and that they had regularly been submitting RT 12s which had been finally assessed.

• There assessee was engaged in providing services of commission agents in India and Nepal for all kinds of earth moving equipment and other machines including accessories and spares manufactured by L & T Komatsu Limited.

• The Department had demanded service tax thereon for the period from July 2003 to March 2005 under the head clearing and forwarding agent services.

• The assessee had filed an appeal before Tribunal along with application for stay of demand, which was pending. A hearing was granted to assessee in matter of stay application, but, it was postponed/adjourned due to non-availability of the Tribunal Bench.

• Pending such application, the Department initiated recovery proceedings and allegedly threatened to take coercive action for recovery relying on CBEC Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013.

• Assessee challenged such circular as invalid.

Assessee's arguments

• The stipulation in the Circular that even though an application for stay of the recovery of the demand has been filed before the appellate forum, recoveries would be proceeded with on the expiry of a stipulated period, and in certain cases immediately, was an invalid stipulation.

• When the stay application remains to be disposed of due to the inability of the appellate authority to take up the application for hearing and for disposal, and without any default on the part of the assessee, it would be arbitrary to penalize the assessee by enforcing the recovery despite the pendency of the application for stay.

• Hence, Sl. Nos. 3, 6, 9, 10 and 11 of Table in para 2 of the impugned Circular were arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution insofar as they sought recovery prior to disposition of pending stay application.

Revenue's arguments

• There is no prohibition on proceeding with recovery of a confirmed demand even immediately after an order has been issued, when no stay is in operation.

• Section 87 of the Finance Act, 1994 does not provide for suspension of the original order when a stay application is pending before an Appellate Authority.

• It is a matter of policy for the Government to decide as to how long it should wait before a recovery of a confirmed demand should be initiated, which had now been decided by the circular dated 1 January, 2013.

• Under section 35F, a pre-deposit is mandatory with the filing of an appeal and an order of dispensation is by way of an exception.

• The impugned Circular did not impinge upon the power of the Appellate Authority to grant a stay.

Issue Involved

• Whether impugned entries of the impugned Circular were invalid in law ?

The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture of air-compressors, garage equipment, hydraulic presses, etc., for which purpose it imported certain components and raw materials. Besides paying the invoice price, it incurred customs duty, freight and handling charges. The accounting year under appeal was the calender year ending on 31-12-1960. For the financial year ending on 31-12-1959, the value of the closing stock, which became opening stock on 1-1-1960 included an ad hoc amount for customs duty and other charges. However, the valuation of closing stock was made without adding customs duty, freight and handling charges for the year ending 31-12-1960. The ITO held such valuation to be defective and, accordingly, made an addition thereon. The ITO made another addition on coming into possession of a letter in which it was found that the foreign principals from whom the assessee purchased components and other material had given a credit in a statement of account sent by them to the assessee which had not been accounted for in the assessee’s books. On appeal, the AAC held that the customs duty, freight and handling charges paid ought to have been included in the value of the closing stock. The AAC also confirmed the addition on account of the credits on the ground that all the credits on account of the purchases had not been accounted for. On second appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the decision of the AAC in respect of the under-valuation of the closing stock observing that both the opening stock and the closing stock should be valued on the same principle, i.e., the market value or the cost, whichever was lower, and that the opening stock could not be valued in a manner different from the valuation of the closing stock. In respect of the addition on account of failure to account for the credit note, the Tribunal held that the question was as to whether the original account given by the foreign party was to be believed or the subsequent account given by it reversing the said entry was to be believed and that the ITO should have probed that matter a little more in detail instead of relying on the first letter, however, since the assessee had not satisfactory explained the credit note and there was failure to account for it in the account books, the addition was to be upheld.

On application under section 256(2) :

The appellant declared the value of their import as shown in the manufacturers' invoice. Customs authorities observed that the price shown in the manufacturer's International Price List was much in excess of the invoiced price. They charged the appellant of misdeclaration and made an assessment on the basis of price list after allowing a marginal diminution of 20% on account of the fact that the machines were used before import. The authorities, however, accepted the declared value for the purpose of debiting it to the import Licence. The appellant contended that the order was arbitrary as no reasons for conclusion on assessable value were given in the adjudication order. There was no basis for arriving at 20% diminution and the discount for bulk purchase was not taken into account. The sections/rules under which assessable value was to be determined were disputed by the parties.

The assessee-company had imported machinery under duty exemption certificate issued by the Ministry of Finance. Because of said certificate, the assessee did not pay any custom duty on imported machinery. However, the custom department disputed the said certificate and called upon the assessee to pay differential amount of custom duty. The assessee paid the said amount without prejudice to its contention that the certificate issued by the Ministry of Finance was valid, legal and proper and no such custom duty was payable. It capitalized the cost of machinery by adding the said payment to the cost of machinery and on that basis, depreciation on the said addition was claimed. The Assessing Officer disallowed the depreciation on addition. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) as well as the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim relying on various judgments of the Supreme Court wherein it has been held that even if the liability is challenged and the legal proceedings are pending, once the amount has gone out of the coffers of the assessee, the assessee would be entitled to capitalize the same.

On appeal to the High Court :

Facts

Assessee, a manufacturer of synthetic filament yarn, under intense pressure of the department, paid, during the period 6-12-1995 to 22-10-1997, the differential duty in respect of the additions to the assessable value of goods on account of transportation, insurance, handling and delivery charges for the clearances made during the period 1-03-1994 to 30-11-1996.

By way of the letters dated 5-10-1995 and 5-12-1995, assessee claimed to have had lodged protest against inclusion of such charges in the assessable value of goods when the Assessing Officer proposed to make such additions; and during the pendency of those proceedings, the amount in question was paid after raising objections. Ultimately, the objections of the assessee were sustained.

Thereafter, on 25-06-1998, the assessee lodged the claim, per section 11B(2) of the Act, for refund of the amount paid.

The Deputy Commissioner rejected the claim so made by the assessee for refund of the duty as being time-barred, while holding that the letters dated 5-10-1995 and 5-12-1995, as filed by the assessee with the Department, were not the letters of protests but were merely the letters of disagreement with the Superintendent on various issues; and that the procedure specified under rule 233B of the Rules was not followed by the assessee.

Assessee argued that they had recorded disagreement with levy of differential duty on transportation, delivery charges; in following words in letter dated 5-12-1995 —

'differential excise duty in case of Transportation/Delivery charges and Insurance Charges is not leviable';

said items 'are permissible deductions for the calculation of assessable values';

department was requested 'not to insist upon recovery on short levied excise duty amount charged in case of transportation/delivery and insurance charges'; and

department's continuous 'insistence and pressure for recovery of the same would be unjustified and against the principle of natural justice.'

Issue Involved

Whether assessee had paid duty under protest ?

The petitioner is aggrieved by the order passed by the Asstt, Supdt, of CE, confirming demand of Addl. excise duty on Fiat cars sold during 1969-71. The Company had fixed the price of the cars at Rs. 14,862, but because of a price control order issued by the G.O.I., the cars were sold at Rs. 13,325, but an endorsement was incorporated in the invoice whereby the price was liable to be upwardly revised in case the petitioners won their case against the price control order. Excise duty was paid after taking assessable value as Rs. 13,434 per car. Pursuant to the S.C. decision lifting the price control order, allowing the company to recover the additional price, Show cause Notices were issued by the Supdt. of CE. calling upon the appellants to pay differential duty of over Rs. 24 lakhs in respect of the addl. price which the company was entitled to recover in accordance with the endorsement in the invoices. After the demand was confirmed the appellant appealed before the Appellate Collr. as well as a single judge of the High Court, but the appeals were rejected. The arguments put forward before the single Judge as well as in this petition, inter alia, are (a) the assessment orders passed by the Department were final and could not be reopened and even if reopened, were hit by one year limitation under Rule 10(b), assessable value is price prevalent at time of sale and the same cannot be hiked up retrospectively.

The appellants in all these cases imported small consignments through shipping lines. These goods were landed and delivered by the shipping company without any extra charge as freight, including landing charges, was paid by the shipping company. The Collector (Appeals) contended that import of goods is not complete till they are landed, pass through Port Trust and are placed before Customs for assessment, and that landing charges should be included in the assessable value. He also added that there is no documentary evidence or receipt to show that the freight paid included landing charges.

The assessee was following the mercantile system of accounting. In the assessment year 1975-76, certain interest on sticky advances accrued to the assessee and the same was included in the assessee’s income by the Assessing Officer. The Commissioner (Appeals) following his earlier order for the assessment year 1973-74, which came to be upheld by the Tribunal, deleted the addition. The Tribunal confirmed the order of the Commissioner (Appeals). The department relying upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in State Bank of Travancore v. CIT [1986] 158 ITR 102/ 24 Taxman 337, sought reference which was opposed by the assessee contending that in view of the Circular bearing No. 201/21/84-ITA-II, dated 9-10-1984, interest on doubtful debts cannot be charged to tax and that the view expressed by the Supreme Court in State Bank of Travancore’s case (supra) that the Circular issued by the Board cannot detract from the Act, is a view which is in direct conflict with the earlier view of the Apex Court in Navnit Lal C. Javeri v. K.K. Sen, AAC [1965] 56 ITR 198.

The petitioners sought to challenge the inclusion of landing charges in the assessable value of a consignment of white synthetic waste imported by them, and also countervailing duty charged on the goods. A preliminary objection, however, was raised by the respondents who, relying on two High Court judgments, contended that the petitioners had not availed of the alternative remedy of appeal under the Customs Act and therefore could not invoke the jurisdiction of the High Court under Art. 226 of the Constitution. The petitioners conceded that writ proceedings were not the appropriate remedy for their challenges but also sought to contend that the remedy of appeal would not be appropriate as they had challenged the legality of the bill of entry form prescribed by the CBEC.

Outer carton packing of prepared or preserved food and confectionery, manufactured by the respondents, was held to be includible in the assessable value by the Assistant Collector, who demanded duty even though he had first approved price lists without including the value of the outer carton. The Collector (Appeals), however, held that the cost of outer cartons could not be included in the value since the cartons were used only for the purpose of transport. The respondents argued that the Assistant Collector could not review his own order and demand duty for the past period as he could take a different view only prospectively. They pleaded that since the demand related to the period prior to the Supreme Court judgment laying down that the cost of packing was includible in the assessable value, the benefit of the High Court judgments passed earlier with a contrary view should be given to them. The departmental authorities pointed out that the outer cartons were necessary for the respondents' wholesale sales throughout and were not required only for transport.

Under the provisions of he Customs Act 1962, the assessee was entitled to pay import duty at concessional rates on spare parts and tools if their value did not exceed 10 per cent of the total value of imported machinery, but if the value exceeded this percentage, he was required to pay duty at higher rates. Section 143 of the Customs Act, 1962, also permitted the assessee to execute a bond, agreeing to pay the difference in duty when demanded by the customs authorities. For the assessment years 1973-74 to 1976-77, the assessee had executed such a bond and imported goods on which only provisional assessments at concessional rates of duty had been made by the customs department and the assessee had also paid duty at such conces-sional rates only. However, since the value of the imported goods exceeded the specified percentage, the assessee made provision in its accounts towards additional customs duty payable, and claimed it as a deduction. The ITO disallowed the claim since no demand had been raised by the customs department. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the claim.

On second appeal:

The revenue authorities, while assessing the value of superfine cement manufactured by the appellants, added packing charges to the price on the ground that the assessable value should be inclusive of packing charges. The appellants contended that superfine cement was not different from ordinary grey portland cement for which packing charges were not included in the assessable value and therefore should also be excluded for their goods. They sought adjournment of the case till the Supreme Court clarified the issue of 'durable and returnable packing'.

The appellants imported ZKL Bearings working out the duty liability on the invoice price. The department, however, sought to enhance the same with reference to revised price list as the order for subject goods had been placed after 1.1.1977 and the same supplier had sold similar goods to another importer after the crucial date at the said revised price.

held.text:
PER RUMA PAL, J. - Although a circular is not binding on a Court or an assessee, it is not open to the revenue to raise the contention that is contrary to a binding circular by the Board. When a circular remains in operation, the revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to the terms of the statute. Despite the decision of the Supreme Court, the department cannot be permitted to take a stand contrary to the instructions issued by the Board. A show-cause notice and demand contrary to existing circulars of the Board are ab initio bad. It is not open to the revenue to advance an argument or file an appeal contrary to the circulars. [Para 10]

The provisions of section 151A are in pari materia with the provisions of section 119 of the Income-tax Act and section 37B of the Central Excise Act. The Parliament introduced section 151A by an amendment to the Customs Act in 1995 but with effect from 27-12-1985 (Act 80 of 1995), when the Supreme Court had already construed identical language in the manner indicated. It may be assumed that the Parliament had legislatively approved the construction by using the exact words so construed again in the Customs Act. There is, therefore, no reason why the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court under the two earlier Acts should not also be determinative of the construction put on the later in respect of a materially similar statutory provision. This was also not argued by the appellant (department). [Para 11]

The relevant circular dated 14-8-1991 provides, inter alia, that 'demurrage' and 'despatch' money may not form a part of assessable value. [Para 12]

The circular dated 14-8-1999 in no uncertain terms excludes demurrage from the assessable value. In the light of the judicial principles enunciated earlier, it was not open to the appellant to either issue the show-cause notice or contend otherwise. The demand based on an assessable value inclusive of demurrage could not be sustained as long as the circular remained operative and as long as the decisions on the issue remain good law. [Para 13]

The submission of the appellant that the respondent had not acted on the basis of the circular and, therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel did not apply is misconceived. The circulars issued by the CBDT under the Income-tax Act and the CBEC under section 37B of the Central Excise Act have been held to be binding primarily on the basis of the language of the statutory provisions buttressed by the need of the adjudicating officers to maintain uniformity in the levy of tax/duty throughout the country. [Para 14]

The stand of the appellant that the Supreme Court had taken the view that demurrage was includible in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) both in the adjudication order and before the Tribunal appears to have been abandoned in the written notes of submission. Apart from the decision of the Constitution Bench in Collector of Central Excise v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 143 ELT 19 on the binding nature of the circulars, in Garden Silk Mills Ltd.'s case (supra) the decision was on landing charges. It did not construe the 1988 Rules. The circular on the other hand was issued on a re-examination of the issue in the light of the GATT Valuation principles as incorporated in the 1988 Rules. [Para 17]

Therefore, demurrage was wrongly included by the adjudicating officer in the assessable value contrary to the directive of the CBEC at a time when the circular had not been withdrawn. [Para 18]

PER P. VENKATARAMA REDDI, J. (CONCURRENT VIEW) : The revenue's appeal is liable to be dismissed in the light of the circular dated 14-8-1991 issued by the CBEC which is traceable to the power conferred on the Board by section 151A of the Customs Act. The purpose of this separate opinion is only to highlight certain doubts as to the correctness of the proposition laid down in the two Dhiren Chemical Industries' cases (supra) - one decided by the Constitution Bench and the other by a three Judge Bench. [Para 20]

It is not in dispute that after the two communications of assessee, the assessee did make payment of the differential duty in question in respect of addition to the assessable value of goods on account of transportation, insurance, handling and delivery charges for the clearances made during the period 1-03-1994 to 30-11-1996. The payment was made during the period 6-12-1995 to 22-10-1997. [Para 22]

The language and contents of the letter dated 5-10-1995, as reproduced hereinabove, leave nothing to doubt or guess that the assessee had pleaded, in unequivocal terms, with the department that duty was not payable on the additions made to the assessable value of goods towards transportation, insurance and handling/delivery charges. The contents of the letter dated 5-12-1995 further make it clear that despite the assessee having lodged the protest by the letter dated 5.10.1995, the department had been insisting for making such payment and hence the assessee put on record emphatic denial of the department's propositions; and the statement had been even to the extent that the insistence for such a payment would be unjust and against the principles of justice. [Para 23]

For their subject, contents and tenor, the said two letters dated 5-10-1995 and 5-12-1995 could only be regarded as the letters of protest. The contention urged on behalf of the department is that for being a protest as envisaged by rule 233B, the assessee ought to have followed the procedure prescribed by the rules and in the present case, such a procedure has not been followed. This contention is of no avail for the department. In the first place, this contention remains rather a matter of form than of substance. Secondly, the requirements of rule 233B cannot be construed in a narrow or hyper-technical manner and essentially, what is required is that substantively, there has to be a protest in writing. Thirdly, as shall be seen hereafter, all the requirements of rule 233B cannot even be employed in the fact situation of the present case. Fourthly and in any case, the rule is procedural in nature and cannot control the substantive provision of section 11B(1) of the Act. [Para 24]

Indisputably, no specific form of protest has been provided in the Rules. The simple and ordinary meaning of the expression 'protest' is: 'to express or record dissent or objection'. The dissent, disagreement, and objection of the assessee had been clear, emphatic, unequivocal, and unambiguous in the communications aforesaid. [Para 25]

So far the requirement of following the procedure prescribed by the Rules is concerned, the same has to be construed from the practical stand point and cannot be employed in a hyper technical manner. [Para 27]

The factors required to be taken into consideration in this case are that the payment was made during the period 6-12-1995 to 22-10-1997 whereas it related to the clearances made during the period 01-03-1994 to 30-11-1996. The assessee's letter dated 05-10-1995 was, in fact, a response to the communication dated 09-09-1995, as received from the Superintendent, Central Excise. It appears that the addition was sought to be insisted upon by the department at the later stage and hence came the protest from the assessee on 05.10.1995 which was followed by the communication dated 05-12-1995. When the department still insisted, the assessee made the payment. It is not in dispute that ultimately, the objections of the assessee were sustained. [Para 28]

In the totality of circumstances, it is very difficult to find as to how the requirements of sub-rule (4) of Rule 233B could have been fulfilled in respect of the clearances which had already been made before the department compelled the assessee to make payment of duty i.e., at least for the clearance made between 01-03-1994 to 05-12-1995. In the present case, in respect of these clearances, which had already been made before the department attempted to include the charges towards freight etc. in the assessable value of goods, Sub-rule (4) can only be held inapplicable. As regards the other period, even if it be taken to be a case of lapse on the part of the assessee, looking to the substantive provision of section 11B(1) of the Act and the ratio of the decisions above-referred, for such omission alone, substance of the matter is not lost altogether that the assessee was indeed protesting against the levy in question. [Para 29]

ITC--OGL--Appendix 10 of Policy AM 1982-83--the letter of credit established on 28.2.1983, continued to be valid on the date of shipment--the import is covered by OGL (ratio of Appellate Tribunal decision in Tara Art Printers, New Delhi v. CC, Bombay). ".........on reference to para (7) of Appendix 10 of 1982-83 Import Policy, we find that it was not clearly spelled out that shipment after 31.3.1983 was permissible only in cases where delay in shipment was on account of longer manufacturing schedule. In our view, if the delivery period of the goods was extended beyond 31.3.1983 due to any reason they could be shipped on or before 31.12.1983 provided the contract entered into on or before 28.2.1983 continued to be in force on the date of shipment. In this case in the first instance the shipment was delayed on account of the country of origin having been erroneously shown in the Letter of Credit as West Germany instead of Sweden necessitating the extension of the Letter of Credit up to 30.8.1983. However, the shipment was delayed further since the intimation regarding the extension of the Letter of Credit was not received by the supplier. Thereafter, the Letter of Credit was amended again on 21.10.1983 to extend its validity up to 31.12.1983. Since the goods were shipped before 31.12.1983 against the Letter of Credit which was established on 28.2.1983 and continued to be valid on the date of shipment, we are of the view that they were covered by the OGL in terms of 1982-83 Import Policy."

2. Valuation--Undervaluation--the change is not sustainable as the Collector's decision to enhance the value of the machine on the basis of contemporary import of 1973 model, is ad hoc and arbitrary (ratio of Tribunal decision in Tara Art Printers New Delhi v. CC, Bombay). "We find that on the question of valuation as well there is sufficient force in the appellants contention that the Collector's decision to enhance the assessable value of the imported machine of 1974 make, on the basis of the price of a similar machine of 1973 model was arbitrary. It is seen that the adjudicating authority did not give any indication of the method employed for the computation of the assessable value of the imported second hand machine of 1974 make on the basis of the price of another second-hand machine of 1973 make. Since, in this case there was no evidence of the importers being related to the suppliers or any amount in excess of the invoice price having been remitted by the importers to the suppliers, the invoice price represented the value of the goods which was determinable under clause (a) of section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962. We find that the Tribunal had taken a similar view in the case of M/s. Tara Art Printers, New Delhi v. Collector of Customs, Bombay (supra) in which the adjudicating authority had determined the assessable value of the second hand printing machine of 1975 on the basis of the value of a second hand machine of 1974 model."

letter stating that he was paying the reassessed amount of duty under protest. Having once agreed to the assessment made by the department, the assessee cannot be permitted to challenge the said assessment or the impugned circular on the basis whereof the assessment was made. The fact that the assessee had initially agreed with the department's assessment has been concealed by the assessee which amounts to suppression of material facts. The assessee has not approached the court with clean hands and does not deserve any relief. In court's opinion, non-mentioning of any and every fact does not amount to suppression of material facts. A material fact is one that would have a bearing on the decision of the court. Even if the assessee mentioned in the writ petition about the factum of he having initially agreed with the department's assessment, decision would not have been any different. This is so because there can be no estoppel against the statute. Section 11A of the Customs Tariff Act does not countenance amendment of the First Schedule to the said Act by issuance of a mere departmental circular. The method in which the First Schedule has been sought to be amended is contrary to the method prescribed by section 11A and as such the circular cannot be sustained. Hence, the fact that the assessee initially agreed with the department's assessment is not a material fact and accordingly the department's point is rejected. [Para 34]

The second point urged by the department is that the assessee has not challenged the show cause-cum-demand notice dated 21-4-2014. In court's view, this is a point without any substance. The said show cause notice is admittedly based on the impugned circular. If the circular is quashed, the show cause notice automatically goes. [Para 35]

In view of what has been discussed above, the impugned circular is bad in law being without jurisdiction and cannot be sustained. The Circular No. 19/2013-CUS., dated 9-5-2013 is quashed and set aside. [Para 36]

Alternative remedy--Merits of the case are being considered by the Court even though the matter is sub-judice before the Tribunal because multiplicity of proceedings will result in harassment to the petitioner. "Ordinarily, we would not have discussed the merits of the case since the point under issue in the present matter which has been decided in favour of the petitioner by the Collector (Appeals), is still sub-judice before the Tribunal and we would have waited for the decision of the Tribunal but looking to the fact that the Department is not satisfied by the order of the Collector (Appeals) and instead of pursuing the matter before the Tribunal, has been issuing notices and the Assistant Collector has even passed assessment orders involving the same question and taking a contrary view than that of the Collector (Appeals) and the Department did not even wait but proceeded to pass the assessment order without waiting for the decision of the Tribunal in spite of repeated requests made by the petitioner, particularly when the High Court had stayed the assessment order in these writ petitions but in the later year, the petitioners could not obtain a stay order, though writ petition had been filed, because of the strike of the lawyers. The petitioner has to file writ petition every now and then. The Tribunal is not a party before us and the matter may not be decided finally by the Tribunal for a number of years. The Department will go on issuing notices and passing the assessment orders which will necessitate filing of appeals or coming to this Court which will be nothing but multiplicity of proceedings and undue harassment to the petitioner. Therefore, in these particular facts and circumstances, we are inclined to consider the merits of the case as well."

Valuation--cost of transportation, depot service charges and unloading, charges have to be excluded as the ex-factory price is ascertainable and these costs have nothing to do with the manufacture of goods (ratio of Supreme Court decisions). "......there is a clear finding that there was an ex-factory price which is ascertainable. ......When the factory price is ascertainable, the excise duty has to be levied on that price. If the assessee transported the goods from its factory to the Depot, cost of transportation has to be excluded, as has been held in Bombay Tyres' case and in Indian Oxygen Ltd.'s case. ....The depot service charges and unloading charges have nothing to do with the manufacture and therefore, that amount is not to be included to ascertain the assessable value for the purpose of payment of central excise duty".
