Limitation--Transportation charges collected through separate bills were not declared in the price lists. There was therefore, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Longer time limit is therefore available to the Department "As regards the limitation it is admitted by the appellants, as already set out above, that they were collecting charges through separate bills and therefore, there was no declaration of these charges in the price list because the prices declared were ex-works. Apparently, therefore, there was a wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts calling for invoking a larger period of 5 years for demanding the differential duty. The show cause notice was, therefore, well within the time. As regards the point.....that the law regarding includibility of loading charges within the factory was clarified only in the year 1988 by the Supreme Court in the Indian Oxygen case it maybe mentioned that the appellants have not taken this plea in their appeal memo or in the course of arguments by the learned advocate. Such a plea in my view is too vague a plea for the purpose of determining the question of limitation of the show cause notice unless the appellants came positively with definite judgments of the legal position which prevented them from showing such charges in the price list..... I direct the Assistant Collector to redetermine the differential duty after the appellants herein have furnished the break-up of the so-called delivery charges incurred towards the loading etc of the goods within the factory of the appellants which alone would be includible the assessable value of the goods. --I observe that admittedly the charges in question were not declared in the price list Furthermore, undisputably the law relating to the determination of the assessable value in the central excise cases required filing of the price list and supplying the relevant information to enable the officers to Judge the correctness of the declaration and assess the value according to law. Hence irrespective of the appellants' own views complete information was required to be supplied to the Department voluntarily--(whether as apart of the price list or a remark or as an enclosure or covering memo). The Department was also required to be vigilant and expected to call for full particulars at the earliest. However, non-supply of the information normally required for assessment amounted to suppression of relevant facts Hence the extended period was available to the Department and the show cause notice was not time barred Once this was the position, the Assistant Collector was required to re-determine the differential duty after the appellants furnished the required break-up. Hence I agree with the learned Technical Member that the matter was required to be remanded for re-determining the correct duty liability."

Replacement import - Marine Insurance Policy in this case covered replacement the warehouse of the importer. The mere fact that the goods have reached Ludhiana town is not enough to conclude that the transit has come to an end. As long as the goods are not cleared by the customs authority and are stored in the customs warehouse, it is futile to suggest that the transit has come to an end and the goods have been received by the importers. Once the erroneous assumption of the Additional Collector on this count is found to be unsustainable, then the submission........that the replacement import is covered by the relevant policy deserves acceptance."

It is well settled that officers working under the Board are bound by the circulars issued by the Board, and that if a particular circular which is beneficial to the interests of the assessee and has been in force throughout the assessment year under consideration and is withdrawn only after the end of the assessment year, the assessee is entitled to have the assessment made and completed only in accordance with the instruction. In this case, the said Circular directing the ITOs to add back the net amount only was in force in the assessment year 1974-75 and was withdrawn only after the expiry of that year. Consequently, the view taken by the ITO and the AAC was not correct.

Earlier in the course of hearing of the appeal the assessee was directed to explain the entries of customs duty payment in the profit and loss account and balance-sheet. In response to the same, the assessee filed a supplemen-tary paper-book on 21-2-2007 explaining the entries made regarding the closing stock to show that the customs duty had been included therein, and had also explained in details as to how the provisions of section 145A introduced with effect from 1-4-1999 would have no effect in view of the overriding provisions of section 43B. These submissions had been briefly adverted to in the order of the Tribunal. One of the paragraph of the order of the Tribunal showed that the contention of the assessee that since inception, that is, from the assessment year 1994-95 till the assessment year 2006-07 the assessee had been following the inclusive method of accounting for customs duty payment while valuing the stock and that was accepted by the Tribunal. Further, the Tribunal had even stated in this paragraph that this claim of the assessee was not contradicted even in the assessment order. In the same paragraph, the Tribunal had also made an observation that in the year under appeal, the customs duty formed part of the closing stock, though the duty was not debited to the profit and loss account and had also referred to the fact that the duty was separately claimed as deduction in the return of income. In one other paragraph, the Tribunal had accepted the assessee's claim in principle and had observed that it was supported by the Special Bench's order of the Tribunal in Indian Communication Network (P.) Ltd. v. IAC [1994] 49 ITD 56 (Delhi), which was approved by the Supreme Court in Berger Paints India Ltd. v. CIT [2004] 266 ITR 99/ 135 Taxman 586. However, the observations made in the said paragraph showed that the Tribunal had considered that the customs duty was not included in the valuation of the closing stock. This observation was at variance with and contradictory to its earlier finding to the effect that the duty had been included in the closing stock as per the consistent accounting practice adopted by the assessee which was accepted in the assessment. It was only in view of the latter contradictory finding that the Tribunal thought it necessary to restore the matter to the Assessing Officer with the direction to examine the applicability of section 145A to the assessee's case. Even if it was assumed for the sake of argument that the case would have had to be restored to the Assessing Officer to be processed with reference to section 145 A notwithstanding the earlier finding of the Tribunal that the customs duty was included in the valuation of the closing stock, the fact that the assessee's argument was based on the order of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra) was not considered by the Tribunal showed that there was a mistake apparent from the record in light of decision of Supreme Court in Honda Siel Power Products Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 165 Taxman 307. [Para 8]

In Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra), it was held that section 43B has overriding effect over section 145A. This decision was referred to by the Tribunal in its order while summarizing the contentions of the department but unfortu-nately it omitted to deal with this decision and considered its applicability while taking a decision to remit the matter to the Assessing Officer with a direction to examine the applicability of section 145A. This omission had caused prejudice to the assessee in the sense that it had given rise to further proceedings before the Assessing Officer involving further delay in finalising the assessment proceedings, when the legal position already stood con-cluded by the binding order of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra). The other mistake committed by the Tribunal to the prejudice of the assessee was its omission to refer to the assessee's plea that in the subsequent years, the Assessing Officer had accepted the assessee's claim under section 43B and assessments had been completed accordingly. [Para 8]

"...the appellants have purchased the plant and machinery on as-is-where-is condition and the appellants have agreed to take upon themselves the cost of dismantling and removal of the equipment. The goods will not become ready for shipment without such dismantling, packing and forwarding. Therefore, they have to be considered as an element of value of the goods for the purposes of section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962. ...it is reasonable to conclude that the services performed by the contractors on behalf of the appellants flows out of the terms of the agreement by which the appellant's had taken upon themselves to incur these charges and that, but for the appellants undertaking to do so, the element of these charges would have gone into the price of the plant and equipment so as to make such an equipment ready for delivery at the port of shipment. In such a view of the matter, therefore, we hold that the Collector was right in including these expenses in the assessable value for finalising the imports made for the Project under the contract registered with the Custom House."

The Assessing Officer noted that the difference of the FMV as determined by the DVO and the amount paid by the assessee was Rs. 15.14 lakhs (Rs. 1.72 crores - Rs. 1.57 crores) and the said difference between the actual consideration and FMV as determined by the DVO was less than 10 per cent. The Assessing Officer thereafter, considering the amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 in line with pronouncements of various Courts and Tribunals, which held that when the margin between the actual consideration and the value ascertained by Departmental valuer was less than 10 per cent, noted that the said difference is liable to be ignored, for the purpose of Assessment. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer accepted the total income as declared by the assessee. [Para 9]

■

The Principal Commissioner did not accept the above finding of the Assessing Officer and held that the Circular No. 8/2018 of CBDT regarding rationalization of section 43CA, section 50C and section-56, clearly mentions that the amendments will take effect from 1-4-2019 and will accordingly apply in relation to assessment year 2019-20 and subsequent years and held that the difference between the stamp duty value and sale consideration should have been added in the income of the assessee, as per the provisions applicable for the year under consideration. [Para 9.2]

■

However, the Principal Commissioner did not comment or give any contrary decision to the case laws relied by the assessee in reply to the show-cause issued to the assessee that the circular no. 8/2018 was to operate retrospectively which was considered by the Assessing Officer in accepting the total income declared by the assessee relying upon the said decisions. It is noted that the assessee has relied upon the orders of the Co-ordinate Bench of Mumbai in the case of Maria Fernandes Cheryl v. ITO, (International Taxation), 2(3)(1), Mumbai [2021] 123 taxmann.com 252/187 ITD 738/85 ITR(T) 674 (Mumbai - Trib.) for assessment year 2011-12 and of the Kolkata Tribunal in the case of Chandra Prakash Jhunjhunwala v. Dy. CIT [2020] 113 taxmann.com 246/181 ITD 185 (Kolkata - Trib.), which have held that the amendment to section 50C brought into the Act by Finance Act, 2018 with effect from 1-4-2019 was to apply retrospectively with effect from 1-4-2003, when the section 50C was brought into statute. The section 56(2)(vii) being pari-materia to section 50C, and the said Circular No. 8/2018 also amending the provisions of section 56, will be applicable to the case of the assessee also and will accordingly the benefit of the said amendment will apply retrospectively in the case of the assessee also and the difference of Rs. 15.14 lakhs between the actual consideration paid and the FMV being less than 10 per cent will have to be ignored for applying the provisions of section 56(2)(vii) in the case of the assessee. Therefore, in the given facts of the case, the view of the Commissioner is not supported by any judicial authority and therefore his action in holding the assessment order passed in this case to be erroneous as well as prejudicial to the interest of the revenue is merely a change of opinion and the same is not sustainable and the same is quashed. [Para 9.3]

As the assessment of the goods had been made only on a provisional basis, with the consent of the appellants, the demands as per the show cause notices are not time-barred. The limitation applies only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessment "......the assessments had been made provisionally under Rule 9B of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 at their own request and on the strength of the provisional duty bond executed by them.......As per Rule 9B, the assessments made on provisional basis have to be finalised eventually and adjustments of duty made. Under Section 11A of the Act, the limitation starts running only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessments. The demands issued as per the show cause notices on 6.11.1984, 10.12.1984 and 43.1985 were, therefore, not time barred, even if the normal time limit of six months were to be applied."

2. In not granting the appellants their request for a personal hearing wherein they wanted to make further submissions regarding certain points, the department has violated the principles of natural justice. "The appellants........argued their case in part and asked for certain clarifications. They expressed their desire to make further submissions on receipt.......The Collector did not grant this further hearing and he proceeded to decide the matter. There has, therefore, been a denial of full opportunity of personal hearing."

3. SPECIAL PACKING: The criterion to judge special packing is, whether it is essential for delivery of the goods in wholesale at the factory gate. As far as glass sheets are concerned, ordinary packing is quite adequate for wholesale deliveries, therefore following the principle of essentiality, the cost of special packing is, in principle, excludable in the instant case. "......the appellants did clear some consignments for delivery at Calcutta in ordinary packing. The number of such consignments may be small but yet they do establish the principle that the goods could be delivered in whole-sale at the factory gate in ordinary packing.........Such ordinary packing is quite adequate for wholesale deliveries at the factory gate and at the market situated very close to the factory.......Following the principle of essentiality as laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, we hold that the cost of special packing was, in principle, excludible in the case of the present appellants also."

4. As jam-packing is not required for the deliveries of glass sheets at the factory gate, laffa charges incurred for jam-packing are excludible. " 'Laffa' charges incurred for jam-packing of the railway wagonsllorries are incurred obviously in those cases only where the goods have to be delivered to a sufficiently long distance. No jam-packing would be required for deliveries at the factory gate. Laffa charges are, therefore, excludible in principle."

5. Loading charges incurred by the appellants beyond the factory gate and the cost of transport, including the cost of transit insurance for the goods are not includible in the assessable value. "Loading charges incurred within the factory gate have to be included in the assessable value. But further loading and un-loading charges, if any, incurred by the appellants for giving delivery of the goods beyond the factory gate, are, in principle, not includible......the cost of transport, including the cost of transit insurance for the goods, is not to be included in the assessable value."

6. The nature of 'miscellaneous charges' is not clear, but if such service is performed in relation to the goods after their removal from the factory gate, such costs are not includible. "The nature of 'miscellaneous charges',........is not clear. However, if such charges were incurred for some service performed in relation to the goods after their removal from the factory gate, such cost would not, in principle, be includible. But if such charges were essential even for giving delivery of the goods at the factory gate, they have to be included."

1. Assessable Value--Assessable value of an imported car is world-car-catalogue Price less 15% failing which manufacturer's Net price to whole-sale dealer's failing both invoice price. "We order that the same basis should be followed in the case of the present appellant also and his car re-assessed on the basis of the World Car Catalogue Price of the same model less 15% discount. ......In case the World Car Catalogue Price is not available with the Customs House, the Customs may ascertain the manufacturer's net price to wholesale dealers in the course of international trade in any other manner. If this course is also not feasible, the assessment may be maintained at the appellant's invoice price. There is no question of granting the 15% discount on the individual export passenger's invoice price.''

2. Assessable Value--Ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges are part of delivery price at the place of importation, hence form a part of assessable value. "Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 requires that valuation should be done on the basis of the price for delivery of the goods at the place of importation. The imported goods have to be valued according to this provision. Seeking analogy of a different enactment which deals with locally manufactured goods is a totally mis-conceived exercise. No imported goods can be delivered at the port of importation in India without incurring the ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges. These charges have, therefore, been correctly added to the basic price of the car."

3, Assessable Value--No depreciation admissible if the car has not been used abroad. "Depreciation is given if the car is possessed and used abroad. Here, the appellant purchased a brand new car and loaded it for shipment to India. He did not use the car abroad. No depreciation as asked for is permissible."

4. Additional duty--Additional duty is also customs duty and not excise duty. "Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 separately specifies the rates for basic customs duty and additional customs duty both of which are to be charged on the imported goods. The additional customs duty is also very much a duty of customs. Just because its rate generally happens to be equivalent to the excise duty chargeable on the like goods manufactured in India, it does not cease to be a customs duty."

5. Air-conditioner fitted in a car, not being an essential components, is separately assessable even if invoice shows composite price for the car and the Air-Conditioner. "An Air-Conditioner is not an essential component of the car. It is not even a standard part of the car. It is an optional accessory and is supplied to only those purchasers of cars who asked for it. The department has, therefore, correctly assessed the Air-Conditioner separately under Head 84.12 of the Tariff."

Valuation: Assessable value for levy of customs duty is to be based on the declared invoiced prices unless proved otherwise by the department. "The onus of proving misdeclaration regarding the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry is on the Department and this can be discharged by the Department only on proving of proper facts, which would discredit the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry and not on the basis of mere suspicion. It is, therefore, on this ground alone that the orders of the lower authorities merit to be set aside."

2. Show Cause notice to the parties for change in invoice prices is necessary otherwise the decision to enhance the valuation can be set aside on this ground also. "What amazes us, is that the show cause notice in this case alleges that the correct price of the imported bearings is Rs. 9.25 per piece whereas the order of the Additional Collector is based on the correct price being Rs. 18.40 per piece. The learned JDR has conceded that the order was passed without furnishing the additional evidence to the appellant and without giving any opportunity to show cause in respect of it. This further seriously undermines the legality of the order."

3. Dissenting view: Per Shri I.J. Rao: Case to be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication. "However, I feel that the omission on the part of the Collector should be allowed to be made good. While I agree that the order should be set aside, I hold that the matter should be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication after disclosing to the appellants the relevant evidence relied on by the department and after giving a reasonable opportunity to them to counter the evidence."

Swatanter Kumar, J. :

The assessee has contended that as the similar claims had been decided in favour of the banks for the assessment years 1991-92 to 1993-94 by Special Bench of the Tribunal, which had not been challenged by the department, the issue had attained finality and could not be disturbed in the subsequent years. [Para 12]

The above contention of the assessee-bank is not impressive. Merely because the orders of the Special Bench of the Tribunal were not assailed in appeal by the department itself, this would not take away the right of the revenue to question the correctness of the orders of assessment, particularly when a question of law is involved. There is no doubt that the earlier order of the Commissioner (Appeals) had merged into the judgment of the Special Bench of the Tribunal and attained finality for that relevant year. Equally, it is true that though the Full Bench of the Kerala High Court specifically overruled the Division Bench judgment of that very Court in the case of South Indian Bank Ltd. (supra ), it did not notice any of the contentions before and principles stated by the Special Bench of the Tribunal in its impugned judgment.

The questions raised in the instant appeal go to the very root of the matter and are questions of law in relation to interpretation of sections 36(1)(vii ) and 36(1)(viia) read with section 36(2). Thus, the findings recorded in the earlier assessment years 1991-92 to 1993-94 would not be binding on the department for subsequent years as well. [Para 13]

Sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) provide for such deductions, which are to be permitted, in accordance with the language of these provisions. A bare reading of these provisions show that sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) are separate items of deduction. These are independent provisions and, therefore, cannot be intermingled or read into each other. It is a settled canon of interpretation of fiscal statutes that they need to be construed strictly and on their plain reading. [Para 16]

The provisions of section 36(1)(vii ) would come into play in the grant of deductions, subject to the limitation contained in section 36(2). Any bad debt or part thereof, which is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts of the assessee for the previous year, is the deduction which the assessee would be entitled to get, provided he satisfies the requirements of section 36(2). Allowing of deduction of bad debts is controlled by the provisions of section 36(2). The argument advanced by the revenue is that it would amount to allowing a double deduction if the provisions of sections 36(1)(vii ) and 36(1)(viia) are permitted to operate independently. There is no doubt that a statute is normally not construed to provide for a double benefit unless it is specifically so stipulated or is clear from the scheme of the Act. As far as the question of double benefit is concerned, the legislature in its wisdom introduced section 36(2)(v ) by the Finance Act, 1985 with effect from 01.04.1985. Section 36(2)(v) concerns itself as a check for claim of any double deduction and has to be read in conjunction with section 36(1)(viia ). It requires the assessee to debit the amount of such debt or part thereof in the previous year to the provision made for that purpose. [Para 17]

Circulars can be issued by the Board to explain or tone down the rigours of law and to ensure fair enforcement of its provisions. These circulars have the force of law and are binding on the income tax authorities, though they cannot be enforced adversely against the assessee. Normally, these circulars cannot be ignored. A circular may not override or detract from the provisions of the Act but it can seek to mitigate the rigour of a particular provision for the benefit of the assessee in certain specified circumstances. So long as the circular is in force, it aids the uniform and proper administration and application of the provisions of the Act. [Para 18]

The assessee submits that if the demand is held sustainable it should be given the benefit of cum-duty-price, considering the subsidy received as inclusive of the excise duty payable. Therefore, such provision is only directory. [Para 43]

Basis on which Circular was issued was arbitrary - Condition of recovery pending stay application read down - Recovery only if delay in disposition is due to fault of assessee : The Circular was purportedly issued in terms of judgment in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The said judgment lays down that mere filing of an appeal does not operate as stay or suspension of the order appealed against. But the Board over-looked the fact that the assessee is not seeking stay only on account of filing of an appeal, but for the reason that the assessee has sought dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied and has a right to demand decision on such application, the right which is created by the statute. Therefore, the very basis of the Circular is untenable, misconceived, wholly illegal and arbitrary. Therefore, the condition of recovery, if no stay is granted within 30 days, is illegal, arbitrary, unjustified and consequently set aside. [Para 44]

Right of consideration in appeal and on an application for waiver of pre-deposit, is a right conferred by the statute and such right cannot be defeated on the basis of Circular, which contemplates that the recovery can be effected, is stay is not granted within 30 days. Therefore, such condition in the Circular is not legal and is therefore set aside with the observation that till such time, the application for waiver of pre-deposit is decided in an appeal filed in terms of the statute, the revenue shall not proceed to recover the same provided that the assessee does not delay the hearing of the appeal directly or indirectly. In the event, the assessee is delaying the decision, the revenue shall be at liberty to move an application before the Commissioner (Appeals) to take the application for waiver of pre-deposit and seek orders thereon in accordance with law. If such an application is filed by the revenue, the Commissioner (Appeals) shall decide the same expeditiously. [Para 46]

Thus, direction to recover the duty demanded and penalty levied, if the stay was not granted within 30 days, contravenes the right of consideration of appeal and of an application for waiver of pre-deposit conferred under section 35F of the Act and is illegal. Such direction to the Administrative Officers to recover the amount pending consideration of application of waiver of pre-deposit is not justified and, thus, not enforceable in law. [Para 47]

Time-limit of 180 days in stay matters before Tribunal is not mandatory - Vacation of stay will take place only if Revenue claims before Tribunal that delay was attributable to assessee :

As per second proviso to section 35C(2A), if an order of stay is made in any proceedings relating to an appeal filed under sub-section (1) of section 35B, the Appellate Tribunal shall dispose of the appeal within a period of 180 days from the date of such order. The further proviso is if an appeal is not disposed of within the period specified in the first proviso, the stay order shall, on the expiry of that period, stand vacated. [Para 48]

Though the right of appeal is a creation of statute and it can be exercised only subject to the conditions specified therein, but the conditions specified have to be in relation to the assessee as something which is required to be complied with by the assessee. But where the assessee has no control over the functioning of the Tribunal, then the provision of vacation of stay cannot be sustained. [Para 51]

The assessee having preferred appeal and that Tribunal being satisfied that condition for dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied is made out, is compelled to pay the duty demanded and penalty levied, if the appeal is not decided within 180 days. The assessee has no control in respect of matters pending before the Tribunal; in the matter of availability of infrastructure; the members of the Tribunal and the workload. Therefore, for the reason that the Tribunal is not able to decide appeal within 180 days, the vacation of stay is a harsh and onerous and unreasonable condition. The condition of vacation of stay for the inability of the Tribunal to decide the appeal is burdening the assessee for no fault of his. Such a condition is onerous and renders the right of appeal as illusory. An order passed by a judicial forum is sought to be annulled for no fault of assessee. [Para 52]

Therefore, such condition of automatic vacation of stay on the expiry of 180 days, has to be read down to mean that after 180 days the revenue has a right to bring to the notice of the Tribunal the conduct of the assessee in delay or avoiding the decision of appeal, so as to warrant an order of vacation of stay. If the provision is not read down in the manner mentioned above, such condition suffers from illegality rendering the right of appeal as redundant. [Para 52]

It is not in dispute that originally the goods in question, being Dialysers were classified under CTH 90189031. The impugned circular has sought to change such classification by bringing Dialysers under CTH 84212900. [Para 26]

Chapter 90 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'optical, photographic, cinematographic, measuring, checking, precision, medical or surgical instruments and apparatus; parts and accessories thereof.' Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to 'instruments and appliances used in medical, surgical, dental or veterinary sciences including scientigraphic apparatus, other electro-medical apparatus and sight-testing instruments. CTH 90189031 specifically pertains to renal dialysis equipment (artificial kidneys, kidney machines and dialysers). [Para 27]

Chapter 84 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'nuclear reactors, boilers, machinery and medical appliances; parts thereof.' Heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to 'centrifuges, including centrifugal dryers; filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus, for liquids or gases.' CTH 84212900 talks of 'filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus for gases.' [Para 28]

Thus, CTH 90189031 specifically provides for dialysers whereas CTH 84212900 provides for generic description of articles. Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to medical instruments whereas heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to goods which are generally used for industrial purposes and do not appear to have any medical use. Hence, the natural classification of dialysers should be under CTH 90189031 as it was prior to issuance of the impugned circular. When a specific tariff heading for classification is available, the goods concerned cannot be classified under a generic tariff heading. A heading with a more specific description of the goods in question shall be preferred to and prevail over a heading with a more general description. Just as a special law in a particular field would prevail over a general law that may be operational in that field, a heading with a more specific description would prevail over a heading with a more general description. In this connection, rule 3(a) of the General Rules for interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act makes it very clear that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description.

If the department intends to classify the goods in question under a heading which is different from the heading under which an assessee classifies such goods, the burden of proof is on the department which has to be discharged by adducing proper evidence. In the instant case, the onus was on the department to justify the change of classification sought to be made by the impugned circular, which onus has not been discharged by the department. Thus, it is evident that the impugned circular is blatantly contrary to the said rule and is thus, not sustainable. [Para 29]

Section 11A of the Customs Tariff Act empowers the Central Government to amend the First Schedule to the said Act. Such amendment may be carried out by notification in the Official Gazette and such notification must be placed before both the Houses of the Parliament for their approval. It is trite law that where a statute empowers an authority to do a certain thing in a certain way that thing must be done only in that way or not at all. All other methods of exercising such power are forbidden. [Para 30]

In the present case, the department sought to amend the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act by issuing the impugned circular. This falls foul of section 11A of the said Act and on this ground also the impugned circular must be set aside. [Para 31]

A circular cannot take away the effect of a notification statutorily issued. [Para 32]

The impugned circular at best contains executive instructions. It is not issued under any statute and has no force of law. It cannot override the statute. Any notice, circular, guidelines etc. which are contrary to statutory laws cannot be enforced. [Para 33]

The department claims that on 6-4-2015 the assessee agreed with the decision of the department and recorded so in writing. It was only two days later, i.e., on 8-4-2015 that the assessee wrote a letter stating that he was paying the reassessed amount of duty under protest. Having once agreed to the assessment made by the department, the assessee cannot be permitted to challenge the said assessment or the impugned circular on the basis whereof the assessment was made. The fact that the assessee had initially agreed with the department's assessment has been concealed by the assessee which amounts to suppression of material facts. The assessee has not approached the court with clean hands and does not deserve any relief.

Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 has to be consistent with the provisions of Section 14(1) of Customs Act, 1962, it has to be held that the Additional Collector was justified in holding that the declared value in respect of the imported goods, being widely at variance with the international price of the goods prevailing at or about the same time when the goods being valued were imported, did not represent the transaction value under Rule 4." 4. Valuation--The adjudicating authority was not right in determining the value of the goods under Rule 8, bypassing Rules 5, 6 and 7, without recording reasons therefor. In terms of Rule 3, the provisions of Customs (Determination of the Price of Imported Goods) Rules have to be applied sequentially. The Addl. Collector's order is not a speaking order and shows non-application of mind. The matter is remanded for reconsideration and disposal within two months. ".......after having held that the declared value or the price paid for the goods could not be deemed as the Transaction Value' the adjudicating authority observed that the value of the imported goods is also not determinable under Rules 5, 6 and 7. Thereafter, he proceeded to determine the value under Rule 8. It is seen that in terms of Rule 3, the provisions of the Customs (Determination of the Price of Imported Goods) Rules 1988 have to be applied sequentially. Hence, the Additional Collector ought to have recorded the reasons for holding that the assessable value of the goods was not determinable in terms of each of the Rules 5, 6 and 7. We find that even while determining the value under Rule 8, the adjudicating authority has not taken into account the fact that the quantity imported by the appellants was larger than quantity covered by the invoices relied upon by the department. For these reasons, we are of the view that the order passed by the Additional Collector in as far as it relates to the valuation of the imported goods is not a speaking order and shows non-application of mind. We are, therefore, of the view that this matter needs to be remanded for reconsideration."

5. Valuation--The assessable value of the goods has to be determined taking into account the actual weight of the goods, as they have been charged by the supplier on weight basis. "........we are not inclined to accept the appellants' contention that the higher weight found of the consignment does not warrant the enhancement of the value since the excess weight could be due to the variation in the thickness of the material. Since the goods have been charged by the supplier on weight basis, their assessable value has necessarily to be determined by taking into account the actual weight of the goods. Hence, we reject the appellants' plea that the assessable value of the goods would continue to be the Transaction value' even when the quantity of goods with reference to weight has been found to be in excess of the invoiced quantity."

6. Penalty--The Addl. Collector has not given a reasoned finding after applying his mind to the question whether the weight of the goods declared by the appellants was an innocent misdeclaration. The question whether the appellants are liable for penalty shall be decided by the Addl. Collector in the de novo proceedings. "........while deciding whether the appellants were liable to penalty, the Additional Collector should have given a reasoned finding after applying his mind to the question whether the weight of the goods declared by the appellants was an innocent misdeclaration on the basis of the shipping documents received by them."

There is no merit in the submission that petitioners should have filed separate petition for each consignment imported by them as it would result in multiplicity of litigation. "The objection is that the petitioners have imported various consignments by different ships and in respect of those diverse consignments separate petition should have been filed. It is difficult to find any merit in the submission, save and except that the respondents desire that there should be multiplicity of litigation. It is difficult to appreciate who would be benefited by filing separate petitions when the relief claimed is identical and it is the petitioners atone who have imported all these consignments."

2. The objection that invoices filed by the petitioners are vague is misconceived. "The second objection raised by Shri Vyas is that the invoices filed by the petitioners arc not very clear but are vague as though the quantity, unit price and amount is set out, other details are not furnished.....In my judgment, the objection raised on behalf of the respondents is totally misconceived."

3. Petitioners allowed clearance on provisional assessment on the basis of invoice value by furnishing a personal bond only. The Department is free to continue departmental adjudication proceedings. "The respondents to allow clearance of the goods covered by bills of entry.......on provisional assessment on the basis of invoice value.........and furnishing only a personal bond without bank guarantee for the difference of amount of duty as claimed by the respondents. This order pertains to valuation dispute only. The respondents will be at liberty to continue any departmental adjudication proceedings and pass order."

Section 122 read with section 124 of the Customs Act 1962 does not provide for giving an opportunity to the Department in adjudication proceedings for confiscations and penalties. 'Taking up the first contention of the appellants that they were not given opportunity to explain, and therefore, the order is ab initio void, we are of the view that the contention is opposed to the scheme of the act. Section 122 read with Section 124 of the Customs Act does not provide for giving an opportunity to the deptt. in adjudication proceedings. The order relied upon by Shri Sunder Rajan reported in CC Bombay v. Walker Anjaria & Sons (P) Ltd. is not relevant to the facts of the instant case."

2. The charge of under invoicing has to be supported by an evidence of right kind of goods. A quotation at a higher rate would not by itself show under invoicing of the goods ought to be imported. "It is also equally settled that the burden of proving the charge of undervaluation lies squarely on the deptt. The charge of under-invoicing has to be supported by an evidence of right kind of goods........A quotation at a higher rate would not by itself show under-invoicing of the goods sought to be imported. For many reasons quotation may disclose higher rate. It is only after the quotations are accepted and contract is concluded and actual sale takes place, the price may then indicate whether there is a case of under-invoicing Ghanshyam Chejra v. CC......Therefore, these instances of quotation relied on by the appellants would not lead to the inference of under-invoicing in the absence of evidence, that these quotations resulted in concluded contract and goods were actually imported in pursuance of the same. The appellants failed to adduce any evidence to prove that in pursuance of these quotations the parties have actually concluded the contract and the goods were actually imported. Therefore, we reject these quotations as leading to the inference of under-invoicing of the imported goods."

3. In the absence of evidence of remitting more than what is indicated in the invoice or of contemporary sales of higher price or that the sellers and buyers are interested in the business of each other, the invoice price cannot be discarded. "In our view in the absence of evidence that the respondents remitted to the foreign supplier more than what is indicated in the invoices, or that there are contemporaneous sale at higher price or that the sellers and buyers are interested in the business of each other, the nature of the Import Policy cannot be treated to be an extra commercial consideration to discard the invoice price."

4. Appellants cannot be permitted to set up a new case at the appeal stage. "The show cause notice proposes to enhance the prices on the basis of 1983 price list. The relevant portion of the show cause notice reads as follows:

'On the basis of foregoing facts it appears that the value of the goods as declared in the invoice is not acceptable under Section 14(1)(a) of the Customs Act 1962. The value of the goods has arrived under Rule of Customs Valuation Rules 1963 read with Section 14(1)(b) of the Customs Act 1962 as shown in Annexure 'A' the prices for the purpose of valuation under Section 14(1)(b) are taken as per 1983 price list for Hungary bearings.' Whereas in the appeal the proposal is to enhance the value of the imported goods, on the basis of 1981 price list. The relevant portion of the appeal reads as follows:

The assessable value of the goods should have been determined on the basis of the manufacturer's 1981 price list.'

In our opinion the appellants cannot be permitted to set up a new case at the appeal stage. Therefore, we accept the finding of the Collector that the invoice price should be accepted in respect of the imports from Hungary."

Invoice value to be taken as the C.I.F. value for calculating duty since that was the original price quoted by the manufacturer, and the price at which the machines were finally bought by the petitioners. "In my view, therefore, the department was wholly wrong in rejecting the invoice value of these two machines imported by the petitioner and, therefore, there is no justification for demanding any additional duty on the basis of the value as suggested by the department."

2. Invoice price being the actual price of the imported items, there is no violation of the provisions of Import and Export (Control) Act, 1947 or of the Import (Control) Order No. 17, as claimed by the Department, and additional customs duty and fines are therefore not maintainable, (ratio of earlier judgment). "In fact the department's attention was drawn to a case of this High Court in the Union of India and Ors. vs. Glaxo Laboratories (India) Ltd., reported in 1984 (17) E.L.T. 284 (Bombay) in which it is expressly stated that the department ought to have taken the actual price as shown in the invoice and they could not have taken into account the import value for the purpose of debiting the licence. However, the department would not follow the said judgment. In my view, the department's action in this behalf is expressly contrary to the law as laid down by this Court in the said judgment. Therefore, on that count also the department has clearly defaulted."

Valuation--Price of the goods imported is not what is stated in the invoice and consequently in the Bill of Entry. "........on a consideration of the entire evidence and the arguments submitted from both sides, we are inclined to agree with the department that the prices of the goods imported is not what is stated in the invoice and consequently in the bill of entry. The correspondence with the trade representative relied upon by the learned advocate, as rightly pointed out by the learned DR, is all subsequent to the importation of the goods."

2. These prices are not available to other importers in India for the said goods. The price has been influenced by consideration other than sale in the present case.

"These prices are not to be divulged to any other party in India. The inference is clear that these prices are not available for other importers in India for the said goods. It is, therefore, clear that the price of the goods in the instant case has been strongly influenced by consideration other than that of sale in the present case. It is for the purpose of promoting future sales in the country that specially reduced price has been given by the suppliers to the appellants. In the light of 20th January 1987 letter, Agent's letter dated 11.8.1986 stating that the suppliers reserved to themselves the right to negotiate the price on case to case basis loses its significance. That right, obviously has been exercised for considerations other than that of sale of the instant goods. That being so, the price is not acceptable under Section 14 of the Customs Act."

3. No merit in the plea of appellants. Value has been rightly arrived at on the basis of price list. "We are of the view that having regard to the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances referred to above, the value of the goods has been rightly arrived at on the basis of price list available in this case. It is significant to note that the appellants have nowhere disputed the authenticity or genuineness of the price list. In these circumstances we do not find any merit in the pleas of the appellants so far as the valuation of the goods is concerned."

4. Clearance under OGL--The goods are covered by OGL, hence the order of confiscation under Sec. 111(d) Cus. Act. is not tenable and is set aside. The redemption fine of Rs. 2,50,000 is also set aside. "We, therefore, after hearing both sides, hold that the goods are covered by OGL. The impugned order confiscating the goods under Section 111(d) of the Customs Act is not tenable. It is, therefore, set aside and consequently the redemption fine of Rs. 25 lakhs is also set aside."

5. Imposition of penalty--Sufficient force in appellants' plea that no penalty having been imposed by the Collector earlier, imposition of the same in remand proceedings was unjustified. Penalty of Rs. 50,000 set aside. "We have considered this plea of the appellants and we find sufficient force in that plea. We, therefore, set aside the penalty of Rs. 50,000/- imposed in the impugned order."

6. Detention Certificate--Because of the delay in readjudication proceedings, the appellants' request for issue of detention certificate may be considered sympathetically. "This is a matter to be considered by the Customs authorities themselves. The Tribunal does not normally come into the picture so far as the detention certificate is concerned because there is no provision in the Customs Act which allows granting of detention certificate. Nevertheless, we are of the view that the appellants' request be considered sympathetically inasmuch as there has been a delay in readjudication proceedings despite an observation of the Tribunal that the Collector is expected to decide the case within four weeks of receipt of the Tribunal's Order No. 168/89-A dated 2.5.1989."

excise duty on manufactured goods, cannot be the basis for granting exemption under the Customs Act, which is a separate and distinct enactment. "The exemptions granted under the Excise Act, which regulates the levy of excise duty or a tax on manufactured goods in the country is a separate and distinct enactment. The exemptions granted under the Excise Duty either in whole or in part are for the purpose of that Act only and they cannot on any principle be the basis for claiming exemptions under the Customs Act." 7. Powers of the C.B.E.C. include framing of regulations prescribing the forms of bills of entry. "Section 157 of the Customs Act expressly empowers the Board to frame regulations prescribing the forms of bills of entries. .......An examination of the 'forms' prescribed by the Board shows that they are made for purposes of the Act. We find no merit in the challenge of the petitioners to the Regulations or the forms prescribed by the Board."

8. 'Landing charges' are includible in the assessable value of imported goods, as value has to be determined at the time and place of importation and the importer cannot take delivery of goods till payment of landing charges. "The value had to be determined at the time and place of importation. The time and place of importation can never be where the ship crosses the territorial waters but must naturally be at the sea port where the goods are actually delivered by the shipmaster. .......Without payment of landing charges, the importer does not and cannot take delivery of the goods at all. We are of the view that this is the true import of Section 14(1) of the Customs Act, which is only made specific in the Customs Valuation Rules of 1963 and the form of Bill of Entry prescribed by the Board. We are, therefore, of the view that 'landing charges' cannot be excluded and the assessment cannot be made on the CIF value of goods. "

9. Exemption claim on packages and containers is remanded to the proper authorities for examination. "On the packages and containers the petitioners" claim is founded on the notifications issued by Government under Section 25 of the Customs Act. Whether the claim is well founded or not has to be examined and decided in the first instance by the authority under the Act. As the authority had not examined and decided the same we must only direct the authority to do that."

From the case records, it was found that the assessee had collected various charges from importers/exporters including passengers for keeping the cargo in transit safely, pending export or customs clearance for home consumption. In holding that keeping safe custody of cargo in transit, pending clearance by the customs would constitute an activity exigible under the above entry, the lower authorities had relied on Circulars of the CBEC which clarified that storage and warehousing service provided by, inter alia, Airport Authority is covered by the entry. The entry cargo handling service was clarified by the CBEC as not covering export cargo and passenger baggage. The clarification was not to the effect that all activities relating to export cargo and passenger baggage were also excluded from levy under other entries. The finding of the Commissioner, that the exceptions provided under cargo handling services with regard to passenger baggage and export cargo could not be claimed under storage and warehousing services, was to be agreed with. [Para 9.2]

Demurrage or wharfage charges were collected, respectively, in relation to clearance of import/export cargo beyond five days and 24 hours. As found by the original authority, these were higher charges for continued storage of cargo collected by the assessee from members of the trade. These were part of the taxable value collected towards storage and warehouse charges. [Para 9.3]

As regards the abandoned cargo, those accrued to the assessee towards storage and warehousing of cargo, which were not taken delivery of by the importer. The procedure for auctioning abandoned cargo and the sharing of the proceeds is prescribed by the Ministry of Finance. These instructions also make it clear that the assessee would receive amounts towards the service of storage and warehousing of cargo under this head. However, the services were not rendered to any person in the case of the abandoned cargo. Therefore, demand under this head was not sustainable. [Para 9.4]

As regards the destination charges, it was found that the assessee had collected the documents representing the consignments brought by Air India and Blue Dart and hand over these to the respective consignees. In cases where the assessee merely collected and handed over the documents to the respective consignees, destination charges would not form part of taxable value under storage and warehousing. [Para 9.5]

As regards the OT charges/penalties, the lower authorities had not given a finding as to the nature and purpose of these penalties but had presumed that these were collected for violations on the part of their clients in relation to storage and warehousing services. The Commissioner (Appeals) did not find this item to be taxable under storage and warehousing. In the absence of a finding as to how that amount was taxable towards any service rendered by the assessee, it was difficult to accept the stand of the revenue in this regard. The assessee had also not explained the nature and purpose of collecting these charges. This matter would be decided after hearing the party afresh. [Para 9.6]

There was considerable merit in the assessee’s submission that there was no suppression of facts, etc. to warrant invocation of larger period. From the orders impugned, one did not find a reliable finding by the authorities that the assessee, a State PSU, had resorted to suppression of the facts to evade appropriate service tax amount. Considering the nature of the activities involved, the Commissioner could not have found with certainty that the assessee had deliberately mis-classified the activities undertaken by it under the head ‘Cargo handling services’ instead of ‘Storage and warehousing services’. Therefore, the authorities could not have validly invoked extended period and imposed penalties. The penal liability of the assessee required reconsideration in the light of section 80. [Para 9.7]

In view of section 75 the assessee was liable to pay interest for delay in payment of the tax found due from it. Therefore, the order of the lower appellate authority as regards interest was to be upheld. [Para 10.1]

A ground raised for the first time before the Tribunal was based on the Circular No. 89/7/2006-ST, dated 18-12-2006. [Para 11]

The lower authorities had no occasion to examine that plea and to determine that liability of the assessee in the light of the same. The Tribunal was not in a position to decide the issue as it was not clear whether the circular applied to the assessee and if the assessee would come under the description of ‘public authority’, as envisaged in the above circular. In any case, records did not indicate that the charges collected by the assessee were deposited with the Government. The circular defines statutory authorities discharging sovereign functions, etc., to be those that deposit the ‘fees’ collected with the Government. [Para 12]

In the circumstances, the appeals were to be allowed by way of a remand. The impugned orders were to be set aside. [Para 13]

Affidavits filed by the Department do not give any satisfactory explanation for the course of action adopted by the Department. Importers cannot wait indefinitely for assessment and the Department should have completed the assessment within a reasonable time. "The affidavit which has been filed leaves much to be explained. The entire grievance in paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 of this affidavit, to the effect that (he petitioners have rushed to the Court and obtained orders without waiting for assessment, has no merit as it is seen that right from the year 1987, the Respondents have, in not a single case of this type, completed the assessment. The importers cannot therefore be expected to wait indefinitely for assessment..........The Respondents, however, have been fully aware throughout, that they are at liberty to complete the assessment. No explanation is given as to why they have not done so for the last four years."

2. Valuation--Department directed to assess Ball Bearings imported from China in accordance with Customs Valuation Rules,. 1988 on the basis of evidence adduced by the importers. "For the purpose of valuation, the Respondents are bound by the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 which prescribe the methods of valuation of imported goods. The Respondents shall determine the value of Ball Bearings imported from China in the cases before them on the basis of the evidence produced before them by the importers in each of these cases and on the basis of any material which may be in the possession of the respondents of which inspection shall be given to the importers, and the same shall be done in accordance with law, including, needless to add, the above Rules."

3. Department submits that all assessments pertaining to Ball Bearings imported from China will be completed promptly. Assessment of goods already cleared on provisional assessment to be completed within 6 months. "Mr. Sethna, who appears for the Respondents, has stated before us........that in all cases relating to Ball Bearings, where it is not proposed to permit clearance of Ball Bearings on provisional assessment of duty under Section 18 of the Customs Act, a show cause notice will be issued to the importer within two weeks of the filing of the Bill of Entry. And after the reply is received, the assessment shall be completed within four weeks thereafter and the order shall be communicated to the importers within that time. In respect, however, of pending assessments relating to the import of Ball Bearings, where goods are already cleared on provisional assessment, the Respondents shall complete final assessments Within six months from today."

Valuation--Deemed value--The real value for purpose of assessment of Customs duty is the international market price at which goods are sold or offered for sale at the time and place of importation. ".............under Section 14(1) of the Act, the value for the purposes of assessment of duty would be the deemed value. Even if the invoice price is proved to be true price as agreed between the parties, for it is the international market price which is the real value for the purpose of Customs duty. Thus the deemed value in terms of Section 14 is the price at which such goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale at the place of importation."

2. ITC--Import licence--Debiting of--Only the C.I.F. value is to be debited to the licence and not the assessable value. ".......there is one kind of valuation for the purpose of assessment to customs duty but another for the purpose of c.i.f. value which is to be debited to the licence. This value to be debited consists of the items viz. the price of the goods and the commission allowed and where the commission is not apparent on the surface, it is the duty of the Customs authorities to find out and add to it the said price so that the price of the goods plus the commission and the freight and insurance would constitute the c.i.f. price for the purpose of debiting to the licence."

"In our view unless it can be shown and proved by the Customs authorities that the importer has paid to the foreign supplier more than what has been reflected in the agreement or invoice the c.i.f value has to be taken as the basis for debiting the licence."

3. ITC--Import licence--Debiting of--Enhanced value cannot be debited to the licence, particularly when the order of enhancement has been appealed against and is not final. "It is true, in the instant case, for the purpose of payment of Customs duty the assessable value has been enhanced by the adjudicating order, but for the purpose of debiting the licence the declared c.i.f. value has to be taken to be the basis in the absence of any finding that the importer has paid something over and above the declared c.i.f. value. The international price of imported goods is a relevant factor for determining the assessable value for the purpose of Customs duty, but the same is not relevant for debiting the import licence. The authorities have to determine the real value of the goods. The import licence speaks only of the c.i.f. value of the goods for the purpose of debiting the licence. The c.i.f. value cannot be equated with the real value of the goods which may be determined by the Customs authorities taking into account all the relevant facts and circumstances of the case. "

"There is another aspect of the matter. Assuming that the value as determined in the adjudication order by which the import licence has to be debited, the said adjudication order is now subject to an appeal before the Tribunal. It is well settled that once an appeal is preferred the decision loses it character of finality and what was once res judicata again become res sub judice."

"Therefore, it is not correct to urge that the licence has to be debited by the enhanced assessable value as determined in adjudication order which may or may not be sustained by the Appellate authority."

4. Import licence--Customs authorities directed to debit the licence with the declared c.i.f. value and return the same to the Appellants, as the licence has not been established to be forged one. "........the case of the forging of the licence has not been established by the Customs authorities."

"..........Even the stand of the Customs authorities in this regard shows that they did not treat the licence as forged. The Customs authorities have allowed the subject goods to be cleared against the very same licence which they have labelled as forged. C.J. Bandi for the Appellant.

N.K. Shastri for the Respondent.

1. Valuation--Invoice value may not be accepted for computing duty if comparable goods are purchased at substantially higher price. "The appellants explanation for increase in the price is that the demand for second hand machinery had gone up and the suppliers therefore raised the prices in case of latter import No evidence in support of this plea has been produced either before the lower authorities or before us. In the absence of any such evidence and the apparently large price differential in the prices of two sets of machines, the imports of which were made in the span of about nine months time, we held that the lower authorities were justified in not accepting low price as reflected in the invoice for the goods".

2. Valuation--Computation of value should preferable be under Rule 3 and 4 if comparable goods are available at different prices. "We would like to observe that in the instant case, the value of comparable goods was available and the correct rule that should have been applied by the lower authorities should have been Rule 3 of the Custom Valuation rules 1963 read with Rule 4 of the said rule. We find that the value of comparable goods imported by the appellants was acceptable to the authorities and as such there was no need for the officers to traverse beyond these rules to Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules."

3. Valuation--Assessee has no grievance if a criterion, less preferable than other available ones, is adopted if it does not put him to disadvantage. "In any case, we find that the appellants had not suffered any disadvantage on this account and probably the value fixed now in terms of the Appellate Collector's order is lower than what might have been fixed in case Rule 3 read with Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules 1963 had been resorted to. We, therefore, find no reason to accede the appellants plea for accepting the invoice value for purpose of assessment."

4. Assessable value includes landing charges. "The inclusion of landing charges in the assessable value is maintainable in law seeing that the expenditure incurred for landing would become an integral component of their intrinsic value and accordingly "the price at which such or like goods are for delivery at the time and place of importation"."

Valuation--Notional landing charges are includible for computing the assessable value (ratio of judgment in Ceat Tyres of India Ltd. v. CC). "In the case law cited as aforesaid under the heading Landing Charges it was held that landing charges are includible in assessable value and the same (landing charges) are to be calculated as a percentage of c.i.f. value taking into account total value of imports and total landing charges."

2. Addl. Duty of Customs (CVD)--Assessable value is the aggregate value inclusive of the customs duties chargeable on the imported goods. "In the case of Ashok Traders v. Union of India.....it was held by the Bombay High Court that section 3(2) of the Customs Tariff Act is constitutionally valid and for purposes of c.v. duty the assessable value of the imported goods is the aggregate value of the imported goods plus customs duty chargeable on that article."

3. Valuation--Packing charges are not excludible in terms of Notfn. 184/76-Cus., where these are included in the value of imported goods (ratio of Bombay High Court judgment in Polyset Corporation v. CC). "....the Bombay High Court after considering the ambit and scope of exemption notification 184/76-Cus held that what are exempt meter this exemption notification from the duty leviable are the goods imported or exported in packages or any portion of the value of the goods so imported. In other words, if packages as such are subject to customs duty they would be exempt from duty. Even then it is not every packages imported that is exempt, it is only when the goods are imported or exported in packages that such packages are exempt provided they satisfy the other conditions laid down in the notification. It was made clear that the said notification does not permit the valuation of goods in packages split up into principal goods and packages and exempt the packages from duty. In the instant case the authorities below have held that the appellants did not satisfy the conditions of the said notification. The same views were reiterated by this Tribunal in the case of M/s. K. Hargovind Dass Co., M/s. Chhaganlal Sons, and others--Final Order No. 468 to 597/92-A dated 29.10.1992.......Thus following the ratio of the said decisions we do not find any infirmity in the impugned orders passed by the authorities below."

Valuation--Assessable Value-value of 'bought out' items includible in assessable value if these were essential parts of the machinery. "......in the absence to any evidence to the contrary, these bought out items have to be taken to be necessary to complete the equipment which the appellants manufactured and supplied....the value of these 'bought out items' has to be treated as part of the cost of the manufacture of the finished goods, and the simple fact that the appellants invoiced them separately would not make any difference."

2. Assessable value: Installation and supervision charges treated as a post-manufacturing activity and not part of manufacturing cost, hence not includible in assessable value. "...installation and supervision charges are to be treated in the nature of post manufacturing expenses, and not part of the manufacturing cost, so as to be included in the assessable value."

3. Assessable Value: Exempted goods remain excisable goods, value of conversion charges includible in assessable value. "The view is well settled by now that by virtue of being exempted under a notification, the given class of goods does not go out of the category of 'excisable goods', once they find a place in or under an item of the CET. (M/s. Vishalandhra Industries Vs. Union of India--1983 ECR 1559D--Delhi, DB). We, are, therefore, of the view that claim of the appellants for exclusion of conversion charges is not tenable."

4. Limitation--Suppression of extended period of (initiation for issuance of show cause notice applicable since fact of 'bought out items' or commission charges, etc. had not been disclosed. "In view of the undisputed position that while filing declaration for clearances free of duty by virtue of Notification No 176/77, the fact of 'bought out items' or conversion charges or other disputed heads has not been disclosed; this by itself can, undisputedly, be considered as suppression within the meaning of Proviso to Section 11A of the Act, thereby extending the period of limitation for issuance of show cause notice to 5 years.......We, therefore, find the pleas of 'time-barred' as not sustainable."

5. Rate of duty applicable is the rate in force on the date on which removals were effected. "We find a manifest error in Collector's approach in this regard, as we do not find any concept in Rule 9A(5), as introduced by the Collector to the effect that when the clearances are not in accordance with law, then the current rate as prevalent on the date of payment of duty would be applicable. We are thus unable to subscribe to the Collector's view that in such circumstances, provisions of Rule 9A(5) would apply. We, therefore, hold that in case any duty was leviable, it would have been in terms of Rule 9A(1)(ii) of the rules."

There was no dispute about the applicability of section 41(1) in the instant case. The only dispute was when the liability to pay customs duty ceased. In other words, the issue was in which year the benefit in respect of customs duty liability by way of remission or cessation thereof accrued to the assessee and when the amount due to cessation of liability had been obtained by the assessee. The assessee company as well as other newspaper companies had filed writ petitions challenging the levy of customs duty by the Government. The Supreme Court vide order dated 6-12-1984 directed the Government of India to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and refix the rate of customs duty afresh, with effect from 1-3-1981. If on such reconsideration the Government decided that there should be any modification in the levy of customs duty or auxiliary duty with effect from 1-3-1981 it would take necessary steps to implement its decision. Until such redetermination of the liability, the Government was directed to recover only Rs. 550 per MT on imported newsprint towards customs duty and auxiliary duty and would not insist upon payment of duty in accordance with the impugned notifications. It was further stipulated in the Supreme Court’s order that even after such redetermination if it was found that any of the petitioners was liable to pay any deficit amount by way of duty, such deficit amount would be paid by such petitioner within four months from the date on which a notice of demand was served on such petitioner by the concerned authority. It was clear from the above order of the Supreme Court that the Government of India was directed to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on newsprint used for printing newspaper, periodicals, etc., with effect from 1-3-1981. Therefore, as on 6-12-1984 the liability of the assessee to pay customs duty, etc., had not ceased because the matter regarding payment of customs duty was to be considered by the Government. As a result of the directions of the Supreme Court, the Government of India had issued notification dated 19-12-1985 and the CBEC also issued a departmental circular on 10-2-1986 determining the customs duty in respect of imported newsprint. It was clear from the notification as well as circular that after examination of the question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on imported newsprint the Government had fixed the rate at Rs. 550 per MT. The notification as well as circular dates fell in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, i.e., 1987-88. Therefore, as a result of the notification and circular of the CBEC the assessee’s liability to pay customs duty had ceased in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88. The assessee thus obtained the benefit in respect of customs duty by way of remission or cessation thereof and the amount obtained by it and/or the value of benefit accrued to it had to be deemed as its profits and gains of business for the assessment year 1987-88. The customs authority by issuing the notice of demand had given effect to the notification dated 19-12-1985 issued by the Government of India and Circular dated 10-2-1986 of CBEC. A notice of demand did not have the effect of cessation or remission of liability of the assessee. The liability of an assessee ceased only under Notification dated 19-12-1985 of the Government of India read with circular of the customs authority dated 10-2-1986. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in confirming the addition made to the total income of the assessee for the assessment year 1987-88 after making necessary adjustments regarding claim, if any, disallowed under section 43B earlier while determining the amount assessable.

The benefit in respect of cessation of customs liability by way of remission or cessation thereof had to be taxed in the assessment year 1987-88 because the assessee obtained the benefit in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88 and if the assessee did not make entry in the relevant accounting year it would not effect operation of the provisions of section 41(1).
