In Sita Ram (supra), it was observed:

"43. Of course, procedure is within the Court's power, but where it pares down pre-judicially the very right, carving the kernel out, it violates the provision creating the right. Appeal is a remedial right and if the remedy is reduced to a husk by procedural excess, the right became a casualty. That cannot be."

Therefore, the rule that object of the Legislature has to be kept in view and a construction consistent with the object has to be placed on the words used if there be ambiguity, is also applicable in construing a taxing enactment.12 Every taxing statute has a fiscal philosophy - a feel of which is necessary to gather the intent and effect of its different clauses13.

Various indirect taxing statutes especially Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 mandates for filing of appeal on the deposit of 10% of the amount of tax in dispute and on deposit of the same the recovery proceedings in respect thereof shall be deemed to be stayed. What deserves to be noticed is that under the Act stay is the consequence of deposit of 10% of the amount of tax in dispute and no independent power expressly under the Act has been conferred on the Appellate Authorities to exercise the power of stay even if a prima facie case is made out or is forthcoming from the Order of the Adjudicating Authority on account of being ultra vires the Act or without jurisdiction or patently illegal etc.

Conclusion:

The emphasis is on deposit of certain percentage of amount of disputed demand. What is demand of duty/penalty in dispute has not been defined under the indirect taxing statutes. Deposits made during the pendency of the proceedings, or even after the order-in-original is passed, have to be taken into consideration for determining and deciding whether condition of pre-deposit of certain percentage of duty/penalty has been satisfied. Earlier deposits do not get obliterated and are not to be treated as inconsequential as rightly pointed out by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of Santani Sales Organisation (supra)in view of the Circular (supra) issued by the Central Board of Excise & Customs. A Circular provides extraneous aid to construction being contemporanea expositio for interpreting a statute with reference to the exposition it has received from contemporary authority i.e., Central Board of Excise & Customs14. The proceedings under indirect taxing statutes culminate in the passing of an Order determining the duty/penalty payable after the imposition of self-assessment of payment of duty/tax and therefore, the entire amount of duty and penalty levied thereon is open to challenge before the Appellate Authorities on the ground of jurisdictional and/or legal errors emanating therefrom. In most of such cases, on the basis of self-assessment of the assessee/dealer duty is declared and deposited along with the returns. If the aggrieved assessee/dealer is to deposit de novo certain percentage of the entire amount of disputed demand of duty/penalty in addition to the amount already declared and deposited with the returns the provisions of Article 265 of the Constitution of India would come into play, thereby making such a mandate of deposit along with the memorandum of appeal a negation of not only the right to violate free access to justice but the right of appeal itself illusory and delusive particularly in the absence of any power of stay of demand conferred on the Appellate Authorities under the various indirect taxing statutes. Though equity and taxation are often strangers, attempts should be made that they do not remain always so and if a construction results in equity rather than injustice, then such a construction should be preferred with promotes justice and fair play which are the facets of rule of law and a part and parcel of Article 14 of the Constitution of India15. Thus, the inevitable conclusion drawn by the Hon'ble High Court of Punjab & Haryana backed up by the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi is fundamentally a correct view.

Background

Recently, the Hon'ble Supreme Court ('SC') vide its judgement in the case of Union of India v. Cosmo Films Ltd. [2023] 149 taxmann.com 473/2023 (72) G.S.T.L. 417/[2023] 97 GST 544 (SC) upheld the constitutional validity of the imposition of 'pre-import' condition in order to avail the exemption of IGST and compensation cess ('cess') under the Advance Authorisation ('AA') scheme, wherein such condition had been incorporated in paragraph 4.14 of the Foreign Trade Policy ('FTP') vide Notification No. 33/2015-2020 w.e.f. 13.10.2017.

While the judgement held in favour of the revenue, the SC vide paragraph 75 of the judgement also granted relief to the respondent who had continued claiming benefits under the AA scheme based on the interim orders of the Gujarat High Court1, thereby directing the department to issue a circular providing appropriate procedure to be followed in order for the respondent to claim refund or input tax credit ('ITC').

Summary of the Circular

Pursuant to such directions of the SC, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs ('Board) has issued Circular No. 16/2023-Customs dated 07.06.2023 ('Circular') which has been made applicable not only to the Cosmo Films Limited but also to all assessees who intend to regularise the failure to fulfil 'pre-import condition' by paying applicable IGST and Cess.

The Board specifically noted that there exists no functionality permitting the payment of Customs duties on a Bill of Entry ('BoE') after giving the Out-of-charge ('OOC') to the goods and thus, such duties are to be paid only vide TR-06 Challan. Further, the Board also clarified that as per GST Law, TR-06 Challan is not a valid document for the availment of ITC and that there is no mechanism of transmission of details of IGST payment made vide TR-06 challan from ICEGATE portal to GSTN portal for flow of ITC. To resolve these aforementioned issues, the Board prescribed a procedure of cancellation of existing OOC, reassessment of such Bills of Entry and generation of 'notional OOC' upon payment of such re-assessed IGST. Under this procedure, the payment of IGST would be against the reassessed BOE and the details of such IGST payment would flow from ICEGATE portal to GSTN portal for flow of ITC.

It is to be noted that under the pre-GST regime, it was a well-settled law that TR-06 challan was considered a duty paying document and thus, a valid document for taking credit by the assessee, as also held in multiple cases2.

Under the GST regime, reference may be made to the provisions regarding the availment of ITC wherein as per Section 16(2)(a) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 ('CGST Act'), one of the primary documentary requirements and conditions to claim ITC by a registered person is the possession of a "tax paying document as may be prescribed". Further, Rule 36(1)(d) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 ('CGST Rules') also specifically states that ITC can be availed on the basis of a "BoE or any similar document prescribed under the Customs Act, 1962 or rules made thereunder for the assessment of integrated tax on imports".

Ironically, while Section 16(2)(a) of CGST Act enables availment of ITC based on a 'tax paying document', the CGST Rules requires a 'Duty assessing document' i.e., BoE for availment of ITC of IGST. The aforementioned Circular refers to the CGST Rules and clarifies that TR-06 Challan is not a valid document for availment of ITC, failing to consider Section 16 of the CGST Act which requires only tax paying document, like TR-06 challan, for the availment of ITC.

Ambiguities resurfacing due to the Circular

As indicated in the circular, the given mechanism of reassessment of BoE to ensure transmission of details of IGST payment from ICEGATE portal to GSTN portal is applicable only in situations where the IGST is paid to regularise the violation of pre-import condition under the AA Scheme. However, other than the aforementioned situation, there are still various scenarios wherein duty is paid only through TR-06 Challan, including but not limited to the following:

i.

Payment of duty upon failure to fulfil export obligations under the EPCG Scheme or AA Scheme;

ii.

Payment of duty upon de-bonding of goods by an EOU;

iii.

Payment of differential Customs duty upon finalisation of provisionally assessed BoEs;

iv.

violation of pre-import condition under the AA Scheme. However, other than the aforementioned situation, there are still various scenarios wherein duty is paid only through TR-06 Challan, including but not limited to the following:

i.

Payment of duty upon failure to fulfil export obligations under the EPCG Scheme or AA Scheme;

ii.

Payment of duty upon de-bonding of goods by an EOU;

iii.

Payment of differential Customs duty upon finalisation of provisionally assessed BoEs;

iv. Payment of differential duty/IGST amount demanded under Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 including payment of Customs duty under protest.

In such aforementioned scenarios, there still arises an impossibility in the availment of ITC basis the standalone TR-06 Challan in the absence of a mechanism to ensure transmission of information from ICEGATE portal to the GSTN portal. It is also uncertain as to whether an assessee can claim refund of IGST paid now by redetermining the quantum of refund for past exports, as per GST law.

Conclusion and parting remarks

While the issuance of said Circular is undoubtedly a step forward with the Board specifically taking cognizance and resolving the issues where payment is made vide TR-06 challan, the Circular has also parallelly opened a Pandora's box and aggravated the concerns of assessees in the aforementioned scenarios wherein no similar procedure has been prescribed to facilitate the availment of ITC legally accrued to such assessees. Such ambiguity continues to cause further confusion and unnecessary litigations among assessees. The additional issue of the jurisdictional customs officers refusing to amend the BOEs despite repeated requests of the importers so as to enable the flow of ITC also adds to the problem. Therefore, even the directions given in the present Circular for reassessment of the BOEs may not achieve the desired results. Additionally, the issue still remains open as to whether an assessee can get their BoEs re-assessed in respect of IGST already paid previously through TR-06 Challan in order to avail ITC.

To conclude, the industry expects the Board to further prescribe similar mechanism and procedure to enable the assessees to avail ITC which are legally accruing to them in the aforementioned scenarios, which is otherwise disallowed to them due to mere procedural ambiguities. Further, the industries may also file a suitable representation before the Government of India/Board, explaining such practical difficulties in the availment of ITC basis a standalone TR-06 Challan and how the absence of such mechanism/procedure as issued under the Circular continues to result in redundancy of efforts, increased ambiguities and the requirement to undertake undue compliances.

Section 14of Customs Duty Act, provides that for the purposes of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 (51 of 1975), the value of the imported goods and export goods shall be the transaction value of such goods, that is to say, the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India for delivery at the time and place of importation, where the buyer and seller of the goods are not related and price is the sole consideration for the sale. The Section further provides that such transaction value in the case of imported goods shall include, in addition to the price as aforesaid, any amount paid or payable for costs and services, including commissions and brokerage, engineering, design work, royalties and licence fees, costs of transportation to the place of importation, insurance, loading, unloading and handling charges to the extent and in the manner specified in the rules made in this behalf. Accordingly, Rule 10 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 provides that in determining the transaction value, there shall be added to the price actually paid or payable for the imported goods, —

(i)

commissions and brokerage, except buying commissions;

(ii)

the cost of containers which are treated as being one for customs purposes with the goods in question;

(iii)

the cost of packing whether for labour or materials;

The Rule further provides that the value of the imported goods shall be the value of such goods, for delivery at the time and place of importation and shall include -

(a)

the cost of transport of the imported goods to the place of importation;

(b)

loading, unloading and handling charges associated with the delivery of the imported goods at the place of importation; and

(c)

the cost of insurance :

Thus, Section 14 read with Rule 10 as state above clearly provides for inclusion of Ocean freight in the value of goods for the levy of Customs duty thereon.

Position post 01.06.2016

W.e.f 01.6.2016, in Section 66D, clause (p)(ii) was deleted which read as follows – "by an aircraft or a vessel from a place outside India up to the customs station of clearance."

Thus, both ocean freight and air freight in case of import became taxable as the entry in negative list has been deleted. However, an exemption has been given in respect of an aircraft by providing Entry No 53 to Notification No. 25/2012-ST. Thus, the whole debate remains in respect of Ocean freight which is brought under Service Tax levy w.e.f. 01.6.2016.

The first question which comes up is whether both Customs Duty and Service Tax can be levied on same value?

In the case of United Shippers Limited v CCE, Thane II [2015 (37) S.T.R. 1043 (Tri. - Mumbai)], as affirmed by Hon'ble Supreme Court it was held that services of Cargo Handling Services can be rendered in respect of such goods only once the customs transaction is completed. It was held by the Court as under:

"Thus when the goods are being transported by the barges from the mother vessel to the jetty onshore, that activity is part of the import transaction of bringing the goods into India from a place outside India. The question of rendering any service in respect of such goods by way of cargo handling or otherwise can take place only after the customs transaction is completed. Therefore, the question of levying to Service Tax the transportation by barges from the mother vessel to the jetty onshore, would not arise at all since the said activity is part of the import transaction leviable to import duty and we hold accordingly."

The C.B.E. & C. has also clarified vide Circular 34/2009, dated 30-11-2009 that "the issue of ineligibility of barge charges in the value (of imported goods) will be governed by the provisions of Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 for the assessment arising in the period from October 10, 2007 onwards."

Introduction

1. This year whole emphasis of the budget is on two aspects, i.e., ease of doing business and to promote make in India. The tariff and non-tariff (legislative) changes are made keeping in view the above objectives in mind. In February, 2016 SVB procedure was revamped. This budget has further simplified the warehousing provisions under the Customs Act. Concept of warehousing stations itself has been removed, permitting the self-governance and promoting privatization of warehousing without any interference of customs/excise officers. It may further be noted that compliance of law is being promoted, however, at the same time duty evasion is being punished.

On tariff part, to promote make in India, exemptions on various finished goods are withdrawn and their raw materials are being exempted subject to actual user conditions. New baggage Rules would permit excess duty free imports. Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty for Manufacture of Excisable Goods) Rules are introduced waving off various prior permission requirements. The new rules are mostly based upon self-declarations.

Details of changes made in customs laws, reasons and effect thereof are discussed hereunder:

Demand of customs duty can be raised in two years from date of import in non-suppression cases

2. Section 28 of the Customs Act providing for demand of customs duty has been amended to provide that demand of customs duty can be raised within period of two years from the date of import of goods. This provision would be applicable even for cases not involving collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts.

2.1 Earlier provision: Earlier the provision provided that customs department can raise demand of duty only within one year from date of import in cases of interpretation of provisions/exemption, etc. However, power to demand duty beyond one year of import was only available in case of suppression or mis-declaration by the assessee.

2.2 Reason of amendment: In cases where issue pertains to classification of imported goods or interpretation of the exemption notification, the assessee argues that there is no suppression on part of the assessee and customs was fully aware of details of goods. In those situations, customs duty could not be recovered for imports beyond one year's period from the date of imports.

From department's point of view, it was felt that due of paucity of time, i.e., one year's period, investigations could not be completed for various assessees and SCNs were not being issued within one year from date of import.

2.3 Effect of amendment: This amendment would give room of additional one year to customs for making detailed investigations and issue SCN.

From assessee's point of view, this would increase the uncertainty of duty demand till two years during which it can be raised even in cases of assessment with complete knowledge of customs officer. Further, in the era of stiff competition, even one SCN demanding duty after period of 20 months of import would have huge impact on assessee's financial planning.

The other class of importer traders would be deeply hit as their customers to whom imported goods are re-sold may not pay them the excess customs duty/differential duty demanded by department.

Thus, proposed amendment is, to some extent contrary to the principal of certainty, as assessee would be unsure of the duty demand, even though the assessment may have been done with the knowledge of the department.

Further, it is also not clear whether the said provision would be applicable even on past imports where one year's period from date of imports has expired and department also does not allege any suppression.

Date of publication in the official gazette

3. Section 25 of the Customs Act grants power to government to issue exemption notification. Section 25(4) of the Customs Act is amended to provide that every notification issued shall come into force on the date of its issue by the Central Government for publication in the Official Gazette. This is being amended so as to omit the requirement of publishing and offering for sale any notification issued by the Directorate of Publicity and Public Relations of CBEC.

The proposed amendment will nullify the effect of decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. By the present amendment second condition shall be removed.

In this decision the Supreme Court followed the case of Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 263 ITR 706 / 132 Taxman 373. Some of the important observations of the Supreme Court in the decision are as follow:

uTax administration is a complex subject. It consists of several aspects. The Government needs to strike a balance in the imposition of tax between collection of revenue on one hand and business-friendly approach on the other hand. Today, Governments have realized that in matters of tax collection, difficulties faced by the business have got to be taken into account. Exemption, undoubtedly, is a matter of policy. Interpretation of an Entry is undoubtedly a quasi-judicial function under the tax laws. Imposition of taxes consists of liability, quantification of liability and collection of taxes. Policy decisions have to be taken by the Government. However, the Government has to work through its senior officers in the matter of difficulties which the business may face, particularly in matters of tax administration. That is where the role of the Board of Revenue comes into play. The said Board takes administrative decisions, which includes the authority to grant administrative reliefs. This is the underlying reason for empowering the Board to issue orders, instructions and directions to the officers under it.

uIn the present case, one was not concerned with deciding the scope and extent of each item in Entry 110. One was essentially concerned in this case with the nature of the powers exercised by the Board/Commissioners under section 3(1A). As stated above, the said circular was issued by the Board by exercising statutory powers vested in it under section 3(1A). Section 3(1A) provides for an enabling power of the Board, which was recognized as an authority under the 1963 Act. The said power was to be exercised in special cases. Granting of administrative reliefs by the Board came within its authority. The said circular was issued for just and fair administration of the 1963 Act. Section 3(1A) is similar to section 119(1) of the 1961 Act. The circulars of this nature are issued by the Board consisting of highest senior officers in the Revenue Department. These circulars are to be respected by the officers working under the supervision of the Board. These circulars are binding on all the authorities administering the tax department.

Meaning of ‘recognised by law for the time being in force’

2. As per section 65(27 ), ‘Commercial training or coaching centre’ does not include any institute or establishment which issues any certificate or diploma or degree or any educational qualification recognised by law for the time being in force.

Usually, there is no problem up to school education. However, in respect of post-school education, there are many issues. Usually, such education is given by University.

As per section 2(f) of the University Grants Commission Act (UGC Act), ‘University’ means a University established or incorporated by or under a Central Act, a Provincial Act or a State Act and includes any such institution, as may, in consultation with University concerned, be recognised by University Grants Commission (UGC), in accordance with the regulations made in this behalf under the UGC Act.

As per section 3 of the UGC Act, any institution of higher education, other than a University, can be notified by the Central Government as ‘deemed university’ and then all provisions of the UGC Act will apply as if it were a University under section 2(f ) of the UGC Act.

Recognition can be granted to a college or a institution run by a trust, a registered society or a body corporate or body incorporated under the Central or the State Act. It is an institution affiliated to or forms a constituent member of a University.

In addition, as per National Policy of Education, 1986, a scheme of autonomous college has been promoted. These are autonomous colleges but degree is granted by University.

All these institutions are created or recognised in terms of powers conferred by statute and, hence, would fall in category of institute/establishment which issues diploma or certificate recognised by law. Degree can be granted only by University or Deemed University - para 3.2 of CBEC Circular No. 107/01/2009-ST, dated January 28, 2009."

Thus, an institute/establishment affiliated to University is exempt even if the degree is granted by University and not by the institute/establishment itself.

2.1 Recognition at the time of provision of service is relevant - What is relevant is that the recognition of institute or establishment should be there at the time of provision of service and not earlier or later. It cannot be said that once recognised, an institute or establishment would remain so even in future or was so in past - para 3.7 of CBEC Circular No. 107/01/2009-ST, dated January 28, 2009 [Probably this is the only statement in the circular which is least controversial].

2.2 Recognition of professional courses - For promotion of professional institutions, a number of Professional Councils have been created under various Acts, like All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), Medical Council of India (MCI), Indian Council for Agricultural Research (ICAR) and Bar Council of India (BCI).

They have been given powers to de-recognise an institution or establishment or a particular course, even if they are recognised by a University, Deemed University or Affiliated College.

[2003]127 TAXMAN 21 (ART) VALUATION OF INVENTORIES LYING IN A BONDED WAREHOUSE

M.S. Prasad*

In Caprihans India Ltd. v. Prakash Chandra [2002] 122 Taxman 862 (Bom.), the company filed the return along with its accounts and audit report. It was mentioned in the notes on accounts that excise duty on finished goods manufactured, and customs duty on raw material imported, which were both lying in the bonded warehouse, were not claimed as liabilities and, therefore, not included in the value of the closing stock. Later, the assessment was reopened on the ground that the taxable event was the manufacture of an excisable article and so the excise and customs duty were includible in the valuation of the closing stock. The High Court held that the reassessment was bad. It held that when the method of accounting followed by the assessee had been accepted by the revenue for subsequent years and duty liability on the bonded goods crystallised only on the date of ex-bounding, it could not be said that there was any reason to believe that any income had escaped assessment. The author of this article discusses the question of valuation of inventories lying in bonded warehouse in the context of the above decision - EDITOR

Caprihans India’s case

1. The Bombay High Court considered the question of valuation of inventories lying in a bonded warehouse in Caprihans India Ltd. v. Prakash Chandra [2002] 122 Taxman 862 . In this case, the company filed a return for the assessment year 1994-95 on November 30, 1994 along with its accounts and audit report. It was mentioned in the notes on accounts that excise duty on finished goods manufactured, and customs duty on raw material imported (the amounts of which were mentioned), which were both lying in the Bonded Warehouse, were not claimed as liabilities and, therefore, not included in the value of the closing stock and as such it had no effect on the profit declared and this was a practice consistently followed by it. The duties were paid on clearance of goods and then accounted for. An assessment was made on December 20, 1996 and was the subject-matter of cross appeals before the Tribunal when the matter came up before the High Court. On November 20, 1997 the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 154/155 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 to the company requiring it to state why the amounts of excise and customs duty should not be included in valuing the closing stock. Proceedings were dropped when the company pointed out that there was no mistake in the assessment order, or in the method of accounting followed by the company as the said duties were payable at the time of clearance from the Bonded Warehouse. On January 21, 2001, a notice under section 148 was issued to the assessee by the Assessing Officer on the ground that the Supreme Court had held in the case of Wallace Flour Mills Co. Ltd. v. CCE that the taxable event was the manufacture of an excisable article and so the excise and customs duties were includible in the valuation of the closing stock. The company paid the said excise and custom duties before the due date for filing of the return and appeared to have furnished evidence thereof along with the return as required under the proviso to section 43B(1) of the Act.

When the company challenged the issue of the notice under section 148 of the Act by way of a writ, the Bombay High Court held:

that interest charges automatically apply to delayed return filings, regardless of whether payments are made through the Electronic Credit or Cash Ledger. The Court observed that the input tax credit and the resultant payment of tax from the Electronic Credit Ledger occurs only when a return is furnished. If there is a delay in furnishing of returns, then there is a delay in the input tax credit coming into the Electronic Credit Ledger and a resultant payment being made to the Government as tax is belated, leading to a levy of interest. From the above, it can be inferred that this matter will take another round of litigation to settle. It is relevant to mention here that the CBIC vide Circular F. No. CBEC-20/01/08/2019-GST, dated 18-9-2020, has clarified that for the period 01-07-2017 to 31-08-2020, field formations in respective jurisdictions may be instructed to recover interest only on net cash tax liability (i.e. that portion of the tax that has been paid by debiting the electronic cash ledger or is payable through cash ledger) and wherever SCNs have been issued on gross tax payable, the same may be kept in Call Book till the retrospective amendment in section 50 of the CGST Act, 2017 is carried out. Despite the circular, which is binding on the department, it has been overlooked, leading to widespread litigations on a Pan India basis.

Additionally, conflicting decisions have been issued by different High Courts on this issue. It is recommended that the Government should make necessary amendment in the said provision and issue detailed guidelines to resolve these ongoing disputes in the upcoming budget.

63. Need for clarity on the treatment of post-sales discounts and incentives

The ambiguity around post-sales discounts and incentives has been there since the inception of the GST law. Section 15(3)(b) of the CGST Act, 2017 allows for the exclusion of post-sales discounts from the taxable value, provided certain conditions are met. These conditions include:

The discount being agreed upon before or at the time of supply.

The discount being linked to a specific invoice.

The recipient of the supply reversing the input tax credit (ITC) attributable to the discount.

Thus, if any of the above conditions are not met, the GST law does not allow the deduction of discounts from the value of supply. The basic issue revolves around whether secondary or post-sales discounts can be deducted from the value of supply. There have been conflicting interpretations of these provisions. Some rulings consider post-sales discounts as a reduction in the original supply value, excluding them from GST, whereas others do not allow any deduction.

However, the debate does not end here. The CBIC had earlier clarified by way of circular14 that such an additional discount would represent the consideration flowing from the supplier of goods to the dealer for the supply made by the dealer to the customer. This additional discount would be liable to be added to the consideration payable by the customer for the purpose of arriving at the value of the supply made by the dealer. However, in view of the industry apprehensions, the given clarification was later withdrawn15 by the CBIC. However, the GST authorities are still following the given view and treating such additional discounts as a form of 'consideration' for a separate supply, attracting GST. In some cases, the authorities treat volume/additional discounts as subsidies and add them to the value of supply in terms of Section 15(2)(e) of the CGST Act, 2017.

This lack of consistency creates a challenging environment for businesses. To address this confusion, the Government needs to make necessary amendments or issue clear guidelines on how to treat various types of post-sales discounts and incentives across different industries.

64. Sale of Repossessed Goods under GST: Complexities for the Banking and NBFC Sectors

Under GST law, tax is levied on the supply of goods, services or both, and the value of such supply is determined in terms of Section 15 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with the CGST Rules, 2017.

For suppliers dealing in buying and selling second-hand goods, Rule 32(5) of the CGST Rules, 2017 provides a specific method for calculating the value of supply. This involves calculating the difference between the selling price and the purchase price, with negative values ignored. Thus, the value is determined based on the margin of the sale made by the supplier rather than the transaction value as per Section 15 of the CGST Act, 2017.

The proviso to Rule 32(5) provides a specific provision for determining the purchase value of repossessed goods from a defaulting borrower who is unregistered under the GST law in the case of recovery of a loan or debt. In such cases, the purchase price is deemed to be the purchase price of such goods by the defaulting borrower reduced by 5 percentage points for every quarter or part thereof between the date of purchase and the date of disposal by the person making such repossession.

Additionally, notifications on CGST rates16 and Compensation Cess17 offer concessional rates for specified old and used vehicles, provided the supplier has not claimed input tax credit.

This principle is not new, but it has seldom been expressed with such clarity and force. The CESTAT traced the issue back to the basic structure of tax law, relying on Justice G.P. Singh’s Principles of Statutory Interpretation, which explains that taxation ordinarily involves three distinct stages: first, the creation of a tax liability; second, the assessment of that liability to determine the amount payable; and third, the recovery of the assessed amount if it is not paid voluntarily. The mere occurrence of a taxable event does not, by itself, make a tax or duty immediately recoverable. In the context of customs law, the duty must first be assessed under the statutory procedure prescribed in Sections 17 and 18 of the Customs Act, 1962, or determined through adjudication proceedings. Only thereafter can it be recovered. Where Parliament intends tax to be collected before assessment, it expressly provides for such a mechanism, as seen in the case of advance tax and tax deducted at source (TDS) under the income-tax laws. The Customs Act contains no comparable provision.

As the CESTAT precisely observed, any amount obtained from an assessee before assessment or adjudication occupies a distinct legal character. Although the money is in the State’s possession, it is not customs duty in the eyes of law. It remains a deposit held by the State in trust until the liability is properly determined, with the State acting merely as a custodian rather than as the owner of the funds.

Deposit vs. Duty: A distinction with profound consequences

The CESTAT’s order places considerable emphasis on the distinction between a deposit and duty—and for good reasons. Although the difference may appear technical at first glance, it carries important legal and financial consequences.

The distinction between a deposit and duty has been repeatedly recognised by the courts. The Madras High Court in Global United Shipping India Pvt. Ltd.2 explained that a deposit is an amount paid pending the determination of liability to safeguard the Revenue’s interests, whereas duty arises only after a statutory assessment crystallises the liability. The Delhi High Court in EBIZ.COM Pvt. Ltd.3 reinforced this principle, holding that money deposited during an investigation retains its character as a deposit even if it is temporarily appropriated towards a demand that is later set aside. In such cases, the State merely holds the money as a custodian and does not acquire it as duty.

The CESTAT in EMD Locomotive Technologies (supra) carried this principle to its logical conclusion. It held that where an amount was not duty when it was paid—because no liability had yet been assessed—it cannot later be converted into duty by a mere change in the department’s characterisation. Neither the issuance of a show cause notice nor the passing of an adjudication order can retrospectively alter the true nature of the payment. This finding has significant practical consequences. It prevents the department from artificially splitting investigation-stage deposits into “pre-deposit” and “duty” components and then using that distinction to restrict or vary the assessee’s entitlement to interest.

The entire deposit must be treated as pre-deposit

The CESTAT held that where an amount deposited during investigation exceeds the mandatory pre-deposit requirement and remains with the Department, the entire amount must be treated as a pre-deposit. The Department cannot arbitrarily classify only 7.5% or 10% as a pre-deposit and treat the balance as duty, since it has no legal right to recover that amount as duty while the appeal is pending. The CESTAT also rejected the Department’s reliance on CBIC Circular No. 984/8/2014-CX dated 16.9.2014, holding that an administrative circular cannot override the statute or binding judicial precedents, and describing the circular’s contrary view as ‘misplaced and unsustainable in law’.

Although the CESTAT has not recorded any specific finding on the vires of the CBIC Circular No. 984/8/2014-CX dated 16.9.2014, it appears to have the effect of implicitly overruling the same. It is anticipated that subsequent judicial pronouncements may address the matter with greater clarity and specificity. In any event, it is well settled that departmental circulars are not binding on the CESTAT in the exercise of its adjudicatory functions.

Interest is not a concession: It is compensatory in nature

There is a broader constitutional and equitable basis for requiring the state to pay interest when it refunds the amount deposited by an assessee. The Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in RHL Profiles Ltd.4, relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in Tata Chemicals Ltd5, and held that the state cannot retain and use money to which it was never lawfully entitled without compensating the person deprived of it. The payment of interest is therefore not a matter of legislative generosity; it is an essential component of restoring the assessee to the position it would have occupied had the money not been wrongly retained.

The Supreme Court reinforced this principle in Pratibha Processors6, holding that interest is compensatory in nature and is intended to make good the loss suffered on account of delayed return of the money. Accordingly, when an assessee succeeds and a refund is eventually sanctioned, interest from the date of deposit is not a windfall but compensation for the period during which the assessee was deprived of its funds.

Other points in provisional assessment

6. The other points that may be considered in respect of provisional assessment under the Customs Act are as follows:

Whether the customs authorities are having discretion to make provisional assessment? Whether the provisional assessment can be claimed as a right?

The case of Sachin Bhupendra Desai v. Union of India 2009 (240) ELT 360 (Cal.) gives answers to the said questions. It was held that -

In the event the petitioner satisfied the Customs Authorities for exercise of their jurisdiction or power under Section 18 for the purpose of provisional assessment of duty, the Customs authorities should adjudicate the matter and decide the same in accordance with the law. The order cannot be construed to be a mandatory direction for release of goods upon making provisional assessment;

Various circumstances have been laid down in Section 18(1) of the Customs Act, and on satisfaction of any one of the said conditions, the Customs authorities have been vested with the discretion to make provisional assessment;

Thus, it is clear that-

The customs authorities have been vested with the discretion to make provisional assessment;

The assessee cannot claim the provisional assessment as right unless he fulfils the conditions for seeking provisional assessment.

Finalization of provisional assessment

7. The provisional assessments are expected to be finalized expeditiously, well within six months. However, in respect of cases involving machinery contracts or large project imports, where imports take place over long period, such finalization may take more time since action can be taken only after all the imports have been made. However, effort should be made to finalize the case within six months of the date of import of the last consignment covered by the contract.

In Sigma Power Productivity Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner of Customs 2014 (304) ELT 19 (Cal.) the customs authorities raised a reasonable doubt as to the transaction value shown in the Bill of Entry at the time of import. The petitioner prayed for a provisional release of the said goods. Since no steps were taken by the authorities, the petitioner approached the High Court. The High Court directed the Department to make a provisional assessment within the specified time and the petitioner was directed to deposit with the authorities the customs duty payable on the value declared by them and also to furnish a bank guarantee of the differential duty after the provisional assessment was made by the Customs authorities and in addition thereto would also submit the P.D. Bond.

The directions of the Court were complied with both by the Department and assessee. After that no steps were taken for the final assessment. The Court directed the department to activate themselves in determining the value under Rule 12 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and to make a final assessment, after adhering to the statutory procedures and the norms and to see that the principles of Natural Justice were not violated.

Procedure for final assessment

8. In Saurastra Cement Ltd. v. CCE, Hamnagar - 2013 (297) ELT 365 (Tri. - Ahd.) the finalization of assessment should have been done by the details of Bill of Entry such as-

Bill of Entry number;

Date of bill of Entry;

Duty provisionally assessed;

Duty finally assessed; and

The difference payable or refundable.

Section 18 is relevant which provides that when the duty leviable on such goods is assessed finally in accordance with the provisions of this Act, then in the case of goods cleared for home consumption or exportation, the amount paid shall be adjusted against the duty finally assessed and if the amount so paid falls short of or is in excess of the duty finally assessed, the importer or the exporter of the goods shall pay the deficiency or be entitled to the refund, as the case may be. The Assessing Officer has to indicate the amount paid and adjusted. In the absence of such details the letter issued cannot be considered as an order finalizing the assessment.

when the respondent pays duty at the time of clearance of goods, the duty is paid on the correct assessable value and correct rate of duty and there is no question of any short payment of duty at the material time and since the respondents have no means and knowledge that price of goods will increase, the assessee could not be faulted for not paying the duty at the clearance of goods. Since there is no suppression of fact or fraud, the assessee cannot be held liable to pay the duty. But the Tribunal of Ahmedabad in the case of Inducto Casts (supra) has a contrary view and held that an assessee has to pay the interest either way he chooses, i.e., if he chooses rule 7 (Provisional assessment) he has to pay the interest under rule 7(4) at the time of finalizalion. In such a case, the interest becomes payable from the first day of month succeeding the month for which such amount is determined till the date of payment thereof. Or if he chooses to assess according to transaction value because the valuation in terms of section 4 shall be the transaction value at the time and place of removal and include in addition the amount charged as price, any amount which the buyer is liable to pay to the assessee in connection with the sale, whether payable at the time of sale or any other time. In this case, since there is a price escalation clause, the amount becomes payable at a later point of time and as such the amount payable to the appellant in terms of price escalation is includible as transaction value as defined in section 4(3)(d ). A similar view was taken by the Tribunal of Chennai in the case of Ennore Foundries Ltd. v. CCE Chennai10 wherein it was held that an assessee has to pay interest for the period between the payment of provisional duty and the payment of differential duty on finalisation of provisional assessment.

Recently, the same issue has been decided by the Division Bench of High Court in the case of CCE v. Rucha Engg. (P.) Ltd.11 where it affirmed the earlier order of the Tribunal and has observed as follows :—

"There is nothing to indicate that there was any time-gap between the date on which the revised rates applicable with retrospective effect were learnt by the assessee and the date on which differential duty was paid. Had that been the case, the levy of interest as under section 11AB could have been considered because of delayed payment of duty, but this is the case wherein the assessee upon learning that the rates of the goods cleared were revised/escalated and therefore, they are liable to pay more duty than already paid at the time of clearance of the goods, has voluntarily paid the duty. Thus, there is no delay."

But the Commissioner (Appeals) of Pune in the case of Spicer India Ltd., In re.12 has given a detailed order and has at least clarified two issues, which were wrongly appreciated by the Delhi Tribunal in the cases of Rajasthan Explosive & Chemicals Ltd. (supra) and D.K. Electrics (supra) and held that :—

(i)During the period 28-9-1996 to 10-5-2001, suppression of fact, etc., was prerequisite for invoking interest under section 11AB and also for imposing penalty under section 11AC. For invoking section 11AB or section 11AC, duty was required to be determined under section 11A(2). With effect from 11-5-2001, suppression of fact and, mis-statement was not necessary for invoking section 11AB; whereas they continued to be necessary for invoking penalty under section 11AC.

(ii)With effect from 11-5-2001, payment of duty under section 11A(2B) was also brought under the purview of section 11AB for interest recovery.

The Commissioner (Appeals) refused to follow the Rucha Engg. (P.) Ltd.’s case (supra) on the ground that it was observed by the Commissioner (Appeals) that there was no determination of duty under section 11A(2) and, therefore, provisions of section 11AB were not attracted. It was held that under section 11AB, as it stood prior to 11-5-2001, there was a reference to only section 11A(2); whereas in the section 11AB as it stands now with effect from 11-5-2001 there is a reference of both section 11A(2) and section 11A(2)(b). Therefore, it is clear that the above decisions will not be applicable for interest recovery under section 11AB with effect from 11-5-2001.

The Commissioner (Appeals) had also wrongly misunderstood the decision of the Tribunal that there is no case of any non-payment, short levy or short payment as envisaged under section 11A(1). But observation of the Tribunal of Delhi in the case of D. K. Electrics ( supra) is acceptable to the extent that amount escalation is unforeseen circumstance and beyond the control of the assessee, and if in these circumstances the assessee is not able to pay duty, it cannot be construed to mean that it failed to pay excise duty. Hence, interest cannot be demanded from the assessee under section 11AB of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

But in customs, the transactions are often sporadic and unrelated to previous ones. Moreover, assessment of the same for determination of customs duty is the first stage of verification of transaction and thus requires a physical presence to avoid tax evasion.

Analyzing the major hiccups The prominent issue in the implementation is the lack of opportunity to be heard. There remains a qualm among the taxpayers that they would not be provided with an adequate opportunity to present their viewpoints and arguments. Even the department acknowledged these issues and subsequently issued a circular wherein they addressed these concerns and directed that proper procedures must be followed. Moreover, it has also been assured that even if a physical hearing is not possible, adequate opportunity via video conferencing or any other method shall be provided but proper execution of the same is still obscure. The taxpayers' worries still seem to accentuate by the fact that virtual hearing may not be congruent with a physical one and can impair the process of decision making. Audi alteram partem even though is one of the primary principles of natural justice, is being disregarded in an inconsiderate way which is evident from the pleas filed by taxpayers in many cases such as DJ Surfactants v. NAC, IT Department, New Delhi [2021] 127 taxmann.com 641/281 Taxman 316 (Delhi), and Axis Wind Farms (Anantapur) (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [WP. No. 11812 of 2021, dated 30/4/2021] wherein while acknowledging the concerns of the taxpayers, various high courts have even granted them intermediate reliefs in form of stay orders against the assessments done under the new regime.

Time taken in the completion of the process remains another huddle in the way of smooth functioning. The entire Turant customs scheme aims at speedy processing as it was assured that the clearance process which usually took 3-4 days would be completed in a few hours. But as of now, this seems to be improbable because there are many instances where for the clearance process of the standard time of 48 hours, the actual time taken exceeded even 4-5 days. Since the scheme is still at a nascent stage, there is hope that this could be reduced to a large extent if not to the promised few hours. The long processing hours also raise concerns regarding demurrage expenses i.e. charges for occupying the port for more than allocated time for the taxpayers who now fear a more expensive trade process. Among other challenges, limited technological knowledge, unstable connectivity, and glitches in the new portal make it difficult to comply with the provisions which may be unjust to the assessee as highlighted in the case of SRC Chemicals (P.) Ltd. v. CBIC [2021] 131 taxmann.com 314 (Bom.) wherein the Bombay High Court granted a refund which could not be claimed earlier due to technical glitches. Concerns are also raised regarding the probability of future jurisdiction issues considering that FAGs are expected to have all India jurisdiction instead of territorial jurisdiction and also regarding the legality of the entire scheme.

India optimistically launched this initiative to pace up to its international counterparts like the UK and Australia who have introduced similar schemes for digital taxation in form of the 'Making Tax Digital Initiative' and 'Digital by Default program' respectively but a concrete verdict on successful implementation of all these schemes still hasn't seen the light of the day.

Conclusion

Faceless Assessment seems to be a good initiative but extension of the same to customs would involve a plethora of challenges and hurdles overcoming which would be a difficult task and the implementation would help us discern whether the new regime would be as pragmatic as it promises or would, as per the fears of taxpayers, turn out to be problematic. Customs involves much more complexities than income tax in terms of assessment and have different demands, creating a new mechanism to address all such demands is difficult but the department has made great efforts in trying to address as many issues as possible. Still, as mentioned above, there remain certain problems that endanger the success of the scheme. Moreover, the difference between planning and execution continues to be another issue on which the department needs work but both the department and the taxpayers must be optimistic for the changes to come with the hope of increased ease of business which shall be beneficial for both.

Section 85 - Appeals to Commissioner (Appeals) - Condonation of delay of 350 days Adjudication order dated June 18, 2004 was delivered to appellant on June 23, 2004 through registered post. Appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) was filed on January 25, 2006. The Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed appeal on ground that same was barred by limitation as appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) ought to have been filed within period of three months from date of communication, i.e., on or before September 22, 2004, and if, for some reason, appeal could not have been filed within period above-mentioned, it could have been filed beyond a further period of three months, i.e. , December 22, 2004. Section 86 - Appeals to Appellate Tribunal - Condonation of delay

The Tribunal cannot condone delay, which has occurred in filing of appeal before lower appellate authority. [Vijay Baburao Petkar’s case (supra)]. If an appeal is not filed by a party within time-limit stipulated in appeal provision, a legal right is accrued to other side on the ground that because of non-filing of appeal, order passed in favour of other side would have been accepted and reached its finality, and therefore, aforesaid legal right cannot be simply brushed aside by filing an application for condonation of delay of 350 days on ground that similar issue is stated to be pending before the Supreme Court. In case of export through merchant exporter, normally, property in goods passes to merchant exporter at the factory gate. Hence, that will be normally place of removal. However, in isolated cases, the port/ICD/CFS can be place of removal depending on facts of the case.

4.2 Validity of case law and departmental circular, after decision of Supreme Court – Though issue has become litigation prone, it can be argued that Supreme Court has only held that place of buyer cannot be 'place of removal'. Port is not the place of buyer. It can also be argued that port is a place 'referable to manufacturer', as the manufacturer continues to be owner of goods till goods are loaded in ship.

It can also be argued that when two interpretations are possible, an interpretation which promotes exports and which is beneficial to assessee should be adopted.

In any case, whatever assessee decides, it is advisable to inform department.

Cenvat Credit of Service Tax on Outward Freight and Outward Insurance

5. In view of clear decision of Supreme Court, place of buyer cannot be 'place of removal' of goods. Hence, Cenvat credit of service tax paid on outward freight and outward insurance of final products from place of factory of manufacturer to place of customer will not be available to manufacturer even if he pays excise duty on FOR price including outward freight and outward insurance.

Even when manufacturer pays excise duty on basis of MRP valuation or production capacity, the Cenavt credit of service tax paid on outward freight or outward insurance will not be available.

It is possible that the definition of 'place of removal' may be suitably amended or some administrative relief may be given.

As per third proviso to rule 4(1) and fifth proviso to rule 4(7) of Cenvat Credit Rules, amended w.e.f. 1-3-2015, the duty paying document is valid only for one year from date of duty paying document.

Thus, if assessee wants to safeguard his eligibility of Cenvat credit, he may take Cenvat credit and immediately reverse before utilisation. This should be done after informing department that he is doing so only to ensure that Cenvat credit is taken within one year from date of duty paying document.

Demands for Past Period

6. Demands for past period from department (in case of Cenvat Credit of service tax paid on outward freight and outward insurance), demands for past period are possible. In my view, demands for period prior to one year cannot sustain and will be held as time barred, though harassment cannot be ruled out.

If show cause notices have already been issued, then those assessees are unlucky. Demand with interest will become payable. Only relief from penalty can be claimed on basis of 'bona fide' belief.

In this year budget various changes are made in customs law in a direction of ease of doing business and reduction in the litigation. Some provisions have been amended to catch loopholes in the existing law. At this stage it may be mentioned that lot more could have been done which is opportunity missed. Some of the major changes are as under:

Definition of importer and exporter expanded to include beneficial owner of the goods

There were situations where the IEC was borrowed by the assessees/importers and the import documents were filed in name of the original IEC holderby some other persons. In case of any dispute, when the customs demand duty from the actual owner of the imported goods, then the actual owner use to take plea that he is not the importer thus duty cannot be demanded from him in terms of section 28 of the customs Act. The said practises were adopted for export goods also.

To curb the said practices, now definition of importer and exporter is expanded to include the beneficial owner of the goods. Thus after amendment of the definition of the importer and exporter, it would not be possible for the IEC borrower to argue that they are not the importer and duty cannot be demanded from them.

Further Section 17 of the Customs Act is amended to simplify the production of documents or information by the importer or exporter or any other person for verification of self-assessment. This amendment is in direction of ease of doing business.

Amendment in the provisions pertaining to refund

Earlier refund arising out of any reassessment was also subject to unjust enrichment. Now Section 27 of the customs Act providing for refund is amended to provide that refund arising out of following two situations would not be subject to unjust enrichment:

Where excess payment of the duty is evident form the self assessed bill of entry

Where duty actually payable is reflected in the reassessed bill of entry in case of reassessment

Thus in situations, where the importer paid duty twice on the very same imports or in a situation where the importer did not claim any available exemption or there is mistake in calculation of duty or other errors which lead to excess payment of customs duty, in all these case, the principal of unjust enrichment would not apply. Thus need for producing books of accounts and charted accountant's certificate showing the amount of excess customs duty as receivables from customs is not required. Thus this is welcome change.

However, the provision does not suggest if the said refund of excess duty is automatic and period of limitation for refund application would be applicable. Further it is also not clear as to whether the reassessment of bill of entry happening because of pending litigation/order of higher authority would also be part of this beneficial scheme.

Advance Ruing

It is now provided that that the Authority for Advance Rulings constituted under section 245-O of the Income-tax Act shall be the Authority for giving advance rulings for the purposes of the Customs Act and the Member of the Indian Revenue Service (Customs and Central Excise), who is qualified to be a Member of the Board, shall be the revenue Member of the Authority. It further provides that transferring the pending applications before the erstwhile Authority for Advance Rulings (Central Excise, Customs and Service Tax) to the Authority of advance ruling under Income tax. The application fee is enhanced to rupees ten thousand and time limit for pronouncing ruling is extended to six months.

Obligation on Person-In charge of vessel

New section 30A is inserted so as to make it obligatory on the personin-charge of a conveyance to deliver the passenger and crew arrival manifest to the customs officer before arrival in the case of an aircraft/vessel and passenger name record information of arriving passengers. The form and manner would be prescribed by Rules framed under Section 157 of the customs Act. In case of any delay in providing such information, the person in charge of a conveyance would be liable for penalty not exceeding fifty thousand Rupees. Corresponding provisions in case of departing vessels is incorporation in Section 41.

Section 46 of the Customs Act is amended and obligation is casted upon the importer to file bill of entry on next day of the arrival of the conveyance and in case of delay additional charges would be imposed. Further section 47 is also amended to provide for payment of interest in case of delay in payment of customs duty.

Section 49 of the customs Act is amended and it is now provided that the imported goods in respect of warehousing bill of entry is filed may also be stored in the public warehouses licenced under section 49 of the customs Act. This is also a good step in ease of doing business.

Section 82 of the customs Act providing for the treatment of label as entry for the goods imported and exported through courier is omitted from the Act and Section 84 is amended to give power to central government to frame rules in this regards.

Even after this amendment, in light of the above Circulars, the view of the Board seemed clear that place of removal has to be determined according to the place where transfer of property takes place. Hence, where the assessee was able to prove that the transfer of property took place at the customer's premises, the benefit of cenvat credit on outward GTA service was allowed as the condition of the input service of outward GTA, being availed 'upto the place of removal' was satisfied.

In my view, the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court has been rendered without considering the subsequent Circulars issued by the Board which have clarified the eligibility of cenvat credit as per the 'place of removal', even after the amendment to the definition of input service w.e.f 01.04.2008. If the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the eligibility of credit on outward GTA service, in all cases, to the factory gate, the same would have been incorporated in the definition of input service instead of the phrase, 'place of removal'.

Further, as per Section 4 of the Central Excise Act, 1944, in cases where there is sale of excisable goods on FOR basis, i.e the sale takes place at the customer's premises, the excise duty is payable on transaction value which is inclusive of freight element. In such cases, if a demand is raised by the Department, denying cenvat credit of service tax paid on such outward GTA service, the assessee would be hard hit as he would have to bear the burden of excise duty as well as service tax on the freight element. This nullifies the main objective of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004, which is to avoid the cascading effect of tax.

Be that as it may, the decision of the Hon'ble Apex court comes as a huge blow to the trade, as in all likelihood, the assessee would be faced with demands from the Department, along with huge interest liability, proposing to deny cenvat credit on outward GTA service used for transportation of goods from factory gate till the customer's premises. The Department may also rely upon the judgment to deny credit on outward GTA service used for transportation of goods till the port in case of export sale, since the Hon'ble Supreme Court has given a finding that the Circular dated 23.08.2007 cannot be made applicable for period post 01.04.2008. Further, after the advent of the Goods & Service Tax (GST) regime, since the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 are not in existence anymore, there is no scope of any relief in the form of retrospective amendment to the definition of 'input service'.

Another question that arises here is the limitation period for raising such demand as per Rule 14 of the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 read with Section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944. If the extended period of limitation is invoked by the Department for raising such demands, it would cause undue hardship to the assessee, as credit on outward GTA service was being allowed by various legal forums, subject to satisfaction of the three conditions mentioned in Circular dated 23.08.2007. Hence, in any case, the demand should be restricted to the normal period of limitation.

CBEC CIRCULARS

SUPREME COURT RULINGS ON EFFECT AND BINDING NATURE OF CBEC CIRCULARS

In some recent decisions under section 37B of the Central Excise Act relating to powers of CBEC to issue circulars, the Supreme Court has emphasised two aspects, viz., ( i) the circulars are binding on the department and it cannot take a stand contrary to the circular even in an appeal, and (ii) benevolent circulars will have retrospective effect whereas oppressive circulars will have prospective effect, and assessee has the right to claim that oppressive circulars are enforceable only prospectively. This article explains these decisions.

The Arviva Industries case

1. In the case of Union of India v. Arviva Industries (I) Ltd. 2007 (209) ELT 5 (SC), the question before the Supreme Court was whether circulars of the CBEC issued under section 37B of the Central Excise Act are binding on the department, and whether the department can take a stand at any stage that such circulars are not binding on it. This was a case relating to customs duty. The CBEC had issued a circular on 25-6-1999 extending the benefit of Brand Rate of Drawback to compensate exporters for the re-rolled steel products and processed fabrics. In an appeal by the revenue, the High Court held that the circulars issued by the CBEC were binding on the department. The department appealed against the High Court judgment and pleaded that the case may be referred to a larger Bench. The Supreme Court cited reference to a string of decisions, both under the Income-tax Act and the Central Excise Act, making it clear and settled that the departmental circulars are binding on the department, and rejected the plea of the department. The Supreme Court agreed with the view taken by the High Court that the circulars issued by the CBEC were binding on the department and that the department could not be permitted to urge that the said circulars were not binding on it. The Supreme Court also quoted with approval the following principles earlier enunciated by them in Commissioner of Customs v. Indian Oil Corporation (2004) 3 SCC 488:

(a)Although a circular is not binding on a court or an assessee, it is not open to the revenue to raise a contention that is contrary to a binding circular by the Board. When a circular remains in operation, the revenue is bound by it and cannot be allowed to plead that it is not valid nor that it is contrary to the terms of the statute.

(b)Despite the decision of this Court, the department cannot be permitted to take a stand contrary to the instructions issued by the Board.

(c)A show-cause notice and demand contrary to the existing circulars of the Board are ab initio bad.

(d)It is not open to the revenue to advance an argument or file an appeal contrary to the circulars.

The Mysore Electrical Industries Ltd. case

2. In the case of CCE v. Mysore Electricals Industries Ltd. 2006 (204) ELT 517 (SC), the question before the Supreme Court was whether an order under section 37B of the Central Excise Act re-classifying a particular commodity can be applied retrospectively. The assessee had filed a classification list in which it had classified a commodity under a particular heading of the Central Excise Tariff, and was paying duty at applicable rate of 5 per cent during the period 24-6-1993 to 22-11-1993 and 1-12-1993 to 27-2-1994. Under a CBEC circular dated 14-7-1994, the classification of this commodity was revised, according to which the duty payable was 20 per cent. Based on this circular, differential duty was demanded from the assessee for the above periods even though the periods fell before the date of the circular. The Tribunal held that the circular could not be given retrospective effect, and accordingly struck down the demand. When the department appealed to the Supreme Court, the assessee contended that the circular was oppressive and against the assessee and hence had to be applied prospectively and not retrospectively. The Supreme Court accepted this contention and dismissed the appeal. The Supreme Court also made it clear that ‘a beneficial circular has to be applied retrospectively while an oppressive circular has to be applied prospectively’ and that ‘when the circular is against the respondents (assessee), they have a right to claim the enforcement of the same prospectively’.

However, where the manufacturer has sold his goods to his dealer and wholesale dealer thereafter does ASS to the customer and incurs expenditure therefore, it cannot be added back to the sale price charged by the manufacturer from the dealer for computing the assessable value. This is more so, where the ASS is done by the dealer many weeks after the goods have been sold to him by the manufacturer. Such a post-sale activity undertaken by the dealer is not relevant for the purpose of excise since the goods have already been marketed to the dealer.

While SVB investigations are essential for ensuring accurate customs valuation, there are certain instances where such investigations are unnecessary, particularly when the revenue implications are negligible. Key exemptions include:

Samples and Prototypes: Imports involving samples or prototypes from related suppliers, which hold minimal commercial value, are exempt from SVB investigations.

Imports with Full Duty Exemption: Where the imported goods are fully exempt from customs duties or the applicable duty rate is nil, SVB investigations are not required, as there is no revenue impact.

Low-Value Imports: Transactions below Rs. 1 lakh, provided the cumulative value of such transactions does not exceed Rs. 25 lakhs in a financial year, are exempt from SVB scrutiny, ensuring that small-scale imports are not unnecessarily delayed.

7. Jurisdictional Framework of SVBs:

Currently, SVBs operate out of five key customs locations across India:

Bengaluru

Chennai

Kolkata

Delhi

Mumbai

The jurisdiction of an SVB is typically determined by the location of the importer's corporate or registered office.

8. Reform of Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) Provisions:

The earlier SVB regime was heavily criticized for its imposition of EDD—1% of the declared assessable value—which could be escalated to 5% in cases of non-compliance with document submission timelines. This was widely regarded as an excessive burden on trade. In response to industry representations, the government eliminated the requirement for EDD in Circular No. 05/2016.

However, under the revised regime, if an importer fails to submit the requisite documentation within 60 days, the customs authorities may impose a security deposit of 5%, valid for an initial period of three months. This deposit can be furnished in the form of either a cash payment or a bank guarantee, providing flexibility to the importer while ensuring compliance with customs requirements.

9. Conclusion:

The SVB's investigatory powers are pivotal in safeguarding the integrity of the customs valuation process, particularly in complex related-party transactions where the declared value may be subject to manipulation. The intricate interplay between contractual terms, such as royalties, and the customs valuation process necessitates careful oversight by SVBs to prevent undervaluation. Importers, for their part, can mitigate the time and cost implications of SVB investigations by ensuring full compliance with documentation requirements and maintaining transparency in their transactional relationships.

Subsequent resale or disposal: The value of any part of the proceeds of any subsequent resale, disposal or use of the imported goods that accrues, directly or indirectly, to the seller. [Rule 10(1)(d) of CVR, 2007]

Other connected payments: All other payments actually made or to be made as a condition of sale of the imported goods, by the buyer to the seller, or by the buyer to a third party to satisfy an obligation of the seller to the extent that such payments are not included in the price actually paid or payable. Finalization of Assessment :

a.

Declared Value is found confirming to Rule 3: Where the declared value as per Bill of Entry has been found confirming to the relevant rule of the CVR,2007 - the provisional assessment done by the customs houses shall be considered the final assessment and accordingly it must be finalized.

b.

Declared Value is found not confirming to Rule 3: Where the declared value as per Bill of Entry is found to be influenced by the relationship or such case as may be applicable, the proper office of the customs house shall issue a show cause notice to the importer within 15 days of the receipt of the Investigation Report (IR) from the Special Valuation Branch (SVB).

Wherever the imports have been cleared through multiple locations, jurisdictional commissioner shall after consulting with other locations, make a proposal for appointment of common adjudicating authority for the matter and after providing enough opportunity to the importer, pass a combined order quantifying the extent of influence on the declared transaction value.
