HEADNOTE: Section 2(23) of the Customs Act, 1962 - Import - Import-takes place when goods enter the land mast

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Valuation; Assessable value has to include unloading charges also, not merely port charges: but any bonus earned for quick unloading should be deducted

FACT: These are ten appeals which relate to the same respondent and involve common facts and issues; hence a combined order. The respondents are manufacturers of fertilizers and imported rock phosphate and sulphur in bulk quantities came to India on chartered ship. The goods were purchased on the high seas and unloading on the Indian coast was the responsibility of the respondents. For this they maintained their own wharf, unloading equipment and staff at Vishakhapatnam. 1.4% by way of landing charges stood already added to the price of the goods. The Assistant Collector held that this 1.4% did not include stevedoring charges which he added separately and recalculated the value at varying rates from Rs. 5.86 to Rs. 9.42 per MT. In appeal the Appellate Collr. set aside the Asst. Collr.'s orders and held that the 1.4% already added as landing charges were the same as unloading charges. The Department is now in appeal against the Appellate Collector's orders.

HELD: Place of importation has to be the land mass of India where goods are unloaded from the ship. Section 2(23). "Place of importation in section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, should take the similar meaning as place of removal of the imported goods, that is, the port gate. Delivery to the importer is effected only here."

2. Port landing charges comprise only wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds; any unloading charges incurred have to be included in the value for assessment in addition to the port landing charges. Section-14. "The 1.4% Port landing charge already added to the respondents, value comprised wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds and not unloading charges from ship to berth. The unloading charges have therefore to be computed and added too."

3. For calculating the unloading charges and despatch money earned because of unloading of chartered vessel before stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs, but if any money is paid as penalty for delayed unloading of the ships the same should be added.

".........despatch money earned because of unloading of the chartered vessel before the stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs. Conversely if the appellants have paid any penalty for delayed unloading of the ship the same should be added to the costs."

HEADNOTE: Section 119 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Central Board of Direct Taxes - Instructions issued by CBDT to subordinate authorities - Whether assessee was right in contending that circular dated 4-10-1969 would be applicable in its case since it was effective during relevant previous year and ITO was wrong in following circular dated 5-12-1974 which was issued while assessment proceedings were pending - Held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of production and distribution of cine pictures. During the previous year ended 18-10-1971, it had purchased the distributorship rights of six pictures. While making the assessments, the ITO followed the CBDT circular, dated 5-12-1974 and held that the cost of two pictures could be allowed as deduction in full against the income of the year and the cost of remaining four pictures was to be allowed only partially. The assessee contained that during the relevant previous year CBDT circular, dated 4-10-1969 was effective and that the ITO was bound to follow it. The AAC, however, upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal :

HELD: The circulars, instructions and directions of the Board are biding on the income-tax authorities as provided in section 119 but a circular is not law, and the assessee is not bound by it. If such circulars, directions or instructions are to the prejudice of the assessee, he may claim the benefit which was available to him under the provisions of law. However, the assessee cannot claim to be assessed in accordance with the old circular which stood modified by the Board’s subsequent circular when the assessment proceedings are pending particularly when the Board’s instruction clearly showed such an intention on the part of the Board.

The Board had specifically directed that all pending assessments may be completed in accordance with 1974 circular. Since the ITO was bound by the Board’s circular in terms of section 119, he was bound to follow the 1974 circular only.

hence, to infer exclusion of section 14 of Limitation Act or principles contained in section 14 would be unduly harsh and would not advance cause of justice; hence, time taken in pursuing remedy before wrong forum bona fide, would be excluded Section 128, read with  section 128A, of the Customs Act, 1962 - Appeals - Condonation of delay - Commissioner (Appeals) - Against an order of Superintendent dated 2-4-1992, passing in pursuance of policy framed by Commissioner, assessee filed appeal before Tribunal on 22-6-1992 - On 12-3-2003, Supreme Court held that appeal was maintainable only before Commissioner (Appeals) - On 23-5-2003, assessee filed appeal before Commissioner (Appeals), which was dismissed as barred by limitation beyond total '60 days plus 30 days' time-limit - Assessee argued that principles of section 14 of Limitation Act would apply to exclude time spent in pursuing remedy before wrong forum and old time-limit applicable before 2001 viz. 180 days, would apply - HELD : Since section 128 does not lay down a long period; hence, to infer exclusion of section 14 or principles contained in section 14 would be unduly harsh and would not advance cause of justice - Hence, time taken in pursuing remedy before wrong forum bona fide, would be excluded - Though periods of limitation are procedural in nature and would ordinarily be applied retrospectively; however, a new law prescribing a shorter period of limitation cannot extinguish existing period of limitation - Time began to run on 3-4-1992 under pre-amended section 128 and Right of appeal within a period of 180 days (including discretionary period of 90 days) from date of said order was a right which vested in assessee - On 12-3-2003, vested right of appeal within period of 180 days had not yet got over and a certain residuary period within which a proper appeal could be filed still remained - Time taken from 12-3-2003 to 23-5-2003, when added to time taken between 3-4-1992 and 22-6-1992, would be within 180 days provided by pre amended section 128 - Hence, present appeal was within time and matter was remanded back for decision on merits [Paras 47 to 53] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: Facts

The assessee is engaged in ship breaking activity at Alang Ship Breaking Yard. The assessee imported a vessel, namely, M.V. Olinda, for the purpose of breaking the same, and filed a Bill of Entry when the vessel was imported on 7-2-1992.

It declared in the said Bill of Entry that the Light Displacement Tonnage of the vessel was 7009 metric tons.

On 19-2-1992, the assessee was informed by the Superintendent of Customs and Central Excise Alang that the Light Displacement Tonnage of the ship is actually 8570 tons and that customs duty was to be levied on this tonnage.

On 3-3-1992, the assessee cleared the vessel on payment of customs duty on the basis of 7009 metric tons and executed a bank guarantee for Rs.19,90,275/- being the difference in customs duty on 1561 metric tons.

On 25-3-1992, the Collector of Customs, Rajkot, directed the Assistant Collector, Bhavnagar to encash the bank guarantee furnished by the assessee.

On 2-4-1992, the Superintendent of Customs and Central Excise sent a letter to the assessee communicating the decision of the Collector, as aforesaid. The bank guarantee was duly encashed on 3-4-1992.

After protesting against the said illegal action of the department in encashing the bank guarantee, the assessee preferred an appeal against the Superintendent's letter dated 2-4-1992 and the Collector's order dated 25-3-1992 before CEGAT.

On 23-6-1998, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Collector dated 25-3-1992.

In the year 2000, the Department preferred an appeal before this Court. On 12-3-2003 CC & CE v. M.P. Steel Corpn. 2003 taxmann.com 1543, the Supreme Court held that since order of Superintendent was passed in pursuance of a policy framed by Collector, it continued to be order of Superintendent and was appealable only before Collector (Appeals) and not Tribunal.

On 23-5-2003, the assessee filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) against the order passed by the Superintendent, Customs dated 2-4-1992 (i.e., within 60 days from date of order of the Supreme Court).

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Transactional value not acceptable for second-hand goods in perfect condition. Reasonable assessment does not call for interference - Undervaluation-Misdeclaration not being deliberate, confiscation and penalty unwarranted -111(d), 111(m)

FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand 1976 model, 4 colour, off-set printing machine and a second-hand 1983 model paper folding machine, both of German make, from the U.K. The declared value of these machines was £ 49,000 and £ 3000.00 respectively. Certificates from Chartered Engineers in support of the transactional value were furnished. However, since the current prices of the machines indicated in the certificates were much lower than the current price indicated by the local agents of the manufacturers of these machines and also because the prices quoted for the year of manufacture were found to be wrong, the Asstt. Collector rejected the certificates. There was a difference of Rs. 10,03,400 between the declared value and the assessable value arrived at by the Department. Alleging deliberate undervaluation with an intention to evade duty, the Asstt. Collector of Customs held both the machines liable to confiscation under section 111(m) of the Customs Act, 1962. The off-set printing machine was held to be liable to confiscation under section 111(d) as well as it was older than 7 years, which was in violation of the provisions of AM 1988-91 Import Policy. Aggrieved by the aforementioned order, the appellants have come in appeal.

HELD: Valuation-Undervaluation established, as machines were in perfect condition, with an expected residual life of 10-12 years, and the depreciation allowed by the adjudicating authority was reasonable. Transactional value not acceptable. "Market of second-hand goods also fluctuates with the market of new goods. If therefore, the certificates issued by the Chartered Engineers have given the prices of new goods at a lower level naturally their estimation of the prices of second-hand goods is also likely to be affected. To that extent the department was right in not placing reliance on the Chartered Engineers' certificates. ........so far as the offset printing machine is concerned, that it has been certified that the machine was found to be in perfect working condition and it had been well maintained and serviced and that no major repairs/reconditioning were necessary. Expected residual life of the machine is estimated at 10 to 12 years. The undisputed service the machine has already completed is about 14 years i.e. from 1976. It is also certified in the said certificate that the machine utilises the current generation of technology and therefore, compares with the latest machinery available in the international market. ........the depreciation of 70% allowed by the adjudicating authority on the price of the new goods in the year of its manufacture, cannot be said to be unreasonable at all. ........Similar comments and assessment of the said Chartered Engineers have been made in respect of the second-hand machine i.e. paper folding machine. .......for a total span of life of 17 to 19 years of the machine, the residual life of 10 to 12 years and other condition being perfect and good the depreciation of 65% allowed by the adjudicating authority cannot on the same reasons be considered unjust. ......We are, therefore, of the view that there has been undervaluation of the machines to the extent upheld in the adjudication order."

2. Freight Insurance—Actual charges being known, with no apparent reason to discard the same, notional charges not to be taken into account. "........the goods have been imported from U.K.. which is farther from India than Germany i.e. freight and insurance charges from Germany are, therefore, likely to be less than those from U.K. Accordingly in the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, there is no reason as to why the actual freight and insurance charges incurred by the appellants from U.K. should not be taken into account rather than the notional freight and insurance charges from Germany to U.K. If, however, the department can find the actual freight and insurance charges liable to be incurred from Germany to India in respect of such machine, they may take them into account. Benefit in respect of valuation of the goods on account of freight and insurance in the light of the above observations may, therefore, be extended to the appellants.

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Invoice value must be accepted unless proved incorrect by the department

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Show cause notice to the parties for change in invoice prices is necessary otherwise the decision to enhance the valuation can be set aside on this ground also

FACT: The appellants imported 15000 pcs. of Miniature Ball Bearings from Singapore and gave the invoice price as CIF 3000 Singapore Dollars i.e. Rs. 17,128.20. The Customs Department at Amritsar did not have the price for the goods and so requested Delhi Customs for the same. On getting the information from Delhi Customs, the Department issued a show cause notice to the party for adopting that rate for valuation i.e. 9.25 per piece However, the Asstt. Collector directed the duty to be paid on Rs. 18.40 per piece i.e. on total value of Rs. 21,76,000/- without giving any further show cause notice to the appellants. This rate of 18.40 per piece was obtained from the Central Warehousing Corporation. The appellants contended that the assessable value was to be based on the declared invoice prices unless the department could prove it incorrect. The department wanted the case to be remanded so that the party was given a proper opportunity of being heard on the evidence.

HELD: Valuation: Assessable value for levy of customs duty is to be based on the declared invoiced prices unless proved otherwise by the department. "The onus of proving misdeclaration regarding the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry is on the Department and this can be discharged by the Department only on proving of proper facts, which would discredit the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry and not on the basis of mere suspicion. It is, therefore, on this ground alone that the orders of the lower authorities merit to be set aside."

2. Show Cause notice to the parties for change in invoice prices is necessary otherwise the decision to enhance the valuation can be set aside on this ground also. "What amazes us, is that the show cause notice in this case alleges that the correct price of the imported bearings is Rs. 9.25 per piece whereas the order of the Additional Collector is based on the correct price being Rs. 18.40 per piece. The learned JDR has conceded that the order was passed without furnishing the additional evidence to the appellant and without giving any opportunity to show cause in respect of it. This further seriously undermines the legality of the order."

3. Dissenting view: Per Shri I.J. Rao: Case to be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication. "However, I feel that the omission on the part of the Collector should be allowed to be made good. While I agree that the order should be set aside, I hold that the matter should be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication after disclosing to the appellants the relevant evidence relied on by the department and after giving a reasonable opportunity to them to counter the evidence."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Natural justice - cross-examination regarding relevant telex cannot be denied. Matter remanded for de novo adjudication. Additional evidence can be filed even though disallowed in appellate proceedings

FACT: The appellants had imported a consignment of 'Dielectric Heater Components of Heat Training Systems, and claimed its clearance under OGL Item No. 476, appendix 6, list 8, part I of the Import & Export Policy 1985-88. However the Addl. Collr. held that for ITC purposes, the goods were classifiable under Sl. No. 462(a) of appendix 3A. He also did not accept the invoice price and ordered enhancement of the assessable value from Rs. 5,15,696/- to Rs. 10,71,721.70 under section 14(1)(h) of the Customs Act. He confiscated the imported goods with an option to redeem on payment of fine of Rs. 10,00,000 and also imposed penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 under section 112(a) of Customs Act. In their appeal to the Tribunal, the appellants sought permission for filing certain additional evidence and a similar request was received from the Department. The appellants also stated that they were denied the opportunity of cross-examination of the two officials whose advice was taken into account and that they were not confronted with the telex relied upon for upward revision of the value which has figured only in the adjudication order.

HELD: Natural justice--principles violated since cross-examination regarding relevant telex was denied to the appellants. Matter remanded to the adjudication authorities. Fresh evidence can be filed (ratio of Supreme Court judgment in Kalra Glue Factory v. Sales Tax Tribunal). "The appellants had pleaded for the cross-examination of Shri Prabhat Kumar which was not granted. We are of the view that there was dental of principles of natural justice.......We ate of the view that telex is very relevant for valuation, and the appellant should have been confronted with the same, and an opportunity should also be given for rebuttal. ...we are of the view that the matter should be remanded. Since cross-examination was also denied, we are of the view that there was denial of principles of natural justice. ......we remand the matter to the adjudicating authority having jurisdiction and give an opportunity to the appellants to cross-examine them. Both the sides are at liberty to file any fresh evidence to substantiate their case in accordance with law. We further order that re adjudication will be done within three months from the receipt of this order."

2. Additional Evidence--The lower authority is free to decide the request of the appellants for admission of any additional evidence on merits as per law for the purpose of de-novo adjudication proceedings before him, even though it was disallowed in the appellate proceedings. "...I would like to observe that learned Brother while he has disallowed the admission of additional evidence......he has observed in the operative portion of the order that both the sides are at liberty to file any fresh evidence to substantiate their case in accordance with law. By way of clarification I would like to add that while we have disallowed the admission of the documents as above for the purpose of the appellate proceedings before us, the lower authority is free to decide the request of the appellants for admission of any additional evidence, as held by learned Brother, on merits as per law for the purpose of de novo adjudication proceedings before him."

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1949 - Writ - Maintainability of - Alternative Remedy - Writ can be invoked a second time if earlier appeal was not disposed of on merits, but was withdrawn to enable parties to come to a settlement and when settlement is prima facie wrong and perverse and delay has caused irreparable damage, alternative remedy is not a bar to maintainability. Valuation--precedent--identical goods cannot be assessed differently for different importers if customs have earlier cleared goods at those rates; quotation of higher rates is not proof of under invoicing. Valuation--clubbing together--different consignments for different importers cannot be clubbed together just because they can be assembled together to make a complete VCR; as individual consignment is for parts, they cannot be held to be in SKD condition. Cus. Act: S. 14. Precedent--ratio of Supreme Court and Cegat decisions must be considered by the authorities. Review--Collector has no review power under the Customs Act and Rules; he can only issue notice, U/s. 129D, so his reviewing his earlier decision is bad in law, Cus. Act: S. 129D, Imports  Exports (Control) Act: S. 167(8)

FACT: The petitioner is an importer of various electronic components of T.V., V.C.R. electronic type-writers etc. In 1987 the petitioner imported two consignments of Printed Circuit Board Sub-Assembly, Remote Control and Miscellaneous Hardware. He also purchased V.C.R. parts from the recognised export houses on 'High seas sales basis'. The goods were duly assessed and some of them kept at the customs bonded warehouse. The customs authorities meanwhile raided the business premises of the petitioners, and charged the petitioners with under-invoicing, and importing complete VCRs in the name of name-lender firms. Various demands were raised in lieu of short levy, fines and penalties, and the petitioner paid under protest a total sum of Rs. 11,11,990.11 and got released the goods, being under pressure to resume production in his factory which was lying closed for want of materials.

HELD: Writ jurisdiction--Maintainability--There is no bar to invoking Writ Jurisdiction a second time on same issue, if the earlier appeal was not disposed of on merits, but was withdrawn to enable parties to come to a settlement. Where the settlement arrived at is prima facie wrong and perverse and delay has already caused irreparable damage to the petitioner, writ appeal is valid and maintainable. Alternative remedy is not a bar to maintainability in such a case. "There is no doubt in my mind that there was some understanding between the writ petitioner and the respondents regarding the manner and mode of assessment to be made. But for one reason or other, the respondents did not rise up to the expectation. The writ petition and the appeal arising out of such writ petition were withdrawn in the expectation that the respondents would judiciously load the value. ........The writ application was not dismissed on merits. It was allowed to be withdrawn to enable the parties to arrive at a settlement. .......As the settlement failed, which is demonstrated by the order of adjudication, the petitioner has challenged the validity of such order. .......Accordingly, it cannot be said that the petitioner cannot invoke the writ jurisdiction for the second time. ......In this case, Collector had adjudicated and passed an order which is highly prejudicial to the petitioner. If this order has to be challenged in the appropriate forum, the petitioner may not get the desired relief for long time to come. This aspect of the matter cannot be overlooked in considering whether the application is maintainable or not. ........On the facts and in the circumstances of this case, I am of the view that the order of adjudication is illegal and manifestly, arbitrary and unreasonable and delay would cause irreparable loss and prejudice to the petitioner. In the premises, the contention that the writ petition is not maintainable cannot be accepted."

HEADNOTE: Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Levy of additional duty - Additional duty (CVD) of customs is calculated on the aggregate of CIF value plus basic duty and any other customs duty

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Additional duty of customs (CVD) is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India--Value for assessment is the landed cost including charges upto point of clearance

Section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Exemption from Customs duty - Exemption notification can be availed of only where its conditions are satisfied--Notification 302/79-CE

FACT: The petitioners imported in February 1983, 51 metric tonnes of High Density Polyethylene Moulding Powder. Customs duty and auxiliary duty was levied on the item at the rate of 50% and 25% respectively of the c.i.f. value and the additional or countervailing duty was fixed at the rate of 42% of c.i.f. value added on to customs duty. The petitioners contended that loading of customs duty on c.i.f. value for the purpose of arriving at countervailing duty is not permissible; that there should be partial exemption of countervailing duty as prescribed by Notification No. 302/79-CE and that landing and port charges were not to be added on the dutiable value of the imported item.

HELD: Additional duty (CVD) duty--Customs duty to be added on to c.i.f. value while determining countervailing duty. "The sub-section opens with the words for the purpose of calculating under Section 3 the additional duty on any imported article....'. It further recites that the value of the imported article shall be the aggregate of (a) the value of the imported article determined under sub-section (1) of Section 14, and (b) any duty of customs chargeable on that article under Section 12 of the Customs Act. In view of the clear statutory provision, it is futile for Dr. Kantawala to submit that the customs duty cannot be loaded on c.i.f. value while determining assessable value for the purpose of additional or countervailing duty." [Section 3(2) of Customs Tariff Act, 1975].

2. Value of imported goods not determined at point of entry--all expenses till goods are cleared from port form part of the value of imported goods. "In our judgment, the taxable event continues till the goods are cleared at Customs barrier for home consumption and all the expenses which are required to be incurred in respect of those imported goods form part of the value of those goods and it is not permissible for the importer to suggest that the value of goods should be determined at the point of time of entry into territorial waters and all expenses incurred thereafter are post-import expenses."

3. Exemption Notification No. 302/79-CE--its impact on countervailing duty--advantage of Notification available only after fulfilling both conditions of the said notification. "The advantage of the notification dated December 4, 1979 is available provided both the conditions are satisfied, the conditions being that the goods are manufactured from raw naphtha and on which the appropriate amount of excise duty has already been paid. It is obvious that the imported goods cannot satisfy the second condition, because the payment of excise duty on raw naphtha can never arise in respect of imported goods." [Notification No. 302/79-CE; CE Rule 8(i)]

4. Additional Duty (CVD): Duties imposed under Section 3(2) of CTA are neither void nor unconstitutional. "It is impossible to accede to the submission of the learned counsel. The two categories of tax-payers cannot be bracketed in the same class and it would be improper to suggest that the goods locally manufactured and the goods imported form the same class. In our judgment, the two categories of goods are not at all comparable and totally distinct and different. Levy of countervailing duty on the value ascertained by addition of customs duty to c.i.f. value cannot be claimed to be discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. .....In our judgment, the Section does not suffer from any vice and cannot be struck down."

FACT: Under the provisions of he Customs Act 1962, the assessee was entitled to pay import duty at concessional rates on spare parts and tools if their value did not exceed 10 per cent of the total value of imported machinery, but if the value exceeded this percentage, he was required to pay duty at higher rates. Section 143 of the Customs Act, 1962, also permitted the assessee to execute a bond, agreeing to pay the difference in duty when demanded by the customs authorities. For the assessment years 1973-74 to 1976-77, the assessee had executed such a bond and imported goods on which only provisional assessments at concessional rates of duty had been made by the customs department and the assessee had also paid duty at such conces-sional rates only. However, since the value of the imported goods exceeded the specified percentage, the assessee made provision in its accounts towards additional customs duty payable, and claimed it as a deduction. The ITO disallowed the claim since no demand had been raised by the customs department. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the claim.

On second appeal:

HELD: In T.M. Abdul Rahim Sahib & Co. v. CIT [1963] 50 ITR 508 , the Madras High Court had held that there can be no liability either notional or legal unless and until a demand had been made by the appropriate authority.

In view of the provisions of section 143 of the Customs Act, the liability for the payment of additional duty arises only when final assessment has been made. The words used in section 143 are 'notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or such other law'. Irrespective of the other provisions in the Act or any other law or item 72A of the Indian Customs and Central Excise Tariff, once a bond is executed under section 143, it is the terms of that bond that would prevail and the other provisions of the Act or any other law or tariff would not be applicable. After the provisional assessment is made, additional liability will arises only when final assessment is made and final demand is raised. Till then there is no liability for additional duty.

Consequently, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in allowing the assessee's claim.

SECTION 145 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961—METHOD OF ACCOUNTING— VALUATION OF WORK-IN-PROGRESS—WHETHER ASSESSEE COULD CHANGE METHOD OF VALUATION OF WORK-IN-PROGRESS FROM MATERIAL COST PLUS DIRECT WAGES TO MATERIAL COST ONLY—HELD, NO

HEADNOTE: Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 - Computed value - ITC Policy 85-88 - Project export--Valuation--assessment without notice to party is violation of principles of Natural Justice--Remanded. Customs Valuation Rules: Rule 8

FACT: The appellants imported from Iraq three lots of 8-10 year old used machinery under ITC Policy 85-88, under the heading 'Project Export'. They declared value of these machinery on the basis of assessment by an independent Chartered Engineer from Iraq. The Asstt. Collr. rejected the certificate of valuation in respect of the third lot and assessed FOB value by allowing the usual 3 years depreciation from the estimated CIF value of new machinery. Hence the appeal.

HELD: Natural Justice:--Enhancement of assessable value to the prejudice of the appellants, without issuing a show cause notice to them is against the principles of natural justice and cannot be upheld. "While enhancing the assessable value to the prejudice of the appellants, by rejecting the declared price of the equipment and machinery which was followed in respect of previous imports, and the contract/agreement for freight and insurance, the Assistant Collector ought to have issued a show cause notice asking them why the declared price, freight & insurance ought not to be accepted. An illegible "Query memo" and reply thereto cannot be treated as a substitute to the "show cause notice" and personal hearing......The order of the Assistant Collector is in violation of principle of natural justice and is liable to be set aside."

CBEC had also issued a circular dated 10-2-1986 intimating that the effective rate of customs duty would be Rs. 550 only from 1-3-1981 to 18-12-1985, and this notification had the effect of cancelling the auxiliary duty. Since the above notification and circular issued by the CBEC fell within the relevant assessment year, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer for this year.

On second appeal : HELD: There was no dispute about the applicability of section 41(1) in the instant case. The only dispute was when the liability to pay customs duty ceased. In other words, the issue was in which year the benefit in respect of customs duty liability by way of remission or cessation thereof accrued to the assessee and when the amount due to cessation of liability had been obtained by the assessee. The assessee company as well as other newspaper companies had filed writ petitions challenging the levy of customs duty by the Government. The Supreme Court vide order dated 6-12-1984 directed the Government of India to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and refix the rate of customs duty afresh, with effect from 1-3-1981. If on such reconsideration the Government decided that there should be any modification in the levy of customs duty or auxiliary duty with effect from 1-3-1981 it would take necessary steps to implement its decision. Until such redetermination of the liability, the Government was directed to recover only Rs. 550 per MT on imported newsprint towards customs duty and auxiliary duty and would not insist upon payment of duty in accordance with the impugned notifications. It was further stipulated in the Supreme Court’s order that even after such redetermination if it was found that any of the petitioners was liable to pay any deficit amount by way of duty, such deficit amount would be paid by such petitioner within four months from the date on which a notice of demand was served on such petitioner by the concerned authority. It was clear from the above order of the Supreme Court that the Government of India was directed to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on newsprint used for printing newspaper, periodicals, etc., with effect from 1-3-1981. Therefore, as on 6-12-1984 the liability of the assessee to pay customs duty, etc., had not ceased because the matter regarding payment of customs duty was to be considered by the Government. As a result of the directions of the Supreme Court, the Government of India had issued notification dated 19-12-1985 and the CBEC also issued a departmental circular on 10-2-1986 determining the customs duty in respect of imported newsprint. It was clear from the notification as well as circular that after examination of the question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on imported newsprint the Government had fixed the rate at Rs. 550 per MT. The notification as well as circular dates fell in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, i.e., 1987-88. Therefore, as a result of the notification and circular of the CBEC the assessee’s liability to pay customs duty had ceased in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88. The assessee thus obtained the benefit in respect of customs duty by way of remission or cessation thereof and the amount obtained by it and/or the value of benefit accrued to it had to be deemed as its profits and gains of business for the assessment year 1987-88. The customs authority by issuing the notice of demand had given effect to the notification dated 19-12-1985 issued by the Government of India and Circular dated 10-2-1986 of CBEC. A notice of demand did not have the effect of cessation or remission of liability of the assessee. The liability of an assessee ceased only under Notification dated 19-12-1985 of the Government of India read with circular of the customs authority dated 10-2-1986. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in confirming the addition made to the total income of the assessee for the assessment year 1987-88 after making necessary adjustments regarding claim, if any, disallowed under section 43B earlier while determining the amount assessable.

The benefit in respect of cessation of customs liability by way of remission or cessation thereof had to be taxed in the assessment year 1987-88 because the assessee obtained the benefit in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88 and if the assessee did not make entry in the relevant accounting year it would not effect operation of the provisions of section 41(1).

Section 36(1)(vii), read with section 36(2), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Bad debts - Assessment year 1987-88 - Whether where there was nothing to show that amount of bad debt had been taken into account in computation of assessee’s income for previous year in which amount of such debt or part thereof was written off and facts revealed that parties were making counter claims against each other, bad debt was rightly disallowed - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Valuation - Customs and Auxiliary Duty both to be included while calculating assessable value for levy of additional duty on consignments of 2-Etaylhexanol (Octanol) a kind of alcohol

FACT: The petitioners imported 2-Etaylhexanol (Octanol) and paid customs & auxiliary duty. The Customs authorities demanded additional duty by including customs duty while determining assessable value. The petitioners filed a petition. Before clearing the goods the petitioners came to know that imported goods were a kind of alcohol on which countervailing duty was not payable but as the customs authorities did not accept their claim the petitioners paid the countervailing duty and amended their petition for refund of countervailing duty of Rs. 3,02,779.40.

HELD: Assessable value--Additional duty--Customs duty includible--the petitioner's contention that customs duty cannot be included while calculating assessable value for levy of additional duty is not correct [ratio of Bombay High Court judgment in Ashok Traders, Kandivli v. UOI & Anr. 1988 (14) ECR 12 (Bombay)]. "Shri Dalvi, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submitted that the amount of customs duty cannot be included while calculating the assessable value for levy and collection of additional duty. The submission is not correct in view of the decision of the Division Bench of this Court....... (Ashok Traders v. Union of India & Another)."

2. Countervailing duty--the petitioner's submission that the levy of countervailing duty by the Department is unlawful is correct as the duty was not payable [ratio of Bombay High Court judgment in Raman Kantilal Bhandari v. UOI & Ors. 1987 (11) ECR 84 (Bombay)]. "The second submission urged by the learned counsel is that the levy of countervailing duty by the Department, was clearly without authority of law. This submission deserves acceptance in view of the decision of single Judge reported in............ (Raman Kantilal Bhandari v. Union of India & Ors.) and which decision is confirmed by Division Bench in the decision........ (Union of India and Others v. Raman Kantilal Bhandari)."

HEADNOTE: Section 18, read with sections 28 and 28AA, of the Customs Act, 1962 and article 226 of the Constitution of India - Interest - On delayed payment of duty/tax - Period prior to 13-7-2006 - Assessee's provisional assessment for December, 1999 to February, 2005 was finalized in 2011-12 and assessee paid differential duty without interest - Department passed order under section 28 demanding interest - Assessee filed writ petition challenging adjudication order on ground that interest was not leviable, as provisional assessments took place prior to 13-7-2006, when there was no provision for levy of interest in section 18 - Department argued that writ was not maintainable against adjudication order in view of alternate appeal remedy - HELD : Since, prior to 13-7-2006, there was no provision in section 18 to charge interest, demand for interest could not be confirmed under section 28 - Since adjudication order was passed without even considering binding precedent of jurisdictional High Court, High Court could interfere in exercise of its writ jurisdiction - Hence, demand for interest was set aside [Paras 10 to 20] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : In case of provisional assessments carried out for period prior to 13-7-2006, there was no provision for interest under section 18 of Customs Act; hence, no demand for interest can be raised by resort to provisions of section 28

FACT: Assessee's provisional assessment for December, 1999 to February, 2005 was finalized in 2011-12 and assessee paid differential duty without interest.

Department passed order under section 28 demanding interest.

Assessee filed writ petition challenging adjudication order on ground that interest was not leviable, as provisional assessments took place prior to 13-7-2006, when there was no provision for levy of interest in section 18.

Department argued that writ was not maintainable against adjudication order in view of alternate appeal remedy.

HELD: It is a well settled legal proposition that where an alternative remedy is available, the High Court would ordinarily not exercise powers under article 226 of the Constitution of India. However, it is equally true that there is no absolute proposition of law that where an alternative remedy is available, the High Court would refuse to exercise powers under article 226 of the Constitution even if the facts so justify. Non-entertainment of petitions under writ jurisdiction by the High Court when an efficacious alternative remedy is available is a rule of self-imposed limitation. It is essentially a rule of policy, convenience and discretion rather than a rule of law. Undoubtedly, it is within the discretion of the High Court to grant relief under article 226 despite the existence of an alternative remedy. However, the High Court must not interfere if there is an adequate efficacious alternative remedy available to the assessee and he has approached the High Court without availing the same unless he has made out an exceptional case warranting such interference or there exist sufficient grounds to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction under article 226. Some exceptions to the rule of alternative remedy are where the statutory authority has not acted in accordance with the provisions of the enactment in question, or in defiance of the fundamental principles of judicial procedure, or has resorted to invoke the provisions which are repealed, or when an order has been passed in total violation of the principles of natural justice. [Para 10]

In the present case, it is the case of the assessee that the adjudicating authority has not acted in accordance with the provisions of the Customs Act and in defiance of the law laid down by the jurisdictional High Court. On the facts as emerging from the record, and for the reasons that follow, this Court is of the view that the availability of an alternative statutory remedy of appeal, would not preclude the Court from entertaining this writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [Para 12]

A perusal of the show cause notice issued to the assessee shows that it has been issued on the ground that the assessee has not paid interest on customs duty which was required to be paid as per the provisions of sub-section (3) of section 18 as well as for recovery of such amount under section 28. However, in the impugned order, the adjudicating authority, before whom various decisions of the Tribunal as well as of this Court had been pointed out in support of the contention that the provisions of section 18(3) would not apply in the present case as the same related to a period prior to insertion of sub-section (3) of section 18, has totally sidestepped the issue, ignored the decision of the jurisdictional High Court and has held the assessee liable for payment of interest on differential duty under section 18(3).

HEADNOTE: Section 129E of the Customs Act, 1962 - Pre-deposit of duty pending appeal - Stay - demurrage charges - predeposit waived

FACT: The point for decision in the appeal is whether rule 9 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 prescribes the inclusion of demurrage charges in the assessable value. The appellants have sought waiver of pre-deposit of Customs duty demanded from them on the demurrage charges incurred by them.

HELD: Stay--Pre-deposit of duty demanded on demurrage charges waived and stay granted till the disposal of the appeal in view of prima facie case. "We, therefore, in this prima facie view, waive the pre-deposit of the duty amount and grant the stay on its realisation during the pendency of these proceedings."

HEADNOTE: Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Provisional assessment of custom duty - Expeditious decision advisable to avoid unnecessary litigation. Department undertakes to finalise pending assessments within 6 months

FACT: Right from 1987, nearly 70 writ petitions similar to the present petitions had been filed pertaining to the import of Ball Bearings manufactured in China and in all the cases, the petitioners had obtained orders for the clearance of their goods on the basis of provisional assessment and the Department was permitted to complete the assessment in accordance with law. However, not a single assessment of this nature had been completed so far. In view of this, although the petitioners wished to withdraw the petitions, the Court asked the Department to file affidavits explaining why no final assessment had been done so far and why the petitioners had to take recourse to this remedy when they could have opted for provisional assessment under section 18, Customs Act.

HELD: Affidavits filed by the Department do not give any satisfactory explanation for the course of action adopted by the Department. Importers cannot wait indefinitely for assessment and the Department should have completed the assessment within a reasonable time. "The affidavit which has been filed leaves much to be explained. The entire grievance in paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 of this affidavit, to the effect that (he petitioners have rushed to the Court and obtained orders without waiting for assessment, has no merit as it is seen that right from the year 1987, the Respondents have, in not a single case of this type, completed the assessment. The importers cannot therefore be expected to wait indefinitely for assessment..........The Respondents, however, have been fully aware throughout, that they are at liberty to complete the assessment. No explanation is given as to why they have not done so for the last four years."

2. Valuation--Department directed to assess Ball Bearings imported from China in accordance with Customs Valuation Rules,. 1988 on the basis of evidence adduced by the importers. "For the purpose of valuation, the Respondents are bound by the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 which prescribe the methods of valuation of imported goods. The Respondents shall determine the value of Ball Bearings imported from China in the cases before them on the basis of the evidence produced before them by the importers in each of these cases and on the basis of any material which may be in the possession of the respondents of which inspection shall be given to the importers, and the same shall be done in accordance with law, including, needless to add, the above Rules."

3. Department submits that all assessments pertaining to Ball Bearings imported from China will be completed promptly. Assessment of goods already cleared on provisional assessment to be completed within 6 months. "Mr. Sethna, who appears for the Respondents, has stated before us........that in all cases relating to Ball Bearings, where it is not proposed to permit clearance of Ball Bearings on provisional assessment of duty under Section 18 of the Customs Act, a show cause notice will be issued to the importer within two weeks of the filing of the Bill of Entry. And after the reply is received, the assessment shall be completed within four weeks thereafter and the order shall be communicated to the importers within that time. In respect, however, of pending assessments relating to the import of Ball Bearings, where goods are already cleared on provisional assessment, the Respondents shall complete final assessments Within six months from today."

Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 has to be consistent with the provisions of Section 14(1) of Customs Act, 1962, it has to be held that the Additional Collector was justified in holding that the declared value in respect of the imported goods, being widely at variance with the international price of the goods prevailing at or about the same time when the goods being valued were imported, did not represent the transaction value under Rule 4." 4. Valuation--The adjudicating authority was not right in determining the value of the goods under Rule 8, bypassing Rules 5, 6 and 7, without recording reasons therefor. In terms of Rule 3, the provisions of Customs (Determination of the Price of Imported Goods) Rules have to be applied sequentially. The Addl. Collector's order is not a speaking order and shows non-application of mind. The matter is remanded for reconsideration and disposal within two months. ".......after having held that the declared value or the price paid for the goods could not be deemed as the Transaction Value' the adjudicating authority observed that the value of the imported goods is also not determinable under Rules 5, 6 and 7. Thereafter, he proceeded to determine the value under Rule 8. It is seen that in terms of Rule 3, the provisions of the Customs (Determination of the Price of Imported Goods) Rules 1988 have to be applied sequentially. Hence, the Additional Collector ought to have recorded the reasons for holding that the assessable value of the goods was not determinable in terms of each of the Rules 5, 6 and 7. We find that even while determining the value under Rule 8, the adjudicating authority has not taken into account the fact that the quantity imported by the appellants was larger than quantity covered by the invoices relied upon by the department. For these reasons, we are of the view that the order passed by the Additional Collector in as far as it relates to the valuation of the imported goods is not a speaking order and shows non-application of mind. We are, therefore, of the view that this matter needs to be remanded for reconsideration."

5. Valuation--The assessable value of the goods has to be determined taking into account the actual weight of the goods, as they have been charged by the supplier on weight basis. "........we are not inclined to accept the appellants' contention that the higher weight found of the consignment does not warrant the enhancement of the value since the excess weight could be due to the variation in the thickness of the material. Since the goods have been charged by the supplier on weight basis, their assessable value has necessarily to be determined by taking into account the actual weight of the goods. Hence, we reject the appellants' plea that the assessable value of the goods would continue to be the Transaction value' even when the quantity of goods with reference to weight has been found to be in excess of the invoiced quantity."

6. Penalty--The Addl. Collector has not given a reasoned finding after applying his mind to the question whether the weight of the goods declared by the appellants was an innocent misdeclaration. The question whether the appellants are liable for penalty shall be decided by the Addl. Collector in the de novo proceedings. "........while deciding whether the appellants were liable to penalty, the Additional Collector should have given a reasoned finding after applying his mind to the question whether the weight of the goods declared by the appellants was an innocent misdeclaration on the basis of the shipping documents received by them."

HEADNOTE: Section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation of imported goods - Rate of duty - relevant date--increased rate applicable at the time of clearance cannot be charged once the goods have been assessed to duty and passed out of customs charge

FACT: In 1981 the petitioners imported consignments of Nonyl Phenol Ethylene Oxide and Methylene Chloride and cleared the same to the bonded warehouse. In 1983 they were served notices advising them that the goods would be sold of not cleared within 10 days and accordingly the customs duty and demurrage charges were paid on 28.2.1983. The petitioners' request on 1.3.1983 to allow the clearances of the said goods was not granted except on payment of the increased customs duty that had come into effect the same day. This petition impugns the demand by the respondents of the increased customs duty.

HELD: Enhanced customs duty cannot be claimed as the goods were "passed out of customs charges". "...on 28th February 1983 ex-bond warehouse operations were to be stopped at 4 p.m. The circular instructs those to whom it is addressed not to allow ex-bond home consumption withdrawals which are sought to be effected after closing hours on 28th February 1983 'even though the Bill of Entry may have been noted before....' In the instant case, we have a situation where Customs duty on the said goods was paid at 2.30 p.m. on 28th February 1983 and the six bills of entry were marked 'passed out of Customs charges'. Therefore, assuming all else, this circular did not entitle the respondents to refuse clearance of the said goods on 28th February 1983. The Respondents cannot, therefore, validly lay claim to the enhanced Customs duty on the said goods that came into effect on the next day."

to the appellate authority. No fetters can be imposed on quasi-judicial authority, as section 37-B of the Central Excise Act and section 151-A of the Customs Act provide that no interference is called for in the case of quasi-judicial appellate authority. The instruction in the present case can be no better when compared to the circulars/notification issued under section 37-B of the Central Excise Act or section 151-A of the Customs Act. [Para 20] The Supreme Court and the High Courts have, while interpreting the scope of interim orders passed by the Appellate Authority, held that not only the undue hardship is relevant, but prima facie case also can be considered. It goes to show that the filing of an appeal and the application under section 35-F of the Central Excise Act or section 129-E of the Customs Act is not an empty formality. A substantial right granted by the statute cannot be casually set at naught by the circular/instruction. It has to be consistent with the statutory right of the assessees. [Para 21]

No recovery can be made in delay in disposing stay application is not attributable to assessee :

The non-consideration of the stay/waiver applications, at times, is because of lack of members to constitute the coram for a bench in the case of Tribunal. [Para 24]

Insofaras Commissioner (Appeals) is concerned, large number of stay petitions are pending disposal. In spite of assessees request for early hearing of the stay/waiver applications the same has not been considered or decided. The inability on the part of the assessees to obtain interim orders is not on account of any delay or inaction on their part, but only due to the administrative difficulties expressed by the Office of the Commissioner (Appeals) and also due to the non-functioning of the Tribunal with its full complement of members for a substantial period of time. [Para 25]

Circulars are more in the nature of guidance to the field formations and cannot bind the Court or the assessee. Circulars issued by the board are not binding on the assessee and cannot override the decision of the Court. Circulars are meant to ensure proper administration of the statute. [Paras 27 to 29]

Present circular/instruction, which though not relatable to section 37-B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 or section 151-A of the Customs Act, 1962 can at best be taken as an instruction to the field formations to initiate proceedings for recovery of revenue dues which the assessee or the importer has failed to pay having suffered an order passed by the adjudicating authority and is pending in appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the CESTAT, as the case may be. It is not mandatory to effect recovery immediately after 30 days as mentioned, as such an intention is not there in the statute. The circular/instruction directs the recovering authority to initiate proceedings for recovery. In the event of stay/waiver application pending and on intimation, the authority should refrain from proceeding further in the recovery proceedings pending an order in the application for stay/waiver. The circular/instruction has no statutory backing for initiating recovery proceedings and hence it is to be read as directory and not mandatory. [Para 30]

Recovery cannot be found fault with but coercive recovery cannot be made, as it would defeat object of right of appeal with stay of demand :

For recovery of dues payable to the revenue, proceedings can be initiated thirty days after filing of the appeal or any time thereafter and the same cannot be found fault with. But the action of the department in resorting to coercive recovery proceedings at an early date without taking into consideration the pendency of the stay/waiver application before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal would necessarily work hardship to the assessees. The right granted under the statute cannot be whittled down by fixing a time limit in an instruction even though the Appellate Authority has not taken up the matter at the stage of waiver of pre-deposit or for stay. The right provided under a statute should not be denied only on the basis of the impugned circular/instruction. [Para 31]

The board has been mulling over this issue as to what should be the correct time limit for initiating recovery proceedings, as the statute is silent on the issue. Different yardsticks have been used from time to time, but one common factor appears to be that the board was conscious of the fact that after filing of the appeal, if stay/waiver applications are filed, reasonable period of time should be granted. In some cases, time limit has been fixed and in some cases it has not been specified. In the present case, the board has clearly fixed the time limit. The question is if the stay/waiver application is not taken up by the appellate forum, can the assessee/appellant be found fault with. The Supreme Court decision in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1999 (73) ELT 519 supra, relied upon did not give a mandate for fixing a time-limit for recovery. All that it stated is that mere filing of appeal is no stay of proceedings. [Para 32]

of an executive direction. It would be wholly unjustified to recover the amount even though, the assessee has filed appeal and an application but the Appellate Authority is not able to decide the applications within 30 days. [Para 38]

Since, the statute has not provided for such consequence, the executive cannot order the recovery of the amount only for the reason, that the application for waiver of pre-deposit has not been decided by the Appellate Authorities. [Para 38] Under section 35F, the Appellate Authority has a power to waive or reduce the amount of pre-deposit, but such power is sought to be taken away only if the Commissioner (Appeals) is not able to decide the application for stay within 30 days. Such a condition is relevant and meaningful, if the Central Government is in a position to ensure that all appeals and/or the applications for dispensation of duty demanded and penalty levied can be decided within a period of 30 days. [Para 39]

If the Central Government has no power to control the working of the Appellate Authorities and also to ensure that all appeals are decided within the time frame, such condition is wholly unwarranted. The assessee has also no control over such Authorities. The Commissioner (Appeals), a quasi-judicial Tribunal, has a jurisdiction to waive the condition of pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied, but such judicial discretion vested in the Authority under the Act cannot be interfered with in any manner administratively. [Para 39]

Since the statute confers a right of appeal on the assessee and also right to make an application to dispense with deposit of the duty demanded and penalty levied in the manner which the Appellate Authority deems appropriate. Therefore, unless such jurisdiction is exercised by the Appellate Authority either way i.e., to grant benefit of waiver or impose such conditions as it may consider appropriate, the Board cannot direct the Administrative Officers to recover the demand raised against the assessee. The statutory right of appeal or of consideration of an application for pre-deposit cannot be frustrated administratively. [Para 40]

An aggrieved party such as an assessee could only file appeal along with an application for waiver of the pre-deposit. It is, thereafter, for the public functionary i.e., Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal to pass an order on such appeal and/or application. The decision on appeal and on application is not within the power and control of the assessee, but depends upon the acts of public functionary. The provisions of a statute relate to performance of a public duty. The failure of the Appellate Authority to decide appeal and/or application would work serious general inconvenience or injustice to persons who have no control over those entrusted with the duty. [Para 41]

The Commissioner (Appeals) is discharging a public duty and that failure to decide an application for waiver of deposit would lead to serious injustice to the assessee, who has no control over the Commissioner (Appeals), who is entrusted with the duty to decide such application. Therefore, such provision is only directory. [Para 43]

Basis on which Circular was issued was arbitrary - Condition of recovery pending stay application read down - Recovery only if delay in disposition is due to fault of assessee :

The Circular was purportedly issued in terms of judgment in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The said judgment lays down that mere filing of an appeal does not operate as stay or suspension of the order appealed against. But the Board over-looked the fact that the assessee is not seeking stay only on account of filing of an appeal, but for the reason that the assessee has sought dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied and has a right to demand decision on such application, the right which is created by the statute. Therefore, the very basis of the Circular is untenable, misconceived, wholly illegal and arbitrary. Therefore, the condition of recovery, if no stay is granted within 30 days, is illegal, arbitrary, unjustified and consequently set aside. [Para 44]

Right of consideration in appeal and on an application for waiver of pre-deposit, is a right conferred by the statute and such right cannot be defeated on the basis of Circular, which contemplates that the recovery can be effected, is stay is not granted within 30 days. Therefore, such condition in the Circular is not legal and is therefore set aside with the observation that till such time, the application for waiver of pre-deposit is decided in an appeal filed in terms of the statute, the revenue shall not proceed to recover the same provided that the assessee does not delay the hearing of the appeal directly or indirectly. In the event, the assessee is delaying the decision, the revenue shall be at liberty to move an application before the Commissioner (Appeals) to take the application for waiver of pre-deposit and seek orders thereon in accordance with law. If such an application is filed by the revenue, the Commissioner (Appeals) shall decide the same expeditiously. [Para 46]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock [Inclusion of freight] - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee-company purchased material on CIF basis - However, in exceptional circumstances, where material was immediately consumed, transport charges were not included in purchase price, but were separately debited to profit and loss account as invoices of transporters were received after consumption of material - Whether, addition on account of non-inclusion of freight inward and import clearing expense to cost of closing inventory, in such cases was not justified, since revenue had accepted assessee's method of valuation of stock in past, especially when revenue failed to demonstrate that impugned method of accounting resulted in material underestimation of profits - Held, yes [Para 7.22] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing and selling of two-wheelers in joint venture with a Japanese company. During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer referred the case to the Transfer Pricing Officer, as there were certain international transaction with its associated enterprises (AEs). It purchased material on CIF basis and ordinarily included freight and cost of delivery of goods in purchase price. However, in exceptional circumstances, where assessee has to immediately lift material, transport charges were not included in purchase price, but were separately debited to profit and loss account, since invoices of transporters were received after consumption of material.

The Assessing Officer added the amount of freight inward and import clearing expenses to cost of closing inventory. The assessee contended that the revenue had accepted its method of valuation in the past. It also contended that the transaction would be revenue neutral in the long run, as similar adjustment would also be required in the opening stock. However, the Dispute Resolution Panel confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On assessee's appeal:

HELD: Though, technically it can be argued that the value of closing inventory must include freight/ import clearing charges, the purchases in question were done under exceptional circumstances for immediate consumption. They were consumed immediately i.e. as soon as raw material entered the factory premises, hence, the question of such purchases being part of closing stock does not arise at all. In such a situation, when freight/import charges were directly debited to the profit and loss account along with the value of the purchases, the question of treating them as part of closing inventory does not arise. The assessee acted and accounted in a proper and acceptable method. Therefore, the relief should be granted on this count alone. [Para 7.14]

Alternatively, the undisputed fact remains that the assessee had been consistently following the said method of accounting in the last many years and the revenue had been accepting these facts and method of accounting without any demur.[Para 7.15]

The contention of the DRP that, the principle of res judicata does not apply in Income-tax proceedings and therefore, the Assessing officer is correct to come to independent conclusion and is not bound by past acceptance of a factual legal point by the department, is untenable. Technically, the principle of res judicata may not apply to the income-tax proceedings as each year is an independent year, yet there ought to be uniformity in treatment and consistency as propounded by the Supreme Court in the case of Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT [1992] 193 ITR 321/60 Taxman 248, where the facts and circumstances were identical. It is a judicially accepted principle that when the facts are same, a uniform view should be adopted for the subsequent years in the income-tax proceedings. Unless there is a material change in the facts, which is neither demonstrated by the Assessing Officer nor DRP, the view which is taken earlier, should not be changed, as held by various courts. [Para 7.16]

In the present case, the revenue rejected the method of accounting, which was consistently followed by the assessee, but it failed to demonstrate with facts and figures that the impugned method of accounting resulted in material underestimation of profits. On the contrary, the assessee demonstrated that the change in the method of accounting for year under appeal would result in loss to the revenue as the opening stock would also require similar adjustment and the cascading effect will be loss to revenue. In this case, the revenue unnecessarily disturbed the consistent method of accounting though it had been accepted in many years. Such tinkering with the method is unjustified when the exercise does not materially alter the profits. Such petty additions should be avoided on the ground of materiality, as AS-1, which talks about materiality, consistency, prudence etc., is part of the I.T. Act after it was notified under section 145(2). [Para 7.22]

In view of above discussion, this ground of the assessee is allowed. [Para 7.25]
