The appellants had followed the same practice as followed by the Department; no differential duty was therefore payable by the appellants. The show cause notice issued on 22-7-2005 was barred by limitation since it covered demand for the period 8/2000 to 7/2004. Along with the Bills of Entry filed by the appellants, the invoice of SABIC/Shell raised on SPL alone had been filed in support of the declared value. No invoice of SPL had been filed with Bills of Entry. Other documents submitted included bill of lading endorsed by SPL in favour of the appellants, test bond, HSS agreement, declaration in terms of Rule 10 of CVR and sale letter by SPL. There was no suppression. In terms of Rule 10 of CVR, appellants had disclosed all relevant information and the manner of computation of value for assessment. Till issuance of Circular No. 32/2004-Cus., dated 11-5-2004, Public Notice No. 145/2002, dated 3-12-2002 of the Custom House had prescribed addition of 2% towards HSS commission to the original invoice for computation of value for assessment of goods purchased on HSS basis. As the service charges realized by SPL covered a host of post importation services, value had to be determined adopting best judgment assessment by addition of 2%. In a show cause notice dt. 26-2-2001 issued to M/s. Hotline Glass Ltd. by Bombay Customs House, it was proposed to revise the value declared (CIF + HSS commission higher than 2%) and to re-assess the goods at CIF + 2%. This notice reflected the practice followed in the Bombay Custom House for computing value for assessment of HSS purchases as adding 2% HSS commission to the CIF value charged by the foreign supplier.

4.6 The impugned order was a consequence of a change in the basis of assessment. Therefore, short levy was not due to any suppression. Therefore, the demand was barred by limitation.

Per Justice U.L. Bhat : Appellant imported 900 metric tonnes of Dimethyl Terphthalate from Spain. It was shipped in vessel M.V. Hero. The vessel was grounded near Greece and the consignment was transferred to another vessel S.S. Vishva Tej. When the respondent filed bill of entry showing the invoice price CIF, the Assistant Collector added the extra freight and insurance charges which the respondent had to bear on account of the grounding of the ship and transfer to another ship, over-ruling the contention of the respondent that such additional expenses could not be included in the assessable value. The Collector (Appeals) set aside this enhancement and assessable value. The department, being aggrieved, has filed the present appeal.

2. An employee of the respondent appeared before us and pleaded for adjournment on the ground that though notice had been received, the respondent could not trace the records. In an appeal filed in 1987, we do not think this is a reasonable request. The request for adjournment is rejected.

3. The declared value includes the normal CIF value. What was sought to be added was the extra freight and insurance charges which the respondent had to incur on account of grounding of the original vessel and transfer to another vessel. Ordinarily, such extra charges are not taken into consideration by the customs house, since the customs house goes by the actual freight or a particular percentage of price. In these circumstances, we are not inclined to interfere. The appeal is dismissed.

2. The appellants are M/s. Shine Petroleum Pvt. Ltd., Chennai and M/s. Elf Gas India Ltd., Bangalore. The first appellant imported Superior Kerosene Oil known as SKO and the second appellant imported Commercial Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG). The issue in both the appeals is one and the same and therefore, we are taking up the matter for issue of a common order.

3. The appellants have a CIF Contract with the foreign supplier. The goods are loaded in vessels and thereafter they reach the port for unloading. A minimum time is given for unloading before which the goods have to be unloaded and this time is known as lay time. If there is a delay in discharge of cargo, due to various reasons, demurrage is charged by the carrier to the supplier of the goods. In turn the supplier collects this demurrage charges from the importers who are the appellants. The point at issue is whether the demurrage charges are to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for customs duty purposes.

4. Revenue proceeded against the appellants in both the cases by way of issue of show cause notice for inclusion of the demurrage charges in the assessable value of the goods imported. In the case of the first appellant, the Adjudicating Authority confirmed a demand of Rs. 79,73,330/-. Interest to the tune of Rs. 28,98,945/- was demanded. Further, a penalty of Rs. 1,08,72,275/- was imposed. The period involved in the case of first appellant is from May 2003 to November 2003. As regards the second appellant, the Commissioner confirmed the duty demand of Rs. 20,38,610/- and imposed equal penalty under Section 114A of the Customs Act. The period involved in the case of second appellant is from October 1999 to November 2004. The appellants strongly challenge the impugned orders of the Commissioner. Therefore, they have come before this Tribunal for relief.

5. Shri G. Shiva Dass, learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the appellants and Smt. Sudha Koka, learned Departmental representative for the Revenue.

6. We heard both sides. The learned advocate took us through the relevant statutory provisions and made the point that the issue of includability of demurrage charges to the assessable value of the imported goods has been exhaustively dealt with in the Tribunal's decision in the case of IOC Ltd. and Others Vs. CC, Calcutta - 2000 (41) RLT 251 (CEGAT-LB)=2000 (122) ELT 615, which was affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2004 (61) RLT 2 (SC)=2004 (165) ELT 257 (SC). The department went in against the above decision by Review Petition which was also dismissed by Apex Court in 2005 (186) ELT A199. The learned advocate pointed out that once there is a CIF contract which includes the freight, no further addition can be made to the freight in respect of the CIF contract. He relied on the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Ispat Industries Ltd. Vs. CC - 2006 (77) RLT 1 (SC)=2006-TIOL-127-SC-Cus. Further, he relied on the Board's Circular dated 14.8.1991, according to which demurrage is not to be included in the assessable value of the imported goods. The idea in all these circulars and decisions is that the demurrage cannot be considered as cost of transportation. It is completely different from the cost of transportation. The learned advocate took us through the decision in the case of IOC and said that the assessable value is value of the goods which are ordinarily sold. He emphasized the word ordinary and said that the demurrage is paid only when there is delay in unloading of the goods and the situation in which there is delay in unloading of goods is not an ordinary situation but in fact it is an extra ordinary situation. In view of this, he submitted that the Tribunal held that demurrage is not includable in the assessable value and this decision has been upheld by the Supreme Court.

"Since the car was one year old there was no reason restricting for only two quarters as it was rightly argued on behalf of the appellant. Once depreciation is permissible it should be given to fully ear since the car was imported after one year from the date of purchase. The Tribunal has been consistently held that 15% trade discount is permissible even in the case of individual who has purchased and brought into India following the earlier decisions, we hold that the appellant is entitled to 15% trade discount. Section 14 of the Customs Act provides for the Customs Tariff Act where a duty of customs is chargeable on any goods by reference to their value, the value of such goods shall be deemed to an price at which such or like goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale, for delivery at the time and place of importation. Such price shall be calculated with reference to rate of exchange as in force on the date on which the bill of entry is presented. Hence the Department was justified in including the freight charges. FACT: The petitioners are engaged in the business of texturising base flat yarn. Base yarn was imported by them and lodged in a warehouse owned by Central Warehousing Corporation. The petitioners filed two bills of entry for removal of the above goods on 16th February, 1983 and 28th February, 1983. Customs duty was paid as per rates applicable on 28th February 1983. All that remained to be done was to pay the warehousing charges and lift the goods from the warehouse. The petitioner's agents came to get release of the goods on 28.2.1983 but to their surprise found that the cash counter was closed at 3 PM instead of 4 PM and delivery counter at 4 PM instead of 5 PM. As duty on the subject goods was increased w.e.f. 1.3.1983 petitioners approached their Association, who registered a protest with the Customs authorities, along with the request that the goods should be treated as having been delivered on 28.2.1983, thus getting the benefits of the pre-budget rates. The Department refused this, and contended that the advancing of working hours was valid because of a circular issued in that behalf.

HELD: Official circulars are not binding on a citizen. Departmental action based on such circulars can be held valid only if legal validity and sanction of the same is proved. Mere cyclostyled instructions, as in the present case, have no legal validity and it is against the principles of equity that the petitioners should be held liable for the consequences, and to pay enhanced customs duty. "The question has now been rightly posed by Mr. Jagtiani the learned Counsel for the Petitioners as to what is the legal sanction for this circular and whether the same can be accepted as a mandate. The learned Counsel for the Respondent Mr. Sethna when questioned could not throw any light on this aspect much less could he effectively answer this very relevant question posed with the necessary consequences that nothing has been shown on this forum to accept the legal validity of this circular, namely, about the authority, the sanction and all other features which go to make out a validly legal circular. In the absence of any such material and even an ostensible explanation which is not coming forth this becomes inescapable to obviously strike down the validity of this circular having no existence in law at all."

2. Warehoused goods--withholding delivery even when a party has been physically present to pay the warehousing charges and lift the goods is a failure on the part of the official staff. Hence, it is fair and just that the consignments should be treated as having been released on 28.2.1983. "...the Petitioners were waiting to offer the warehousing charges between 3 p.m. and 4 p.m. and thereby they could have obtained delivery between 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. as usual, the Petitioners' assertion that even this was not done by the staff within that time also even though they were just awaiting their turn for which the entire blame lies with the staff is not seriously controverted. ......I have no reservation in my mind that......they would be liable to pay customs duty as was prevailing on 28th February 1983 and not enhanced customs duty that came into force on 1st March 1983. This result therefore appears to be unescapable."

3. Warehoused goods--Non-presentation of Bank Certificates is not sufficient ground to deny delivery of goods from warehouse as all other formalities had been complied with. "As rightly contended by Mr. Jagtiani the learned Counsel it is the monetary transaction which has the direct nexus to the schedule time of 4 p.m. which was advanced to 3 p.m. and it has nothing to do with the physical presentation of the discharge certificate from the bank and according to him if the moneys were offered before 4 p.m. then it becomes immaterial in so far as the presentation of the document is concerned because customs duty is admittedly paid earlier and warehousing charges are effered on the spot.......In my opinion the object as enunciated by sub-clause (b) does not embrace within its fold the presentation of the discharge certificate from any bank. In a way that would be only incidental because the main count would be about the payment of customs duty and the payment of warehousing charges."

Per Justice P. Venkatarama Reddi :

The respondent herein imported certain consignment of superior kerosene oil which was sold to it by Indian Oil Corporation on high sea sale basis. The controversy in this appeal is about the assessable value of the imported goods under Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962. The Assistant Commissioner of Customs assessed the value on the basis of final invoices raised by Indian Oil Corporation, Madras, which included CIF value, service charges plus other charges. Amongst 'other charges' were demurrage, wharfage and stock loss. The respondent-assessee filed an appeal and contended inter alia that these charges were not includible in the assessable value for the reason that they were post-importation charges and an addition of CIF value at the rate of one percent having already been made in terms of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 to cover the landing charges, no further addition could be made under the above heads. The appellate Commissioner accepted the contention of the appellant and allowed the appeal in respect of the above mentioned three items. However, the appeal was dismissed as regards bank charges and ocean losses with which we are not concerned. The appeal filed by the Revenue in CEGAT, Chennai Bench, was dismissed on 12.1.1999 following its earlier decision in Final Order Nos. 84 and 85 of 1998. The learned Counsel appearing for the parties are not in a position to tell us whether that order of the Tribunal has become final. Be that as it may, the legality of the Tribunal's order dated 12.1.1999 dismissing the Revenue's appeal has been assailed in this appeal by the Revenue.

2. According to Section 14(1) of the Customs Act, the value for the purpose of charging customs duty on imported goods shall be deemed to be the price at which they are ordinarily sold or offered for sale for delivery at the time and place of importation, in the course of international trade provided that the seller and buyer have no mutual business interests and price is the sole consideration for the transaction. However, sub-section (1A) which was added to Section 14 in the year 1988 provides as follows:-

"(1A) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), the price referred to in that sub-section in respect of imported goods shall be determined in accordance with the rules made in this behalf."

3. Pursuant to sub-section (1A) of Section 14 and in exercise of rule making power under Section 156, the Central Government framed the Customs Valuation (Department of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988. The relevant portion of Rule 9(2) is extracted hereunder:-

"For the purposes of sub-section (1) and sub-section (1A) of Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 (52 of 1962) and these rules, the value of the imported goods shall be the value of such goods, for delivery at the time and place of importation and shall include-

(a)

the cost of transport of the imported goods to the place of importation;

(b)

loading, unloading and handling charges associated with the delivery of the imported goods at the place of importation; and

(c)

the cost of insurance:

Provided that

(i)

where the cost of transport referred to in clause (a) is not ascertainable, such cost shall be twenty per cent of the free on board value of the goods;

(ii)

the charges referred to in clause (b) shall be one per cent of the free on board value of the goods plus the cost of transport referred to in clause (a) plus the cost of insurance referred to in clause (C);

(iii)

where the cost referred to in clause (c) is not ascertainable, such cost shall be 1.125% of free on board value of the goods;

take the list price of the manufacturer as the starting point. He argued that the rules of valuation that have been adopted in the instant case was in consonance with the long standing practice of the Department and even if the long standing practice is not in conformity with statutory provisions, the long established practice of the Department must prevail. I am unable to uphold this contention. The long standing practice has not been proved by an evidence. Moreover, the long standing practice cannot override the provisions of an Act of Parliament. 9. Lastly it does not appear that there is any conflict between Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation Rules and Section 14(1) of the Customs Act. On the other hand, Rule 8 has been made applicable subject to the provisions of Section 14 of the Customs Act.

10. Both the Assistant Collector of Customs and the Collector of Customs (Appeals) have ignored the provisions of Rule 8(2)(ii) and 8(2)(iv). The endeavour of the Department has been to realise highest possible amount of duty from the petitioner, whether permitted by law or not. In the facts of this case, an arbitrary and fictitious valuation of the car has been fixed for a second hand car taking into account the price of a new car. A copy of 'Parker's Car Price Guide, April 1992 has been produced in Court. That contains the price of second hand cars in the United Kingdom. The price of 1985 model jaguar cars which are similar in description has been valued at less than £ 3,000. It does not appear on what basis the list price of a new car was taken for ascertaining the value of the second hand car. It is also not known how the figure of depreciation was arrived at. The depreciation in India at the moment is 20% per annum for a car for the Income Tax purpose.

11. In my view, the valuation has been arrived it in total disregard to the provision of Section 14 and also the provisions of Rule 8. In the premises, there will be an order of Certiorari as prayed for in terms of prayer (b) of the petition. The order dated 3rd April, 1992 passed by the Assistant Collector of Customs is ex facie erroneous and is accordingly set aside. The Assistant Collector of Customs, Respondent No. 1 is directed to make a fresh assessment in conformably with the provisions of Section 14(1) of the Customs Act as also keeping in mind the provisions of Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation Rules. I make it clear that Rule 8 must be construed and applied in a manner not to make the provisions of Section 14(1) of the Customs Act nugatory.

12. The car is now lying at the site of the Calcutta Port Trust for a long time. It is apprehended by the petitioner that the car would get rusty and unusable altogether. It has also been stated that a sum of Rs. 600/- per day is being paid by the petitioner to the Port authorities by way of demurrage charges and he will have to go on paying the demurrage charge even if the case goes on endlessly. Therefore, the petitioner has prayed for an interim order for release of the car.

13. Therefore, the following interim order is passed. The petitioners shall be entitled to get release of the car upon payment of Rs. 3 lakhs in cash towards duty and upon furnishing a Bank Guarantee of a sum of Rs. 3 lakhs on a scheduled bank to the satisfaction of the Collector of Customs, Calcutta. Upon payment of the sum of Rs. 3 lakhs and furnishing the Bank Guarantee as aforesaid, the Customs Department must release the car to the petitioner within 48 hours thereafter. The petitioner, who is present in court, has given an undertaking to court through his counsel that he will not sell or dispose of or alienate the car in any manner whatsoever till the Customs proceedings are completed. The petitioner will, however, produce the car once on the first Monday of every month at the Customs House, 15/1, Strand Road, Calcutta between 10 A.M. and 11 A.M. for inspection by the Assistant Collector of Customs and such inspection must be completed within 1 hour's time.

14. The respondents have argued this case needlessly for 3 days. What is fun to the Department is death to an individual writ petitioner. Therefore, the respondents must pay costs of this application assessed at 200 GMs. to the petitioner and such costs must be paid within a fortnight's time.

15. The writ petition is finally disposed of as above.

16. The respondents have prayed for stay of operation of this order. In the facts and circumstances of this case, I find no reason to grant any stay and accordingly the said prayer is rejected.

17. All parties shall act on a signed copy of the operative part of this order on the usual undertaking.

We agree with the Ld. We do not find any justification for enhancing the value of the imported goods on the said basis. FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand offset press against a letter of credit for Rs. 1,99,867.00 opened on 28.2.1983 and valid for negotiation up to 30.8.1983, subsequently extended up to 31.12.1983. The appellants claimed clearance of the machine under OGL in terms of para 7 of Appendix 10 of the Import Policy 1982-83. However, the Customs held that the goods could not be allowed clearance as changes of fundamental nature had been made in the letter of credit. The Collector ordered confiscation of the machine with an option to redeem it on payment of Rs. 65,000/-. He also ordered enhancement of its value to Rs. 2,57,162/- on the basis of contemporaneous import of identical machine of 1973 model.

HELD: ITC--OGL--Appendix 10 of Policy AM 1982-83--the letter of credit established on 28.2.1983, continued to be valid on the date of shipment--the import is covered by OGL (ratio of Appellate Tribunal decision in Tara Art Printers, New Delhi v. CC, Bombay). ".........on reference to para (7) of Appendix 10 of 1982-83 Import Policy, we find that it was not clearly spelled out that shipment after 31.3.1983 was permissible only in cases where delay in shipment was on account of longer manufacturing schedule. In our view, if the delivery period of the goods was extended beyond 31.3.1983 due to any reason they could be shipped on or before 31.12.1983 provided the contract entered into on or before 28.2.1983 continued to be in force on the date of shipment. In this case in the first instance the shipment was delayed on account of the country of origin having been erroneously shown in the Letter of Credit as West Germany instead of Sweden necessitating the extension of the Letter of Credit up to 30.8.1983. However, the shipment was delayed further since the intimation regarding the extension of the Letter of Credit was not received by the supplier. Thereafter, the Letter of Credit was amended again on 21.10.1983 to extend its validity up to 31.12.1983. Since the goods were shipped before 31.12.1983 against the Letter of Credit which was established on 28.2.1983 and continued to be valid on the date of shipment, we are of the view that they were covered by the OGL in terms of 1982-83 Import Policy."

"We find that on the question of valuation as well there is sufficient force in the appellants contention that the Collector's decision to enhance the assessable value of the imported machine of 1974 make, on the basis of the price of a similar machine of 1973 model was arbitrary. It is seen that the adjudicating authority did not give any indication of the method employed for the computation of the assessable value of the imported second hand machine of 1974 make on the basis of the price of another second-hand machine of 1973 make. Since, in this case there was no evidence of the importers being related to the suppliers or any amount in excess of the invoice price having been remitted by the importers to the suppliers, the invoice price represented the value of the goods which was determinable under clause (a) of section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962. We find that the Tribunal had taken a similar view in the case of M/s. Tara Art Printers, New Delhi v. FACT: Appellants, manufacturers of glass sheets, charged from their customers the price of the goods as well as extra charges on account of special packing, cost of transport, forwarding charges, breakage risk and miscellaneous charges. The dispute was whether the charges for the extras were includible in the assessable value of the goods. When the same issue had gone to the High Court earlier, the appellants had contended that they realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers and not from their local buyers. The High Court held that as the appellants realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers, the extra charges were in principle excludible from the assessable value, and further, ordered the department of investigate the assertion of the facts made by the appellants. While the matter was under enquiry, the department received some information that the appellants were indulging in under-valuation of their goods. The Anti-Evasion staff of the department scrutinised the documents of the appellants and came to the conclusion that the appellants had highly inflated the costs of the extra items so as to camouflage the true assessable value of the goods. On this ground, show cause notices were issued demanding differential excise duty of Rs. 1,88,84,508.57 and also a penalty of Rs. 50 lakhs was imposed on the appellants for making false and mis-leading declarations. Confiscation of the plant and machinery of the appellants in lieu of a fine was also ordered. The appellants contended that the show-cause notices issued by the department were time-barred as they were issued beyond the normal time of six months. Further, the appellants pointed out that there has been a violation of principles of natural justice as their request to make further clarifications on the matter, was not honoured by the department. The question as to which of the items of extras should be held to be excludible for determining the assessable value of the goods was also taken up in the instant case.

HELD: As the assessment of the goods had been made only on a provisional basis, with the consent of the appellants, the demands as per the show cause notices are not time-barred. The limitation applies only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessment "......the assessments had been made provisionally under Rule 9B of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 at their own request and on the strength of the provisional duty bond executed by them.......As per Rule 9B, the assessments made on provisional basis have to be finalised eventually and adjustments of duty made. Under Section 11A of the Act, the limitation starts running only from the date of adjustment of duty after finalisation of the provisional assessments. The demands issued as per the show cause notices on 6.11.1984, 10.12.1984 and 43.1985 were, therefore, not time barred, even if the normal time limit of six months were to be applied."

2. In not granting the appellants their request for a personal hearing wherein they wanted to make further submissions regarding certain points, the department has violated the principles of natural justice. "The appellants........argued their case in part and asked for certain clarifications. They expressed their desire to make further submissions on receipt.......The Collector did not grant this further hearing and he proceeded to decide the matter. There has, therefore, been a denial of full opportunity of personal hearing."

certain additions to be made for expenses out of India on basis of FOB value - In some cases, certain expenses incurred outside India (like license fee, tool amortization costs, free material supplied etc.) are required to be added for valuation of customs duty. In such cases, these should be added in 'FOB value' for purpose of adding freight (20% of FOB value) or insurance (1.125% of FOB value), if actual freight or insurance is not available. Barge/lighterage charges includible - In some cases, the ship is not brought upto jetty. Goods are discharged at outer anchorage. This may be for various reasons, e.g. (a) deep draught at port (b) Ports are busy (c) Odd dimensional or heavy lifts or hazardous cargo discharged at anchorage. Charges for brining the goods from outer anchorage are known as 'barging/lighterage charges'.

As per Explanation to rule 10(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 [inserted w.e.f. 10-10-2007], ship demurrage charges on chartered vessels, lighterage or barge charges are includible - - confirmed in MF(DR) circular No. 34/2009-Cus dated 30-11-2009.

Mode of computation of freight of time chartered/daughter vessel has been specified in MF(DR) circular No. 4/2006-Cus dated 12-1-2006.

Once freight upto port of unloading is included in assessable value, further expenses on account of lighterage and stevedoring are not includible - CC v. Hindustan Copper (2016) 331 ELT 99 (CESTAT).

Freight from port or airport to ICD/CFS not includible in customs value - If goods are imported by sea or air and transshipped to another customs station in India, handling charges associated with such transshipment are not includible in Assessable Value - fifth proviso to rule 10(2) of Customs Valuation Rules as amended w.e.f. 26-9-2017 [It was forth proviso upto 26-9-2017].

Thus, transshipment costs from port to ICDs, port to port, port to CFS, Airport to Airport etc. within India will not be part of assessable value - para 6 of MF(DR) circular No. 39/2017-Cus dated 26-9-2017.

Sea freight to be considered even when goods brought by air in emergency - In Bombay Dyeing and Mfg Co. v. CC - 1993 (63) ELT 557 (CEGAT) and ORWO Films v. Collector - 1991 (56) ELT 805 (CEGAT), it has been held that if goods are normally imported by sea, then sea freight should be considered for calculating the value under section 14 of Customs Act, even if goods are actually imported by air due to emergency requirement. It was held that air freight can be considered only if goods are normally imported by air. - confirmed in CC v. State Trading Corporation of India 1998(100) ELT 11 (SC). [This is correct on the principle that 'normal price' has to be considered for customs valuation.]

Tribunal, in Orwo Films v. CC - 1991 (56) ELT 805 (CEGAT) have held that if sea freight of such goods is available, only that freight should be added to FOB value to arrive at CIF value and actual air freight should not be considered.

Deduction if freight refunded and addition if additional freight charged - If part of freight is refunded (due to unloading of charter vessel before stipulated time - called 'despatch money'), it is deductible from cost and does not form part of assessable value - CC v. Shimoga Steels Ltd. 1997(89) ELT 93 (CEGAT) * CC v. Associated Cement Co. Ltd. 1998(104) ELT 395 (CEGAT) * Reliance Industries Ltd. v. CC 2004 (174) ELT 344 (CESTAT). In BHEL v. CC 1983(13) ELT 358 = 1983 ECR 1266 (CEGAT), it was held that any rebate granted by shipping line is allowable as deduction, even if allowed subsequently as even at the time of packing of cargo, it is known that this rebate will be forthcoming.

If appellant gets dispatch money on quick turn around of the vessel, its deduction is allowable - Indian Farmer Fertilizer Coop Ltd. v. CCE (2012) 284 ELT 266 (CESTAT).

Alternative remedy--Merits of the case are being considered by the Court even though the matter is sub-judice before the Tribunal because multiplicity of proceedings will result in harassment to the petitioner. "Ordinarily, we would not have discussed the merits of the case since the point under issue in the present matter which has been decided in favour of the petitioner by the Collector (Appeals), is still sub-judice before the Tribunal and we would have waited for the decision of the Tribunal but looking to the fact that the Department is not satisfied by the order of the Collector (Appeals) and instead of pursuing the matter before the Tribunal, has been issuing notices and the Assistant Collector has even passed assessment orders involving the same question and taking a contrary view than that of the Collector (Appeals) and the Department did not even wait but proceeded to pass the assessment order without waiting for the decision of the Tribunal in spite of repeated requests made by the petitioner, particularly when the High Court had stayed the assessment order in these writ petitions but in the later year, the petitioners could not obtain a stay order, though writ petition had been filed, because of the strike of the lawyers. The petitioner has to file writ petition every now and then. The Tribunal is not a party before us and the matter may not be decided finally by the Tribunal for a number of years. The Department will go on issuing notices and passing the assessment orders which will necessitate filing of appeals or coming to this Court which will be nothing but multiplicity of proceedings and undue harassment to the petitioner. Therefore, in these particular facts and circumstances, we are inclined to consider the merits of the case as well."

Valuation--cost of transportation, depot service charges and unloading, charges have to be excluded as the ex-factory price is ascertainable and these costs have nothing to do with the manufacture of goods (ratio of Supreme Court decisions). "......there is a clear finding that there was an ex-factory price which is ascertainable. ......When the factory price is ascertainable, the excise duty has to be levied on that price. If the assessee transported the goods from its factory to the Depot, cost of transportation has to be excluded, as has been held in Bombay Tyres' case and in Indian Oxygen Ltd.'s case. ....The depot service charges and unloading charges have nothing to do with the manufacture and therefore, that amount is not to be included to ascertain the assessable value for the purpose of payment of central excise duty".

CCE. expenses incurred towards the loading of the goods within the factory are required to be included in the assessable value of the goods Since a separate break-up of these charges is not given out of the total transportation cost or delivery charges collected by the assessee from its customers, the case has necessarily to be remanded for determining the charges collected towards loading and handling of the goods within the factory for the purpose of charging duty thereon and I order accordingly." Limitation--Transportation charges collected through separate bills were not declared in the price lists. There was therefore, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts. Longer time limit is therefore available to the Department "As regards the limitation it is admitted by the appellants, as already set out above, that they were collecting charges through separate bills and therefore, there was no declaration of these charges in the price list because the prices declared were ex-works. Apparently, therefore, there was a wilful mis-statement or suppression of facts calling for invoking a larger period of 5 years for demanding the differential duty. The show cause notice was, therefore, well within the time. As regards the point.....that the law regarding includibility of loading charges within the factory was clarified only in the year 1988 by the Supreme Court in the Indian Oxygen case it maybe mentioned that the appellants have not taken this plea in their appeal memo or in the course of arguments by the learned advocate. Such a plea in my view is too vague a plea for the purpose of determining the question of limitation of the show cause notice unless the appellants came positively with definite judgments of the legal position which prevented them from showing such charges in the price list..... I direct the Assistant Collector to redetermine the differential duty after the appellants herein have furnished the break-up of the so-called delivery charges incurred towards the loading etc of the goods within the factory of the appellants which alone would be includible the assessable value of the goods. --I observe that admittedly the charges in question were not declared in the price list Furthermore, undisputably the law relating to the determination of the assessable value in the central excise cases required filing of the price list and supplying the relevant information to enable the officers to Judge the correctness of the declaration and assess the value according to law. Hence irrespective of the appellants' own views complete information was required to be supplied to the Department voluntarily--(whether as apart of the price list or a remark or as an enclosure or covering memo). The Department was also required to be vigilant and expected to call for full particulars at the earliest. However, non-supply of the information normally required for assessment amounted to suppression of relevant facts Hence the extended period was available to the Department and the show cause notice was not time barred Once this was the position, the Assistant Collector was required to re-determine the differential duty after the appellants furnished the required break-up. Hence I agree with the learned Technical Member that the matter was required to be remanded for re-determining the correct duty liability."

Replacement import - Marine Insurance Policy in this case covered replacement the warehouse of the importer. The mere fact that the goods have reached Ludhiana town is not enough to conclude that the transit has come to an end. As long as the goods are not cleared by the customs authority and are stored in the customs warehouse, it is futile to suggest that the transit has come to an end and the goods have been received by the importers. Once the erroneous assumption of the Additional Collector on this count is found to be unsustainable, then the submission........that the replacement import is covered by the relevant policy deserves acceptance."

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - EPCG scheme - Valuation - Board's circular - requires consultation with DGFT at Board's level before revising value of imports - since the matter is in second round of litigation before CESTAT, it is too late to act according to Board's circular. (Para 4)

SC), it has been held that Standing Orders/instructions/directions issued by department are not binding on assessing authority as he is quasi-judicial authority. He has to act independently in exercise of his quasi-judicial powers. The Standing Orders/instructions/directions issued for smooth functioning of assessment and work in no way interferes with discretion of assessment authority - same view in Life Style International v. UOI (2011) 271 ELT 190 (Bom HC DB). In Tolin Rubbers P Ltd. v. CC 2004 (163) ELT 289 (SC), it was held that even in case of second hand goods, valuation is required to be done on basis of transaction value, unless it is rejected due to exceptional circumstances as indicated in rule 4(2) of Customs Valuation Rules [now rule 3(2)]. In this case, valuation done on basis of depreciation method was rejected by SC - same view in Vadilal Diary International Ltd. v. CC 2005 (180) ELT 436 (SC) - followed in Balaji Office Equipment v. CC (2007) 216 ELT 611 (CESTAT).

There is no standard value for purpose of used second hand goods. The second hand market of used goods is highly volatile and it is possible for assessee to bargain and obtain best prices. In each case, it would not be possible for importer to produce invoice of original manufacturer when he is obtaining goods from trader. In such case, transaction value cannot be rejected without valid reasons - New Techno Graphics v. ACCE (2008) 222 ELT 260 (CESTAT).

In Bala Krishna Pillai v. CC 2003 (156) ELT 414 (CEGAT), it was held that valuation should be done as per provisions of Customs Act and not as per 'long standing practice'. In this case, it was held that when price of car duly certified by manufacturer is available, valuation on basis of price list (list price) is not permissible.

Depreciation guidelines are against valuation rules - In Sree Rajendra Mills Ltd. v. CC 1997(90) ELT 68 (CEGAT), it was (indeed very rightly) held that the provision of scale of depreciation for valuation is against the very spirit of section 14 of Customs Act and Customs Valuation Rules. - . - . - Normally, invoice value (transaction value) should form the basis of assessable value and which value should not be disregarded without laying a basis for the same. - . - . - . - Having a comparable value is not a pre-condition for accepting transaction value. - . - . - Transaction value can be discarded if the transaction is such that it was not in normal course of business and there were some extraneous factors having a bearing on the price or the basis of price. — . - . - In case the authorities have doubt that the second hand machinery was not valued correctly, they should have caused necessary investigation.

However, in Sima Khatib v. CC 2004 (166) ELT 119 (CESTAT), it was observed that depreciation method has been accepted by Technical committee under WTO agreement, and hence that method can be adopted for practical guidance in India.

Pre-importation expenses to be added - Pre-importation expenses like dismantling charges are to be added in case of second hand machinery - Bombay Dyeing v. CC - 1991(51) ELT 65 (CEGAT) - confirmed in Bombay Dyeing & Mfg v. CC 1997 AIR SCW 1427 = AIR 1997 SC 1329 = 90 ELT 276 (SC). * Essar Gujarat Ltd. v. HEADNOTE: Rule 3 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1963 – Determination of the method of valuation - Valuation - Invoice value may not be accepted for computing duty if satisfactory explanation for substantial price difference between comparable goods is missing-Value may preferably be computed under Rule 3 and 4 if comparable goods are avail able-Assessment made by adopting even a less preferable criteria is maintainable if the assessee is not put to disadvantage - Assessable value--Landing charges form a part of assessable value

FACT: The appellants imported certain second-hand machines. The Customs authorities did not accept the invoice price on the plea that similar machines had been imported by the same assessee at a much higher price while the time gap between the two imports was not much. The goods were valued under Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules keeping in view appreciation of prices depreciation insurance, freight and landing charges. Collector (Appeals) upheld the order except that he allowed depreciation @ 10% as against 6-1/4% allowed by the lower authorities.

HELD: 1. Valuation--Invoice value may not be accepted for computing duty if comparable goods are purchased at substantially higher price. "The appellants explanation for increase in the price is that the demand for second hand machinery had gone up and the suppliers therefore raised the prices in case of latter import No evidence in support of this plea has been produced either before the lower authorities or before us. In the absence of any such evidence and the apparently large price differential in the prices of two sets of machines, the imports of which were made in the span of about nine months time, we held that the lower authorities were justified in not accepting low price as reflected in the invoice for the goods".

2. Valuation--Computation of value should preferable be under Rule 3 and 4 if comparable goods are available at different prices. "We would like to observe that in the instant case, the value of comparable goods was available and the correct rule that should have been applied by the lower authorities should have been Rule 3 of the Custom Valuation rules 1963 read with Rule 4 of the said rule. We find that the value of comparable goods imported by the appellants was acceptable to the authorities and as such there was no need for the officers to traverse beyond these rules to Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules."

3. Valuation--Assessee has no grievance if a criterion, less preferable than other available ones, is adopted if it does not put him to disadvantage. "In any case, we find that the appellants had not suffered any disadvantage on this account and probably the value fixed now in terms of the Appellate Collector's order is lower than what might have been fixed in case Rule 3 read with Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules 1963 had been resorted to. We, therefore, find no reason to accede the appellants plea for accepting the invoice value for purpose of assessment."

4. Assessable value includes landing charges. "The inclusion of landing charges in the assessable value is maintainable in law seeing that the expenditure incurred for landing would become an integral component of their intrinsic value and accordingly "the price at which such or like goods are for delivery at the time and place of importation"."

It is well settled that officers working under the Board are bound by the circulars issued by the Board, and that if a particular circular which is beneficial to the interests of the assessee and has been in force throughout the assessment year under consideration and is withdrawn only after the end of the assessment year, the assessee is entitled to have the assessment made and completed only in accordance with the instruction. In this case, the said Circular directing the ITOs to add back the net amount only was in force in the assessment year 1974-75 and was withdrawn only after the expiry of that year. Consequently, the view taken by the ITO and the AAC was not correct.

HELD: Earlier in the course of hearing of the appeal the assessee was directed to explain the entries of customs duty payment in the profit and loss account and balance-sheet. In response to the same, the assessee filed a supplemen-tary paper-book on 21-2-2007 explaining the entries made regarding the closing stock to show that the customs duty had been included therein, and had also explained in details as to how the provisions of section 145A introduced with effect from 1-4-1999 would have no effect in view of the overriding provisions of section 43B. These submissions had been briefly adverted to in the order of the Tribunal. One of the paragraph of the order of the Tribunal showed that the contention of the assessee that since inception, that is, from the assessment year 1994-95 till the assessment year 2006-07 the assessee had been following the inclusive method of accounting for customs duty payment while valuing the stock and that was accepted by the Tribunal. Further, the Tribunal had even stated in this paragraph that this claim of the assessee was not contradicted even in the assessment order. In the same paragraph, the Tribunal had also made an observation that in the year under appeal, the customs duty formed part of the closing stock, though the duty was not debited to the profit and loss account and had also referred to the fact that the duty was separately claimed as deduction in the return of income. In one other paragraph, the Tribunal had accepted the assessee's claim in principle and had observed that it was supported by the Special Bench's order of the Tribunal in Indian Communication Network (P.) Ltd. v. IAC [1994] 49 ITD 56 (Delhi), which was approved by the Supreme Court in Berger Paints India Ltd. v. CIT [2004] 266 ITR 99/ 135 Taxman 586. However, the observations made in the said paragraph showed that the Tribunal had considered that the customs duty was not included in the valuation of the closing stock. This observation was at variance with and contradictory to its earlier finding to the effect that the duty had been included in the closing stock as per the consistent accounting practice adopted by the assessee which was accepted in the assessment. It was only in view of the latter contradictory finding that the Tribunal thought it necessary to restore the matter to the Assessing Officer with the direction to examine the applicability of section 145A to the assessee's case. Even if it was assumed for the sake of argument that the case would have had to be restored to the Assessing Officer to be processed with reference to section 145 A notwithstanding the earlier finding of the Tribunal that the customs duty was included in the valuation of the closing stock, the fact that the assessee's argument was based on the order of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra) was not considered by the Tribunal showed that there was a mistake apparent from the record in light of decision of Supreme Court in Honda Siel Power Products Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 165 Taxman 307. [Para 8]

In Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra), it was held that section 43B has overriding effect over section 145A. This decision was referred to by the Tribunal in its order while summarizing the contentions of the department but unfortu-nately it omitted to deal with this decision and considered its applicability while taking a decision to remit the matter to the Assessing Officer with a direction to examine the applicability of section 145A. This omission had caused prejudice to the assessee in the sense that it had given rise to further proceedings before the Assessing Officer involving further delay in finalising the assessment proceedings, when the legal position already stood con-cluded by the binding order of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra). The other mistake committed by the Tribunal to the prejudice of the assessee was its omission to refer to the assessee's plea that in the subsequent years, the Assessing Officer had accepted the assessee's claim under section 43B and assessments had been completed accordingly. [Para 8]

Key judicial precedents on valuation of related parties :

Mere relationship is not sufficient for denial of transaction value, it must be established that the relationship has influenced the price

The transaction price between the two parties must be influenced by their relationship in order to question the valuation of such a transaction. The rejection of transaction value can only be done after due verification and undertaking the exercise as to what influenced the price and cogent reasons to be recorded for such price not being the sole consideration. [CCE v. Sanjivani Non-Ferrous Trading (P) Ltd., 2019 (365) ELT 3 (SC)]

Burden of proof for proving the value in question is not appropriate is in the hands of department

The burden of proof for proving the value in question is not appropriate is in the hands of departments and if departments fail in that, the benefit of doubt goes to importer. For proving the transaction value being influenced by relationship, relevant comparable proof needs to be taken which incorporates adjustments as to the price with respect to declaration made by supplier in his exporting country, but not relying on the fact that how such declaration was procured with.

Non reliance of document submitted by the appellant for value of similar supplier for same goods is not acceptable. The department had relied on some declaration made by a foreign supplier without seeing the fact that supplier had enhanced the value in that foreign country to get more incentive benefit offered by that country. Fact to be considered by the authority and hence strict rules of evidence do not apply to adjudication proceedings though adjudicating officer has to examine the probative value of documents on which reliance is placed. [Commissioner of Customs v. South India Television (P) Ltd. 2007 taxmann.com 910/214 ELT 3 (SC)]

Commodity price fluctuation in the international market must be taken into consideration

The transaction value agreed by both the parties cannot be questioned merely on the basis that there is increase in prices in the international market between the time of contract and actual shipment of the product as there was no collusion between the parties, as well the payment was received within the same terms under which the contract was entered into and there was actual no misstatement or undervaluation and the case was also not falling under any of the criteria as mentioned under Rule 4(2) of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988. Department as well cannot rely on or take base the prices, which are almost a month after the actual date of contract, as the product dealt with is highly fluctuating in the international market. [Commissioner of Customs v. Aggarwal Industries Ltd. [2011 (272) E.L.T. 641 (S.C.)]]

Arbitrary addition of value cannot be made especially when importer provides complete cost & margin details

Department enhanced the value of imports on the ground that the sale price of the goods in India were exorbitantly higher than the declared value. the value was enhanced subject to a 20% allowance for profit margin. The importer contested such enhancement and submitted that the selling price in India was inclusive of the costs of transport, insurance, storage, and taxes. Enhancement was set aside as the Tribunal opined that the department had failed to accurately ascertain the cost of the goods at the hands of the importer namely post-importation expenditure and the price at which the imported goods were sold. It was held that post-importation expenses supported by documentary evidence must necessarily be considered to arrive at the cost price and the department's method of fixing 20% as the importer's profit margin based on the sale price of the goods was held to be improper. IMCD GROUP B.V. INDIA v. COMMISSIONER OF CUS. (IMPORT) 2014 (301) E.L.T. 259 (Tri. - Mumbai)]

Agreement with the related parties must considered as a whole including addendums entered therein

Price of the transaction when such price is actually paid and duly payable by such procurer of product or item, such price should be accepted as transaction value. When addendum to memorandum of agreement was entered into by the parties for reduction in the value of such product, such addendum needs to be accepted and cannot be questioned on the ground that memorandum of agreement do not contain such provision for price variation. [Chaudhary Ship Breakers v. Commissioner of Customs [2010] 1 taxmann.com 412/259 ELT 161 (SC)]

Extraordinary circumstances must be taken into consideration while arriving at a value

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Valuation: Invoice value - goods contracted for import at certain price have to be assessed ad valorem at that (invoice) price

FACT: Parle Products Pvt. Ltd., imported two lots of machines from Italy. Dispute arose between them and the Customs Authorities as to the C.I.F. value of the machines for calculating duty, because the Italian firm who sold the machines had revised the prices during the period when import formalities were being dispensed with, but they finally agreed to the original price fixed by them. The Department's contention being that the enhanced price was the acceptable C.I.F. value, they claimed that the goods were under-invoiced and fines of Rs. 21,000 and 16,000 were imposed in lieu of confiscation. The fines were paid under protest, but later reduced to Rs. 5000 and Rs. 3000, after the importers went up in appeal. The revision applications filed by them were rejected and subsequently they filed the present writ petitions.

HELD: Invoice value to be taken as the C.I.F. value for calculating duty since that was the original price quoted by the manufacturer, and the price at which the machines were finally bought by the petitioners. "In my view, therefore, the department was wholly wrong in rejecting the invoice value of these two machines imported by the petitioner and, therefore, there is no justification for demanding any additional duty on the basis of the value as suggested by the department."

2. Invoice price being the actual price of the imported items, there is no violation of the provisions of Import and Export (Control) Act, 1947 or of the Import (Control) Order No. 17, as claimed by the Department, and additional customs duty and fines are therefore not maintainable, (ratio of earlier judgment). "In fact the department's attention was drawn to a case of this High Court in the Union of India and Ors. vs. Glaxo Laboratories (India) Ltd., reported in 1984 (17) E.L.T. 284 (Bombay) in which it is expressly stated that the department ought to have taken the actual price as shown in the invoice and they could not have taken into account the import value for the purpose of debiting the licence. However, the department would not follow the said judgment. In my view, the department's action in this behalf is expressly contrary to the law as laid down by this Court in the said judgment. Therefore, on that count also the department has clearly defaulted."

FACT: Facts

Assessee's appeal along with stay application was pending before High Court.

Pending stay application, Department initiated recovery proceedings in pursuance of CESTAT order in favour of revenue.

Such action was taken in accordance with Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013.

Assessee argued that CBEC had no power to issue such Circular and, in any event, Sl. Nos. 3, 6, 9, 10 and 11 of para 2 of Circular were invalid.

Issue Involved

Whether recovery proceedings were valid in law ?

HELD: A. Board has power to instructions such as those issued in impugned Circular :

Power under Customs Act comes from section 151A : Insofar as section 151A of the Customs Act is concerned, it is worded widely and includes power of the Board to issue instructions, orders and directions for the purpose of uniformity in classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty thereon or for the implementation of any other provisions of the Act or any other law for the time being in force insofar as they relate to any prohibition, restriction or procedure for import or exports of goods. The power of the Board, therefore, to issue any orders, instructions, or directions for the implementation of the provisions of the Act if the Board considers it necessary and expedient to do so cannot be questioned. Recovery of customs duty with or without interest and penalty would certainly arise out of the provisions made in the Customs Act, 1962 and the Rules made thereunder. For example, section 142 of the Customs Act pertains to recovery of sums to the Government. The Customs (Attachment of Property of Defaulters for Recovery of Government Dues) Rules, 1995 provides for the procedure for such recoveries. In that view of the matter, power of the Board to issue such instructions for recovery of customs duty would flow from section 151A of the Customs Act, 1962. [Para 11]

Section 37B of Excise Act does not directly empower issuance of such Circular : Section 37B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, however, is not so widely worded. It empowers the Board, if it considers necessary and expedient to do so for the purpose of uniformity in classification of excisable goods or with respect to levy of duty of excise on such goods, to issue orders, instructions and directions to the Central Excise Officers as deemed fit. The powers of the Board, therefore, can be exercised for the purpose of uniformity in classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty of excise on such goods. When read in conjunction, both the elements touching the powers of the Board would have a bearing on the question of classification of the goods or with the levy of duty of excise on such goods. It is highly questionable whether recovery of excise duty along with interest and penalty can form part of matter of any instructions the Board may issue in exercise of powers under section 37B of the Central Excise Act. However, this issue was not examined in view of provisions of rule 31 of Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 12]

The respondent-assessee was engaged in the business of construction. She constructed a complex during the assessment years 1993-94 to 1996-97. On completion of project in the assessment year 1996-97, the assessee, after taking into consideration the profits offered in the assessment years 1993-94 and 1994-95, offered the balance profit for taxation in the assessment year 1996-97. The Assessing Officer rejected the books of account maintained by the assessee and referred the matter to the departmental valuation cell. The valuation cell determined the value of the property at a much higher amount as against the declared value. The Assessing Officer, after making adjustments to the valuation report, completed assessment under section 143(3) by making addition. Appeal against the said order was rejected by the appellate authority. On further appeal, the assessee contended that since the department had decided by virtue of the Board circular not to make detailed scrutinies for the assessment year 1996-97 if the income declared was more than 30 per cent of the income declared in 1995-96, the assessment itself was bad. The Tribunal accepted the contention and allowed the appeal. In the instant appeal, the appellant submitted that the instructions in the circular were not binding on the Tribunal or the Court nor were available for execution to any judicial authority.

ITO, (International Taxation), 2(3)(1), Mumbai [2021] 123 taxmann.com 252/187 ITD 738/85 ITR(T) 674 (Mumbai - Trib.) for assessment year 2011-12 and of the Kolkata Tribunal in the case of Chandra Prakash Jhunjhunwala v. Dy. CIT [2020] 113 taxmann.com 246/181 ITD 185 (Kolkata - Trib.), which have held that the amendment to section 50C brought into the Act by Finance Act, 2018 with effect from 1-4-2019 was to apply retrospectively with effect from 1-4-2003, when the section 50C was brought into statute. The section 56(2)(vii) being pari-materia to section 50C, and the said Circular No. 8/2018 also amending the provisions of section 56, will be applicable to the case of the assessee also and will accordingly the benefit of the said amendment will apply retrospectively in the case of the assessee also and the difference of Rs. 15.14 lakhs between the actual consideration paid and the FMV being less than 10 per cent will have to be ignored for applying the provisions of section 56(2)(vii) in the case of the assessee. Therefore, in the given facts of the case, the view of the Commissioner is not supported by any judicial authority and therefore his action in holding the assessment order passed in this case to be erroneous as well as prejudicial to the interest of the revenue is merely a change of opinion and the same is not sustainable and the same is quashed. 5.5-9 Cost of Transport upto port should be added

Cost of transport, loading, unloading and handling charges as associated with the delivery of imported goods to the place of importation is to be added in 'Assessable Value'. [Rule 10(2)(a) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 as amended w.e.f. 26-9-2017]

Till 26-9-2017, the words were only 'cost of transportation'. The words in rule 10(2)(b) covered loading, uploading and handling charges associated with the delivery of the imported goods at the place of importation [This covered landing charges at the place of import].

Now, clause (a) covers loading, unloading and handling charge at the load port (i.e. from where goods were exported] are includible in the customs value. Landing charges at the port of import are not includible - para 4.2 of MF(DR) circular No. 39/2017-Cus dated 26-9-2017.

In other words, CIF value is the basis for valuation. If the goods are imported by air, the air freight will be very high. Hence, in case air freight is higher than 20% of FOB price of goods, only 20% of FOB price will be added for Customs Valuation purposes.

If cost of transport is not ascertainable, it will be taken as 20% of FOB value of goods. However, cost of transport within India is not to be considered.

In NGEF Ltd. v. CC - 1996(84) ELT 62 (CEGAT 3 member bench), it was held that freight and insurance costs have to be added even in case of re-importation of exported goods as per provisions of section 20(1) of Customs Act.

Calculation of FOB value if certain additions to be made for expenses out of India on basis of FOB value - In some cases, certain expenses incurred outside India (like license fee, tool amortization costs, free material supplied etc.) are required to be added for valuation of customs duty. In such cases, these should be added in 'FOB value' for purpose of adding freight (20% of FOB value) or insurance (1.125% of FOB value), if actual freight or insurance is not available.

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, read with rules 4 and 9 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988, rule 10 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and Article 14 of the Constitution of India - Valuation of Imported Goods - Transaction Value - General - Period prior to October 2007 - Vide Notification dated 5-7-1990, customs valuation rules provided that loading, unloading and handling charges will be added to value at 1 per cent of CIF (FOB value plus freight plus insurance) irrespective of actual charges - Assessee claimed that actual charges in its case were merely Rs. 69.98 paisa but customs department added a fictional sum of Rs. 15,214.69 in value at 1 per cent of CIF value, which was arbitrary, irrational and unconstitutional - HELD : Scheme of valuation under section 14 (prior to its substitution in 2007) and valuation rules of 1988 is to take into consideration actual price of goods, except where some charges are unascertainable, in which case only, deemed additions are made - Additions in respect of cost of transport and insurance under rule 9(2) read with proviso thereto are made on actual basis and percentage-based fictional additions are made only if actual charges are unascertainable - Addition in respect of 'loading, unloading and handling charges' under rule 9(2)(b) read with proviso (ii) thereto at 1 per cent of CIF, even in those cases where actual cost paid on such an account is available and ascertainable, is ultra vires section 14 and is also arbitrary and violative of Article 14 - Therefore, proviso (ii) to rule 9(2) was read down to mean that deemed addition at 1 per cent of CIF would apply only when actual charges are not ascertainable [Paras 21 to 36] [In favour of assessee]Customs : Deemed addition in respect of 'loading, unloading and handling charges' under rule 9(2)(b) of Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 at 1 per cent of CIF, even where actual charges are available, is ultra vires section 14; hence, said deemed addition at 1 per cent of CIF would apply only if actual charges are not ascertainable

FACT: The assessees challenged constitutional validity of proviso (ii) of rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 inserted by Notification No. 39/90, dated 5-7-1990.

The assessee claimed that the actual loading, unloading and handling charges amounted to Rs. 69.98 paisa as per the tariff of the International Airport Authority of India, Madras (now Chennai). The assessee argued that such a notional fixation of the handling charges with the addition of 1 per cent of CIF value, irrespective of the nature of goods, size of the cargo, was in total disregard to total handling charges, even when such actual handling charges could be ascertained. Same was irrational, arbitrary and ultra vires.

The department argued that it was found impossible to ascertain the actual amounts incurred towards loading, unloading and handling charges while making the assessment as they varied depending upon the quantities and place of import. It was argued that once this uniformity is achieved with the aforesaid provisions, merely because some would be getting the benefit while others would suffer certain detriment, is no reason for invalidating the provision when many others would be getting the benefit thereof as well. The percentage had been fixed by the rule making authority after taken into consideration the overall picture.

Earlier in the course of hearing of the appeal the assessee was directed to explain the entries of customs duty payment in the profit and loss account and balance-sheet. In response to the same, the assessee filed a supplemen-tary paper-book on 21-2-2007 explaining the entries made regarding the closing stock to show that the customs duty had been included therein, and had also explained in details as to how the provisions of section 145A introduced with effect from 1-4-1999 would have no effect in view of the overriding provisions of section 43B. These submissions had been briefly adverted to in the order of the Tribunal. One of the paragraph of the order of the Tribunal showed that the contention of the assessee that since inception, that is, from the assessment year 1994-95 till the assessment year 2006-07 the assessee had been following the inclusive method of accounting for customs duty payment while valuing the stock and that was accepted by the Tribunal. Further, the Tribunal had even stated in this paragraph that this claim of the assessee was not contradicted even in the assessment order. In the same paragraph, the Tribunal had also made an observation that in the year under appeal, the customs duty formed part of the closing stock, though the duty was not debited to the profit and loss account and had also referred to the fact that the duty was separately claimed as deduction in the return of income. In one other paragraph, the Tribunal had accepted the assessee's claim in principle and had observed that it was supported by the Special Bench's order of the Tribunal in Indian Communication Network (P.) Ltd. v. IAC [1994] 49 ITD 56 (Delhi), which was approved by the Supreme Court in Berger Paints India Ltd. v. CIT [2004] 266 ITR 99/ 135 Taxman 586. However, the observations made in the said paragraph showed that the Tribunal had considered that the customs duty was not included in the valuation of the closing stock. This observation was at variance with and contradictory to its earlier finding to the effect that the duty had been included in the closing stock as per the consistent accounting practice adopted by the assessee which was accepted in the assessment. It was only in view of the latter contradictory finding that the Tribunal thought it necessary to restore the matter to the Assessing Officer with the direction to examine the applicability of section 145A to the assessee's case. Even if it was assumed for the sake of argument that the case would have had to be restored to the Assessing Officer to be processed with reference to section 145 A notwithstanding the earlier finding of the Tribunal that the customs duty was included in the valuation of the closing stock, the fact that the assessee's argument was based on the order of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra) was not considered by the Tribunal showed that there was a mistake apparent from the record in light of decision of Supreme Court in Honda Siel Power Products Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 165 Taxman 307. [Para 8]

In Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra), it was held that section 43B has overriding effect over section 145A. This decision was referred to by the Tribunal in its order while summarizing the contentions of the department but unfortu-nately it omitted to deal with this decision and considered its applicability while taking a decision to remit the matter to the Assessing Officer with a direction to examine the applicability of section 145A. This omission had caused prejudice to the assessee in the sense that it had given rise to further proceedings before the Assessing Officer involving further delay in finalising the assessment proceedings, when the legal position already stood con-cluded by the binding order of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra). The other mistake committed by the Tribunal to the prejudice of the assessee was its omission to refer to the assessee's plea that in the subsequent years, the Assessing Officer had accepted the assessee's claim under section 43B and assessments had been completed accordingly. [Para 8]

Appellants, manufacturers of glass sheets, charged from their customers the price of the goods as well as extra charges on account of special packing, cost of transport, forwarding charges, breakage risk and miscellaneous charges. The dispute was whether the charges for the extras were includible in the assessable value of the goods. When the same issue had gone to the High Court earlier, the appellants had contended that they realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers and not from their local buyers. The High Court held that as the appellants realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers, the extra charges were in principle excludible from the assessable value, and further, ordered the department of investigate the assertion of the facts made by the appellants. While the matter was under enquiry, the department received some information that the appellants were indulging in under-valuation of their goods. The Anti-Evasion staff of the department scrutinised the documents of the appellants and came to the conclusion that the appellants had highly inflated the costs of the extra items so as to camouflage the true assessable value of the goods. On this ground, show cause notices were issued demanding differential excise duty of Rs. 1,88,84,508.57 and also a penalty of Rs. 50 lakhs was imposed on the appellants for making false and mis-leading declarations. Confiscation of the plant and machinery of the appellants in lieu of a fine was also ordered. The appellants contended that the show-cause notices issued by the department were time-barred as they were issued beyond the normal time of six months. Further, the appellants pointed out that there has been a violation of principles of natural justice as their request to make further clarifications on the matter, was not honoured by the department. The question as to which of the items of extras should be held to be excludible for determining the assessable value of the goods was also taken up in the instant case.

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Valuation; Assessable value has to include unloading charges also, not merely port charges: but any bonus earned for quick unloading should be deducted

FACT: These are ten appeals which relate to the same respondent and involve common facts and issues; hence a combined order. The respondents are manufacturers of fertilizers and imported rock phosphate and sulphur in bulk quantities came to India on chartered ship. The goods were purchased on the high seas and unloading on the Indian coast was the responsibility of the respondents. For this they maintained their own wharf, unloading equipment and staff at Vishakhapatnam. 1.4% by way of landing charges stood already added to the price of the goods. The Assistant Collector held that this 1.4% did not include stevedoring charges which he added separately and recalculated the value at varying rates from Rs. 5.86 to Rs. 9.42 per MT. In appeal the Appellate Collr. set aside the Asst. Collr.'s orders and held that the 1.4% already added as landing charges were the same as unloading charges. The Department is now in appeal against the Appellate Collector's orders.

HELD: Place of importation has to be the land mass of India where goods are unloaded from the ship. Section 2(23). "Place of importation in section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, should take the similar meaning as place of removal of the imported goods, that is, the port gate. Delivery to the importer is effected only here."

2. Port landing charges comprise only wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds; any unloading charges incurred have to be included in the value for assessment in addition to the port landing charges. Section-14. "The 1.4% Port landing charge already added to the respondents, value comprised wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds and not unloading charges from ship to berth. The unloading charges have therefore to be computed and added too."

3. For calculating the unloading charges and despatch money earned because of unloading of chartered vessel before stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs, but if any money is paid as penalty for delayed unloading of the ships the same should be added.

".........despatch money earned because of unloading of the chartered vessel before the stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs. Conversely if the appellants have paid any penalty for delayed unloading of the ship the same should be added to the costs."
