Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of export goods - Transaction value - General - Periods 2004-05 and 2005-06 - Assessee imported diamonds and exported them showing value-addition of 5 to 10 per cent - Department challenged FOB value of exports arguing that no processing was carried out and all exports took place within 1-4 days of import and export goods were overvalued to claim export incentives - Assessee claimed that processing had been carried out by assortment, sieving, boiling, segregation, etc. - HELD : In absence of any condition that value-addition must result out of any specific processing, value-addition may be achieved by trading as well - Simple processes like sieving, boiling and assorting could also achieve value-addition - In any case, value-addition is a subject matter of examination by DGFT; Customs Department can merely examine FOB value - Hence, declared FOB value cannot be rejected on ground that value-addition could not have been achieved [Paras 18.1 to 18.10] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Whether value-addition has been made or whether same has been correctly shown, is a subject matter of examination by DGFT; Customs Department can merely examine FOB value and cannot reject declared FOB value on ground that value-addition shown by assessee could not have been achieved  Excise  Customs : Circular trading viz. import and export of same goods many times, cannot be alleged to reject FOB value of exports when CIF value of imports was accepted each time

HEADNOTE: Section 119 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Central Board of Direct Taxes - Instructions issued by CBDT to subordinate authorities - Whether assessee was right in contending that circular dated 4-10-1969 would be applicable in its case since it was effective during relevant previous year and ITO was wrong in following circular dated 5-12-1974 which was issued while assessment proceedings were pending - Held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of production and distribution of cine pictures. During the previous year ended 18-10-1971, it had purchased the distributorship rights of six pictures. While making the assessments, the ITO followed the CBDT circular, dated 5-12-1974 and held that the cost of two pictures could be allowed as deduction in full against the income of the year and the cost of remaining four pictures was to be allowed only partially. The assessee contained that during the relevant previous year CBDT circular, dated 4-10-1969 was effective and that the ITO was bound to follow it. The AAC, however, upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal :

HELD: The circulars, instructions and directions of the Board are biding on the income-tax authorities as provided in section 119 but a circular is not law, and the assessee is not bound by it. If such circulars, directions or instructions are to the prejudice of the assessee, he may claim the benefit which was available to him under the provisions of law. However, the assessee cannot claim to be assessed in accordance with the old circular which stood modified by the Board’s subsequent circular when the assessment proceedings are pending particularly when the Board’s instruction clearly showed such an intention on the part of the Board.

The Board had specifically directed that all pending assessments may be completed in accordance with 1974 circular. Since the ITO was bound by the Board’s circular in terms of section 119, he was bound to follow the 1974 circular only.

Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. 1997(93) ELT 194 (CEGAT). [As it is not 'normal price'].

Freight is addible, not hire charges - In Essar Steels Ltd. v. CC 2003 (156) ELT 42 (CEGAT), the importer had hired vessels on time charter basis. Actual time taken by vessel in carrying imported goods was much less than the number of days for which vessels were under time charter hire. It was held that though company was liable to pay for hire charges, the same were not used to carry imported goods. Hence, freight should be assessed on the basis of actual days used for transportation of goods and not on entire hire charges. 'Freight' is cost of transport of imported goods while 'hire charges' is payment made for hire of vessel on time charter basis. There is distinction between the two. - - In the concurring judgment, it was rightly held that only 'normal transport charges' are required to be added - view confirmed in CC v. Essar Steel Ltd. "The aforesaid provisions of the Act, therefore, clearly show that after the imported goods are discharged from the vessel at the wharf the importer cannot immediately take delivery thereof. The imported goods remain in the custody of the Port Trust Authorities till they are, inter alia, cleared for home consumption. This being the position the goods cannot be cleared and delivery taken without their being valued and assessed and, thereafter, duty being paid. Section 14 of the Act provides that the value of the goods shall be deemed to be the price of the goods for the delivery at the time and place of importation in the course of international trade. The value has to be determined with relation to the time when physical delivery to the importer can take place. Physical delivery can take place only after the bill of entry, inter alia, for home consumption is filed and it is the value at that point of time which would be relevant. It is evident that there normally will be some lapse of time between the time when the shipper discharges the goods and the time when the bill of entry is filed. The landing charges, which are imposed at or after the time of the discharge of the goods and prior to the clearance being granted under Section 47 of the Act, necessarily have to be an element which have to be taken into account in determining the value thereof for the purpose of assessing the customs duty which would be chargeable" (Para 14)

The assessee is engaged in ship breaking activity at Alang Ship Breaking Yard. The assessee imported a vessel, namely, M.V. Olinda, for the purpose of breaking the same, and filed a Bill of Entry when the vessel was imported on 7-2-1992.

On 3-3-1992, the assessee cleared the vessel on payment of customs duty on the basis of 7009 metric tons and executed a bank guarantee for Rs.19,90,275/- being the difference in customs duty on 1561 metric tons.

After protesting against the said illegal action of the department in encashing the bank guarantee, the assessee preferred an appeal against the Superintendent's letter dated 2-4-1992 and the Collector's order dated 25-3-1992 before CEGAT.

On 23-6-1998, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Collector dated 25-3-1992.

"The nature of 'miscellaneous charges',........is not clear. However, if such charges were incurred for some service performed in relation to the goods after their removal from the factory gate, such cost would not, in principle, be includible. But if such charges were essential even for giving delivery of the goods at the factory gate, they have to be included."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Transactional value not acceptable for second-hand goods in perfect condition. Reasonable assessment does not call for interference - Undervaluation-Misdeclaration not being deliberate, confiscation and penalty unwarranted -111(d), 111(m)

FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand 1976 model, 4 colour, off-set printing machine and a second-hand 1983 model paper folding machine, both of German make, from the U.K. The declared value of these machines was £ 49,000 and £ 3000.00 respectively. Certificates from Chartered Engineers in support of the transactional value were furnished. However, since the current prices of the machines indicated in the certificates were much lower than the current price indicated by the local agents of the manufacturers of these machines and also because the prices quoted for the year of manufacture were found to be wrong, the Asstt. Collector rejected the certificates. There was a difference of Rs. 10,03,400 between the declared value and the assessable value arrived at by the Department. Alleging deliberate undervaluation with an intention to evade duty, the Asstt. Collector of Customs held both the machines liable to confiscation under section 111(m) of the Customs Act, 1962. The off-set printing machine was held to be liable to confiscation under section 111(d) as well as it was older than 7 years, which was in violation of the provisions of AM 1988-91 Import Policy. Aggrieved by the aforementioned order, the appellants have come in appeal.

HELD: Valuation-Undervaluation established, as machines were in perfect condition, with an expected residual life of 10-12 years, and the depreciation allowed by the adjudicating authority was reasonable. Transactional value not acceptable. "Market of second-hand goods also fluctuates with the market of new goods. If therefore, the certificates issued by the Chartered Engineers have given the prices of new goods at a lower level naturally their estimation of the prices of second-hand goods is also likely to be affected. To that extent the department was right in not placing reliance on the Chartered Engineers' certificates. ........so far as the offset printing machine is concerned, that it has been certified that the machine was found to be in perfect working condition and it had been well maintained and serviced and that no major repairs/reconditioning were necessary. Expected residual life of the machine is estimated at 10 to 12 years. The undisputed service the machine has already completed is about 14 years i.e. from 1976. It is also certified in the said certificate that the machine utilises the current generation of technology and therefore, compares with the latest machinery available in the international market. ........the depreciation of 70% allowed by the adjudicating authority on the price of the new goods in the year of its manufacture, cannot be said to be unreasonable at all. ........Similar comments and assessment of the said Chartered Engineers have been made in respect of the second-hand machine i.e. paper folding machine. .......for a total span of life of 17 to 19 years of the machine, the residual life of 10 to 12 years and other condition being perfect and good the depreciation of 65% allowed by the adjudicating authority cannot on the same reasons be considered unjust. ......We are, therefore, of the view that there has been undervaluation of the machines to the extent upheld in the adjudication order."

2. Freight Insurance—Actual charges being known, with no apparent reason to discard the same, notional charges not to be taken into account. "........the goods have been imported from U.K.. which is farther from India than Germany i.e. freight and insurance charges from Germany are, therefore, likely to be less than those from U.K. Accordingly in the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, there is no reason as to why the actual freight and insurance charges incurred by the appellants from U.K. should not be taken into account rather than the notional freight and insurance charges from Germany to U.K. If, however, the department can find the actual freight and insurance charges liable to be incurred from Germany to India in respect of such machine, they may take them into account. Benefit in respect of valuation of the goods on account of freight and insurance in the light of the above observations may, therefore, be extended to the appellants.

All the 11 appellants in this case imported wood by a vessel from Trinidad through a dealer in Hongkong and declared a value of US $ 321 per cbm. The Customs authorities, however, enhanced the assessable value to US $ 420 per cbm. on the basis of a telex message sent by the Charterers to the Master of the vessel that the approximate value of the wood carried in the ship was US $ 420 per cbm. The appellants question the basis of this valuation and also the correctness of the Deptt. relying on the telex as sole evidence for determining the assessable value without following the procedure for valuation laid down under Sec. 14 of the Customs Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Invoice value must be accepted unless proved incorrect by the department

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Show cause notice to the parties for change in invoice prices is necessary otherwise the decision to enhance the valuation can be set aside on this ground also

FACT: The appellants imported 15000 pcs. of Miniature Ball Bearings from Singapore and gave the invoice price as CIF 3000 Singapore Dollars i.e. Rs. 17,128.20. The Customs Department at Amritsar did not have the price for the goods and so requested Delhi Customs for the same. On getting the information from Delhi Customs, the Department issued a show cause notice to the party for adopting that rate for valuation i.e. 9.25 per piece However, the Asstt. Collector directed the duty to be paid on Rs. 18.40 per piece i.e. on total value of Rs. 21,76,000/- without giving any further show cause notice to the appellants. This rate of 18.40 per piece was obtained from the Central Warehousing Corporation. The appellants contended that the assessable value was to be based on the declared invoice prices unless the department could prove it incorrect. The department wanted the case to be remanded so that the party was given a proper opportunity of being heard on the evidence.

HELD: Valuation: Assessable value for levy of customs duty is to be based on the declared invoiced prices unless proved otherwise by the department. "The onus of proving misdeclaration regarding the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry is on the Department and this can be discharged by the Department only on proving of proper facts, which would discredit the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry and not on the basis of mere suspicion. It is, therefore, on this ground alone that the orders of the lower authorities merit to be set aside."

2. Show Cause notice to the parties for change in invoice prices is necessary otherwise the decision to enhance the valuation can be set aside on this ground also. "What amazes us, is that the show cause notice in this case alleges that the correct price of the imported bearings is Rs. 9.25 per piece whereas the order of the Additional Collector is based on the correct price being Rs. 18.40 per piece. The learned JDR has conceded that the order was passed without furnishing the additional evidence to the appellant and without giving any opportunity to show cause in respect of it. This further seriously undermines the legality of the order."

3. Dissenting view: Per Shri I.J. Rao: Case to be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication. "However, I feel that the omission on the part of the Collector should be allowed to be made good. While I agree that the order should be set aside, I hold that the matter should be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication after disclosing to the appellants the relevant evidence relied on by the department and after giving a reasonable opportunity to them to counter the evidence."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Natural justice - cross-examination regarding relevant telex cannot be denied. Matter remanded for de novo adjudication. Additional evidence can be filed even though disallowed in appellate proceedings

FACT: The appellants had imported a consignment of 'Dielectric Heater Components of Heat Training Systems, and claimed its clearance under OGL Item No. 476, appendix 6, list 8, part I of the Import & Export Policy 1985-88. However the Addl. Collr. held that for ITC purposes, the goods were classifiable under Sl. No. 462(a) of appendix 3A. He also did not accept the invoice price and ordered enhancement of the assessable value from Rs. 5,15,696/- to Rs. 10,71,721.70 under section 14(1)(h) of the Customs Act. He confiscated the imported goods with an option to redeem on payment of fine of Rs. 10,00,000 and also imposed penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 under section 112(a) of Customs Act. In their appeal to the Tribunal, the appellants sought permission for filing certain additional evidence and a similar request was received from the Department. The appellants also stated that they were denied the opportunity of cross-examination of the two officials whose advice was taken into account and that they were not confronted with the telex relied upon for upward revision of the value which has figured only in the adjudication order.

HELD: Natural justice--principles violated since cross-examination regarding relevant telex was denied to the appellants. Matter remanded to the adjudication authorities. Fresh evidence can be filed (ratio of Supreme Court judgment in Kalra Glue Factory v. Sales Tax Tribunal). "The appellants had pleaded for the cross-examination of Shri Prabhat Kumar which was not granted. We are of the view that there was dental of principles of natural justice.......We ate of the view that telex is very relevant for valuation, and the appellant should have been confronted with the same, and an opportunity should also be given for rebuttal. ...we are of the view that the matter should be remanded. Since cross-examination was also denied, we are of the view that there was denial of principles of natural justice. ......we remand the matter to the adjudicating authority having jurisdiction and give an opportunity to the appellants to cross-examine them. Both the sides are at liberty to file any fresh evidence to substantiate their case in accordance with law. We further order that re adjudication will be done within three months from the receipt of this order."

2. Additional Evidence--The lower authority is free to decide the request of the appellants for admission of any additional evidence on merits as per law for the purpose of de-novo adjudication proceedings before him, even though it was disallowed in the appellate proceedings. "...I would like to observe that learned Brother while he has disallowed the admission of additional evidence......he has observed in the operative portion of the order that both the sides are at liberty to file any fresh evidence to substantiate their case in accordance with law. By way of clarification I would like to add that while we have disallowed the admission of the documents as above for the purpose of the appellate proceedings before us, the lower authority is free to decide the request of the appellants for admission of any additional evidence, as held by learned Brother, on merits as per law for the purpose of de novo adjudication proceedings before him."

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1949 - Writ - Maintainability of - Alternative Remedy - Writ can be invoked a second time if earlier appeal was not disposed of on merits, but was withdrawn to enable parties to come to a settlement and when settlement is prima facie wrong and perverse and delay has caused irreparable damage, alternative remedy is not a bar to maintainability. Valuation--precedent--identical goods cannot be assessed differently for different importers if customs have earlier cleared goods at those rates; quotation of higher rates is not proof of under invoicing. Valuation--clubbing together--different consignments for different importers cannot be clubbed together just because they can be assembled together to make a complete VCR; as individual consignment is for parts, they cannot be held to be in SKD condition. Cus. Act: S. 14. Precedent--ratio of Supreme Court and Cegat decisions must be considered by the authorities. Review--Collector has no review power under the Customs Act and Rules; he can only issue notice, U/s. 129D, so his reviewing his earlier decision is bad in law, Cus. Act: S. 129D, Imports  Exports (Control) Act: S. 167(8)

FACT: The petitioner is an importer of various electronic components of T.V., V.C.R. electronic type-writers etc. In 1987 the petitioner imported two consignments of Printed Circuit Board Sub-Assembly, Remote Control and Miscellaneous Hardware. He also purchased V.C.R. parts from the recognised export houses on 'High seas sales basis'. The goods were duly assessed and some of them kept at the customs bonded warehouse. The customs authorities meanwhile raided the business premises of the petitioners, and charged the petitioners with under-invoicing, and importing complete VCRs in the name of name-lender firms. Various demands were raised in lieu of short levy, fines and penalties, and the petitioner paid under protest a total sum of Rs. 11,11,990.11 and got released the goods, being under pressure to resume production in his factory which was lying closed for want of materials.

HELD: Writ jurisdiction--Maintainability--There is no bar to invoking Writ Jurisdiction a second time on same issue, if the earlier appeal was not disposed of on merits, but was withdrawn to enable parties to come to a settlement. Where the settlement arrived at is prima facie wrong and perverse and delay has already caused irreparable damage to the petitioner, writ appeal is valid and maintainable. Alternative remedy is not a bar to maintainability in such a case. "There is no doubt in my mind that there was some understanding between the writ petitioner and the respondents regarding the manner and mode of assessment to be made. But for one reason or other, the respondents did not rise up to the expectation. The writ petition and the appeal arising out of such writ petition were withdrawn in the expectation that the respondents would judiciously load the value. ........The writ application was not dismissed on merits. It was allowed to be withdrawn to enable the parties to arrive at a settlement. .......As the settlement failed, which is demonstrated by the order of adjudication, the petitioner has challenged the validity of such order. .......Accordingly, it cannot be said that the petitioner cannot invoke the writ jurisdiction for the second time. ......In this case, Collector had adjudicated and passed an order which is highly prejudicial to the petitioner. If this order has to be challenged in the appropriate forum, the petitioner may not get the desired relief for long time to come. This aspect of the matter cannot be overlooked in considering whether the application is maintainable or not. ........On the facts and in the circumstances of this case, I am of the view that the order of adjudication is illegal and manifestly, arbitrary and unreasonable and delay would cause irreparable loss and prejudice to the petitioner. In the premises, the contention that the writ petition is not maintainable cannot be accepted."

The appellants manufacture weighing machines which are sold from their depots in different regions at varying prices. On the appellants quoting the price at Calcutta as the assessable value, the Excise Dept. charged them with mis-declaration as the sale prices at various depots were higher. The Department also claimed that the duty had not been paid on some of the machines removed from the factory. The appellants were asked to furnish the details of their pricing pattern, and when this was not forthcoming a show cause notice was issued demanding payment of duty based on the highest sale price; payment of duty short levied, and also a penalty.

The appellants contended that the Calcutta price represented the true assessable value and that the difference in prices at their depots was due to post clearance deductible expenses like insurance, freight and handling charges; that the show cause notice was time barred as it was served 6 months after the date of issue; that the earlier acceptance of the Department of certain contract prices should not be revoked; that a comprehensive check of the documents would prove that duty had been paid on all the machines removed.

The Department conceded that the case should be remanded and a verification made of the appellants' contention regarding removals, but claimed an extended time limit for the show cause notice on the ground of mis-declaration.

1. Assessable Value--Assessable value of an imported car is world-car-catalogue Price less 15% failing which manufacturer's Net price to whole-sale dealer's failing both invoice price. "We order that the same basis should be followed in the case of the present appellant also and his car re-assessed on the basis of the World Car Catalogue Price of the same model less 15% discount. ......In case the World Car Catalogue Price is not available with the Customs House, the Customs may ascertain the manufacturer's net price to wholesale dealers in the course of international trade in any other manner. If this course is also not feasible, the assessment may be maintained at the appellant's invoice price. There is no question of granting the 15% discount on the individual export passenger's invoice price.''

2. Assessable Value--Ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges are part of delivery price at the place of importation, hence form a part of assessable value. "Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 requires that valuation should be done on the basis of the price for delivery of the goods at the place of importation. The imported goods have to be valued according to this provision. Seeking analogy of a different enactment which deals with locally manufactured goods is a totally mis-conceived exercise. No imported goods can be delivered at the port of importation in India without incurring the ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges. These charges have, therefore, been correctly added to the basic price of the car."

3, Assessable Value--No depreciation admissible if the car has not been used abroad. "Depreciation is given if the car is possessed and used abroad. Here, the appellant purchased a brand new car and loaded it for shipment to India. He did not use the car abroad. No depreciation as asked for is permissible."

4. Additional duty--Additional duty is also customs duty and not excise duty. "Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 separately specifies the rates for basic customs duty and additional customs duty both of which are to be charged on the imported goods. The additional customs duty is also very much a duty of customs. Just because its rate generally happens to be equivalent to the excise duty chargeable on the like goods manufactured in India, it does not cease to be a customs duty."

5. Air-conditioner fitted in a car, not being an essential components, is separately assessable even if invoice shows composite price for the car and the Air-Conditioner. "An Air-Conditioner is not an essential component of the car. It is not even a standard part of the car. It is an optional accessory and is supplied to only those purchasers of cars who asked for it. The department has, therefore, correctly assessed the Air-Conditioner separately under Head 84.12 of the Tariff."

The assessee had provided in its accounts import duty on newsprint imported by it at Rs. 825 per metric ton. for the period from 1981 to 1985. The Assessing Officer noticed that the Supreme Court in its judgment dated 6-12-1984 had allowed the Government to recover only Rs. 550 per metric ton. He added the amount of difference between provision made for customs duty and the amount actually payable by the assessee as per the judgment of the Supreme Court. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the judgment of the Supreme Court did not have the effect of cancelling the levy and deleted the addition for the assessment year 1985-86. The Assessing Officer again included the said amount in the assessee’s income for the assessment year under consideration because the Government had issued a notification on 19-12-1985 and abolished the auxiliary duty and fixed the import duty at Rs. 550 per MT. The Assessing Officer also noticed that the CBEC had also issued a circular dated 10-2-1986 intimating that the effective rate of customs duty would be Rs. 550 only from 1-3-1981 to 18-12-1985, and this notification had the effect of cancelling the auxiliary duty. Since the above notification and circular issued by the CBEC fell within the relevant assessment year, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer for this year.

On second appeal :

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for custom - Reference to Larger Bench - Assessable value - Demurrage charges - whether demurrage charges could be excluded from assessable value in cases of imports made after 2.3.2001 even where assessments were provisional - referred to Larger Bench in view of doubts about correctness of CESTAT's earlier judgments (Paras 8  9)

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - goods manufactured in USA and Italy supplied to appellant by trader in Singapore - export declaration of manufacturers produced by Deptt. show higher value than price at which trader sold goods to appellant - documents procured by Deptt. neither bear any signatures nor attested and are photocopies - no statement of manufacturers brought on record - prices of goods consistent with prices of contemporaneous imports - invoice signed by US supplier produced by appellant - enhancement of value not sustainable - appeals allowed (Paras 8  9)

HEADNOTE: Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 - Levy of additional duty - Additional duty (CVD) of customs is calculated on the aggregate of CIF value plus basic duty and any other customs duty

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Additional duty of customs (CVD) is not violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India--Value for assessment is the landed cost including charges upto point of clearance

Section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Exemption from Customs duty - Exemption notification can be availed of only where its conditions are satisfied--Notification 302/79-CE

FACT: The petitioners imported in February 1983, 51 metric tonnes of High Density Polyethylene Moulding Powder. Customs duty and auxiliary duty was levied on the item at the rate of 50% and 25% respectively of the c.i.f. value and the additional or countervailing duty was fixed at the rate of 42% of c.i.f. value added on to customs duty. The petitioners contended that loading of customs duty on c.i.f. value for the purpose of arriving at countervailing duty is not permissible; that there should be partial exemption of countervailing duty as prescribed by Notification No. 302/79-CE and that landing and port charges were not to be added on the dutiable value of the imported item.

HELD: Additional duty (CVD) duty--Customs duty to be added on to c.i.f. value while determining countervailing duty. "The sub-section opens with the words for the purpose of calculating under Section 3 the additional duty on any imported article....'. It further recites that the value of the imported article shall be the aggregate of (a) the value of the imported article determined under sub-section (1) of Section 14, and (b) any duty of customs chargeable on that article under Section 12 of the Customs Act. In view of the clear statutory provision, it is futile for Dr. Kantawala to submit that the customs duty cannot be loaded on c.i.f. value while determining assessable value for the purpose of additional or countervailing duty." [Section 3(2) of Customs Tariff Act, 1975].

2. Value of imported goods not determined at point of entry--all expenses till goods are cleared from port form part of the value of imported goods. "In our judgment, the taxable event continues till the goods are cleared at Customs barrier for home consumption and all the expenses which are required to be incurred in respect of those imported goods form part of the value of those goods and it is not permissible for the importer to suggest that the value of goods should be determined at the point of time of entry into territorial waters and all expenses incurred thereafter are post-import expenses."

3. Exemption Notification No. 302/79-CE--its impact on countervailing duty--advantage of Notification available only after fulfilling both conditions of the said notification. "The advantage of the notification dated December 4, 1979 is available provided both the conditions are satisfied, the conditions being that the goods are manufactured from raw naphtha and on which the appropriate amount of excise duty has already been paid. It is obvious that the imported goods cannot satisfy the second condition, because the payment of excise duty on raw naphtha can never arise in respect of imported goods." [Notification No. 302/79-CE; CE Rule 8(i)]

4. Additional Duty (CVD): Duties imposed under Section 3(2) of CTA are neither void nor unconstitutional. "It is impossible to accede to the submission of the learned counsel. The two categories of tax-payers cannot be bracketed in the same class and it would be improper to suggest that the goods locally manufactured and the goods imported form the same class. In our judgment, the two categories of goods are not at all comparable and totally distinct and different. Levy of countervailing duty on the value ascertained by addition of customs duty to c.i.f. value cannot be claimed to be discriminatory and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. .....In our judgment, the Section does not suffer from any vice and cannot be struck down."

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Depreciation - Car (used) - 1993 model car imported in 1996 and bill of entry filed on 31.8.1996 - Car was cleared by Customs on 28.3.2005 - Depreciation for post importation period i.e. from 31.8.96 to 28.3.2005 is not permissible for determining assessable value as value at the time of import/filing of bill of entry is to be adopted - Appeal dismissed with liberty to file suit for damages against Customs (Paras 3,4, 7  9)

FACT: Under the provisions of he Customs Act 1962, the assessee was entitled to pay import duty at concessional rates on spare parts and tools if their value did not exceed 10 per cent of the total value of imported machinery, but if the value exceeded this percentage, he was required to pay duty at higher rates. Section 143 of the Customs Act, 1962, also permitted the assessee to execute a bond, agreeing to pay the difference in duty when demanded by the customs authorities. For the assessment years 1973-74 to 1976-77, the assessee had executed such a bond and imported goods on which only provisional assessments at concessional rates of duty had been made by the customs department and the assessee had also paid duty at such conces-sional rates only. However, since the value of the imported goods exceeded the specified percentage, the assessee made provision in its accounts towards additional customs duty payable, and claimed it as a deduction. The ITO disallowed the claim since no demand had been raised by the customs department. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the claim.

On second appeal:

HELD: In T.M. Abdul Rahim Sahib & Co. v. CIT [1963] 50 ITR 508 , the Madras High Court had held that there can be no liability either notional or legal unless and until a demand had been made by the appropriate authority.

In view of the provisions of section 143 of the Customs Act, the liability for the payment of additional duty arises only when final assessment has been made. The words used in section 143 are 'notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or such other law'. Irrespective of the other provisions in the Act or any other law or item 72A of the Indian Customs and Central Excise Tariff, once a bond is executed under section 143, it is the terms of that bond that would prevail and the other provisions of the Act or any other law or tariff would not be applicable. After the provisional assessment is made, additional liability will arises only when final assessment is made and final demand is raised. Till then there is no liability for additional duty.

Consequently, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in allowing the assessee's claim.

SECTION 145 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961—METHOD OF ACCOUNTING— VALUATION OF WORK-IN-PROGRESS—WHETHER ASSESSEE COULD CHANGE METHOD OF VALUATION OF WORK-IN-PROGRESS FROM MATERIAL COST PLUS DIRECT WAGES TO MATERIAL COST ONLY—HELD, NO

The value of leather tanning machinery imported by the appellants was assessed by the lower authorities on the basis of ruling prices as per the price lists in force on the date of opening of letter of credit. The appellants argued that even though the prices of the machinery had more than doubled, the foreign suppliers had agreed to adhere to the old prices quoted in the proforma invoices. The (departmental authorities, however, were of the view that the concept of value under Section 14 was a deemed value and not necessarily the invoice value of a particular importer.

III. Section 11A, read with section 33A of the Central Excise Act, 1944, article 226 of the Constitution of India, section 73 of the Finance Act, 1994 and section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Recovery - Of duty or tax not levied/paid or short-levied/paid or erroneously refunded - Adjudication of demand - Assessee challenged an adjudication order on ground that : (a) it was passed almost 9 months after conclusion of hearing i.e., beyond period of 15 days/1 month specified in circular dated 5-8-2003, (b) it did not consider various submissions/evidences put forth by assessee - Department argued that impugned order was correct and even otherwise, in view of alternative remedy of appeal, writ was not maintainable - HELD : Submissions and evidences put forth by assessee were not considered, which can only be attributed to delay in passing order and, thus, delay had caused prejudice to assessee - Since impugned order was contrary to already laid down parameters of law, assessee could not be relegated to alternate remedy by way of appeal - Hence, matter was remanded back for fresh hearing and passing of order [Paras 5 to 10] [In favour of assessee]

HEADNOTE: Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 - Computed value - ITC Policy 85-88 - Project export--Valuation--assessment without notice to party is violation of principles of Natural Justice--Remanded. Customs Valuation Rules: Rule 8

FACT: The appellants imported from Iraq three lots of 8-10 year old used machinery under ITC Policy 85-88, under the heading 'Project Export'. They declared value of these machinery on the basis of assessment by an independent Chartered Engineer from Iraq. The Asstt. Collr. rejected the certificate of valuation in respect of the third lot and assessed FOB value by allowing the usual 3 years depreciation from the estimated CIF value of new machinery. Hence the appeal.

HELD: Natural Justice:--Enhancement of assessable value to the prejudice of the appellants, without issuing a show cause notice to them is against the principles of natural justice and cannot be upheld. "While enhancing the assessable value to the prejudice of the appellants, by rejecting the declared price of the equipment and machinery which was followed in respect of previous imports, and the contract/agreement for freight and insurance, the Assistant Collector ought to have issued a show cause notice asking them why the declared price, freight & insurance ought not to be accepted. An illegible "Query memo" and reply thereto cannot be treated as a substitute to the "show cause notice" and personal hearing......The order of the Assistant Collector is in violation of principle of natural justice and is liable to be set aside."

The question involved in the instant appeal is as to whether ship demurrage charges paid by the assessee-importer on the import of the goods were to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for purpose of levy of customs duty.

ELT 207 = 42 RLT 181 (CEGAT).

Stamp duty payable to State Government - Stamp Duty payable to State Government cannot be added in assessable value of imported goods. - Umi Special Steel v. CC 2001(137) ELT 174 (CEGAT) * Tata Yodogawa v. CC 2001(135) ELT 960 (CEGAT).

Computer Software - Note that software imports are exempt from customs duty. Software embedded or pre-loaded in machine is to be classified along with the machine. This will also be case when software is brought separately, but as a 'set'. If tangible software e.g. operating software or application software loaded on disk, floppy, CD-ROM etc. is imported, it will be classifiable as software under heading 8523 - CC (Import), Mumbai PN 39/2007 dated 3-12-2007 - same view in Indusind Media v. CC (2019) 368 ELT 235 (SC).

In Bharti Airtel v. CC (2012) 286 ELT 270 (CESTAT), it was held that software imported separately has to be classified and valued separately, even if imported along with computer. Even peripheral devices like memory devices and systems software are to be treated independently. However, software embedded/etched/burnt into hardware has to be considered as part of hardware and its value forms part of the computer.

In Bhagyanagar Metals v. CCE (2009) 67 taxmann.com 33 = 241 ELT 63 (CESTAT), it was held that value of software which is necessary for functioning of the equipment and is embedded into it in includible in assessable value of the main equipment - same view in Indusind Media v. CC (2019) 368 ELT 235 (SC).

In Bharti Airtel v. CC (2012) 286 ELT 270 (CESTAT) it was held that software embedded in telecom equipment is part of telecom equipment and included in its value.

5.6-1 Interest on deferred payment

Interest on deferred payment, if shown separately in the Invoice cannot be added - CBI&C Clarification No. F.3/12/57-Cus VI dated 27-7-1987 - quoted and followed in Bharat Foam Udyog (P.) Ltd. v. ACC - 1993 (67) ELT 445 (Coll Appl) - same view in Zenith Steel Pipes v. CC - (1995) 80 ELT 886 (CEGAT 3 member bench) * CC v. Bharat Foam Udyog P Ltd. 1997(93) ELT 69 (CEGAT). However, if there is a fixed charge payable irrespective of date of payment, it will not be allowed as deduction even if such fixed charge is termed as 'interest' - Themis Agencies v. CC 1998(104) ELT 487 (CEGAT).

CBI&C has further clarified vide circular No. 20/97-Cus dated 17.6.1997, that interest charged on deferred payment should normally not be added in the assessable value, if (a) Interest element has no nexus with or bearing on value of goods (b) Interest is shown separately in invoice (c) There is no financing agreement/arrangement or any special relationship between importer and exporter, influencing the declared price (d) Price declared is the price actually paid or payable in the ordinary course of trade. However, interest can be added if there is evidence to indicate a nexus between price of goods and interest element, and where circumstances also indicate that this element has also influenced selling price.

In CC v. Jayant Oil Mills (P) Ltd. 1998 AIR SCW 4018 = AIR 1999 SC 1569 = 1998(100) ELT 10 (SC) also, it was confirmed that interest on delayed payment goes to banker and not to seller. It is not addible to assessable value.

5.6-2 Demurrage

Demurrage is of two types - (a) Ship Demurrage when whole ship is chartered and demurrage is payable when ship was not unloaded within specified time (b) demurrage payable to port trust as goods are not cleared from port within prescribed time.

Demurrage charges payable to port trust - Demurrage payable to port trust as goods were not cleared in time is a post landing event, i.e. after goods are landed in the port. In any case, valuation is required to be done on 'ordinary price'. Demurrage cannot be termed as part of 'normal' or 'ordinary' price of a product and hence not includible.

Demurrage charges are after goods are imported. These are post importation charges and not includible in assessable value - CCE v. Mangalore Refinery (2015) 325 ELT 214 (SC). - followed in CC v. MGM International Exports (2022) 380 ELT 3 (SC).

Circular No. 5 of 2016 dated 09.02.2016

Taking into account various representations made by trade and industry in relation to the delays in finalisation of SVB investigations, continued uncertainty due to provisional assessment, increase in transaction costs due to extra duty deposits and burdensome procedure of renewal of SVB borders, the procedures were streamlined vide this Circular. The key points to be noted under this Circular are:

(i)

The SVB is to function under the supervisory control of the jurisdictional Chief Commissioner/Principal Commissioner.

(ii)

The Director General of Valuation (DGoV) shall support the Commissioners by issuing advisories on legal issues and guidance notes.

(iii)

The Extra Duty Deposit as a security was abolished. However, failure to provide documents and information within 60 days of requisition would attract 5% of the declared assessable value to be imposed by the Commissioner for a period not exceeding the next three months along with granting of 60 more days to provide the information.

(iv)

In case the information is not submitted within the extended period as well, the Commissioner in charge of SVB may consider the use of other provisions of the Customs Act for obtaining documents. Information from an importer for conducting investigations.

(v)

The SVB was to no longer issue an appealable order and instead, convey its investigative findings by way of an investigation report to the referring customs formation for finalizing the provisional assessments.

(vi)

A questionnaire was also introduced by the Department to be filled by the importer, to enable the jurisdictional officer to take a decision on whether a case needs to be referred to SVB for investigations.

(vii)

Three categories were exempted from SVB investigations – import of samples and prototypes from related sellers; imports from related sellers where duty chargeable (including additional duty of Customs, etc.) is unconditionally fully exempted or nil; any transaction where the value of imported goods is less than Rs.1 Lakh but cumulatively these transactions do not exceed Rs. 25 Lakhs in any financial year.

(viii)

Cases which may be considered for SVB investigations along with the procedure for considering reference to SVB; procedure for cases where reference to SVB was not required; procedure in SVB; finalization of assessments; instructions in relation to change in circumstances surrounding the sale were also provided.

(ix)

The DGoV was to facilitate co-ordination amongst the SVBs. Once a case was registered by the SVB, detailed information regarding the same along with the IEC Code of the importer should be entered in the Central Registry Database (CRD) maintained by the DGoV and they shall monitor the progress of the investigations and report to the Board cases involving any inordinate delays.

The assessee has contended that as the similar claims had been decided in favour of the banks for the assessment years 1991-92 to 1993-94 by Special Bench of the Tribunal, which had not been challenged by the department, the issue had attained finality and could not be disturbed in the subsequent years. [Para 12]

The above contention of the assessee-bank is not impressive. Merely because the orders of the Special Bench of the Tribunal were not assailed in appeal by the department itself, this would not take away the right of the revenue to question the correctness of the orders of assessment, particularly when a question of law is involved. There is no doubt that the earlier order of the Commissioner (Appeals) had merged into the judgment of the Special Bench of the Tribunal and attained finality for that relevant year. Equally, it is true that though the Full Bench of the Kerala High Court specifically overruled the Division Bench judgment of that very Court in the case of South Indian Bank Ltd. (supra ), it did not notice any of the contentions before and principles stated by the Special Bench of the Tribunal in its impugned judgment.

The questions raised in the instant appeal go to the very root of the matter and are questions of law in relation to interpretation of sections 36(1)(vii ) and 36(1)(viia) read with section 36(2). Thus, the findings recorded in the earlier assessment years 1991-92 to 1993-94 would not be binding on the department for subsequent years as well. [Para 13]

Sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) provide for such deductions, which are to be permitted, in accordance with the language of these provisions. A bare reading of these provisions show that sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) are separate items of deduction. These are independent provisions and, therefore, cannot be intermingled or read into each other. It is a settled canon of interpretation of fiscal statutes that they need to be construed strictly and on their plain reading. [Para 16]

The provisions of section 36(1)(vii ) would come into play in the grant of deductions, subject to the limitation contained in section 36(2). Any bad debt or part thereof, which is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts of the assessee for the previous year, is the deduction which the assessee would be entitled to get, provided he satisfies the requirements of section 36(2). Allowing of deduction of bad debts is controlled by the provisions of section 36(2). The argument advanced by the revenue is that it would amount to allowing a double deduction if the provisions of sections 36(1)(vii ) and 36(1)(viia) are permitted to operate independently. There is no doubt that a statute is normally not construed to provide for a double benefit unless it is specifically so stipulated or is clear from the scheme of the Act. As far as the question of double benefit is concerned, the legislature in its wisdom introduced section 36(2)(v ) by the Finance Act, 1985 with effect from 01.04.1985. Section 36(2)(v) concerns itself as a check for claim of any double deduction and has to be read in conjunction with section 36(1)(viia ). It requires the assessee to debit the amount of such debt or part thereof in the previous year to the provision made for that purpose. [Para 17]

Circulars can be issued by the Board to explain or tone down the rigours of law and to ensure fair enforcement of its provisions. These circulars have the force of law and are binding on the income tax authorities, though they cannot be enforced adversely against the assessee. Normally, these circulars cannot be ignored. A circular may not override or detract from the provisions of the Act but it can seek to mitigate the rigour of a particular provision for the benefit of the assessee in certain specified circumstances. So long as the circular is in force, it aids the uniform and proper administration and application of the provisions of the Act. [Para 18]

Basis on which Circular was issued was arbitrary - Condition of recovery pending stay application read down - Recovery only if delay in disposition is due to fault of assessee : The Circular was purportedly issued in terms of judgment in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The said judgment lays down that mere filing of an appeal does not operate as stay or suspension of the order appealed against. But the Board over-looked the fact that the assessee is not seeking stay only on account of filing of an appeal, but for the reason that the assessee has sought dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied and has a right to demand decision on such application, the right which is created by the statute. Therefore, the very basis of the Circular is untenable, misconceived, wholly illegal and arbitrary. Therefore, the condition of recovery, if no stay is granted within 30 days, is illegal, arbitrary, unjustified and consequently set aside. [Para 44]

Right of consideration in appeal and on an application for waiver of pre-deposit, is a right conferred by the statute and such right cannot be defeated on the basis of Circular, which contemplates that the recovery can be effected, is stay is not granted within 30 days. Therefore, such condition in the Circular is not legal and is therefore set aside with the observation that till such time, the application for waiver of pre-deposit is decided in an appeal filed in terms of the statute, the revenue shall not proceed to recover the same provided that the assessee does not delay the hearing of the appeal directly or indirectly. In the event, the assessee is delaying the decision, the revenue shall be at liberty to move an application before the Commissioner (Appeals) to take the application for waiver of pre-deposit and seek orders thereon in accordance with law. If such an application is filed by the revenue, the Commissioner (Appeals) shall decide the same expeditiously. [Para 46]

Thus, direction to recover the duty demanded and penalty levied, if the stay was not granted within 30 days, contravenes the right of consideration of appeal and of an application for waiver of pre-deposit conferred under section 35F of the Act and is illegal. Such direction to the Administrative Officers to recover the amount pending consideration of application of waiver of pre-deposit is not justified and, thus, not enforceable in law. [Para 47]

Time-limit of 180 days in stay matters before Tribunal is not mandatory - Vacation of stay will take place only if Revenue claims before Tribunal that delay was attributable to assessee :

As per second proviso to section 35C(2A), if an order of stay is made in any proceedings relating to an appeal filed under sub-section (1) of section 35B, the Appellate Tribunal shall dispose of the appeal within a period of 180 days from the date of such order. The further proviso is if an appeal is not disposed of within the period specified in the first proviso, the stay order shall, on the expiry of that period, stand vacated. [Para 48]

Though the right of appeal is a creation of statute and it can be exercised only subject to the conditions specified therein, but the conditions specified have to be in relation to the assessee as something which is required to be complied with by the assessee. But where the assessee has no control over the functioning of the Tribunal, then the provision of vacation of stay cannot be sustained. [Para 51]

The assessee having preferred appeal and that Tribunal being satisfied that condition for dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied is made out, is compelled to pay the duty demanded and penalty levied, if the appeal is not decided within 180 days. The assessee has no control in respect of matters pending before the Tribunal; in the matter of availability of infrastructure; the members of the Tribunal and the workload. Therefore, for the reason that the Tribunal is not able to decide appeal within 180 days, the vacation of stay is a harsh and onerous and unreasonable condition. The condition of vacation of stay for the inability of the Tribunal to decide the appeal is burdening the assessee for no fault of his. Such a condition is onerous and renders the right of appeal as illusory. An order passed by a judicial forum is sought to be annulled for no fault of assessee. [Para 52]

Therefore, such condition of automatic vacation of stay on the expiry of 180 days, has to be read down to mean that after 180 days the revenue has a right to bring to the notice of the Tribunal the conduct of the assessee in delay or avoiding the decision of appeal, so as to warrant an order of vacation of stay. If the provision is not read down in the manner mentioned above, such condition suffers from illegality rendering the right of appeal as redundant. [Para 52]

(1) Whether Section 145A overrides the provisions of Section 36(1)(iii)?

The proviso to section 36(1)(iii) incorporated in Part D of Chapter IV of the Act providing for the 'Method of Computation of Total Income', will override provisions of section 145A, which is incorporated in Chapter IV of the Act relating to 'procedure for assessment'. The words in the proviso to section 36(1) 'whether capitalised or not' will override the accounting practice followed in the books of account by the assessee. In the present case, the assessee has admittedly capitalised the interest paid on the borrowed capital. The assesse also did not claim that the land in question was put to use in the assessment years in question. Mere purchase of the land in the years in question out of the borrowed capital does not entitle the assessee to claim such interest paid on borrowed capital as a deductible expenditure in the present assessment years merely on the basis of method of accounting prescribed under section 145A which was brought in the statute to undo the effect of the decision of the Delhi High Court in Chamber of Tax Consultants v. Union of India [2017] 87 taxmann.com 92 [2018] 252 Taxman 77/400 ITR 178 (Delhi) which quashed the CBDT Notification No. 87 of 2016 dated 29.9.2016 finding it to be ultra vires. The method of accounting provided for the valuation of inventory under section 145A does not determine the allowability of the expenditure. The proviso to section 36(1)(iii), which says that such a claim of deduction will be allowed in the assessment years when it was put to use, will override the provisions contained in section 145A. [Mahindra World City Developers Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax, Company Circle-IV(1), Chennai [2019] 107 taxmann.com 16 (Madras)]

(2) Is it necessary to add customs duty (not yet paid) to the value of imported materials kept at customs bonded warehouse?

According to section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962, customs duty shall be levied on goods imported into or exported from India. Section 2(23) of the said Act defines 'import' as bringing into India from a place outside India. Section 2(27) of the said Act defines India as including the territorial waters of India. Therefore, the taxable event occurs when goods enter the territorial waters of India. Duty liability has arisen but is only deferred by deposit in the bonded warehouse. Deposit in the bonded warehouse does not extinguish the duty liability. Therefore, the duty element should be added for making the adjustments under section 145A. ["Issues on Tax Audit" by ICAI]

(3) Is a Deposit made with port trust in the nature of the tax, duty, cess or fee liable to be added under Section 145A to the cost of imports?

Deposit made with port trust will not fall under the category of tax, duty, cess or fee as mentioned in section 145A. The deposit made with the port trust is not includible in the computation made under section 145A, if it does not fall in the category of tax, duty, cess or fee levied under any law. Hence, the same shall be liable to be included in the adjustments made under section 145A only if it is shown that the payment was made under the authority of any law. Further, since the deposit so made is refundable to the assessee, then also the question of including the same under section 145A does not arise. [Mazagaon Dock Ltd. v. ITO [2017] 85 taxmann.com 213 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

It is not in dispute that originally the goods in question, being Dialysers were classified under CTH 90189031. The impugned circular has sought to change such classification by bringing Dialysers under CTH 84212900. [Para 26]

Chapter 90 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'optical, photographic, cinematographic, measuring, checking, precision, medical or surgical instruments and apparatus; parts and accessories thereof.' Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to 'instruments and appliances used in medical, surgical, dental or veterinary sciences including scientigraphic apparatus, other electro-medical apparatus and sight-testing instruments. CTH 90189031 specifically pertains to renal dialysis equipment (artificial kidneys, kidney machines and dialysers). [Para 27]

Chapter 84 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'nuclear reactors, boilers, machinery and medical appliances; parts thereof.' Heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to 'centrifuges, including centrifugal dryers; filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus, for liquids or gases.' CTH 84212900 talks of 'filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus for gases.' [Para 28]

Thus, CTH 90189031 specifically provides for dialysers whereas CTH 84212900 provides for generic description of articles. Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to medical instruments whereas heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to goods which are generally used for industrial purposes and do not appear to have any medical use. Hence, the natural classification of dialysers should be under CTH 90189031 as it was prior to issuance of the impugned circular. When a specific tariff heading for classification is available, the goods concerned cannot be classified under a generic tariff heading. A heading with a more specific description of the goods in question shall be preferred to and prevail over a heading with a more general description. Just as a special law in a particular field would prevail over a general law that may be operational in that field, a heading with a more specific description would prevail over a heading with a more general description. In this connection, rule 3(a) of the General Rules for interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act makes it very clear that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description.

If the department intends to classify the goods in question under a heading which is different from the heading under which an assessee classifies such goods, the burden of proof is on the department which has to be discharged by adducing proper evidence. In the instant case, the onus was on the department to justify the change of classification sought to be made by the impugned circular, which onus has not been discharged by the department. Thus, it is evident that the impugned circular is blatantly contrary to the said rule and is thus, not sustainable. [Para 29]

Section 11A of the Customs Tariff Act empowers the Central Government to amend the First Schedule to the said Act. Such amendment may be carried out by notification in the Official Gazette and such notification must be placed before both the Houses of the Parliament for their approval. It is trite law that where a statute empowers an authority to do a certain thing in a certain way that thing must be done only in that way or not at all. All other methods of exercising such power are forbidden. [Para 30]

In the present case, the department sought to amend the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act by issuing the impugned circular. This falls foul of section 11A of the said Act and on this ground also the impugned circular must be set aside. [Para 31]

A circular cannot take away the effect of a notification statutorily issued. [Para 32]

The impugned circular at best contains executive instructions. It is not issued under any statute and has no force of law. It cannot override the statute. Any notice, circular, guidelines etc. which are contrary to statutory laws cannot be enforced. [Para 33]

Procedure for cases where reference to SVB is not required

Where it is decided by the Commissioner of customs that a reference to SVB is not necessary, the Customs House shall issue a reference number to the importer and the Risk Management Division to indicate that the transaction has been examined from the point of view of need for SVB inquiries and it has been decided not to refer the same for SVB investigations.

Procedure in Special Valuation Branch Upon receipt of all related records from the referring customs formation, the SVB shall assign a case number and update the Central Registry Database (CRD) maintained by DGoV.

SVB shall commence inquiries. During the course of which the Deputy Commissioner / Asst. Commissioner (SVB) may call for further documents or information as required. The importer shall also be given suitable opportunity to submit evidence in support of the declared value.

The SVBs shall, as far as possible, complete the investigations and issue its findings within two months from the date of receipt of information. If not completed, extension may be obtained from Commissioner/Chief Commissioner.

Upon completing investigations, the SVB shall submit the findings before the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner. Upon approval by the Principal Commissioner / Commissioner, an Investigation Report (IR, for short) shall be prepared. A copy of the IR shall also be sent to the DGoV.

Finalisation of assessments

If SVB finds that the declared value is conforming to Rule 3 of the CVR, 2007, the provisional assessments shall be finalized without issuing any adjudication order,

However, when investigative findings of SVB are that the declared value has been influenced by the circumstances surrounding the sale, the proper officer shall issue a show cause notice to the importer within 15 days of the receipt of the IR, under intimation to the concerned SVB.

In cases where imports have been cleared through multiple customs locations, SVB shall take a proposal to CBEC recommending appointment of a common adjudicating authority.

The adjudicating authority shall, after following the principles of natural justice, pass an order quantifying the extent of influence on the declared transaction value.

Change in circumstances surrounding the sale

In any case where, the circumstances of sale or terms and conditions of the agreement between the buyer and related seller change, or any other payments of the kind referred under Rule 10 (1) (c), (d) & (e) of the CVR, 2007 become payable, the importers shall be required to declare the same at the place of import in the prescribed format.

The system of renewal of SVB orders has been discontinued with immediate effect.

Transitory provisions in respect of pending investigations

Transitory provisions in respect of pending investigations are contained in CBE&C circular No. 4/2016-Cus dated 9-2-2016.

A system of one-time declaration is being provided. Importers, in respect of whom SVB orders are pending renewal, shall submit to the jurisdictional SVB, a one-time declaration in the prescribed format by 31-3-2016.

In cases where the importer files declaration in Annexure 1, the process of renewal would be treated as dispensed with. The SVB shall immediately inform the Custom stations to immediately discontinue obtaining Extra Duty Deposit and finalize the related provisional assessments, before 30-6-2016.

In cases where a change in circumstances surrounding the sale has been stated in the declaration by importer, the SVB inquiry shall be initiated.

In cases, where EDD has been enhanced to 5%, due to the importer not having provided information or documents necessary for SVB inquiries, the Commissioner shall immediately take recourse to appropriate provisions under the Customs Act for obtaining the necessary documents for investigations and subsequently dispense with the EDD.

All existing cases should be disposed of latest by 31-10-2016.

On second appeal : HELD: There was no dispute about the applicability of section 41(1) in the instant case. The only dispute was when the liability to pay customs duty ceased. In other words, the issue was in which year the benefit in respect of customs duty liability by way of remission or cessation thereof accrued to the assessee and when the amount due to cessation of liability had been obtained by the assessee. The assessee company as well as other newspaper companies had filed writ petitions challenging the levy of customs duty by the Government. The Supreme Court vide order dated 6-12-1984 directed the Government of India to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and refix the rate of customs duty afresh, with effect from 1-3-1981. If on such reconsideration the Government decided that there should be any modification in the levy of customs duty or auxiliary duty with effect from 1-3-1981 it would take necessary steps to implement its decision. Until such redetermination of the liability, the Government was directed to recover only Rs. 550 per MT on imported newsprint towards customs duty and auxiliary duty and would not insist upon payment of duty in accordance with the impugned notifications. It was further stipulated in the Supreme Court’s order that even after such redetermination if it was found that any of the petitioners was liable to pay any deficit amount by way of duty, such deficit amount would be paid by such petitioner within four months from the date on which a notice of demand was served on such petitioner by the concerned authority. It was clear from the above order of the Supreme Court that the Government of India was directed to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on newsprint used for printing newspaper, periodicals, etc., with effect from 1-3-1981. Therefore, as on 6-12-1984 the liability of the assessee to pay customs duty, etc., had not ceased because the matter regarding payment of customs duty was to be considered by the Government. As a result of the directions of the Supreme Court, the Government of India had issued notification dated 19-12-1985 and the CBEC also issued a departmental circular on 10-2-1986 determining the customs duty in respect of imported newsprint. It was clear from the notification as well as circular that after examination of the question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on imported newsprint the Government had fixed the rate at Rs. 550 per MT. The notification as well as circular dates fell in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, i.e., 1987-88. Therefore, as a result of the notification and circular of the CBEC the assessee’s liability to pay customs duty had ceased in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88. The assessee thus obtained the benefit in respect of customs duty by way of remission or cessation thereof and the amount obtained by it and/or the value of benefit accrued to it had to be deemed as its profits and gains of business for the assessment year 1987-88. The customs authority by issuing the notice of demand had given effect to the notification dated 19-12-1985 issued by the Government of India and Circular dated 10-2-1986 of CBEC. A notice of demand did not have the effect of cessation or remission of liability of the assessee. The liability of an assessee ceased only under Notification dated 19-12-1985 of the Government of India read with circular of the customs authority dated 10-2-1986. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in confirming the addition made to the total income of the assessee for the assessment year 1987-88 after making necessary adjustments regarding claim, if any, disallowed under section 43B earlier while determining the amount assessable.

The benefit in respect of cessation of customs liability by way of remission or cessation thereof had to be taxed in the assessment year 1987-88 because the assessee obtained the benefit in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88 and if the assessee did not make entry in the relevant accounting year it would not effect operation of the provisions of section 41(1).

FACT: Assessee's provisional assessment for December, 1999 to February, 2005 was finalized in 2011-12 and assessee paid differential duty without interest.

Department passed order under section 28 demanding interest.

Assessee filed writ petition challenging adjudication order on ground that interest was not leviable, as provisional assessments took place prior to 13-7-2006, when there was no provision for levy of interest in section 18.

Department argued that writ was not maintainable against adjudication order in view of alternate appeal remedy.

HELD: It is a well settled legal proposition that where an alternative remedy is available, the High Court would ordinarily not exercise powers under article 226 of the Constitution of India. However, it is equally true that there is no absolute proposition of law that where an alternative remedy is available, the High Court would refuse to exercise powers under article 226 of the Constitution even if the facts so justify. Non-entertainment of petitions under writ jurisdiction by the High Court when an efficacious alternative remedy is available is a rule of self-imposed limitation. It is essentially a rule of policy, convenience and discretion rather than a rule of law. Undoubtedly, it is within the discretion of the High Court to grant relief under article 226 despite the existence of an alternative remedy. However, the High Court must not interfere if there is an adequate efficacious alternative remedy available to the assessee and he has approached the High Court without availing the same unless he has made out an exceptional case warranting such interference or there exist sufficient grounds to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction under article 226. Some exceptions to the rule of alternative remedy are where the statutory authority has not acted in accordance with the provisions of the enactment in question, or in defiance of the fundamental principles of judicial procedure, or has resorted to invoke the provisions which are repealed, or when an order has been passed in total violation of the principles of natural justice. [Para 10]

In the present case, it is the case of the assessee that the adjudicating authority has not acted in accordance with the provisions of the Customs Act and in defiance of the law laid down by the jurisdictional High Court. On the facts as emerging from the record, and for the reasons that follow, this Court is of the view that the availability of an alternative statutory remedy of appeal, would not preclude the Court from entertaining this writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation of imported goods - Rate of duty - relevant date--increased rate applicable at the time of clearance cannot be charged once the goods have been assessed to duty and passed out of customs charge

FACT: In 1981 the petitioners imported consignments of Nonyl Phenol Ethylene Oxide and Methylene Chloride and cleared the same to the bonded warehouse. In 1983 they were served notices advising them that the goods would be sold of not cleared within 10 days and accordingly the customs duty and demurrage charges were paid on 28.2.1983. The petitioners' request on 1.3.1983 to allow the clearances of the said goods was not granted except on payment of the increased customs duty that had come into effect the same day. This petition impugns the demand by the respondents of the increased customs duty.

HELD: Enhanced customs duty cannot be claimed as the goods were "passed out of customs charges". "...on 28th February 1983 ex-bond warehouse operations were to be stopped at 4 p.m. The circular instructs those to whom it is addressed not to allow ex-bond home consumption withdrawals which are sought to be effected after closing hours on 28th February 1983 'even though the Bill of Entry may have been noted before....' In the instant case, we have a situation where Customs duty on the said goods was paid at 2.30 p.m. on 28th February 1983 and the six bills of entry were marked 'passed out of Customs charges'. Therefore, assuming all else, this circular did not entitle the respondents to refuse clearance of the said goods on 28th February 1983. The Respondents cannot, therefore, validly lay claim to the enhanced Customs duty on the said goods that came into effect on the next day."

No fetters can be imposed on quasi-judicial authority, as section 37-B of the Central Excise Act and section 151-A of the Customs Act provide that no interference is called for in the case of quasi-judicial appellate authority. Circulars are more in the nature of guidance to the field formations and cannot bind the Court or the assessee. Circulars issued by the board are not binding on the assessee and cannot override the decision of the Court. Circulars are meant to ensure proper administration of the statute. [Paras 27 to 29]

Present circular/instruction, which though not relatable to section 37-B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 or section 151-A of the Customs Act, 1962 can at best be taken as an instruction to the field formations to initiate proceedings for recovery of revenue dues which the assessee or the importer has failed to pay having suffered an order passed by the adjudicating authority and is pending in appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the CESTAT, as the case may be. It is not mandatory to effect recovery immediately after 30 days as mentioned, as such an intention is not there in the statute. The circular/instruction directs the recovering authority to initiate proceedings for recovery. In the event of stay/waiver application pending and on intimation, the authority should refrain from proceeding further in the recovery proceedings pending an order in the application for stay/waiver. The circular/instruction has no statutory backing for initiating recovery proceedings and hence it is to be read as directory and not mandatory. [Para 30]

Recovery cannot be found fault with but coercive recovery cannot be made, as it would defeat object of right of appeal with stay of demand :

For recovery of dues payable to the revenue, proceedings can be initiated thirty days after filing of the appeal or any time thereafter and the same cannot be found fault with. But the action of the department in resorting to coercive recovery proceedings at an early date without taking into consideration the pendency of the stay/waiver application before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal would necessarily work hardship to the assessees. The right granted under the statute cannot be whittled down by fixing a time limit in an instruction even though the Appellate Authority has not taken up the matter at the stage of waiver of pre-deposit or for stay. The right provided under a statute should not be denied only on the basis of the impugned circular/instruction. [Para 31]

The board has been mulling over this issue as to what should be the correct time limit for initiating recovery proceedings, as the statute is silent on the issue. Different yardsticks have been used from time to time, but one common factor appears to be that the board was conscious of the fact that after filing of the appeal, if stay/waiver applications are filed, reasonable period of time should be granted. In some cases, time limit has been fixed and in some cases it has not been specified. In the present case, the board has clearly fixed the time limit. The question is if the stay/waiver application is not taken up by the appellate forum, can the assessee/appellant be found fault with. The Supreme Court decision in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1999 (73) ELT 519 supra, relied upon did not give a mandate for fixing a time-limit for recovery. All that it stated is that mere filing of appeal is no stay of proceedings. [Para 32]
