of an executive direction. It would be wholly unjustified to recover the amount even though, the assessee has filed appeal and an application but the Appellate Authority is not able to decide the applications within 30 days. [Para 38]

Since, the statute has not provided for such consequence, the executive cannot order the recovery of the amount only for the reason, that the application for waiver of pre-deposit has not been decided by the Appellate Authorities. [Para 38] Under section 35F, the Appellate Authority has a power to waive or reduce the amount of pre-deposit, but such power is sought to be taken away only if the Commissioner (Appeals) is not able to decide the application for stay within 30 days. Such a condition is relevant and meaningful, if the Central Government is in a position to ensure that all appeals and/or the applications for dispensation of duty demanded and penalty levied can be decided within a period of 30 days. [Para 39]

If the Central Government has no power to control the working of the Appellate Authorities and also to ensure that all appeals are decided within the time frame, such condition is wholly unwarranted. The assessee has also no control over such Authorities. The Commissioner (Appeals), a quasi-judicial Tribunal, has a jurisdiction to waive the condition of pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied, but such judicial discretion vested in the Authority under the Act cannot be interfered with in any manner administratively. [Para 39]

Since the statute confers a right of appeal on the assessee and also right to make an application to dispense with deposit of the duty demanded and penalty levied in the manner which the Appellate Authority deems appropriate. Therefore, unless such jurisdiction is exercised by the Appellate Authority either way i.e., to grant benefit of waiver or impose such conditions as it may consider appropriate, the Board cannot direct the Administrative Officers to recover the demand raised against the assessee. The statutory right of appeal or of consideration of an application for pre-deposit cannot be frustrated administratively. [Para 40]

An aggrieved party such as an assessee could only file appeal along with an application for waiver of the pre-deposit. It is, thereafter, for the public functionary i.e., Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal to pass an order on such appeal and/or application. The decision on appeal and on application is not within the power and control of the assessee, but depends upon the acts of public functionary. The provisions of a statute relate to performance of a public duty. The failure of the Appellate Authority to decide appeal and/or application would work serious general inconvenience or injustice to persons who have no control over those entrusted with the duty. [Para 41]

The Commissioner (Appeals) is discharging a public duty and that failure to decide an application for waiver of deposit would lead to serious injustice to the assessee, who has no control over the Commissioner (Appeals), who is entrusted with the duty to decide such application. Therefore, such provision is only directory. [Para 43]

Basis on which Circular was issued was arbitrary - Condition of recovery pending stay application read down - Recovery only if delay in disposition is due to fault of assessee :

The Circular was purportedly issued in terms of judgment in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The said judgment lays down that mere filing of an appeal does not operate as stay or suspension of the order appealed against. But the Board over-looked the fact that the assessee is not seeking stay only on account of filing of an appeal, but for the reason that the assessee has sought dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied and has a right to demand decision on such application, the right which is created by the statute. Therefore, the very basis of the Circular is untenable, misconceived, wholly illegal and arbitrary. Therefore, the condition of recovery, if no stay is granted within 30 days, is illegal, arbitrary, unjustified and consequently set aside. [Para 44]

Right of consideration in appeal and on an application for waiver of pre-deposit, is a right conferred by the statute and such right cannot be defeated on the basis of Circular, which contemplates that the recovery can be effected, is stay is not granted within 30 days. Therefore, such condition in the Circular is not legal and is therefore set aside with the observation that till such time, the application for waiver of pre-deposit is decided in an appeal filed in terms of the statute, the revenue shall not proceed to recover the same provided that the assessee does not delay the hearing of the appeal directly or indirectly. In the event, the assessee is delaying the decision, the revenue shall be at liberty to move an application before the Commissioner (Appeals) to take the application for waiver of pre-deposit and seek orders thereon in accordance with law. If such an application is filed by the revenue, the Commissioner (Appeals) shall decide the same expeditiously. [Para 46]

HEADNOTE: IV. Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock [Inclusion of freight] - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee-company purchased material on CIF basis - However, in exceptional circumstances, where material was immediately consumed, transport charges were not included in purchase price, but were separately debited to profit and loss account as invoices of transporters were received after consumption of material - Whether, addition on account of non-inclusion of freight inward and import clearing expense to cost of closing inventory, in such cases was not justified, since revenue had accepted assessee's method of valuation of stock in past, especially when revenue failed to demonstrate that impugned method of accounting resulted in material underestimation of profits - Held, yes [Para 7.22] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing and selling of two-wheelers in joint venture with a Japanese company. During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer referred the case to the Transfer Pricing Officer, as there were certain international transaction with its associated enterprises (AEs). It purchased material on CIF basis and ordinarily included freight and cost of delivery of goods in purchase price. However, in exceptional circumstances, where assessee has to immediately lift material, transport charges were not included in purchase price, but were separately debited to profit and loss account, since invoices of transporters were received after consumption of material.

The Assessing Officer added the amount of freight inward and import clearing expenses to cost of closing inventory. The assessee contended that the revenue had accepted its method of valuation in the past. It also contended that the transaction would be revenue neutral in the long run, as similar adjustment would also be required in the opening stock. However, the Dispute Resolution Panel confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On assessee's appeal:

HELD: Though, technically it can be argued that the value of closing inventory must include freight/ import clearing charges, the purchases in question were done under exceptional circumstances for immediate consumption. They were consumed immediately i.e. as soon as raw material entered the factory premises, hence, the question of such purchases being part of closing stock does not arise at all. In such a situation, when freight/import charges were directly debited to the profit and loss account along with the value of the purchases, the question of treating them as part of closing inventory does not arise. The assessee acted and accounted in a proper and acceptable method. Therefore, the relief should be granted on this count alone. [Para 7.14]

Alternatively, the undisputed fact remains that the assessee had been consistently following the said method of accounting in the last many years and the revenue had been accepting these facts and method of accounting without any demur.[Para 7.15]

The contention of the DRP that, the principle of res judicata does not apply in Income-tax proceedings and therefore, the Assessing officer is correct to come to independent conclusion and is not bound by past acceptance of a factual legal point by the department, is untenable. Technically, the principle of res judicata may not apply to the income-tax proceedings as each year is an independent year, yet there ought to be uniformity in treatment and consistency as propounded by the Supreme Court in the case of Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT [1992] 193 ITR 321/60 Taxman 248, where the facts and circumstances were identical. It is a judicially accepted principle that when the facts are same, a uniform view should be adopted for the subsequent years in the income-tax proceedings. Unless there is a material change in the facts, which is neither demonstrated by the Assessing Officer nor DRP, the view which is taken earlier, should not be changed, as held by various courts. [Para 7.16]

In the present case, the revenue rejected the method of accounting, which was consistently followed by the assessee, but it failed to demonstrate with facts and figures that the impugned method of accounting resulted in material underestimation of profits. On the contrary, the assessee demonstrated that the change in the method of accounting for year under appeal would result in loss to the revenue as the opening stock would also require similar adjustment and the cascading effect will be loss to revenue. In this case, the revenue unnecessarily disturbed the consistent method of accounting though it had been accepted in many years. Such tinkering with the method is unjustified when the exercise does not materially alter the profits. Such petty additions should be avoided on the ground of materiality, as AS-1, which talks about materiality, consistency, prudence etc., is part of the I.T. Act after it was notified under section 145(2). [Para 7.22]

In view of above discussion, this ground of the assessee is allowed. [Para 7.25]

HELD: I. Old section 14 v. New section 14 amended from October 2007 : A reading of the unamended section 14 would show that the earlier/old principle was to find the valuation of goods 'by reference to their value'. It introduced a deeming/fictional provision by stipulating that the value of the goods would be the price at which such or like goods are 'ordinarily sold, or offered for sale'. Under the new provision, however, the valuation is based on the transaction price namely, the price 'actually paid or payable for the goods'. Even when the old provision provided the formula of the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale, at that time also if the goods in question were sold for a particular price, that could be taken into consideration for arriving at the valuation of goods. The very expression 'ordinarily sold, or offered for sale' would indicate that the price at which these goods are actually sold would be the price at which they are ordinarily sold or offered for sale. Of course, under the old provision, under certain circumstances, the authorities could discard the price mentioned in the invoice. However, that is only when it is found that the price mentioned in the invoice is not the reflection of the price at which these are ordinarily sold or offered for sale. To put it otherwise, the reason for discarding the price mentioned in the invoice could be only when the said price appeared to be suppressed one. In such a case, the authorities could say that generally such goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale at a different price and take that price into consideration for the purpose of levying the duty. It could, however, be done only if there was evidence to show that ordinarily the price at which these goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale is higher than the price mentioned in the invoice. In fact, this fundamental concept is retained even now while introducing the concept of 'transaction value' under the amended provision. More importantly, the rules viz. Valuation Rules, 1988 had incorporated this very principle of 'transaction value' even under the old provision. No doubt, as per this provision existing today generally the price mentioned is to be accepted as it is the transaction value. However, this very provision stipulates the circumstances under which that price can be discarded. In any case, having regard to the question with which we are concerned in the present appeals, such a change in the provision may not have much effect. [Para 21]

The underlying principle contained in amended sub-section (1) of section 14 is to consider transaction value of the goods imported or exported for the purpose of customs duty. Transaction value is stated to be a price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India for delivery at the time and place of importation. Therefore, it is the price which is actually paid or payable for delivery at the time and place of importation, which is to be treated as transaction value. However, this sub-section (1) further makes it clear that the price actually paid or payable for the goods will not be treated as transaction value where the buyer and the seller are related with each other. In such cases, there can be a presumption that the actual price which is paid or payable for such goods is not the true reflection of the value of the goods. This section also provides that normal price would be the sole consideration for the sale. However, this may be subject to such other conditions which can be specified in the form of Rules made in this behalf. [Para 22]

As per the first proviso of the amended section 14(1), in the transaction value of the imported goods, certain charges are to be added which are in the form of amount paid or payable for costs and services including commissions and brokerage, engineering, design work, royalties and licence fees, costs of transportation to the place of importation, insurance, loading, unloading and handling charges to the extent and in the manner which can be prescribed in the Rules. Sub-section (2) of section 14, which remains the same, is an overriding provision which empowers the Board to fix tariff values for any class of imported goods or export goods under certain circumstances. [Para 23]

In contrast, in the unamended section 14, sub-section (1A) stipulated that the price referred to in sub-section (1) in respect of imported goods shall be determined in accordance with Rules made in this behalf. Therefore, Rules can be made in determining the price. However, these Rules have to be subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), the underline principle whereof, as stated above, is to taken into consideration actual price of the goods unless it is impermissible because of certain circumstances stipulated therein. [Para 24]

HEADNOTE: Section  56,  read with sections  50C  and  263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income from other sources  -  Chargeable as  (Revision) - Assessment year  2016-17  - Assessee, an individual engaged in business of manufacturing, export and sales against Form-H of electrical wiring accessories, filed return processed under section 143(1) - Case was reopened under section 147 on ground that assessee purchased an immovable property for consideration significantly lower than circle rate - Assessee held 1/3rd share in property - On assessee’s request disputing circle rate vis-à-vis FMV, Assessing Officer referred matter to DVO, who determined FMV at ?5.16 crores; assessee’s 1/3rd share came to ?1.72 crores, leaving a difference of ?15.14 lakhs, being less than 10 per cent of consideration - Assessing Officer, after considering assessee’s response, applied amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 (treated as retrospective), and accepted that variation below 10 per cent between sale consideration and DVO-determined value was to be ignored, thereby accepting returned income - Principal Commissioner invoked section 263 (including Explanation 2) to revise assessment, holding that Circular No. 8/2018 applied prospectively and that difference between stamp duty value and sale consideration should have been added to assessee’s income - Whether since view of Principal Commissioner was not supported by any judicial authority, his action in treating assessment order as erroneous and prejudicial to interest of revenue was merely a change of opinion and unsustainable - Held, yes [Para 9.3] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, an individual engaged in the business of manufacturing, export and sales against Form-H of electrical wiring accessories, filed a return declaring income of about Rs. 33.64 lakhs for assessment year 2016-17, which was processed under section 143(1).

■

The case was reopened under section 147 on the ground that an immovable property was purchased for consideration significantly lower than the circle rate, thereby attracting the provision of section 56(2) (viib). The total consideration for the property was about Rs. 4.71 crores against circle rate of about Rs. 9.01 crores; the assessee held a 1/3rd share with consideration of about Rs. 1.57 crores (about Rs. 1.54 crores paid by cheque and about Rs. 2.92 lakhs as TDS). On the assessee’s request disputing circle rate vis-à-vis FMV, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to the DVO, who in his valuation report, ascertained the FMV of the said property at Rs. 5.16 crores, accounting for 1/3rd share of the assessee, the FMV was arrived at Rs. 1.72 crores.

■

The Assessing Officer issued notice calling for explanation on applicability of section 56(2)(viib) and considered the assessee’s response, applied the amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 (treated as retrospective), and accepted that a variation below 10 per cent between the sale consideration and the DVO-determined value should be ignored, thereby accepting the returned income. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment at total income of Rs. 33.64 lakhs as declared by the assessee.

■

The Principal Commissioner invoked section 263, holding that Circular No. 8/2018 applied prospectively from assessment year 2019-20, and thus the Assessing Officer erred in not adding the difference of Rs.15.14 lakh.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The Assessing Officer noted that the difference of the FMV as determined by the DVO and the amount paid by the assessee was Rs. 15.14 lakhs (Rs. 1.72 crores - Rs. 1.57 crores) and the said difference between the actual consideration and FMV as determined by the DVO was less than 10 per cent. The Assessing Officer thereafter, considering the amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 in line with pronouncements of various Courts and Tribunals, which held that when the margin between the actual consideration and the value ascertained by Departmental valuer was less than 10 per cent, noted that the said difference is liable to be ignored, for the purpose of Assessment. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer accepted the total income as declared by the assessee. [Para 9]

■

Valuation--Price of the goods imported is not what is stated in the invoice and consequently in the Bill of Entry. "........on a consideration of the entire evidence and the arguments submitted from both sides, we are inclined to agree with the department that the prices of the goods imported is not what is stated in the invoice and consequently in the bill of entry. The correspondence with the trade representative relied upon by the learned advocate, as rightly pointed out by the learned DR, is all subsequent to the importation of the goods."

2. These prices are not available to other importers in India for the said goods. The price has been influenced by consideration other than sale in the present case.

"These prices are not to be divulged to any other party in India. The inference is clear that these prices are not available for other importers in India for the said goods. It is, therefore, clear that the price of the goods in the instant case has been strongly influenced by consideration other than that of sale in the present case. It is for the purpose of promoting future sales in the country that specially reduced price has been given by the suppliers to the appellants. In the light of 20th January 1987 letter, Agent's letter dated 11.8.1986 stating that the suppliers reserved to themselves the right to negotiate the price on case to case basis loses its significance. That right, obviously has been exercised for considerations other than that of sale of the instant goods. That being so, the price is not acceptable under Section 14 of the Customs Act."

3. No merit in the plea of appellants. Value has been rightly arrived at on the basis of price list. "We are of the view that having regard to the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances referred to above, the value of the goods has been rightly arrived at on the basis of price list available in this case. It is significant to note that the appellants have nowhere disputed the authenticity or genuineness of the price list. In these circumstances we do not find any merit in the pleas of the appellants so far as the valuation of the goods is concerned."

4. Clearance under OGL--The goods are covered by OGL, hence the order of confiscation under Sec. 111(d) Cus. Act. is not tenable and is set aside. The redemption fine of Rs. 2,50,000 is also set aside. "We, therefore, after hearing both sides, hold that the goods are covered by OGL. The impugned order confiscating the goods under Section 111(d) of the Customs Act is not tenable. It is, therefore, set aside and consequently the redemption fine of Rs. 25 lakhs is also set aside."

5. Imposition of penalty--Sufficient force in appellants' plea that no penalty having been imposed by the Collector earlier, imposition of the same in remand proceedings was unjustified. Penalty of Rs. 50,000 set aside. "We have considered this plea of the appellants and we find sufficient force in that plea. We, therefore, set aside the penalty of Rs. 50,000/- imposed in the impugned order."

6. Detention Certificate--Because of the delay in readjudication proceedings, the appellants' request for issue of detention certificate may be considered sympathetically. "This is a matter to be considered by the Customs authorities themselves. The Tribunal does not normally come into the picture so far as the detention certificate is concerned because there is no provision in the Customs Act which allows granting of detention certificate. Nevertheless, we are of the view that the appellants' request be considered sympathetically inasmuch as there has been a delay in readjudication proceedings despite an observation of the Tribunal that the Collector is expected to decide the case within four weeks of receipt of the Tribunal's Order No. 168/89-A dated 2.5.1989."

excise duty on manufactured goods, cannot be the basis for granting exemption under the Customs Act, which is a separate and distinct enactment. "The exemptions granted under the Excise Act, which regulates the levy of excise duty or a tax on manufactured goods in the country is a separate and distinct enactment. The exemptions granted under the Excise Duty either in whole or in part are for the purpose of that Act only and they cannot on any principle be the basis for claiming exemptions under the Customs Act." 7. Powers of the C.B.E.C. include framing of regulations prescribing the forms of bills of entry. "Section 157 of the Customs Act expressly empowers the Board to frame regulations prescribing the forms of bills of entries. .......An examination of the 'forms' prescribed by the Board shows that they are made for purposes of the Act. We find no merit in the challenge of the petitioners to the Regulations or the forms prescribed by the Board."

8. 'Landing charges' are includible in the assessable value of imported goods, as value has to be determined at the time and place of importation and the importer cannot take delivery of goods till payment of landing charges. "The value had to be determined at the time and place of importation. The time and place of importation can never be where the ship crosses the territorial waters but must naturally be at the sea port where the goods are actually delivered by the shipmaster. .......Without payment of landing charges, the importer does not and cannot take delivery of the goods at all. We are of the view that this is the true import of Section 14(1) of the Customs Act, which is only made specific in the Customs Valuation Rules of 1963 and the form of Bill of Entry prescribed by the Board. We are, therefore, of the view that 'landing charges' cannot be excluded and the assessment cannot be made on the CIF value of goods. "

9. Exemption claim on packages and containers is remanded to the proper authorities for examination. "On the packages and containers the petitioners" claim is founded on the notifications issued by Government under Section 25 of the Customs Act. Whether the claim is well founded or not has to be examined and decided in the first instance by the authority under the Act. As the authority had not examined and decided the same we must only direct the authority to do that."
The issue under dispute was whether overtime charges paid to customs officers should be included in the assessable value of fertilizers imported by the appellant.

From the case records, it was found that the assessee had collected various charges from importers/exporters including passengers for keeping the cargo in transit safely, pending export or customs clearance for home consumption. In holding that keeping safe custody of cargo in transit, pending clearance by the customs would constitute an activity exigible under the above entry, the lower authorities had relied on Circulars of the CBEC which clarified that storage and warehousing service provided by, inter alia, Airport Authority is covered by the entry. The entry cargo handling service was clarified by the CBEC as not covering export cargo and passenger baggage. The clarification was not to the effect that all activities relating to export cargo and passenger baggage were also excluded from levy under other entries. The finding of the Commissioner, that the exceptions provided under cargo handling services with regard to passenger baggage and export cargo could not be claimed under storage and warehousing services, was to be agreed with. [Para 9.2]

Demurrage or wharfage charges were collected, respectively, in relation to clearance of import/export cargo beyond five days and 24 hours. As found by the original authority, these were higher charges for continued storage of cargo collected by the assessee from members of the trade. These were part of the taxable value collected towards storage and warehouse charges. [Para 9.3]

As regards the abandoned cargo, those accrued to the assessee towards storage and warehousing of cargo, which were not taken delivery of by the importer. The procedure for auctioning abandoned cargo and the sharing of the proceeds is prescribed by the Ministry of Finance. These instructions also make it clear that the assessee would receive amounts towards the service of storage and warehousing of cargo under this head. However, the services were not rendered to any person in the case of the abandoned cargo. Therefore, demand under this head was not sustainable. [Para 9.4]

As regards the destination charges, it was found that the assessee had collected the documents representing the consignments brought by Air India and Blue Dart and hand over these to the respective consignees. In cases where the assessee merely collected and handed over the documents to the respective consignees, destination charges would not form part of taxable value under storage and warehousing. [Para 9.5]

As regards the OT charges/penalties, the lower authorities had not given a finding as to the nature and purpose of these penalties but had presumed that these were collected for violations on the part of their clients in relation to storage and warehousing services. FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand offset printing machine and claimed clearance under OGL (Import Policy 1982-83), declaring an assessable value of Rs. 4,96,306. The goods arrived during import policy period 1983-84 when they ceased to be covered by OGL. The appellants claimed benefit of condition 7 of Appx. 10 of Policy Book for AM 1982-83, according to which, if an importer had entered into a firm contract before 28.2.1983 but the goods could not be shipped before 31.3.1983 on account of the longer delivery period involved, the shipment may be allowed up to 31.3.1984. The Additional Collector of Customs denied them this benefit on the ground that although the original contract was dated 14.10.1982 and a letter of credit was opened on 9.12.1982, there had been a change of contract subsequently reducing the price of the machine and the latter contract, which is a firm contract, was entered into only in the 1983-84 policy period when the machine was withdrawn from the OGL List, and therefore the import was unauthorised. He confiscated the machine, fixed its value at Rs. 5,62,984 on the basis of contemporary import of such a machine by some other party, and imposed a fine of Rs. 1,25,000 in lieu of confiscation.

HELD: The appellants are not entitled to the benefit of condition 7, Appx. 10 of Import Policy 1982-83 as the machine was not imported under the original contract dated 14.10.1982, but under a subsequent contract reducing the price of the machine, and this contract is to be treated as a "firm contract". The import is therefore unauthorised as it was effected during 1983-84 policy period when the subject goods were not covered by OGL. "Here, though one contract was entered into before 28.2.1983, the subject import is not the one made pursuant to that contract but was under a new contract entered into somewhere in January-February 1984 as is evident from the letter dated 3.2.1984 from the supplier as also by issuance of afresh invoice dated 29.3.1984. ...Even assuming that because the same machine is brought and the same is in relation to the contract entered into on 14.10.1982, then also the contract entered into at that time could not be taken as a firm contract, as subsequently, there has been an alteration in the most essential ingredient in a contract of sale, namely the purchase price and if that could be done, the contract initially entered into could not be taken as a firm contract. Here however is a clear case of substitution of the original contract by a new contract of purchase at the reduced price."

UOI (2009) 3 SCC 365 = 235 ELT 193 (SC), it has been held that Standing Orders/instructions/directions issued by department are not binding on assessing authority as he is quasi-judicial authority. He has to act independently in exercise of his quasi-judicial powers. The Standing Orders/instructions/directions issued for smooth functioning of assessment and work in no way interferes with discretion of assessment authority. No instructions to adjudicating or appellate authority - CBI&C (Board) cannot issue instructions or directions to customs officer acting as adjudicating authority or appellate authority. Standardisation of Board circulars - CBI&C has introduced standardised system from 1994 for numbering the orders/clarifications issued. As per the system, first number will be running serial number starting from 1.1.1994 (This method is used for circulars under CGST and IGST but not used for customs circulars, where fresh serial number starts every year). Second number will be serial number of order issued during the year. Last two digits will be year of issuing the order. Suffix 'Cus' will indicate circular issued by customs wing. - CBI&C circular Nos. 23/23/94-CX dated 16-2-1994, 9/95-Cus dated 31-1-1995 and 4/98-Cus dated 23-2-1998.

For example, circular No. 16/2015-Cus is 16th circular issued in 2015 issued in year 2015 by customs wing of CBI&C.

Functioning of Board - Board members look after various functions. The distribution of work among CBI&C members has been notified in MF(DR) Officer Order No. 66/2015 dated 28-5-2015.

Some functions are directly looked after by Chairman. It is not necessary that decisions of CBI&C must be taken at a meeting of all members of Board. In Bihar Public Service Commission v. Manoj Kumar Pandey 1997 AIR SCW 41, it was observed - 'In a multi-member body, it may not be feasible for every member to associate personally and directly with decision making in respect of every matter. It would, therefore, be permissible to constitute committees of members or authorise a member to consider the manifold matters which may come up for consideration before the body'.

Functions of Board can be entrusted to other officers or authority - Central Government can entrust functions of CBI&C to any officer of Central Government or State Government or any local authority, by issuing notification. Such delegation can be conditional or unconditional [section 6 of Customs Act].

9.1-1 Powers of customs officers

Section 5(1) of Customs Act provides that an officer of customs may exercise the powers and discharge the duties conferred on him or imposed on him, subject to conditions and limitations as may be imposed by CBI&C.

Proper Officer - 'Proper officer' in relation to any function to be performed under Customs Act, means the officer of customs who is assigned those functions by CBI&C or Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs under section 5 of Customs Act - Section 2(34) of Customs Act, [words in italics inserted w.e.f. 30-3-2022 vide Finance Act, 2022].

Senior can exercise powers of junior - Section 5(2) of Customs Act specifies that a Customs Officer may exercise powers and discharge duties conferred on any other Customs Officer subordinate to him e.g. powers conferred on Appraiser can be exercised by Assistant Commissioner or Dy. Commissioner.

CBIC can assign functions to any officer of customs as 'proper officer' - Without prejudice to the provisions contained in section 5(1) of Customs Act, the Board (CBIC) may, by notification, assign such functions as it may deem fit, to an officer of customs who shall be the proper officer in relation to such functions - section 5(1A) of Customs Act, inserted w.e.f. 30-3-2022.

Valuation--Deemed value--The real value for purpose of assessment of Customs duty is the international market price at which goods are sold or offered for sale at the time and place of importation. ".............under Section 14(1) of the Act, the value for the purposes of assessment of duty would be the deemed value. Even if the invoice price is proved to be true price as agreed between the parties, for it is the international market price which is the real value for the purpose of Customs duty. Thus the deemed value in terms of Section 14 is the price at which such goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale at the place of importation."

2. ITC--Import licence--Debiting of--Only the C.I.F. value is to be debited to the licence and not the assessable value. ".......there is one kind of valuation for the purpose of assessment to customs duty but another for the purpose of c.i.f. value which is to be debited to the licence. This value to be debited consists of the items viz. the price of the goods and the commission allowed and where the commission is not apparent on the surface, it is the duty of the Customs authorities to find out and add to it the said price so that the price of the goods plus the commission and the freight and insurance would constitute the c.i.f. price for the purpose of debiting to the licence."

"In our view unless it can be shown and proved by the Customs authorities that the importer has paid to the foreign supplier more than what has been reflected in the agreement or invoice the c.i.f value has to be taken as the basis for debiting the licence."

3. ITC--Import licence--Debiting of--Enhanced value cannot be debited to the licence, particularly when the order of enhancement has been appealed against and is not final. "It is true, in the instant case, for the purpose of payment of Customs duty the assessable value has been enhanced by the adjudicating order, but for the purpose of debiting the licence the declared c.i.f. value has to be taken to be the basis in the absence of any finding that the importer has paid something over and above the declared c.i.f. value. The international price of imported goods is a relevant factor for determining the assessable value for the purpose of Customs duty, but the same is not relevant for debiting the import licence. The authorities have to determine the real value of the goods. The import licence speaks only of the c.i.f. value of the goods for the purpose of debiting the licence. The c.i.f. value cannot be equated with the real value of the goods which may be determined by the Customs authorities taking into account all the relevant facts and circumstances of the case. "

"There is another aspect of the matter. Assuming that the value as determined in the adjudication order by which the import licence has to be debited, the said adjudication order is now subject to an appeal before the Tribunal. It is well settled that once an appeal is preferred the decision loses it character of finality and what was once res judicata again become res sub judice."

"Therefore, it is not correct to urge that the licence has to be debited by the enhanced assessable value as determined in adjudication order which may or may not be sustained by the Appellate authority."

4. Import licence--Customs authorities directed to debit the licence with the declared c.i.f. value and return the same to the Appellants, as the licence has not been established to be forged one. "........the case of the forging of the licence has not been established by the Customs authorities."

"..........Even the stand of the Customs authorities in this regard shows that they did not treat the licence as forged. The Customs authorities have allowed the subject goods to be cleared against the very same licence which they have labelled as forged. They have also purported to debit the very same licence with the assessable value as determined by the adjudicating authority. The adjudicating authority has passed an order for release of the goods upon payment of redemption fine in lieu of confiscation against the very same licence. In our view, the Customs authority cannot take inconsistent stand by accepting the licence as valid for some purpose and by treating it as forged and thus being non-existent for some other purpose."

The original Circular No.3/2018 [F.No.279/MISC.142/2007-ITJ(PT)], dated 11-7-2018 issued by the CBDT, is applicable to the assessee, under consideration, for both the appeals of the assessee, and therefore the Tribunal has rightly dismissed the appeals of the revenue, on account of low tax effect, in pursuance of the said circular. Later on, the CBDT has modified the para No. 10 of said Circular No. 3/2018, dated 11-7-2018. The revenue pointed out that above modified Circular No. 3/2018 dated 11-7-2018 (supra), stated that in certain circumstances, the matter should be heard on merit, even if addition made by the Assessing Officer, is less than the prescribed monetary limit, specified in the modified Circular No. 3/2018 dated 11-7-2018. The ITAT does not agree with the revenue, because, in the assessee's case under consideration, the addition was made by the Assessing Officer, based on the information received from the state police department and not on the basis of enforcement agencies such as CBI/ED/DRI/SFIO/Directorate General of GST Intelligences (DGGI), which is mentioned in the modified said Circular No. No. 3/2018 (supra). Hence, even modified Circular No. No. 3/2018 (modified on 20-8-2018,) is not applicable, to the assessee's case under consideration. The various agencies defined in the circular, such as, CBI/ED/DRI/SFIO/Directorate General of GST Intelligences (DGGI), are exhaustive in nature. Exhaustive means comprehensive, thorough or tending to exhaust and no further 'word'/'Agency' should be added. It is a settled position of law that an act done by the assessee, which is legal, when it was done, cannot be made illegal by enacting a new circular. Therefore, it is found that even in modified said Circular No. No. 3/2018 (supra), state police department, is not mentioned, by CBDT, therefore, the said modified circular does not apply to the assessee's case under consideration. The claim of the revenue, to recall the order of the Tribunal, and to hear on merit, is misconceived. Hence, based on these facts and position in law, it is noted that miscellaneous application filed by the revenue deserve to be dismissed. Accordingly, the miscellaneous application filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 8]

On application under section 256(2) : HELD: There is no controversy about the principle that the opening stock cannot be valued in a manner different from the valuation of the closing stock. Both have to be valued on the basis of the same principle. The opening stock for the year under reference was loaded with the value of the proportionate costs of customs duty, freight and handling charges. The closing stock did not have such an addition made to it. In order to bring the two on the same level, it was necessary to disturb the valuation either of the opening stock or of the closing stock. The Tribunal preferred to disturb the closing stock by valuing it on the same principle according to which the opening stock was valued. The assessee suggested that the customs duty, freight and handling charges should have been deducted from the opening stock, to bring the principle of its valuation in accord with the principle which had been adopted for valuing the closing stock. The adoption of this procedure would have hardly brought about any change in the results and would not have adversely affected the interest of the revenue. It would, on the other hand, have given to the assessee the benefit of avoiding the inconvenience and difficulty of splitting up the charges in question and allocating the same in proper proportions to the numerous components and materials. This would have regularised the assessee's balance-sheets in all the subsequent years. The insistence of the department in disturbing the closing stock instead of the opening stock and the approval to this practice given by the Tribunal did give rise to question of law which could appropriately be referred to the High Court. However, that question did not arise from out of the order of the Tribunal, who never considered the merits or demerits of the alternative procedure of disturbing instead the opening stock on the same basis, on which the closing stock was valued. The suggestion made before the Tribunal by the assessee was to deduct the sum of custom duty, freight etc. from the purchases. There was no suggestion to make a suitable deduction from out of the value of the opening stock, as now suggested. The Tribunal had not applied its mind to the suggestion of a deduction from the opening stock and had said nothing about this in its order. Thus, the question as to whether the Tribunal was justified in law in holding that on no account the opening stock could be revalued to make it consistent with the system adopted for valuation of closing stock, could not be said to arise out of the order of the Tribunal.

Further, the assessee agreed that the opening stock included customs duty and incidental charges. There was, therefore, sufficient material for the Tribunal to hold that the closing stock might necessarily be valued likewise. Thus, the question as to whether there was any material on which the Tribunal could hold that the closing stock might necessarily include the customs duties and incidental charges was not a question which the Tribunal could refer to the High Court.

So far as question regarding credit note was concerned the Tribunal came to its conclusion after assessing the evidence before it. It was competent to determine the sufficiency of the evidence before it. The inference drawn by the Tribunal from the evidence on record was a finding of fact and its refusal to make a reference, as desired by the assessee, called for no interference.

Under those circumstances, there was no merit in the instant petition which, accordingly, was to be dismissed.

Commissioner (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be, it may impose such conditions while dispensing with the pre-deposit pending appeal after taking into consideration the interest of the revenue. It goes to show that the filing of an appeal and the application under section 35-F of the Central Excise Act or section 129-E of the Customs Act is not an empty formality. A substantial right granted by the statute cannot be casually set at naught by the circular/instruction. It has to be consistent with the statutory right of the assessees. [Para 21]

Circulars are more in the nature of guidance to the field formations and cannot bind the Court or the assessee. Circulars issued by the board are not binding on the assessee and cannot override the decision of the Court. Circulars are meant to ensure proper administration of the statute. [Paras 27 to 29]

Present circular/instruction, which though not relatable to section 37-B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 or section 151-A of the Customs Act, 1962 can at best be taken as an instruction to the field formations to initiate proceedings for recovery of revenue dues which the assessee or the importer has failed to pay having suffered an order passed by the adjudicating authority and is pending in appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the CESTAT, as the case may be. It is not mandatory to effect recovery immediately after 30 days as mentioned, as such an intention is not there in the statute. The circular/instruction directs the recovering authority to initiate proceedings for recovery. In the event of stay/waiver application pending and on intimation, the authority should refrain from proceeding further in the recovery proceedings pending an order in the application for stay/waiver. The circular/instruction has no statutory backing for initiating recovery proceedings and hence it is to be read as directory and not mandatory. [Para 30]

Recovery cannot be found fault with but coercive recovery cannot be made, as it would defeat object of right of appeal with stay of demand :

But the action of the department in resorting to coercive recovery proceedings at an early date without taking into consideration the pendency of the stay/waiver application before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal would necessarily work hardship to the assessees. The right granted under the statute cannot be whittled down by fixing a time limit in an instruction even though the Appellate Authority has not taken up the matter at the stage of waiver of pre-deposit or for stay. Payment made to the Collaborators in lumpsum was for the transfer of technical knowledge. Construing this payment as buyer's commission, the Asstt. Collector held that in terms of Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules, a loading of 21/2% service charges was required to be added to the invoice value of the third party suppliers. On appeal, the Collector (Appeals) set aside the above order on the grounds that in view of the machineries having been supplied by a third party, in the absence of any specific provision in the Collaboration agreement for the payment of service charges, the payment made to the Collaborators is not to be included in the assessable value of the goods. Hence this Revenue appeal.

HELD: Department's application suffers from infirmities--Collector had given the authorisation for filing the appeal without expressing any opinion about the legality or propriety of the order as specified under section 129A--Specific grounds of appeal not raised by the Department. "On going through the records we find that neither authorisation given by the Collector is in the proper Order nor appeal filed by the Department is in proper form. Section 129-A(2) specifies that before giving authorisation to file an appeal Collector should express about the illegality or impropriety of the order against which the appeal is to be filed and direct the proper Officer to appeal on his behalf to the Appellate Tribunal against such order. In this authorisation the Collector simply authorises the Assistant Collector to file an appeal without expressing any opinion about the legality or otherwise of the order and, as such, there is no proper authorisation for filing the appeal. We find that presentation of appeal also is not in the proper form since neither department has filed any grounds of appeal nor it is clear on which points department is seeking relief in the absence of grounds of appeal. Form No. CA-3 should be accompanied with statement of facts and grounds of appeal but we find that appeal form is accompanied with number of pages in the form of commentary consisting of comments on the impugned order without raising specific grounds. The appeal filed by the department is liable to be dismissed on these preliminary grounds."

2. Valuation--Department's' allegation of undervaluation is not supported by any evidence--in the absence of specific allocation, notional value cannot be added to the invoice value on account of buying commission or handling charges-Collector's order upheld. "The burden lies on the department to prove undervaluation. The department ought to make out a case for undervaluation with sufficient evidence and to prove that value shown in the invoice was not the real value. There is no evidence to show that similar goods were sold at higher price or that the collaborators acted as agents to the foreign Suppliers in getting commission or due to their services resulted in reduction of value. Further payment made to the collaborators for transfer of technical know-how and such lumpsum payment was made to their services where it is not possible for that reason to allocate the charges to individual consignments imported through them, no notional value can be added to the invoice value on account of buying commission or handling charges as it was rightly dealt with in the impugned order. We do not find any infirmity in the impugned order."

Sec. 15(1)(b): Rate of duty applicable to imported goods cleared from the warehouse under Sec. 68 is the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse, hence the goods are not entitled to concessional assessment as the Bill of Entry was for clearance of goods from the warehouse. "According to Section 15(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, the rate of duty and tariff valuation, If any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force..........(b) in the case of goods cleared from the warehouse under Section 68, on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse. In the present ease, the goods, were admittedly sought to be cleared from the warehouse under Section 68. Therefore, Section 15(1)(b) squarely applies to the facts of the case. The appellants' contention that it should be deemed that constructively the Bill of Entry was one for home consumption attracting Section 15(1)(a) is devoid of substance and unacceptable. There is no running away from the fact that the Bill of Entry was one for clearance of goods from the warehouse".

2. Relevant date for rate of duty applicable is determined by procedural law contained in Sec. 15, there being no vested right to the concession granted by the notification, therefore the concessional rate was rightly denied. "Thereafter the question whether a particular consignment was eligible for the concessional rate was to be determined only by the provisions of the Customs Act. Section 15 lays down the relevant date for determination of inter alia the rate of duty in different situations. The situation in the present case is the one described in Section 15(1)(b). We cannot find fault with the denial of the concessional rate under the notification in respect of the present consignment."

3. Civil Court, and not a quasi-judicial authority, is the proper forum for grievances regarding delay and negligence of the authorities leading to increased duty burden on the assessee. "The appellants seem to be nursing a sense of grievance, apparently with cause, that the delay in Customs clearance of the goods has resulted in an increased duty burden on them. The proper forum for agitation of this matter is not quasi-judicial authorities functioning under the Act".

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Second-hand machines falling in different age groups are not comparable. Value to be determined for each type

FACT: The appellants imported second-hand printing machines and declared their value as Rs. 2,81,193. It was noticed in the docks that in addition to the declared machines, one additional two-colour offset printing machine had been imported. This was attributed by the appellants to mistake on the part of supplier. The Department did not accept the declared value and charged the importer with under-valuation and evasion of duty. The value was determined by the Addl. Collector as Rs. 6,65,000 on the basis of value of similar machines imported by M/s. D.S. Sawant & Sons and the price list issued by M/s. Jackal International Co., a well known supplier of second-hand machines.

HELD: It is not legal to compare the price of imported second-hand machines falling in different age groups (ratio of earlier Tribunal decisions). Provision of Section 14(1)(a) of the C.A. 1962 can hardly be of any help in determining the valuation. The value should be determined on the basis of unit price of each type of machine as indicated in the supplier's invoice. "......the order passed by the Additional Collector determining the price of the imported second-hand Solna 225. Two Colour offset printing machines, on the basis of the import price of a similar machine imported by another importer and the price of the 'Guilltone 45' Polar 115 Electromat on the basis of the price list issued by another supplier of second-hand machinery is not sustainable. In our view the assessable value of the imported goods comprising of two second-hand "Solna 225--Two Colour offset printing machines" and one old "Guilltone 45' Polar 15 Electromat" machine was determinable on the basis of the unit price of each type of machine as indicated in the supplier's invoice. Since the case records do not contain the invoice and the Chartered Engineer's certificate, we remand the case to the Assistant Collector for determining the assessable value of the machines and the consequential relief to the appellants if any."

HEADNOTE: Sections 14  1515(3)(a) of the Customs Act, 1962 - Conversion of assessable value from foreign currency into Indian rupees

FACT: The appellants filed this appeal because they had to pay a higher amount of customs duty on goods imported by them as the customs authorities converted the freight amount shown in the invoice in foreign currency to Indian rupees though they had already paid the freight in Indian rupees

HELD: Assessable value of imported goods was rightly converted from foreign currency into Indian rupees as per Sec. 15(3)(a) of the Customs Act. "At the relevant time provisions of section 15(3)(a) of the Act stipulated how the value of the imported goods was to be converted from foreign currency into Indian rupees. The appellants have not disputed the fact that the rate of exchange for conversion of dollars into rupees adopted by the Custom House in their case was different from that notified by the Government. Their contention is that they had paid the freight amount in Indian rupees and that amount alone could be added to the value of the goods. In the face of a clear legal position in this behalf, we see no merit in this contention of the appellants."

2. Any special agreement between the Government of India and any international financial institution cannot override the provisions of the Customs Act. "... any special agreement between the Government of India and any foreign Government/financial institution (I.D.A. in the present case) cannot override the provisions of Customs Act. We have no hesitation, therefore, in upholding the finding of the Appellate Collector on this ground."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Discounts--World Catalogue Price less 15% discount, falling which manufacturer's net price to wholesale dealers; failing both, invoice price without discount/depreciation if not used before shipment. Ocean freight, marine insurance, and landing charges are part of delivery price,  are includible (CUS. Act, 1962--S. 14). Addl. Duty (CVD) is customs duty and not excise duty (Customs Tariff Act, 1975, S. 3). Classification--Air-conditioner is an optional accessory and is assessable separately U/H 84.12 CTA, even if invoice shows composite price

FACT: The appellant imported a new Toyota starlet car and claimed 15% discount on the invoiced price for the purpose of computing customs duty. This was rejected. Appeal also failed. Before the Tribunal, assessable value of the said car has been disputed.

HELD: 1. Assessable Value--Assessable value of an imported car is world-car-catalogue Price less 15% failing which manufacturer's Net price to whole-sale dealer's failing both invoice price. "We order that the same basis should be followed in the case of the present appellant also and his car re-assessed on the basis of the World Car Catalogue Price of the same model less 15% discount. ......In case the World Car Catalogue Price is not available with the Customs House, the Customs may ascertain the manufacturer's net price to wholesale dealers in the course of international trade in any other manner. If this course is also not feasible, the assessment may be maintained at the appellant's invoice price. There is no question of granting the 15% discount on the individual export passenger's invoice price.''

2. Assessable Value--Ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges are part of delivery price at the place of importation, hence form a part of assessable value. "Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 requires that valuation should be done on the basis of the price for delivery of the goods at the place of importation. The imported goods have to be valued according to this provision. Seeking analogy of a different enactment which deals with locally manufactured goods is a totally mis-conceived exercise. No imported goods can be delivered at the port of importation in India without incurring the ocean freight, marine insurance and landing charges. These charges have, therefore, been correctly added to the basic price of the car."

3, Assessable Value--No depreciation admissible if the car has not been used abroad. "Depreciation is given if the car is possessed and used abroad. Here, the appellant purchased a brand new car and loaded it for shipment to India. He did not use the car abroad. No depreciation as asked for is permissible."

4. Additional duty--Additional duty is also customs duty and not excise duty. "Section 3 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 separately specifies the rates for basic customs duty and additional customs duty both of which are to be charged on the imported goods. The additional customs duty is also very much a duty of customs. Just because its rate generally happens to be equivalent to the excise duty chargeable on the like goods manufactured in India, it does not cease to be a customs duty."

5. Air-conditioner fitted in a car, not being an essential components, is separately assessable even if invoice shows composite price for the car and the Air-Conditioner. "An Air-Conditioner is not an essential component of the car. It is not even a standard part of the car. It is an optional accessory and is supplied to only those purchasers of cars who asked for it. The department has, therefore, correctly assessed the Air-Conditioner separately under Head 84.12 of the Tariff."

1.1-5 Common aspects of Customs and CGST

There are some common or similar provisions in Customs and CGST.

Both are Central Acts and derive power of levy from Constitution.

Both are under administrative control of one Board (Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs) (CBI&C) under Ministry of Finance.

Departmental organizational hierarchy is same from top upto Assistant Commissioner level.

Classification Tariffs of CGST and customs are based on HSN and principles of classification are identical.

Principles of deciding 'Assessable Value' are similar i.e. both are principally based on 'transaction value'.

Concept of 'related person' for valuation purposes appears in Customs as well as CGST. Principle of 'piercing of corporate veil' can apply in both cases.

Provisions of refund, including principle of 'unjust enrichment' are similar. Provisions for interest for delayed payment are also similar.

Provisions of raising demand for short levy, non-levy or erroneous refund are similar. Provisions in respect of recovery, mandatory penalty etc. are also similar.

Provisions for granting exemptions from duty - partial or full - conditional or unconditional are similar.

Powers of search and seizure are quite similar.

CGST and customs law make provisions of arrests and prosecution of offences.

Provisions in respect of Authority for Advance Ruling are similar.

Appeal provisions are similar in some aspects.

1.1-6 Changes in Customs Law made vide Finance Act, 2025

Nirmala Sitharaman, Minister of Finance, Government of India, presented Budget for 2025-2026 on 1-2-2025 at 11 AM. Finance Bill, 2025 was also presented. The Bill was passed by Parliament and became Act on 29-3-2025 after receiving assent of President. The provisions are effective from 29-3-2025.

One major change is abolition of Settlement Commission w.e.f. 1-4-2025. Another important change is introduction of Voluntary revision of entry post clearance, for which section 18A of Customs Act has been introduced w.e.f. 29-3-2025.

1.1-7 Provisional Collection of Taxes after introduction of Budget

Finance Bill is introduced in Lok Sabha, which proposes change in duty rates of customs and Central Excise. However, Finance Bill is passed after a period of about 60 to 75 days.

To take care of the situation, Provisional Collection of Act, 2023 [earlier it was Provisional Collection of Act, 1931] provides that if Bill is introduced with declaration that any provision of the Bill shall have immediate effect, the provision shall be effective from midnight of the day on which Finance Bill is introduced in Parliament. Such declaration is valid for 75 days. If the Bill is not passed within that period, the excess tax collected becomes refundable.

The provisions are as follows -

Where a Bill to be introduced in Parliament on behalf of the Government provides for the imposition or increase of a duty of customs or excise with or without change in tariff classification, the Central Government may cause to be inserted in the Bill a declaration that it is expedient in the public interest that any provision of the Bill relating to such imposition or increase shall have immediate effect under Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 2023 - section 3 of Provisional Collection of Act, 2023.

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of pig iron.

During the period June 1998 to August 1998, the assessee imported Low Ash Metallurgical (LAM) Coke under seven Bills of Entry, against four advance licenses without payment of —

basic customs duty (BCD) levied under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962,

special customs duty (SCD) levied under section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996,

special additional duty (SAD) levied under section 3A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and

anti-dumping duty (ADD) levied under section 9A of Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

The department sought to deny exemptions on failure to fulfil export obligation.

Pending final adjudication of notice by the Commissioner, the assessee duly paid the entire duty payable towards BCD, SAD and SCD after considering partial exports already made. The assessee did not make any payment towards ADD.

The department confirmed duty demands along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent as per bond.

Tribunal enhanced ADD as per revised notification but reduced interest to 15 per cent.

The assessee challenged Anti-dumping duty, interest and penalty and other computations.

Assessee's Arguments

Basic customs duty and the special customs duty as well as special additional duty was payable by the assessee.

However, anti-dumping duty was not payable at all, as assessee was exempt under Notification No. 69 of 2000.

Notification No. 30 of 1997 did not stipulate that in the event of default, interest would become payable; hence, interest was not payable.

Since assessment was provisional, there was no provision for collection of interest for the period in dispute as section 18 was amended to include such a provision only prospectively with effect from 2006.

In any case, Anti-dumping duty could not be added for purposes of computing customs duty, special customs duty and special additional duty.

Also no penalty is imposable inasmuch as nothing contumacious was done by the assessee and the export obligation could not be fulfilled only because of bona fide commercial impossibility.

Since appeal before Tribunal was filed by assessee, he could not be worse off in an appeal filed only by the assessee herein to CESTAT and that on the assumption that the assessee was liable to pay anti-dumping duty, they should only pay the said duty at the lower rate prescribed by the Commissioner as revenue had not appealed to the Tribunal against the Commissioner's order.

Revenue's Arguments

The exemption contained in Anti-dumping duty Notification 69 of 2000 was only prospective and, hence Anti-dumping duty had to be paid for the relevant period.

Interest was payable as Notification No. 30 of 1997 independently levied a charge of interest.

Order of Tribunal was correct in law.

(DSD&M) meant for filtering blood are classifiable under Tariff Item 84212900 as 'Filtering or purifying machinery'.

Assessee challenged said circular and consequent classification as invalid.

HELD: It is not in dispute that originally the goods in question, being Dialysers were classified under CTH 90189031. The impugned circular has sought to change such classification by bringing Dialysers under CTH 84212900. [Para 26] Chapter 90 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'optical, photographic, cinematographic, measuring, checking, precision, medical or surgical instruments and apparatus; parts and accessories thereof.' Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to 'instruments and appliances used in medical, surgical, dental or veterinary sciences including scientigraphic apparatus, other electro-medical apparatus and sight-testing instruments. CTH 90189031 specifically pertains to renal dialysis equipment (artificial kidneys, kidney machines and dialysers). [Para 27]

Chapter 84 of the Customs Tariff Act has the caption 'nuclear reactors, boilers, machinery and medical appliances; parts thereof.' Heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to 'centrifuges, including centrifugal dryers; filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus, for liquids or gases.' CTH 84212900 talks of 'filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus for gases.' [Para 28]

Thus, CTH 90189031 specifically provides for dialysers whereas CTH 84212900 provides for generic description of articles. Heading 9018 under Chapter 90 pertains to medical instruments whereas heading 8421 under Chapter 84 pertains to goods which are generally used for industrial purposes and do not appear to have any medical use. Hence, the natural classification of dialysers should be under CTH 90189031 as it was prior to issuance of the impugned circular. When a specific tariff heading for classification is available, the goods concerned cannot be classified under a generic tariff heading. A heading with a more specific description of the goods in question shall be preferred to and prevail over a heading with a more general description. Just as a special law in a particular field would prevail over a general law that may be operational in that field, a heading with a more specific description would prevail over a heading with a more general description. In this connection, rule 3(a) of the General Rules for interpretation of the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act makes it very clear that the heading which provides the most specific description shall be preferred to headings providing a more general description.

If the department intends to classify the goods in question under a heading which is different from the heading under which an assessee classifies such goods, the burden of proof is on the department which has to be discharged by adducing proper evidence. In the instant case, the onus was on the department to justify the change of classification sought to be made by the impugned circular, which onus has not been discharged by the department. Thus, it is evident that the impugned circular is blatantly contrary to the said rule and is thus, not sustainable. [Para 29]

Section 11A of the Customs Tariff Act empowers the Central Government to amend the First Schedule to the said Act. Such amendment may be carried out by notification in the Official Gazette and such notification must be placed before both the Houses of the Parliament for their approval. It is trite law that where a statute empowers an authority to do a certain thing in a certain way that thing must be done only in that way or not at all. All other methods of exercising such power are forbidden. [Para 30]

In the present case, the department sought to amend the First Schedule to the Customs Tariff Act by issuing the impugned circular. This falls foul of section 11A of the said Act and on this ground also the impugned circular must be set aside. [Para 31]

A circular cannot take away the effect of a notification statutorily issued. [Para 32]

The impugned circular at best contains executive instructions. It is not issued under any statute and has no force of law. It cannot override the statute. Any notice, circular, guidelines etc. which are contrary to statutory laws cannot be enforced. [Para 33]

The appellant opted to adopt the invoice value of the imported goods and agreed to loading of 20 per cent as per the circular of the Special Valuation Branch, and went on periodically paying 20 per cent loaded value under the impression that the assessment was provisional. His application for refund was rejected as time barred on the ground that he had not specifically requested for treating the assessment as provisional.

The circulars, instructions and directions of the Board are biding on the income-tax authorities as provided in section 119 but a circular is not law, and the assessee is not bound by it. If such circulars, directions or instructions are to the prejudice of the assessee, he may claim the benefit which was available to him under the provisions of law. However, the assessee cannot claim to be assessed in accordance with the old circular which stood modified by the Board’s subsequent circular when the assessment proceedings are pending particularly when the Board’s instruction clearly showed such an intention on the part of the Board.

The Board had specifically directed that all pending assessments may be completed in accordance with 1974 circular. Since the ITO was bound by the Board’s circular in terms of section 119, he was bound to follow the 1974 circular only.

IT APPEAL NO. 441 (BOM.) OF 1976-77 [ASSESSMENT YEAR 1972-73]

C.J. Bandi for the Appellant.

N.K. Shastri for the Respondent.

1. Valuation--Invoice value may not be accepted for computing duty if comparable goods are purchased at substantially higher price. "The appellants explanation for increase in the price is that the demand for second hand machinery had gone up and the suppliers therefore raised the prices in case of latter import No evidence in support of this plea has been produced either before the lower authorities or before us. In the absence of any such evidence and the apparently large price differential in the prices of two sets of machines, the imports of which were made in the span of about nine months time, we held that the lower authorities were justified in not accepting low price as reflected in the invoice for the goods".

2. Valuation--Computation of value should preferable be under Rule 3 and 4 if comparable goods are available at different prices. "We would like to observe that in the instant case, the value of comparable goods was available and the correct rule that should have been applied by the lower authorities should have been Rule 3 of the Custom Valuation rules 1963 read with Rule 4 of the said rule. We find that the value of comparable goods imported by the appellants was acceptable to the authorities and as such there was no need for the officers to traverse beyond these rules to Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules."

3. Valuation--Assessee has no grievance if a criterion, less preferable than other available ones, is adopted if it does not put him to disadvantage. "In any case, we find that the appellants had not suffered any disadvantage on this account and probably the value fixed now in terms of the Appellate Collector's order is lower than what might have been fixed in case Rule 3 read with Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules 1963 had been resorted to. We, therefore, find no reason to accede the appellants plea for accepting the invoice value for purpose of assessment."

4. Assessable value includes landing charges. "The inclusion of landing charges in the assessable value is maintainable in law seeing that the expenditure incurred for landing would become an integral component of their intrinsic value and accordingly "the price at which such or like goods are for delivery at the time and place of importation"."

Valuation--Notional landing charges are includible for computing the assessable value (ratio of judgment in Ceat Tyres of India Ltd. v. CC). "In the case law cited as aforesaid under the heading Landing Charges it was held that landing charges are includible in assessable value and the same (landing charges) are to be calculated as a percentage of c.i.f. value taking into account total value of imports and total landing charges."

2. Addl. Duty of Customs (CVD)--Assessable value is the aggregate value inclusive of the customs duties chargeable on the imported goods. "In the case of Ashok Traders v. Union of India.....it was held by the Bombay High Court that section 3(2) of the Customs Tariff Act is constitutionally valid and for purposes of c.v. duty the assessable value of the imported goods is the aggregate value of the imported goods plus customs duty chargeable on that article."

3. Valuation--Packing charges are not excludible in terms of Notfn. 184/76-Cus., where these are included in the value of imported goods (ratio of Bombay High Court judgment in Polyset Corporation v. CC). "....the Bombay High Court after considering the ambit and scope of exemption notification 184/76-Cus held that what are exempt meter this exemption notification from the duty leviable are the goods imported or exported in packages or any portion of the value of the goods so imported. In other words, if packages as such are subject to customs duty they would be exempt from duty. Even then it is not every packages imported that is exempt, it is only when the goods are imported or exported in packages that such packages are exempt provided they satisfy the other conditions laid down in the notification. It was made clear that the said notification does not permit the valuation of goods in packages split up into principal goods and packages and exempt the packages from duty. In the instant case the authorities below have held that the appellants did not satisfy the conditions of the said notification. The same views were reiterated by this Tribunal in the case of M/s. K. Hargovind Dass Co., M/s. Chhaganlal Sons, and others--Final Order No. 468 to 597/92-A dated 29.10.1992.......Thus following the ratio of the said decisions we do not find any infirmity in the impugned orders passed by the authorities below."
