"7...If the submissions of learned counsel for the assessee are accepted, it would mean that there is no scope for filing an appeal. In that case, there is no question of a decision of this Court on the point being rendered. Obviously, the assessee will not file an appeal questioning the view expressed vis-a-vis the circular. It has to be the revenue authority who has to question that. To lay content with the circular would mean that the valuable right of challenge would be denied to him and there would be no scope for adjudication by the High Court or the Supreme Court. That would be against very concept of majesty of law declared by this Court and the binding effect in terms of article 141 of the Constitution." (p. 106)

Again the Supreme Court in the matter of CCE v. Hindoostan Spg. & Wvg. M. Ltd. has affirmed the view that department can challenge the validity and authenticity of a circular/clarification. The assessee cannot challenge the department if department is ignoring the circular/clarification and following the statutory provisions.

Whether reimbursement of expenses is not subject to service tax?

Upto April 18, 2006, service tax is payable only on gross amount charged for service rendered. Before April 18, 2006, there was a Board circular stating that reimbursable expenses were not included in the assessable value for the purpose of levy of service tax. If a service provider incurs some expenditure on behalf of customer, that amount is not part of service provided and will not be taxable. The expenses which are reimbursed by the client are taxable only from April 18, 2006, i.e., as per Service tax (Determination of value) Rules, 2006.

As per rule 5(1) of the Service tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, the cost or expenditure which is incurred by the service provider in the course of providing taxable service is to be included in the value of taxable services.

In Malabar Management Services (P.) Ltd. v. CST [2008] 14 STT 107 - The assessee was providing Business Auxiliary Services to the ICICI Bank to market the bank’s personal loans. They were reimbursed by the bank in respect of expenses on salary of personnel, infrastructural expenses like rent, electricity, telephone charges, stationary, etc. But the bank charged service tax only on the consideration and not on the reimbursed expenses. As per the agreement made between bank and the assessee, there was a fixed rate of commission which was mentioned in the agreement. The department demanded service tax on the reimbursed amount. Finally, the Tribunal held that reimbursable expenses were not part of the assessable value in view the fact that the consideration was already fixed in the agreement.

Whether the coaching for the PGPM course or part-time students in the Executive MBA course come within the purview of ‘commercial training or coaching’ and is liable to service tax?

As per CBEC Circular F.No. 137/71/2006-CX, dated November 1, 2006, a commercial concern is an institution or establishment that is primarily engaged in commercial activities. The Board clarified that the principal activity of institutes like IIT’s or IIMs is to impart education without the objective of making profit and, therefore, such institutes cannot be called commercial concerns even if they charge for some of their activities.

In the matter of Great Lakes Institute of Management Ltd. v. CST [2008] 12 STT 296 the Hon’ble Tribunal has held that—

"6. We find that the appellants are recognized as a charitable organization under the Income-tax Act, 1961. Though the appellants earned some surplus income from the activity of imparting education, we hold that activity they are engaged in is predominantly one of public utility benefiting eligible youth thereby sub-serving a much larger interest of providing useful talents to the industry and ultimately the economy of the country. No individual is gaining any monetary benefit out of the activity of GLTM. The appellants are housed in a small facility in Saidapet and propose to re-locate to spacious premises and own building to be constructed. They have already allocated most of the savings to achieve this objective. We find that the appellants are acting strictly in accordance with the MOA, imparting quality education which has received well deserved recognition.

VALUATION FOR CUSTOMS DUTY

5.1

Value for purpose of Customs Act

Customs duty is payable as a percentage of 'Value' often called 'Assessable Value' or 'Customs Value'. The Value may be either (a) 'Value' as defined in section 14(1) of Customs Act or (b) Tariff value prescribed under section 14(2) of Customs Act.

Basic principles of valuation of imported goods in customs have been summarized in chapter 6 of CBI&C's Customs Manual, 2023.

Tariff Value - Tariff Value can be fixed by CBI&C (Board) for any class of imported goods or export goods. CBI&C should consider trend of value of such or like goods while fixing tariff value. Once so fixed, duty is payable as percentage of this value. (The percentage applicable is as prescribed in Customs Tariff Act). Fixing tariff value is not permitted under GATT convention. However, the provision of fixing tariff values has been retained.

Once tariff value has been notified, customs duty cannot be paid on basis of transaction value - CC v. Ashirvad Udyog (2014) 43 GST 56 = 40 taxmann.com 449 (Mad HC DB).

Customs Valuation on basis of transaction value - Section 14(1) of Customs Act states that 'value' of imported and export goods will be 'transaction value' of such goods i.e. the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India for delivery at the time and place of importation, or for export from India for delivery at the time and place of exportation, where the buyer and seller of the goods are not related and price is the sole consideration for the sale, subject to such other conditions as may be specified in the rules made in this behalf.

Accordingly Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 have been notified effective from 10-10-2007.

In Wipro Ltd. v. ACC (2015) 52 GST 47 = 58 taxmann.com 123 = 319 ELT 177 (SC), it has been held objective of section 14 of Customs Act is to accept actual cost paid or payable for customs valuation. Any fictional cost (like landing charges, insurance, freight etc.) can be added only when actual cost is not ascertainable. The intention of section 14 of Customs Act is to pay customs duty on price 'actually paid or actually payable for the goods'.

Addition to transaction value - First proviso to section 14(1) states that such transaction value in the case of imported goods shall include, in addition to the price as aforesaid [i.e. as specified in section 14(1)], any amount that the buyer is liable to pay for costs and services, including commissions and brokerage, engineering, design work, royalties and licence fees, costs of transportation to the place of importation, insurance, loading, unloading and handling charges to the extent and in the manners specified in the Rules.

Though the proviso does not specifically say so, it is obvious that only those expenses which are relating to imported goods alone can be added.

Rate of foreign exchange - Third proviso to section 14(1) states that such price shall be calculated with reference to the rate of exchange as in force on the date on which a bill of entry is presented under section 46, or a shipping bill or bill of export, as the case may be, is presented under section 50. As per Explanation (a) to section 14(2), the rate of exchange will be determined by CBI&C or ascertained in such manner as CBI&C may direct.

Tariff value - Section 14(2) empowers CBI&C to fix tariff values of imported goods or export goods by issuing a notification.

Valuation Rules if transaction value is not determinable - If there is no sale or buyer or seller are related or price is not the sole consideration, value of the goods will be determined as per Valuation Rules [Clause (ii) of second proviso to section 14(1)].

Valuation Rules are applicable only if value is not determinable under section 14(1) of Customs Act - CCE v. Hindustan Lever (2015) 325 ELT 7 (SC).

See Division Two for text of Valuation Rules.

The question now was whether the Circular of the Board would be applicable to an assessment year falling prior to the date when the Circular was issued. In other words, whether the Circular of the Board will have a retrospective effect. The Circulars were issued in March and October, 2006, whereas the assessment year involved in the instant case was 2004-05. [Para 12] Ordinarily the Circulars issued by the CBDT cannot have retrospective effect. Only law can be made retrospective if it is so provided in the statute. There should be something in the Circular making it effective retrospectively. Such retrospective Circulars may be binding on the departmental officers but the Courts and also the Tribunals are free to examine whether the Circular so issued curtails retrospectively a right granted to a taxpayer by the statute or by an earlier issued Circular. Similarly, if a Circular retrospectively creates a duty on a taxpayer then the Court and the Tribunal may intervene to hold against retrospective effect of such Circular. A Circular giving concessions can be withdrawn only prospectively. [Para 12.4]

Where a Circular is issued after the completion of an assessment then such assessment cannot be prejudicially affected by such circular. It cannot be even used in reassessment proceedings for that year. However, where a new Circular has occupied the field before the beginning of the assessment year then it will be binding on the Assessing Officer and the assessee cannot take the benefit of an earlier Circular. [Para 12.5]

In view of the above, it could be said that the Circular No. 4, dated 29-3-2006 and Circular No. 8/2006, dated 6-10-2006 were not made effective retros-pectively. Secondly, at the beginning of the assessment year, no such Circular was in operation. The field was occupied by rule 6DD(f )(ii) which allowed exemption to the assessee in case of purchases made directly from the producers of hides and skins without complying with any of the conditions mentioned in Circular No. 08/2006, dated 6-10-2006 which supplemented/clarified earlier Circular No. 4 of 29-3-2006. The Circulars sought to impose conditions for claiming exemptions from rigours of section 40A(3) and for getting benefit of rule 6DD(f)( ii) in case of direct purchases from producers of hides and skins. Retrospective effect of these Circulars is not permissible. Rule 6DD(f)(ii ) provided a benefit to the assessee without conditions attached with that rule. Such conditions not originally provided in the rule create rigours to the assessee and restrict the scope of the benefit. It is equivalent to legislation, though subordinate, therefore, cannot be retrospective, unless specifically provided in the statute or in the Circulars. In addition to this, these two Circulars also neutralized/withdrew the effect of rule 6DD(l) which conferred benefit to the assessee if it made purchases from agents by making cash payments. [Para 13]

The Madras High Court in the case of CIT v. K.K.S.K. Leather Processor (P.) Ltd. [2007] 292 ITR 669held that where payments were made to small vendors, who came from surrounding villages to sell the skins to the assessee, provisions of section 40A(3) could not be invoked. Following the said decision of the Madras High Court, it was to be held that payments made in cash for purchases made by the assessee directly from producers would be covered by rule 6DD(f)(ii ) and, therefore, disallowance could not be made out of such payments under section 40A(3). [Para 15]

Regarding the payments made to agents for purchase of raw hides/skins, the issue was covered by the decisions of the Tribunal in the cases of Dy. CIT v. Hind Industries Ltd. [2008] 26 SOT 196 (Delhi)and Sri Renukeswara Rice Mills v. ITO [2005] 93 ITD 263 (Bang.). [Para 16]

The department had not shown any authority for the proposition that under such circumstances, rule 6DD(l) would not be applicable. Accordingly, entire payment made by the assessee to producers of the raw hides/skins or to their agents for such purchases would not be hit by the provisions of section 40A(3). The Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly deleted the addition. [Para 17]

Per Ruma Pal, J. : Between 1994 and 1999, M/s Indian Oil Corporation Ltd., the respondent herein, imported various petroleum products and crude oil into India. These goods were carried to different ports in India by vessels chartered for this purpose. Throughout this period, the respondent had cleared the imported goods upon payment of customs duty without protest by the custom authorities.

2. On 15th March 2000, the respondent received a show cause notice sent by the Commissioner of Customs, Calcutta, the appellant before us, alleging that the respondent had wilfully misdeclared the value of the goods while making entries under Section 46 of the Customs Act, 1962 by deliberately suppressing that the demurrage charges had been paid to the ship owners under the charter party agreements. Since, according to the show cause notice payment for the demurrage had been made through the negotiating bank, the bank charges and the demurrage paid were includible in the customs value of the goods. On this basis, the assessable value was alleged to be Rs. 60,26,05,71,604/-. The respondent was therefore asked to show cause why extra duty to the tune of Rs. 9,75,98,31,199/- should not be realised and why penalty should not be levied against the respondent and its officers.

3. According to the respondent, the 17th to 20th March, 2000 were holidays. On 21st March, the respondent asked for time to file a written reply to the show cause notice. This was rejected by the appellant and the demand was confirmed on 30th March 2000. Penalty equivalent to the amount of the duty determined was also levied. In addition, interest @20 per cent per annum was imposed.

4. The respondent filed appeals before the Commissioner of Customs (Appeals). The appeals were rejected. The respondent preferred a further appeal before the Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal (CEGAT). The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the respondent on grounds which are briefly summarized :

(1)

The Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) had issued a Circular on 14th August 1991 in which it was said that the demurrage did not form part of the assessable value of the goods imported; the circular was binding on the Revenue and the Department could not contend otherwise;

(2)

The decision of this Court in Garden Silk Ltd. vs. Union of India 1999 (113) ELT 358* relied upon by the Revenue was not an authority for the proposition that demurrage payable on account of delay in discharging goods from a vessel was includible in the value of goods while assessing the customs duty payable thereon.

(3)

Under Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 the assessable value of the imported goods must be the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold. The payment of demurrage was not an incident of an ordinary sale. An extraordinary expenditure, like demurrage, could not be included in the assessable value of the imported goods.

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Invoice value must be accepted unless proved incorrect by the department

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Show cause notice to the parties for change in invoice prices is necessary otherwise the decision to enhance the valuation can be set aside on this ground also

FACT: The appellants imported 15000 pcs. of Miniature Ball Bearings from Singapore and gave the invoice price as CIF 3000 Singapore Dollars i.e. Rs. 17,128.20. The Customs Department at Amritsar did not have the price for the goods and so requested Delhi Customs for the same. On getting the information from Delhi Customs, the Department issued a show cause notice to the party for adopting that rate for valuation i.e. 9.25 per piece However, the Asstt. Collector directed the duty to be paid on Rs. 18.40 per piece i.e. on total value of Rs. 21,76,000/- without giving any further show cause notice to the appellants. This rate of 18.40 per piece was obtained from the Central Warehousing Corporation. The appellants contended that the assessable value was to be based on the declared invoice prices unless the department could prove it incorrect. The department wanted the case to be remanded so that the party was given a proper opportunity of being heard on the evidence.

HELD: Valuation: Assessable value for levy of customs duty is to be based on the declared invoiced prices unless proved otherwise by the department. "The onus of proving misdeclaration regarding the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry is on the Department and this can be discharged by the Department only on proving of proper facts, which would discredit the price mentioned in the Bill of Entry and not on the basis of mere suspicion. It is, therefore, on this ground alone that the orders of the lower authorities merit to be set aside."

2. Show Cause notice to the parties for change in invoice prices is necessary otherwise the decision to enhance the valuation can be set aside on this ground also. "What amazes us, is that the show cause notice in this case alleges that the correct price of the imported bearings is Rs. 9.25 per piece whereas the order of the Additional Collector is based on the correct price being Rs. 18.40 per piece. The learned JDR has conceded that the order was passed without furnishing the additional evidence to the appellant and without giving any opportunity to show cause in respect of it. This further seriously undermines the legality of the order."

3. Dissenting view: Per Shri I.J. Rao: Case to be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication. "However, I feel that the omission on the part of the Collector should be allowed to be made good. While I agree that the order should be set aside, I hold that the matter should be remanded to the Collector for fresh adjudication after disclosing to the appellants the relevant evidence relied on by the department and after giving a reasonable opportunity to them to counter the evidence."

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Levy of duty - Valuation of goods - Whether ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purpose - Held, no [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]Excise  Customs : Ship demurrage charges paid by assessee/importer on import of goods were not liable to be included in assessable value of goods imported for customs duty purposes

FACT: The question involved in the instant appeal is as to whether ship demurrage charges paid by the assessee-importer on the import of the goods were to be included in the assessable value of the goods imported for purpose of levy of customs duty.

HELD: The demurrage charges are admittedly incurred after the goods reached at Indian ports and, therefore, it is a post-importation event. Such charges, therefore, cannot form part of the transaction value. [Para 5]

In view of the aforesaid, the appeal filed by the revenue was liable to be dismissed.

compel the AO to follow the instructions of the CBDT. This is not to say that the Court is bound by the instructions of CBDT. All that is required to be said is that, so far as the officials of the Department are concerned, it is not open to them to say that they would not follow the instructions of the CBDT and carry matters in appeals and references [ABC India Ltd. v. DCIT [1996] 86 Taxman 267 (Gau.)]. Circulars beneficial to assessees are also binding on authorities - Circulars beneficial to the assessee which tone down the rigour of the law and are issued in exercise of the statutory powers u/s 119 are binding on the authorities in the administration of the 1961 Act. The benefit of such circulars is admissible to the assessee even though the circulars might have departed from the strict tenor of the statutory provision and mitigated the rigour of the law. The Apex Court, however, clarified that the CBDT cannot pre-empt a judicial interpretation of the scope and ambit of a provision of the 1961 Act. Also, a circular cannot impose on the taxpayer a burden higher than what the Act itself, on a true interpretation, envisages. The task of interpretation of the law is the exclusive domain of the Courts. However, the CBDT has the statutory power u/s 119 to tone down the rigour of the law for the benefit of the assessee by issuing circulars to ensure a proper administration of the fiscal statute and such circulars would be binding on the authorities administering the 1961 Act [Keshavji Ravji & Co. v. CIT [1990] 49 Taxman 87 (SC)].

Onus to prove applicability of circulars, etc. - Mere raising objection in terms of CBDT Circular is not enough, CBDT Circulars continue to bind Revenue and if they contain any conditions, whether such conditions are attracted or not would have to be proved and established by Revenue [PCIT v. Nawany Construction Co. (P.) Ltd. [2018] 98 taxmann.com 294/258 Taxman 365 (Bom.)].

Prospective/retrospective application - Circulars that are in force during the year of assessment are the circulars that have to be applied. Circulars which were issued subsequent to the relevant period cannot be applied to a period anterior thereto [CIT v. N.T. Ramarao (HUF) [1987] 31 Taxman 5 (AP)].

Circulars in nature of concession can be withdrawn prospectively only. So long as a circular issued u/s 119 is applied and enforced, it would be binding on the departmental authorities to ensure a uniform and proper administration and application of the Income-tax Act. Such circulars cannot be withdrawn retrospectively as they could operate only prospectively [DCIT v. Sree Janardhana Mills [2009] 311 ITR 439 (Mad.)].

Modification/withdrawal of circulars - The circular issued by the CBDT existing at the beginning of the AY will be applicable and the subsequent modification of the circular will have no relevance [CIT v. Geeva Films [1983] 141 ITR 632 (Ker.)].

Where a circular affecting the assessee's rights is withdrawn only after the end of the relevant AY, the instructions given under that circular will govern the assessment for that year, irrespective of when such assessment is actually made [CIT v. B. M. Edward, India Sea Foods [1979] 2 Taxman 252/119 ITR 334 (Ker. - FB)].

Condoning delay in filing revised return - Where application filed for condoning delay in filing a revised return to clarify irregularities in ex-parte assessment order on account of mental health problem of assessee had been turned down by CBDT not on merits but on interpretation of proviso to s. 119(1) stating that relief as sought for would amount to interference with powers and jurisdiction of a quasijudicial authority, CBDT misunderstood the scope of the provision as discretion, if exercised, would merely result in enabling assessee to file a revised return, no more, no less [Anjalika Kriplani v. CBDT [2017] 82 taxmann.com 152/248 Taxman 149 (Delhi)].

Compounding of offence - CBDT can issue instructions to control Commissioner's discretion u/s 279(2) to compound offence [Y. P. Chawla v. M. P. Tiwari [1992] 63 Taxman 538 (SC)].

Press release - Circulars issued by CBDT have statutory force and would be binding on every income-tax authority although such may not be the case with regard to press releases issue by the CBDT for information of the public [CIT v. Anjum M. H. Ghaswala [2001] 119 Taxman 352 (SC)].

Decision in the case of State of Kerala v. Kurian Abraham (P.) Ltd. (dated 16.02.2008)

In this decision the Supreme Court followed the case of Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 263 ITR 706 / 132 Taxman 373. Some of the important observations of the Supreme Court in the decision are as follow:

uTax administration is a complex subject. It consists of several aspects. The Government needs to strike a balance in the imposition of tax between collection of revenue on one hand and business-friendly approach on the other hand. Today, Governments have realized that in matters of tax collection, difficulties faced by the business have got to be taken into account. Exemption, undoubtedly, is a matter of policy. Interpretation of an Entry is undoubtedly a quasi-judicial function under the tax laws. Imposition of taxes consists of liability, quantification of liability and collection of taxes. Policy decisions have to be taken by the Government. However, the Government has to work through its senior officers in the matter of difficulties which the business may face, particularly in matters of tax administration. That is where the role of the Board of Revenue comes into play. The said Board takes administrative decisions, which includes the authority to grant administrative reliefs. This is the underlying reason for empowering the Board to issue orders, instructions and directions to the officers under it.

uIn the present case, one was not concerned with deciding the scope and extent of each item in Entry 110. One was essentially concerned in this case with the nature of the powers exercised by the Board/Commissioners under section 3(1A). As stated above, the said circular was issued by the Board by exercising statutory powers vested in it under section 3(1A). Section 3(1A) provides for an enabling power of the Board, which was recognized as an authority under the 1963 Act. The said power was to be exercised in special cases. Granting of administrative reliefs by the Board came within its authority. The said circular was issued for just and fair administration of the 1963 Act. Section 3(1A) is similar to section 119(1) of the 1961 Act. The circulars of this nature are issued by the Board consisting of highest senior officers in the Revenue Department. These circulars are to be respected by the officers working under the supervision of the Board. These circulars are binding on all the authorities administering the tax department.

FACT: These are ten appeals which relate to the same respondent and involve common facts and issues; hence a combined order. The respondents are manufacturers of fertilizers and imported rock phosphate and sulphur in bulk quantities came to India on chartered ship. The goods were purchased on the high seas and unloading on the Indian coast was the responsibility of the respondents. For this they maintained their own wharf, unloading equipment and staff at Vishakhapatnam. 1.4% by way of landing charges stood already added to the price of the goods. The Assistant Collector held that this 1.4% did not include stevedoring charges which he added separately and recalculated the value at varying rates from Rs. 5.86 to Rs. 9.42 per MT. In appeal the Appellate Collr. set aside the Asst. Collr.'s orders and held that the 1.4% already added as landing charges were the same as unloading charges. The Department is now in appeal against the Appellate Collector's orders.

HELD: Place of importation has to be the land mass of India where goods are unloaded from the ship. Section 2(23). "Place of importation in section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962, should take the similar meaning as place of removal of the imported goods, that is, the port gate. Delivery to the importer is effected only here."

2. Port landing charges comprise only wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds; any unloading charges incurred have to be included in the value for assessment in addition to the port landing charges. Section-14. "The 1.4% Port landing charge already added to the respondents, value comprised wharfage charges and conveying charges from wharf to transit sheds and not unloading charges from ship to berth. The unloading charges have therefore to be computed and added too."

3. For calculating the unloading charges and despatch money earned because of unloading of chartered vessel before stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs, but if any money is paid as penalty for delayed unloading of the ships the same should be added.

".........despatch money earned because of unloading of the chartered vessel before the stipulated bay time should be deducted from the costs. Conversely if the appellants have paid any penalty for delayed unloading of the ship the same should be added to the costs."

HEADNOTE: Section 49 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Storage of imported goods in warehouse pending clearance - Departmental instructions have no legal binding. Budget clearances - if documents are presented timely but office is prematurely closed, the importer has to be given advantage. Technicalities--procedural lapse in not presenting bank certificate is no ground to deny clearance

FACT: The petitioners are engaged in the business of texturising base flat yarn. Base yarn was imported by them and lodged in a warehouse owned by Central Warehousing Corporation. The petitioners filed two bills of entry for removal of the above goods on 16th February, 1983 and 28th February, 1983. Customs duty was paid as per rates applicable on 28th February 1983. All that remained to be done was to pay the warehousing charges and lift the goods from the warehouse. The petitioner's agents came to get release of the goods on 28.2.1983 but to their surprise found that the cash counter was closed at 3 PM instead of 4 PM and delivery counter at 4 PM instead of 5 PM. As duty on the subject goods was increased w.e.f. 1.3.1983 petitioners approached their Association, who registered a protest with the Customs authorities, along with the request that the goods should be treated as having been delivered on 28.2.1983, thus getting the benefits of the pre-budget rates. The Department refused this, and contended that the advancing of working hours was valid because of a circular issued in that behalf.

HELD: Official circulars are not binding on a citizen. Departmental action based on such circulars can be held valid only if legal validity and sanction of the same is proved. Mere cyclostyled instructions, as in the present case, have no legal validity and it is against the principles of equity that the petitioners should be held liable for the consequences, and to pay enhanced customs duty. "The question has now been rightly posed by Mr. Jagtiani the learned Counsel for the Petitioners as to what is the legal sanction for this circular and whether the same can be accepted as a mandate. The learned Counsel for the Respondent Mr. Sethna when questioned could not throw any light on this aspect much less could he effectively answer this very relevant question posed with the necessary consequences that nothing has been shown on this forum to accept the legal validity of this circular, namely, about the authority, the sanction and all other features which go to make out a validly legal circular. In the absence of any such material and even an ostensible explanation which is not coming forth this becomes inescapable to obviously strike down the validity of this circular having no existence in law at all."

2. Warehoused goods--withholding delivery even when a party has been physically present to pay the warehousing charges and lift the goods is a failure on the part of the official staff. Hence, it is fair and just that the consignments should be treated as having been released on 28.2.1983. "...the Petitioners were waiting to offer the warehousing charges between 3 p.m. and 4 p.m. and thereby they could have obtained delivery between 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. as usual, the Petitioners' assertion that even this was not done by the staff within that time also even though they were just awaiting their turn for which the entire blame lies with the staff is not seriously controverted. ......I have no reservation in my mind that......they would be liable to pay customs duty as was prevailing on 28th February 1983 and not enhanced customs duty that came into force on 1st March 1983. This result therefore appears to be unescapable."

3. Warehoused goods--Non-presentation of Bank Certificates is not sufficient ground to deny delivery of goods from warehouse as all other formalities had been complied with. "As rightly contended by Mr. Jagtiani the learned Counsel it is the monetary transaction which has the direct nexus to the schedule time of 4 p.m. which was advanced to 3 p.m. and it has nothing to do with the physical presentation of the discharge certificate from the bank and according to him if the moneys were offered before 4 p.m. then it becomes immaterial in so far as the presentation of the document is concerned because customs duty is admittedly paid earlier and warehousing charges are effered on the spot.......In my opinion the object as enunciated by sub-clause (b) does not embrace within its fold the presentation of the discharge certificate from any bank. In a way that would be only incidental because the main count would be about the payment of customs duty and the payment of warehousing charges."

Assessable Value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Second hand machinery - depreciation method for determining assessable value to be adopted in absence of transaction value as new machines were purchased abroad and imported after use for some period and as basis for declared value estimated by chartered engineer not disclosed - rate of depreciation adopted as per Board's circular dt. 19.11.87 held to be reasonable

Excise & Customs : A CHA cannot be expected to be a better expert on customs valuation than customs officer; hence, his license cannot be revoked merely because he did not advise importer/revenue to add certain expenses in value, especially when there was no evidence that he was aware that said expenses were includible

In Varsha Plastics v. UOI (2009) 3 SCC 365 = 235 ELT 193 (SC), it has been held that Standing Orders/instructions/directions issued by department are not binding on assessing authority as he is quasi-judicial authority. He has to act independently in exercise of his quasi-judicial powers. The Standing Orders/instructions/directions issued for smooth functioning of assessment and work in no way interferes with discretion of assessment authority. No instructions to adjudicating or appellate authority - CBI&C (Board) cannot issue instructions or directions to customs officer acting as adjudicating authority or appellate authority. Thus, no instructions can be issued for classification of goods in a particular way. No instructions can be issued to Principal Commissioner/Commissioner or Commissioner (Appeals) in exercise of their appellate functions - Orient Paper Mills Ltd. v. UOI - AIR 1969 SC 48 = 1978 (2) ELT - J345 (SC) * Ramchandra Art v. UOI 2002(139) ELT 540 (Guj HC DB). This is also made clear by proviso to section 37B of CEA [and also section 151A of Customs Act].

(In practice, Board instructions are given much more weightage than even Court orders!).

Standardisation of Board circulars - CBI&C has introduced standardised system from 1994 for numbering the orders/clarifications issued. As per the system, first number will be running serial number starting from 1.1.1994 (This method is used for circulars under CGST and IGST but not used for customs circulars, where fresh serial number starts every year). Second number will be serial number of order issued during the year. Last two digits will be year of issuing the order. Suffix 'Cus' will indicate circular issued by customs wing. - CBI&C circular Nos. 23/23/94-CX dated 16-2-1994, 9/95-Cus dated 31-1-1995 and 4/98-Cus dated 23-2-1998.

For example, circular No. 16/2015-Cus is 16th circular issued in 2015 issued in year 2015 by customs wing of CBI&C.

Functioning of Board - Board members look after various functions. The distribution of work among CBI&C members has been notified in MF(DR) Officer Order No. 66/2015 dated 28-5-2015.

Some functions are directly looked after by Chairman. It is not necessary that decisions of CBI&C must be taken at a meeting of all members of Board. In Bihar Public Service Commission v. Manoj Kumar Pandey 1997 AIR SCW 41, it was observed - 'In a multi-member body, it may not be feasible for every member to associate personally and directly with decision making in respect of every matter. It would, therefore, be permissible to constitute committees of members or authorise a member to consider the manifold matters which may come up for consideration before the body'.

Functions of Board can be entrusted to other officers or authority - Central Government can entrust functions of CBI&C to any officer of Central Government or State Government or any local authority, by issuing notification. Such delegation can be conditional or unconditional [section 6 of Customs Act].

9.1-1 Powers of customs officers

Section 5(1) of Customs Act provides that an officer of customs may exercise the powers and discharge the duties conferred on him or imposed on him, subject to conditions and limitations as may be imposed by CBI&C.

Proper Officer - 'Proper officer' in relation to any function to be performed under Customs Act, means the officer of customs who is assigned those functions by CBI&C or Principal Commissioner/Commissioner of Customs under section 5 of Customs Act - Section 2(34) of Customs Act, [words in italics inserted w.e.f. 30-3-2022 vide Finance Act, 2022].

Senior can exercise powers of junior - Section 5(2) of Customs Act specifies that a Customs Officer may exercise powers and discharge duties conferred on any other Customs Officer subordinate to him e.g. powers conferred on Appraiser can be exercised by Assistant Commissioner or Dy. Commissioner.

CBIC can assign functions to any officer of customs as 'proper officer' - Without prejudice to the provisions contained in section 5(1) of Customs Act, the Board (CBIC) may, by notification, assign such functions as it may deem fit, to an officer of customs who shall be the proper officer in relation to such functions - section 5(1A) of Customs Act, inserted w.e.f. 30-3-2022.

5.6

Exclusions from Assessable value of customs

Interpretative Note to rule 3 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 provide that following charges shall be excluded :

(a)

Charges for construction, erection, assembly, maintenance or technical assistance undertaken after importation of plant, machinery or equipment

(b)

Cost of transport after importation

(c)

Duties and taxes in India

Other payments from buyer to seller that do not relate to imported goods are not part of the customs value.

In Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. CCE 2000 AIR SCW 572 = 2000 (3) SCC 472 = AIR 2000 SC 1013 = 116 ELT 422 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that this note does not mean that charges other than those covered in clauses (a) to (c) are available to be included in the value of imported goods - followed in CC v. J K Corporation Ltd. (2007) 208 ELT 485 (SC) - quoted in CC v. Toyota Kirloskar Motor P Ltd. (2007) 213 ELT 4 (SC).

This is also made clear in interpretative note to rule 4 of Customs Valuation Rules.

Expenses incurred in customs area after landing not includible in customs valuation - In CC v. Indian Potash (2009) 234 ELT 507 (CESTAT), packing of imported goods was done in customs area to meet requirements of Fertilizer Price Control Order. It was held that this packing cost is not includible as taxable event has reached when goods reached customs barrier and bill of entry filed. Hence cost incurred after landing of goods is not includible.

Erection, testing and commissioning after importation - Erection, testing and commissioning charges are post importation expenses and are not required to be considered for purpose of customs value, as per interpretative note 3 to Customs Valuation Rules.

Cost of erection, test and commissioning is not includible. - Andhra Pradesh Gas Corpn v. CC 2001(136) ELT 860 (CEGAT). Supervision and technical charges for supervision of erection and commissioning are not includible in assessable value - Bilt Chemicals v. CC (2004) 168 ELT 247 (CESTAT).

Charges for setting up a plant in India are not includible in assessable value of plant, especially as importer was at liberty to get it erected from person other than supplier - NCL Industries Ltd. v. CC 2005 (189) ELT 193 (CESTAT 2 v.1 order).

However, in Mukund Ltd. v. CC 1999(112) ELT 479 (CEGAT), it was held that apart from design and engineering charges, supervision charges in India during erection, commissioning and performance guarantee tests are includible in Assessable Value, as it is part of whole engineering package. However, training charges are not includible. - confirmed in Mukand Ltd. v. CC 2000(120) ELT 30 (SC 3 member bench) stating that supply of basic design and engineering drawings and supervision of erection, testing and commissioning based thereon are includible as both are parts and conditions of the contract [This is based on particular facts, probably because it was held as payment made as condition of sale and hence includible as per rule 9(1)(e) of Customs Valuation Rules. Otherwise, normally, erection and commissioning charges after importation are not includible in assessable value].

Bank charges - Bank charges paid to banker for services rendered by them is not consideration of goods given to seller. It is not includible. - EXIM India Oil Co. v. CC 2001(131) ELT 207 = 42 RLT 181 (CEGAT).

Stamp duty payable to State Government - Stamp Duty payable to State Government cannot be added in assessable value of imported goods. - Umi Special Steel v. CC 2001(137) ELT 174 (CEGAT) * Tata Yodogawa v. CC 2001(135) ELT 960 (CEGAT).

Computer Software - Note that software imports are exempt from customs duty.

HEADNOTE: Section 15 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff valuation of imported goods - Rate of duty - relevant date--increased rate applicable at the time of clearance cannot be charged once the goods have been assessed to duty and passed out of customs charge

FACT: In 1981 the petitioners imported consignments of Nonyl Phenol Ethylene Oxide and Methylene Chloride and cleared the same to the bonded warehouse. In 1983 they were served notices advising them that the goods would be sold of not cleared within 10 days and accordingly the customs duty and demurrage charges were paid on 28.2.1983. The petitioners' request on 1.3.1983 to allow the clearances of the said goods was not granted except on payment of the increased customs duty that had come into effect the same day. This petition impugns the demand by the respondents of the increased customs duty.

HELD: Enhanced customs duty cannot be claimed as the goods were "passed out of customs charges". "...on 28th February 1983 ex-bond warehouse operations were to be stopped at 4 p.m. The circular instructs those to whom it is addressed not to allow ex-bond home consumption withdrawals which are sought to be effected after closing hours on 28th February 1983 'even though the Bill of Entry may have been noted before....' In the instant case, we have a situation where Customs duty on the said goods was paid at 2.30 p.m. on 28th February 1983 and the six bills of entry were marked 'passed out of Customs charges'. Therefore, assuming all else, this circular did not entitle the respondents to refuse clearance of the said goods on 28th February 1983. The Respondents cannot, therefore, validly lay claim to the enhanced Customs duty on the said goods that came into effect on the next day."
2005 taxmann.com 1016 (New Delhi - CESTAT) (LB)[18-07-2005] G.M. Pens International Ltd. vs. Collector of Customs  (Sea-Port), Chennai

Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Rule 5 of the Customs Valuation (DPIG) Rules, 1988 - Assessable value - loading of value of imported goods on the basis of unsustainable admission and value of contemporaneous imports which took place after 6 months after the present import not sustainable when quantity imported is also different - Value of branded goods imported by the same appellant cannot be adopted for the goods in question - Appeal allowed (Para 3)

excise duty on manufactured goods, cannot be the basis for granting exemption under the Customs Act, which is a separate and distinct enactment. "The exemptions granted under the Excise Act, which regulates the levy of excise duty or a tax on manufactured goods in the country is a separate and distinct enactment. The exemptions granted under the Excise Duty either in whole or in part are for the purpose of that Act only and they cannot on any principle be the basis for claiming exemptions under the Customs Act." 7. Powers of the C.B.E.C. include framing of regulations prescribing the forms of bills of entry. "Section 157 of the Customs Act expressly empowers the Board to frame regulations prescribing the forms of bills of entries. .......An examination of the 'forms' prescribed by the Board shows that they are made for purposes of the Act. We find no merit in the challenge of the petitioners to the Regulations or the forms prescribed by the Board."

8. 'Landing charges' are includible in the assessable value of imported goods, as value has to be determined at the time and place of importation and the importer cannot take delivery of goods till payment of landing charges. "The value had to be determined at the time and place of importation. The time and place of importation can never be where the ship crosses the territorial waters but must naturally be at the sea port where the goods are actually delivered by the shipmaster. .......Without payment of landing charges, the importer does not and cannot take delivery of the goods at all. We are of the view that this is the true import of Section 14(1) of the Customs Act, which is only made specific in the Customs Valuation Rules of 1963 and the form of Bill of Entry prescribed by the Board. We are, therefore, of the view that 'landing charges' cannot be excluded and the assessment cannot be made on the CIF value of goods. "

9. Exemption claim on packages and containers is remanded to the proper authorities for examination. "On the packages and containers the petitioners" claim is founded on the notifications issued by Government under Section 25 of the Customs Act. Whether the claim is well founded or not has to be examined and decided in the first instance by the authority under the Act. As the authority had not examined and decided the same we must only direct the authority to do that."

2001 taxmann.com 486 (CEGAT- Kolkata)[06-08-2001] Sushil Halwai vs. Commissioner of Customs (Port), Calcutta

ELT 207 = 42 RLT 181 (CEGAT).

Stamp duty payable to State Government - Stamp Duty payable to State Government cannot be added in assessable value of imported goods. - Umi Special Steel v. CC 2001(137) ELT 174 (CEGAT) * Tata Yodogawa v. CC 2001(135) ELT 960 (CEGAT).

Computer Software - Note that software imports are exempt from customs duty. Software embedded or pre-loaded in machine is to be classified along with the machine. This will also be case when software is brought separately, but as a 'set'. If tangible software e.g. operating software or application software loaded on disk, floppy, CD-ROM etc. is imported, it will be classifiable as software under heading 8523 - CC (Import), Mumbai PN 39/2007 dated 3-12-2007 - same view in Indusind Media v. CC (2019) 368 ELT 235 (SC).

In Bharti Airtel v. CC (2012) 286 ELT 270 (CESTAT), it was held that software imported separately has to be classified and valued separately, even if imported along with computer. Even peripheral devices like memory devices and systems software are to be treated independently. However, software embedded/etched/burnt into hardware has to be considered as part of hardware and its value forms part of the computer.

In Bhagyanagar Metals v. CCE (2009) 67 taxmann.com 33 = 241 ELT 63 (CESTAT), it was held that value of software which is necessary for functioning of the equipment and is embedded into it in includible in assessable value of the main equipment - same view in Indusind Media v. CC (2019) 368 ELT 235 (SC).

In Bharti Airtel v. CC (2012) 286 ELT 270 (CESTAT) it was held that software embedded in telecom equipment is part of telecom equipment and included in its value.

5.6-1 Interest on deferred payment

Interest on deferred payment, if shown separately in the Invoice cannot be added - CBI&C Clarification No. F.3/12/57-Cus VI dated 27-7-1987 - quoted and followed in Bharat Foam Udyog (P.) Ltd. v. ACC - 1993 (67) ELT 445 (Coll Appl) - same view in Zenith Steel Pipes v. CC - (1995) 80 ELT 886 (CEGAT 3 member bench) * CC v. Bharat Foam Udyog P Ltd. 1997(93) ELT 69 (CEGAT). However, if there is a fixed charge payable irrespective of date of payment, it will not be allowed as deduction even if such fixed charge is termed as 'interest' - Themis Agencies v. CC 1998(104) ELT 487 (CEGAT).

CBI&C has further clarified vide circular No. 20/97-Cus dated 17.6.1997, that interest charged on deferred payment should normally not be added in the assessable value, if (a) Interest element has no nexus with or bearing on value of goods (b) Interest is shown separately in invoice (c) There is no financing agreement/arrangement or any special relationship between importer and exporter, influencing the declared price (d) Price declared is the price actually paid or payable in the ordinary course of trade. However, interest can be added if there is evidence to indicate a nexus between price of goods and interest element, and where circumstances also indicate that this element has also influenced selling price.

In CC v. Jayant Oil Mills (P) Ltd. 1998 AIR SCW 4018 = AIR 1999 SC 1569 = 1998(100) ELT 10 (SC) also, it was confirmed that interest on delayed payment goes to banker and not to seller. It is not addible to assessable value.

5.6-2 Demurrage

Demurrage is of two types - (a) Ship Demurrage when whole ship is chartered and demurrage is payable when ship was not unloaded within specified time (b) demurrage payable to port trust as goods are not cleared from port within prescribed time.

Demurrage charges payable to port trust - Demurrage payable to port trust as goods were not cleared in time is a post landing event, i.e. after goods are landed in the port. In any case, valuation is required to be done on 'ordinary price'. Demurrage cannot be termed as part of 'normal' or 'ordinary' price of a product and hence not includible.

Demurrage charges are after goods are imported. These are post importation charges and not includible in assessable value - CCE v. Mangalore Refinery (2015) 325 ELT 214 (SC). - followed in CC v. MGM International Exports (2022) 380 ELT 3 (SC).

HEADNOTE: Section 129B read with Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Orders of Appelalte Tribunal - Rectification application cannot be used as a medium for rearguing lost points - Valuation: Landed cost is the assessable value; so additions of freight and insurance is in order: Discounts cannot be allowed where invoice value is available

FACT: The appellants had imported two Toyota Corona 1600 DLX Sedans. They presented the manufacturer's invoice at the lime of assessment of Customs duly. The Customs authorities determined duty payable after adding freight, insurance and landing charges to the invoice price. Though the importers claimed 15% discount on the manufacturer's price, as well as exclusion of freight, insurance and landing charges, these claims were rejected by the Asstt. Collr. On appeal the Tribunal upheld the Asstt. Collr.'s valuation. Depreciation claims in respect of car accessories like stereo AC were also disallowed. After this the importers submitted applications for rectification of mistakes which, they argued, were obvious and apparent in the earlier order. Their main contention is that as value should have been fixed at place of removal (the market in Japan) insurance and transportation expenses etc., were to be deducted. Besides, the Department was bound by promissory estoppel to allow a discount of 15% in view of a Departmental circular providing for this discount.

HELD: Rectification application cannot be used for re-arguing those points which were already discussed and settled by the Tribunal. As there is no apparent misapplication of law by the Tribunal, earlier decision cannot be disturbed. "under the garb of a rectification application, it is not open to a party to avail it as a further chance of re-arguing the matter or calling upon the Tribunal to review the basis of the decision. Such a course would be beyond the scope of an application for rectification. The "mistakes" repeatedly urged by the applicants were the contentions raised in the main appeals and Tribunal has taken a particular view. It may be argued that they are debatable conclusions. But rectification applications are not intended for re-opening a decision."

Valuation: Tribunal decision that valuation is to be based on prices at the point of landing is upheld. Hence adding of freight, insurance etc. are correct. Deduction of 15% from market price on ground of promissory estoppel is not relevant because the calculation was based on the manufacturer's invoice, whereas deductions were allowed in those cases where the calculation was based on international prices (in. the absence of manufacturer's invoice). "The Tribunal has in the main order held that the prices at which the goods were delivered at the point of landing in India was relevant and not the price at which the transactions took place in Tokyo. The adding of freight, insurance and landing charges was held to be correct. The claim for discount was rejected by the Tribunal for the reasons already stated. The Assessment of the air-conditioners and other accessories were upheld on merits. As rightly urged by the JDR, no promissory estoppel would arise."

Assessable value - Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Second hand machinery - rate of depreciation allowed under Income Tax Act, not to be applied - no justification for enhancement of value on the ground of price rise since the date of manufacture - depreciation as per rate prescribed under Customs law to be allowed and thereafter freight, insurance and landing charges to be added to arrive at CIF value (Para 9)

1986 taxmann.com 245 (CEGAT- NEW DELHI) (SB)[30-09-1986] Collector of Customs, Cochin vs. T. Gulam Mahamood Assadi & Sons

The assessees challenged constitutional validity of proviso (ii) of rule 9(2) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988 inserted by Notification No. 39/90, dated 5-7-1990.

The assessee claimed that the actual loading, unloading and handling charges amounted to Rs. 69.98 paisa as per the tariff of the International Airport Authority of India, Madras (now Chennai). However, the Customs Authorities, on the basis of the impugned notification added a sum of Rs. 15,214.69 paisa at 1 per cent of CIF value.

The assessee argued that such a notional fixation of the handling charges with the addition of 1 per cent of CIF value, irrespective of the nature of goods, size of the cargo, was in total disregard to total handling charges, even when such actual handling charges could be ascertained. Same was irrational, arbitrary and ultra vires.

The department argued that it was found impossible to ascertain the actual amounts incurred towards loading, unloading and handling charges while making the assessment as they varied depending upon the quantities and place of import. Finding this difficulty in actual practice and in order to achieve certainty, one per cent of the CIF value was fixed to be included in the assessable value. It was argued that once this uniformity is achieved with the aforesaid provisions, merely because some would be getting the benefit while others would suffer certain detriment, is no reason for invalidating the provision when many others would be getting the benefit thereof as well. The percentage had been fixed by the rule making authority after taken into consideration the overall picture.

11.4

Valuation of goods

Even if there is provision in respect of self assessment, Valuation Rules have not been changed.

As per rule 11 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007, the importer has to file declaration about full 'value' of goods. If the assessing officer has doubts about the truth and accuracy of 'value' as declared, he can ask importer to submit further information, details and documents. If the doubt persists, the assessing officer can reject the value declared by importer. [rule 12 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007]. If the importer requests, the assessing officer has to give reasons for doubting the value declared by importer. [rule 12(2)]. If the value declared by importer is rejected, the assessing officer can value imported goods on other basis e.g. value of identical goods, value of similar goods etc. as provided in Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.

Assessing Officer should not arbitrarily reject the declared value and increase the assessable value. He should follow due process of law and issue appealable order. - MF(DR) circular No. 16/2003-Cus dated 17-3-2003.

In Escorts Ltd. v. UOI 1998(97) ELT 211 (SC), it was held that when there is no dispute about classification and rate of duty, assessment on the Bill of Entry itself is an assessment order. It is 'across the counter' affair and no separate formal assessment order is necessary.

11.4-1 Special Valuation Branch

Customs have Special Valuation Branch (SVB) which keeps eye on possible under-valuation of goods. Its function is mainly to investigate the valuation of such imported goods from related parties. SVB investigates the impact of such relationship on the invoice value of the imported goods.

CBI&C had issued Circular No. 5/2016 dated 9-2-2016 issued to streamline procedure of investigation by SVB.

In Pernod Richard India P. Ltd. v. UOI (2023) 3 Centax 112 (Bom HC DB), it was held that CBIC Circular No. 5/2016 dated 9-2-2016 in respect of bond and bank guarantee for provisional release of goods applies only during investigation. Once investigation is completed, 100% bank guarantee for differential duty can be demanded for provisional release of goods under CBIC Circular No. 38/2016-Cus dated 22-8-2016 and assessment can be completed.

11.4-2 Appeal is to be filed and not refund, even if self assessment made

It was held that assessment of Bill of Entry is an appealable order and appeal is required to be filed and not a refund claim. There is no 'assessment' by customs officer w.e.f. 8-4-2011. Hence, it was thought that now refund claim can be filed as you cannot file appeal against your own assessment and there is no 'appealable order'.

However, in ITC Ltd. v. CCE (2019) 368 ELT 216 (SC 3 member bench), it has been held that appeal is required to be filed and not refund claim, even in respect of self assessment.

2. As per section 65(27 ), ‘Commercial training or coaching centre’ does not include any institute or establishment which issues any certificate or diploma or degree or any educational qualification recognised by law for the time being in force.

Usually, there is no problem up to school education. However, in respect of post-school education, there are many issues. Usually, such education is given by University.

As per section 2(f) of the University Grants Commission Act (UGC Act), ‘University’ means a University established or incorporated by or under a Central Act, a Provincial Act or a State Act and includes any such institution, as may, in consultation with University concerned, be recognised by University Grants Commission (UGC), in accordance with the regulations made in this behalf under the UGC Act.

As per section 3 of the UGC Act, any institution of higher education, other than a University, can be notified by the Central Government as ‘deemed university’ and then all provisions of the UGC Act will apply as if it were a University under section 2(f ) of the UGC Act.

Recognition can be granted to a college or a institution run by a trust, a registered society or a body corporate or body incorporated under the Central or the State Act. It is an institution affiliated to or forms a constituent member of a University.

In addition, as per National Policy of Education, 1986, a scheme of autonomous college has been promoted. These are autonomous colleges but degree is granted by University.

All these institutions are created or recognised in terms of powers conferred by statute and, hence, would fall in category of institute/establishment which issues diploma or certificate recognised by law. Degree can be granted only by University or Deemed University - para 3.2 of CBEC Circular No. 107/01/2009-ST, dated January 28, 2009."

Thus, an institute/establishment affiliated to University is exempt even if the degree is granted by University and not by the institute/establishment itself.

2.1 Recognition at the time of provision of service is relevant - What is relevant is that the recognition of institute or establishment should be there at the time of provision of service and not earlier or later. It cannot be said that once recognised, an institute or establishment would remain so even in future or was so in past - para 3.7 of CBEC Circular No. 107/01/2009-ST, dated January 28, 2009 [Probably this is the only statement in the circular which is least controversial].

2.2 Recognition of professional courses - For promotion of professional institutions, a number of Professional Councils have been created under various Acts, like All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), Medical Council of India (MCI), Indian Council for Agricultural Research (ICAR) and Bar Council of India (BCI).

They have been given powers to de-recognise an institution or establishment or a particular course, even if they are recognised by a University, Deemed University or Affiliated College.

1. Landing charges are levied by the respective port authority on goods imported into India. Such charges normally work out, on an average, to around 1 % of the C.I.F. price of the goods. As a part of the cost of delivery of the goods at the place of importation, these charges form a component of the assessable value of the goods for levy of customs duty.

2. The customs duties have to be assessed and paid before the goods could be cleared from the port premises. Since the amount of actual landing charges that would be levied on the consignment at the time of its clearance is not known at the earlier stage of assessment and payment of customs duties, it has been an established practice in the Customs Houses to adopt an average rate, worked out on the basis of the total landing charges collected and the total C.I.F. value of the goods imported in the previous year(s). The average rate of landing charges so determined is revised periodically on the basis of actuals of the preceding year(s) at the respective port.

3. The same practice was followed in the case of present respondents and landing charges at the average rate of 1% were added to their C.I.F. price. However, in the present case, the Ld. Collector (Appeals) accepted the claim of the respondents that the actual amount of landing charges alone should be added for arriving at the assessable value. The department, perturbed by the implications of this order, is now in appeal before us.

4. We cannot support the Ld. Appellate Collector's order for the simple reason that it would make the working of the assessment procedures almost impractical. We have already stated in the preceding paragraph that the actuals are not known in advance when duties are assessed and paid. If the respondents' point were to be accepted, lakhs of assessments all over the country would have to be made on provisional basis. The statutory provisional assessment procedure itself involves complicated formalities, including execution of a bond and giving of bank guarantee/security etc. After the actuals become available, such lakhs of assessments would have to be re-opened, resulting In refunds or recoveries. Rare cases apart, the amounts involved in each individual case would be very small. This is so because the landing charges themselves form only a fraction of the import price and the difference between the average amount and the actual amount would further be a fraction of that fraction. A Division Bench of the Hon'ble Gujarat High Court [1982 ELT 203 (GUJ.) ] Prabhat Cotton Silk Mills Ltd. v. Union of India, had an occasion to comment adversely on the litigation involved in numerous challenges to validity of inclusion of landing charges in the customs assessable value. The considerations which had weighed with the Hon'ble High Court, inter alia, were enormous number of cases on the one hand (running into hundreds of thousands) and pettiness of the amounts involved in individual cases on the other. We observe that while the amounts, by way of a fraction of the landing charges themselves, would, by and large, be still more tiny in individual cases, the number of consignments imported over the years has grown. We hear almost every day the trade and industry clamoring for simplification of procedures in our country. And yet in the present case the respondents ask us to support undoing of a simplification which, by a practice accepted since over a century, has become an established part of the customs assessment. We see nothing wrong or illegal in averaging of the landing charges. The interpretation of law has to be a practical one. Taken as a whole, neither the Government nor the importers stand to lose or gain. We see no reason, therefore, to upset the existing procedure and thereby add enormous amount of infructuous work for the custom houses as well as for lakhs of importers.

5. In the result, we set aside the impugned order-in-appeal and restore the Assistant Collector's Order-in-Original. The appeal of the department is, accordingly, allowed.

FACT: The respondents had imported certain plant and machinery. In terms of an agreement the respondents' Collaborators were selecting the machinery. There were no specific charges for this service. Payment made to the Collaborators in lumpsum was for the transfer of technical knowledge. Construing this payment as buyer's commission, the Asstt. Collector held that in terms of Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules, a loading of 21/2% service charges was required to be added to the invoice value of the third party suppliers. On appeal, the Collector (Appeals) set aside the above order on the grounds that in view of the machineries having been supplied by a third party, in the absence of any specific provision in the Collaboration agreement for the payment of service charges, the payment made to the Collaborators is not to be included in the assessable value of the goods. Hence this Revenue appeal.

HELD: Department's application suffers from infirmities--Collector had given the authorisation for filing the appeal without expressing any opinion about the legality or propriety of the order as specified under section 129A--Specific grounds of appeal not raised by the Department. "On going through the records we find that neither authorisation given by the Collector is in the proper Order nor appeal filed by the Department is in proper form. Section 129-A(2) specifies that before giving authorisation to file an appeal Collector should express about the illegality or impropriety of the order against which the appeal is to be filed and direct the proper Officer to appeal on his behalf to the Appellate Tribunal against such order. In this authorisation the Collector simply authorises the Assistant Collector to file an appeal without expressing any opinion about the legality or otherwise of the order and, as such, there is no proper authorisation for filing the appeal. We find that presentation of appeal also is not in the proper form since neither department has filed any grounds of appeal nor it is clear on which points department is seeking relief in the absence of grounds of appeal. Form No. CA-3 should be accompanied with statement of facts and grounds of appeal but we find that appeal form is accompanied with number of pages in the form of commentary consisting of comments on the impugned order without raising specific grounds. The appeal filed by the department is liable to be dismissed on these preliminary grounds."

2. Valuation--Department's' allegation of undervaluation is not supported by any evidence--in the absence of specific allocation, notional value cannot be added to the invoice value on account of buying commission or handling charges-Collector's order upheld. "The burden lies on the department to prove undervaluation. The department ought to make out a case for undervaluation with sufficient evidence and to prove that value shown in the invoice was not the real value. There is no evidence to show that similar goods were sold at higher price or that the collaborators acted as agents to the foreign Suppliers in getting commission or due to their services resulted in reduction of value. Further payment made to the collaborators for transfer of technical know-how and such lumpsum payment was made to their services where it is not possible for that reason to allocate the charges to individual consignments imported through them, no notional value can be added to the invoice value on account of buying commission or handling charges as it was rightly dealt with in the impugned order. We do not find any infirmity in the impugned order."

Per Justice U.L. Bhat : Appellant imported 900 metric tonnes of Dimethyl Terphthalate from Spain. It was shipped in vessel M.V. Hero. The vessel was grounded near Greece and the consignment was transferred to another vessel S.S. Vishva Tej. When the respondent filed bill of entry showing the invoice price CIF, the Assistant Collector added the extra freight and insurance charges which the respondent had to bear on account of the grounding of the ship and transfer to another ship, over-ruling the contention of the respondent that such additional expenses could not be included in the assessable value. The Collector (Appeals) set aside this enhancement and assessable value. The department, being aggrieved, has filed the present appeal.

2. An employee of the respondent appeared before us and pleaded for adjournment on the ground that though notice had been received, the respondent could not trace the records. In an appeal filed in 1987, we do not think this is a reasonable request. The request for adjournment is rejected.

3. The declared value includes the normal CIF value. What was sought to be added was the extra freight and insurance charges which the respondent had to incur on account of grounding of the original vessel and transfer to another vessel. Ordinarily, such extra charges are not taken into consideration by the customs house, since the customs house goes by the actual freight or a particular percentage of price. In these circumstances, we are not inclined to interfere. The appeal is dismissed.

letter stating that he was paying the reassessed amount of duty under protest. Having once agreed to the assessment made by the department, the assessee cannot be permitted to challenge the said assessment or the impugned circular on the basis whereof the assessment was made. The fact that the assessee had initially agreed with the department's assessment has been concealed by the assessee which amounts to suppression of material facts. The assessee has not approached the court with clean hands and does not deserve any relief. In court's opinion, non-mentioning of any and every fact does not amount to suppression of material facts. A material fact is one that would have a bearing on the decision of the court. Even if the assessee mentioned in the writ petition about the factum of he having initially agreed with the department's assessment, decision would not have been any different. This is so because there can be no estoppel against the statute. Section 11A of the Customs Tariff Act does not countenance amendment of the First Schedule to the said Act by issuance of a mere departmental circular. The method in which the First Schedule has been sought to be amended is contrary to the method prescribed by section 11A and as such the circular cannot be sustained. Hence, the fact that the assessee initially agreed with the department's assessment is not a material fact and accordingly the department's point is rejected. [Para 34]

The second point urged by the department is that the assessee has not challenged the show cause-cum-demand notice dated 21-4-2014. In court's view, this is a point without any substance. The said show cause notice is admittedly based on the impugned circular. If the circular is quashed, the show cause notice automatically goes. [Para 35]

In view of what has been discussed above, the impugned circular is bad in law being without jurisdiction and cannot be sustained. The Circular No. 19/2013-CUS., dated 9-5-2013 is quashed and set aside. [Para 36]

Special Valuation Branch In the Circular No. 1/98 – Cus. Dated 01.01.1998, the first set of instructions were given to the Special Valuation Branch in relation to the transactions involving special relationships. At that point of time, the SVBs were located only at Chennai, Calcutta, Delhi and Mumbai. As per the Circular, any decision taken in respect of a particular case in any of the four major Custom Houses was to be followed by all the other Custom Houses/formations. According to this Circular, where in the declaration prescribed under the Custom Valuation (Determination of Price of Imported Goods) Rules, 1988, the importer himself has made an averment that the transactions are between related persons in accordance with Rule 2(2) of the Valuation Rules, 1988 and there is a prima facie justification for further enquiry, the concerned case of import may be referred to the SVB of the concerned Custom House, where a separate case file would be opened and a registration number assigned to the case. The Notification further deals with the explanation regarding various determining factors to investigate the transactions between 'related persons.'

In terms of Circular No. 11 of 2001 – Cus. Dated 23.02.2001, it was stipulated that it would be imperative for the Commissioner of Customs to critically examine the issues involved and decide whether it merits detailed enquiries by SVB and adoption of the provisional assessment procedure.

In each and every case, the decision would be taken at his level before provisional assessment is ordered and matter referred to SVB. There would be however no need to obtain Commissioners' approval for imports made under different bills of entry, in a particular case, once the case has been registered with SVB. An Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) on 1% on the assessable value of goods was to be paid. If the questionnaire regarding relevant information was not completed within 30 days of receipt, the Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) payable increased from 1% to 5%.

Circular No. 5 of 2016 dated 09.02.2016

Taking into account various representations made by trade and industry in relation to the delays in finalisation of SVB investigations, continued uncertainty due to provisional assessment, increase in transaction costs due to extra duty deposits and burdensome procedure of renewal of SVB borders, the procedures were streamlined vide this Circular. The key points to be noted under this Circular are:

(i)

The SVB is to function under the supervisory control of the jurisdictional Chief Commissioner/Principal Commissioner.

(ii)

The Director General of Valuation (DGoV) shall support the Commissioners by issuing advisories on legal issues and guidance notes.

(iii)

The Extra Duty Deposit as a security was abolished. However, failure to provide documents and information within 60 days of requisition would attract 5% of the declared assessable value to be imposed by the Commissioner for a period not exceeding the next three months along with granting of 60 more days to provide the information.

(iv)

In case the information is not submitted within the extended period as well, the Commissioner in charge of SVB may consider the use of other provisions of the Customs Act for obtaining documents. Information from an importer for conducting investigations.

(v)

The SVB was to no longer issue an appealable order and instead, convey its investigative findings by way of an investigation report to the referring customs formation for finalizing the provisional assessments.

(vi)

A questionnaire was also introduced by the Department to be filled by the importer, to enable the jurisdictional officer to take a decision on whether a case needs to be referred to SVB for investigations.

(vii)

Three categories were exempted from SVB investigations – import of samples and prototypes from related sellers; imports from related sellers where duty chargeable (including additional duty of Customs, etc.) is unconditionally fully exempted or nil; any transaction where the value of imported goods is less than Rs.1 Lakh but cumulatively these transactions do not exceed Rs. 25 Lakhs in any financial year.

(viii)

Cases which may be considered for SVB investigations along with the procedure for considering reference to SVB; procedure for cases where reference to SVB was not required; procedure in SVB; finalization of assessments; instructions in relation to change in circumstances surrounding the sale were also provided.
