FACT: The appellants imported certain second-hand machines. The Customs authorities did not accept the invoice price on the plea that similar machines had been imported by the same assessee at a much higher price while the time gap between the two imports was not much. The goods were valued under Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules keeping in view appreciation of prices depreciation insurance, freight and landing charges. Collector (Appeals) upheld the order except that he allowed depreciation @ 10% as against 6-1/4% allowed by the lower authorities.

HELD: 1. Valuation--Invoice value may not be accepted for computing duty if comparable goods are purchased at substantially higher price. "The appellants explanation for increase in the price is that the demand for second hand machinery had gone up and the suppliers therefore raised the prices in case of latter import No evidence in support of this plea has been produced either before the lower authorities or before us. In the absence of any such evidence and the apparently large price differential in the prices of two sets of machines, the imports of which were made in the span of about nine months time, we held that the lower authorities were justified in not accepting low price as reflected in the invoice for the goods".

2. Valuation--Computation of value should preferable be under Rule 3 and 4 if comparable goods are available at different prices. "We would like to observe that in the instant case, the value of comparable goods was available and the correct rule that should have been applied by the lower authorities should have been Rule 3 of the Custom Valuation rules 1963 read with Rule 4 of the said rule. We find that the value of comparable goods imported by the appellants was acceptable to the authorities and as such there was no need for the officers to traverse beyond these rules to Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules."

3. Valuation--Assessee has no grievance if a criterion, less preferable than other available ones, is adopted if it does not put him to disadvantage. "In any case, we find that the appellants had not suffered any disadvantage on this account and probably the value fixed now in terms of the Appellate Collector's order is lower than what might have been fixed in case Rule 3 read with Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules 1963 had been resorted to. We, therefore, find no reason to accede the appellants plea for accepting the invoice value for purpose of assessment."

4. Assessable value includes landing charges. "The inclusion of landing charges in the assessable value is maintainable in law seeing that the expenditure incurred for landing would become an integral component of their intrinsic value and accordingly "the price at which such or like goods are for delivery at the time and place of importation"."

For doing that, the power of exemption conferred by section 9 of the A.P. Act has to be exercised."

In C.S.T. v. Indra Industries [2001] 248 ITR 338 (SC), a three-Judge Bench referred to the above case and purported to distinguish it as follows:

"The observations in para 18 of the judgment in Bengal Iron Corporation case can, at best, apply only when a case of estoppel against a statute is made out."

In Wilh Wilhelmsen v. CIT [1996] 87 Taxman 269/221 ITR 244 (SC), a two-Judge Bench, having referred to section 5(8) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, observed thus:

"The provision is clear. It requires no elaboration. It is, however, evident that the power so conferred on the Central Board of Revenue has to be exercised for the purposes of and within the four corners of the Act".

There is yet another important judgment in case of Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan [2003] 132 Taxman 373 / 263 ITR 706, in which their lordship observed,

"We do not think the circular in any way takes away or curtails the jurisdiction of the Assessing Officer to assess the income of the assessee before him. In our view, therefore, it is erroneous to say that the impugned Circular No. 789 dated April 13, 2000, is ultra vires the provisions of section 119 of the Act. In our judgment, the powers conferred upon the Central Board of Direct Taxes by sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 119 are wide enough to accommodate such a circular."

Simply in this case, it is not said that the circular can override the provision of law in any manner, instead it provide that the circular is according to the power enshrined under section 119 of the Act. But the observation of Supreme Court in case of the Collector of Central Excise v. Dhiren Chemical Industries [2002] 254 ITR 554 was very bold. In this case the Supreme Court, in a small judgment without explaining the precedence on the relevance and scope of circular, interpreting the phrase, "appropriate", observed:

"We need to make it clear that, regardless of the interpretation that we have placed on the said phrase, if there are circulars which have been issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs which place a different interpretation upon the said phrase, that interpretation will be binding upon the Revenue."

There is no discussion of the reasons and precedence on the subject of circular.

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for customs - Natural justice - cross-examination regarding relevant telex cannot be denied. Matter remanded for de novo adjudication. Additional evidence can be filed even though disallowed in appellate proceedings

FACT: The appellants had imported a consignment of 'Dielectric Heater Components of Heat Training Systems, and claimed its clearance under OGL Item No. 476, appendix 6, list 8, part I of the Import & Export Policy 1985-88. However the Addl. Collr. held that for ITC purposes, the goods were classifiable under Sl. No. 462(a) of appendix 3A. He also did not accept the invoice price and ordered enhancement of the assessable value from Rs. 5,15,696/- to Rs. 10,71,721.70 under section 14(1)(h) of the Customs Act. He confiscated the imported goods with an option to redeem on payment of fine of Rs. 10,00,000 and also imposed penalty of Rs. 1,00,000 under section 112(a) of Customs Act. In their appeal to the Tribunal, the appellants sought permission for filing certain additional evidence and a similar request was received from the Department. The appellants also stated that they were denied the opportunity of cross-examination of the two officials whose advice was taken into account and that they were not confronted with the telex relied upon for upward revision of the value which has figured only in the adjudication order.

HELD: Natural justice--principles violated since cross-examination regarding relevant telex was denied to the appellants. Matter remanded to the adjudication authorities. Fresh evidence can be filed (ratio of Supreme Court judgment in Kalra Glue Factory v. Sales Tax Tribunal). "The appellants had pleaded for the cross-examination of Shri Prabhat Kumar which was not granted. We are of the view that there was dental of principles of natural justice.......We ate of the view that telex is very relevant for valuation, and the appellant should have been confronted with the same, and an opportunity should also be given for rebuttal. ...we are of the view that the matter should be remanded. Since cross-examination was also denied, we are of the view that there was denial of principles of natural justice. ......we remand the matter to the adjudicating authority having jurisdiction and give an opportunity to the appellants to cross-examine them. Both the sides are at liberty to file any fresh evidence to substantiate their case in accordance with law. We further order that re adjudication will be done within three months from the receipt of this order."

2. Additional Evidence--The lower authority is free to decide the request of the appellants for admission of any additional evidence on merits as per law for the purpose of de-novo adjudication proceedings before him, even though it was disallowed in the appellate proceedings. "...I would like to observe that learned Brother while he has disallowed the admission of additional evidence......he has observed in the operative portion of the order that both the sides are at liberty to file any fresh evidence to substantiate their case in accordance with law. By way of clarification I would like to add that while we have disallowed the admission of the documents as above for the purpose of the appellate proceedings before us, the lower authority is free to decide the request of the appellants for admission of any additional evidence, as held by learned Brother, on merits as per law for the purpose of de novo adjudication proceedings before him."

HEADNOTE: Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1949 - Writ - Maintainability of - Alternative Remedy - Writ can be invoked a second time if earlier appeal was not disposed of on merits, but was withdrawn to enable parties to come to a settlement and when settlement is prima facie wrong and perverse and delay has caused irreparable damage, alternative remedy is not a bar to maintainability. Cus. Act: S. 14. Precedent--ratio of Supreme Court and Cegat decisions must be considered by the authorities. Act: S. 129D, Imports  Exports (Control) Act: S. 167(8)

FACT: The petitioner is an importer of various electronic components of T.V., V.C.R. electronic type-writers etc. In 1987 the petitioner imported two consignments of Printed Circuit Board Sub-Assembly, Remote Control and Miscellaneous Hardware. He also purchased V.C.R. parts from the recognised export houses on 'High seas sales basis'. The goods were duly assessed and some of them kept at the customs bonded warehouse. The customs authorities meanwhile raided the business premises of the petitioners, and charged the petitioners with under-invoicing, and importing complete VCRs in the name of name-lender firms. Various demands were raised in lieu of short levy, fines and penalties, and the petitioner paid under protest a total sum of Rs. 11,11,990.11 and got released the goods, being under pressure to resume production in his factory which was lying closed for want of materials.

HELD: Writ jurisdiction--Maintainability--There is no bar to invoking Writ Jurisdiction a second time on same issue, if the earlier appeal was not disposed of on merits, but was withdrawn to enable parties to come to a settlement. Where the settlement arrived at is prima facie wrong and perverse and delay has already caused irreparable damage to the petitioner, writ appeal is valid and maintainable. Alternative remedy is not a bar to maintainability in such a case. "There is no doubt in my mind that there was some understanding between the writ petitioner and the respondents regarding the manner and mode of assessment to be made. But for one reason or other, the respondents did not rise up to the expectation. The writ petition and the appeal arising out of such writ petition were withdrawn in the expectation that the respondents would judiciously load the value. ........The writ application was not dismissed on merits. It was allowed to be withdrawn to enable the parties to arrive at a settlement. .......As the settlement failed, which is demonstrated by the order of adjudication, the petitioner has challenged the validity of such order. .......Accordingly, it cannot be said that the petitioner cannot invoke the writ jurisdiction for the second time. ......In this case, Collector had adjudicated and passed an order which is highly prejudicial to the petitioner. If this order has to be challenged in the appropriate forum, the petitioner may not get the desired relief for long time to come. This aspect of the matter cannot be overlooked in considering whether the application is maintainable or not. ........On the facts and in the circumstances of this case, I am of the view that the order of adjudication is illegal and manifestly, arbitrary and unreasonable and delay would cause irreparable loss and prejudice to the petitioner. In the premises, the contention that the writ petition is not maintainable cannot be accepted."

Transaction value at the time and place of importation

Price should be at the time and place of importation.

Place of importation - Place of importation means the customs station, where the goods are brought for being cleared for home consumption or for being removed for deposit in a warehouse - rule 2(da) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2017 as amended on 26-9-2017.

Price should be for delivery at the place of importation - Value at the place of importation does not mean that only expenses till goods enter Indian Customs water should be included. Import is an integrated process which culminates when goods land on land-mass of India so that they can be introduced in stream of supplies to form part of mass of goods within the country. Thus, all expenses upto the destination port, including freight, transit insurance, unloading and handling charges are to be included.

In Essar Oil Ltd. v. CC 2004 (174) ELT 379 (CESTAT), it was held that landmass of India where unloading occurs (usually a wharf of jetty) is the place of importation and all expenses incurred for bringing goods there are includible. In addition, 1% 'landing charges' [for loading, unloading and handling charges for delivery at the port] are also includible in Assessable Value.

5.2-1 Price must be the sole consideration

Price should be sole consideration for sale. If there is other consideration, it should be added to the transaction value.

In Jindal Photo Films v. CC 2002(141) ELT 202 (CEGAT), it was held that license fee related to know-how embedded in machine has to be added to Assessable Value. In this case, the foreign supplier had not charged license fee but had stated that if semi-processed raw material is not purchased from the foreign supplier, flat annual license fee will be payable for seven years. It was thus obvious that price was not the sole consideration and hence the license fee, which was additional consideration, was addible.

Price to include value of intellectual property contained in it - A software cannot be valued on basis of price of CD. In Globe Entertainment v. CC 2005 (180) ELT 258 (CESTAT), it was held that value of video cassettes cannot be valued on basis of material cost plus recording charges. Value of intellectual property i.e. serial recorded in cassettes has also to be taken into consideration. It is not value of material but value of intellectual property which is recorded in the cassettes.

5.2-2 Price in case of high sea sale

Price relevant for customs valuation under section 14(1) is the price for delivery at time and place of importation.

High sea sale (HSS) means sale of goods by transfer of documents before clearance of goods from customs.

In case of high sea sale (HSS), price charged by importer to assessee would form the assessable value and not the invoice issued to the importer by foreign supplier. - National Wire v. CC 2000(122) ELT 810 (CEGAT) * Godavari Fertilizers v. CC (1996) 81 ELT 535 (CEGAT).

If the purchase is on high seas, the selling price will be naturally higher than the price at which the original buyer imported the goods. However, even if price is lower, the duty will be payable on price at which goods are sold on high seas basis to final importer. Original price at which original buyer purchased the goods cannot be basis for valuation - Excel Glasses Ltd. v. CC 2004 (166) ELT 496 (CESTAT) (In this case, price was lower due to one year delay in arrival of ship).

In Tata Power Co. Ltd. v. CC (2009) 240 ELT 742 (CESTAT), the sale was on high seas. The agreement provided that service charges for services like tender negotiations, participation in international bidding etc. were payable. Bank charges, facilitation fee, demurrage and survey fees were payable at fixed rates as per agreement. It was held that all these are includible as the charges were condition of sale of goods.

Only actual cost incurred by ultimate buyer is to be considered. Inclusion of 2% notional commission cannot be done after 2007 amendment - Indian Farmers Fertilisers Coop Ltd. v. PCC (2020) 373 ELT 530 (CESTAT).

12.5-10 Any value addition done to goods after place of removal is not to be considered for valuation.

Department has clarified that if any value addition is done by assessee by processing the goods after removal from factory, cost of such processing is not to be added in Assessable Value, if such process does not amount to 'manufacture' - CBE&C circular No. 138/08/2000-CX.4 dated 3.1.2001. In Rashtriya Ispat Nigam v. CCE 2005 (179) ELT 65 (CESTAT), assessee was clearing iron and steel products from factory to stock yards. While selling the goods from stock yard, these were cut and bent. Charges for cutting and bending were separately collected as 'surcharge'. It was held that this 'surcharge' is not to be added for valuation, as goods removed from factory and those sold from depot are not 'such goods'. Goods sold from stockyard were not 'same' as those cleared from factory.

In CCE v. Akay Cosmetics 2005 (182) ELT 294 (SC 3 member bench), it was observed, 'Value as defined u/s 4(4)(d) [as existing prior to 30-6-2000], was co-related to price at the factory gate. Therefore, costs (expenses) for factors upto the stage of 'price' at the factory gate alone could be taken into account. When the 'value' for the purposes of section 4 was the price at factory gate, the costs which are includible upto that stage alone are includible. Cost is the function of time and place u/s 4(4)(d). In this case, it was held that cost of secondary packing done after removal of goods from factory is not includible. It was held that since price at factory gate is available, deduction for expenses in respect of freight, insurance and handling charges is not allowable [If the factory gate price was available, where was the question of deduction of freight, insurance and handling? The issue is not clear from the judgment] [decision under old section 4 but principle is applicable to new section 4 also].

Transit Insurance

12.5-11 The principle applicable to freight should hold good for insurance charges also, as insurance expenses are really part of the transport charges. - - CBE&C, vide its circular No. 643/34/2002-CX dated 1-7-2002 has confirmed that transit insurance will be allowed as deduction if shown separately in invoice. In Escorts JCB Ltd. v. CCE 2002 AIR SCW 4372 = 53 RLT 1 = 146 ELT 31 (SC), it was held that as per section 39 of Sale of Goods Act, delivery of goods to carrier is prima facie delivery of goods to buyer. Ownership in the property may not have relevance in so far as insurance of goods sold during the transit is concerned. It is not necessary that insurance of the goods and ownership of goods must always go together.

In Nirlon Ltd. v. CCE 2005 (190) ELT 334 (CESTAT), it was held that transit insurance is allowable as deduction. - same view in Yamuna Motors v. CCE (2014) 301 ELT 524 (CESTAT) * CCE v. Jai Mata Glass Ltd. (2013) 295 ELT 737 (CESTAT).

In Rama Vision Ltd. v. CCE (2005) 185 ELT 296 (CESTAT), it was held that even if there is excess collection towards insurance charges, the difference is not includible in assessable value of goods - relying on Baroda Electric Meters Ltd. v. CCE 1997 (94) ELT 13 (SC 3 member) - same view in LML Ltd. v. CCE (2007) 211 ELT 440 (CESTAT).

In Gujarat Borosil v. CCE (2010) 253 ELT 610 (CESTAT), price of goods (glass bottles) were ex-works. If customer wanted delivery, it was given by charging 7%. Goods were packed in special packing and glasses broken during transit were replaced. It was held that charges for transit insurance/special packing are not includible in assessable value.

Self insurance charges addible - In Gujarat Borosil v. CCE (2007) 217 ELT 367 (CESTAT), assessee was collecting 7% amount was 'insurance charges'. Actual insurance premium paid was much less. I am afraid in the face of apparent deficiencies annexed to that circular which are already discussed and which are highlighted by the learned Single Judge Bharucha J. in the other matter this provision hardly goes to the rescue of the Department because the generalised provision contained in Section 157 cannot be so spaciously extended so as to invest an authority and power in the Board even to suddenly change the working hours and that too by a simple circular. FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand offset press against a letter of credit for Rs. 1,99,867.00 opened on 28.2.1983 and valid for negotiation up to 30.8.1983, subsequently extended up to 31.12.1983. The appellants claimed clearance of the machine under OGL in terms of para 7 of Appendix 10 of the Import Policy 1982-83. However, the Customs held that the goods could not be allowed clearance as changes of fundamental nature had been made in the letter of credit. The Collector ordered confiscation of the machine with an option to redeem it on payment of Rs. 65,000/-. He also ordered enhancement of its value to Rs. 2,57,162/- on the basis of contemporaneous import of identical machine of 1973 model.

HELD: ITC--OGL--Appendix 10 of Policy AM 1982-83--the letter of credit established on 28.2.1983, continued to be valid on the date of shipment--the import is covered by OGL (ratio of Appellate Tribunal decision in Tara Art Printers, New Delhi v. CC, Bombay). ".........on reference to para (7) of Appendix 10 of 1982-83 Import Policy, we find that it was not clearly spelled out that shipment after 31.3.1983 was permissible only in cases where delay in shipment was on account of longer manufacturing schedule. In our view, if the delivery period of the goods was extended beyond 31.3.1983 due to any reason they could be shipped on or before 31.12.1983 provided the contract entered into on or before 28.2.1983 continued to be in force on the date of shipment. In this case in the first instance the shipment was delayed on account of the country of origin having been erroneously shown in the Letter of Credit as West Germany instead of Sweden necessitating the extension of the Letter of Credit up to 30.8.1983. However, the shipment was delayed further since the intimation regarding the extension of the Letter of Credit was not received by the supplier. Thereafter, the Letter of Credit was amended again on 21.10.1983 to extend its validity up to 31.12.1983. Since the goods were shipped before 31.12.1983 against the Letter of Credit which was established on 28.2.1983 and continued to be valid on the date of shipment, we are of the view that they were covered by the OGL in terms of 1982-83 Import Policy."

"in fact, the power of remand by the Commissioner (Appeals) has been taken away by amending Section 35A with effect from 11.5.2001 under the Finance Bill, 2001. Under the Notes to clause 122 of the said Bill it is stated that clause 122 seeks to amend Section 35A so as to withdraw the power of the Commissioner (A) to remand matters back to the adjudicating authority for fresh consideration." Pursuant to the above judgement, board vide instructions (F. No. 275/34/2006-CX.8A) dated 18.02.2010 directed that Commissioner (Appeals) should follow the said Hon'ble Apex Court judgement strictly and in terms of the board's instruction dated 25.07.2008, Commissioner (Appeals) should resort to the method of further enquiry in such cases where it may be necessary before passing the order as prescribed under appeal procedure. Although, there has hardly been any impact on the intended appellate authorities across the country resulting into mounting of cases where Commissioners (Appeals) referred the matter back to original authority without giving effect to the aforesaid amendment. There may be another spell of debate or discussion on the position of binding nature of departmental circulars/instructions on the Commissioner (Appeals). However, it is a well settled law that board's instructions are binding on the field formation but it seems that departmental circulars may not be binding on the assessee, quasi-judicial authorities [including the Commissioner (Appeals)] and the courts.

Accordingly, the saga of confusion with respect to the power of remand of the Commissioner (Appeals) under the Customs Act, has been in continuation till now. There are many such cases where the Commissioner (Appeals) has referred the matters back to the original adjudicating authority. One of the aforesaid cases, in the matter of Rajesh Khanna v. Commissioner of Custom 2010 (262) E.L.T. 399 (Tri. - Kolkata), CESTAT, Eastern Bench, Kolkata, held that there was no infirmity in remand order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and appellant contention that the Commissioner (Appeals) has no power in view of the amended section 128A(3) of Customs Act, was rejected. The relevant part of the judgment is extracted here;

"I find that in the present case the adjudicating authority imposed the penalty of Rs. 5,000/- on the appellant as the appellant issued invoices in respect of the confiscated goods having different descriptions of the goods and value. The Commissioner (Appeals) simply sent back the matter to the adjudicating authority to look into the issue for imposition of penalty on the appellant afresh. In these circumstances I find no infirmity in the impugned order. The appeal is dismissed."

Impact on the trade:

It is pertinent to observe from the above discussion that there is a catch-22 situation in the trade as well as in appellate authorities with respect to such issue of power of remand. Now, with this amendment, Commissioner (Appeals) is conferred with the clear power of remand in certain prescribed matters such as inter alia,where an order or decision has been passed without following the principles of natural justice. This particular clause will provide a huge breathing space to the Commissioner (Appeals) and considering the wide scope of interpretational reach of the phrase 'natural justice', same will have a tangible impact on overall litigation management of the country.

Hon'ble Finance Minister is his budget speech has said that certain changes to the Customs Act, 1962 are proposed to smoothen dispute resolution processes and to reduce litigation but it is not understandable that how the instant amendment in section 128A (3) of the customs act, would serve such intended purpose of the government to reduce litigation in the days to come. The answer must be lies in the lap of future.

Conclusion

It is hoped that the appellate authorities will act with utmost maturity and discipline in dealing with the said sub-section 128A(3) of the customs act in the coming days, keeping in mind the larger interest of the nation, since consistency and discipline are of far greater importance than winning or losing proceedings in any court of law.

The assessee has contended that as the similar claims had been decided in favour of the banks for the assessment years 1991-92 to 1993-94 by Special Bench of the Tribunal, which had not been challenged by the department, the issue had attained finality and could not be disturbed in the subsequent years. [Para 12]

The above contention of the assessee-bank is not impressive. Merely because the orders of the Special Bench of the Tribunal were not assailed in appeal by the department itself, this would not take away the right of the revenue to question the correctness of the orders of assessment, particularly when a question of law is involved. There is no doubt that the earlier order of the Commissioner (Appeals) had merged into the judgment of the Special Bench of the Tribunal and attained finality for that relevant year. Equally, it is true that though the Full Bench of the Kerala High Court specifically overruled the Division Bench judgment of that very Court in the case of South Indian Bank Ltd. The questions raised in the instant appeal go to the very root of the matter and are questions of law in relation to interpretation of sections 36(1)(vii ) and 36(1)(viia) read with section 36(2). Thus, the findings recorded in the earlier assessment years 1991-92 to 1993-94 would not be binding on the department for subsequent years as well. [Para 13]

Sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) provide for such deductions, which are to be permitted, in accordance with the language of these provisions. A bare reading of these provisions show that sections 36(1)(vii) and 36(1)(viia) are separate items of deduction. These are independent provisions and, therefore, cannot be intermingled or read into each other. It is a settled canon of interpretation of fiscal statutes that they need to be construed strictly and on their plain reading. [Para 16]

The provisions of section 36(1)(vii ) would come into play in the grant of deductions, subject to the limitation contained in section 36(2). Any bad debt or part thereof, which is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts of the assessee for the previous year, is the deduction which the assessee would be entitled to get, provided he satisfies the requirements of section 36(2). Allowing of deduction of bad debts is controlled by the provisions of section 36(2). The argument advanced by the revenue is that it would amount to allowing a double deduction if the provisions of sections 36(1)(vii ) and 36(1)(viia) are permitted to operate independently. There is no doubt that a statute is normally not construed to provide for a double benefit unless it is specifically so stipulated or is clear from the scheme of the Act. As far as the question of double benefit is concerned, the legislature in its wisdom introduced section 36(2)(v ) by the Finance Act, 1985 with effect from 01.04.1985. Section 36(2)(v) concerns itself as a check for claim of any double deduction and has to be read in conjunction with section 36(1)(viia ). It requires the assessee to debit the amount of such debt or part thereof in the previous year to the provision made for that purpose. [Para 17]

Circulars can be issued by the Board to explain or tone down the rigours of law and to ensure fair enforcement of its provisions. These circulars have the force of law and are binding on the income tax authorities, though they cannot be enforced adversely against the assessee. Normally, these circulars cannot be ignored. A circular may not override or detract from the provisions of the Act but it can seek to mitigate the rigour of a particular provision for the benefit of the assessee in certain specified circumstances. So long as the circular is in force, it aids the uniform and proper administration and application of the provisions of the Act. [Para 18]

For recovery of dues payable to the revenue, proceedings can be initiated thirty days after filing of the appeal or any time thereafter and the same cannot be found fault with. But the action of the department in resorting to coercive recovery proceedings at an early date without taking into consideration the pendency of the stay/waiver application before the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal would necessarily work hardship to the assessees. The right granted under the statute cannot be whittled down by fixing a time limit in an instruction even though the Appellate Authority has not taken up the matter at the stage of waiver of pre-deposit or for stay. The right provided under a statute should not be denied only on the basis of the impugned circular/instruction. [Para 31]

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of goods for Customs - Transactional value not acceptable for second-hand goods in perfect condition. Reasonable assessment does not call for interference - Undervaluation-Misdeclaration not being deliberate, confiscation and penalty unwarranted -111(d), 111(m)

FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand 1976 model, 4 colour, off-set printing machine and a second-hand 1983 model paper folding machine, both of German make, from the U.K. The declared value of these machines was £ 49,000 and £ 3000.00 respectively. Certificates from Chartered Engineers in support of the transactional value were furnished. However, since the current prices of the machines indicated in the certificates were much lower than the current price indicated by the local agents of the manufacturers of these machines and also because the prices quoted for the year of manufacture were found to be wrong, the Asstt. Collector rejected the certificates. There was a difference of Rs. 10,03,400 between the declared value and the assessable value arrived at by the Department. Alleging deliberate undervaluation with an intention to evade duty, the Asstt. Collector of Customs held both the machines liable to confiscation under section 111(m) of the Customs Act, 1962. The off-set printing machine was held to be liable to confiscation under section 111(d) as well as it was older than 7 years, which was in violation of the provisions of AM 1988-91 Import Policy. Aggrieved by the aforementioned order, the appellants have come in appeal.

HELD: Valuation-Undervaluation established, as machines were in perfect condition, with an expected residual life of 10-12 years, and the depreciation allowed by the adjudicating authority was reasonable. Transactional value not acceptable. "Market of second-hand goods also fluctuates with the market of new goods. If therefore, the certificates issued by the Chartered Engineers have given the prices of new goods at a lower level naturally their estimation of the prices of second-hand goods is also likely to be affected. To that extent the department was right in not placing reliance on the Chartered Engineers' certificates. ........so far as the offset printing machine is concerned, that it has been certified that the machine was found to be in perfect working condition and it had been well maintained and serviced and that no major repairs/reconditioning were necessary. Expected residual life of the machine is estimated at 10 to 12 years. The undisputed service the machine has already completed is about 14 years i.e. from 1976. It is also certified in the said certificate that the machine utilises the current generation of technology and therefore, compares with the latest machinery available in the international market. ........the depreciation of 70% allowed by the adjudicating authority on the price of the new goods in the year of its manufacture, cannot be said to be unreasonable at all. ........Similar comments and assessment of the said Chartered Engineers have been made in respect of the second-hand machine i.e. paper folding machine. .......for a total span of life of 17 to 19 years of the machine, the residual life of 10 to 12 years and other condition being perfect and good the depreciation of 65% allowed by the adjudicating authority cannot on the same reasons be considered unjust. ......We are, therefore, of the view that there has been undervaluation of the machines to the extent upheld in the adjudication order."

2. Freight Insurance—Actual charges being known, with no apparent reason to discard the same, notional charges not to be taken into account. "........the goods have been imported from U.K.. which is farther from India than Germany i.e. freight and insurance charges from Germany are, therefore, likely to be less than those from U.K. Accordingly in the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, there is no reason as to why the actual freight and insurance charges incurred by the appellants from U.K. should not be taken into account rather than the notional freight and insurance charges from Germany to U.K. If, however, the department can find the actual freight and insurance charges liable to be incurred from Germany to India in respect of such machine, they may take them into account. Benefit in respect of valuation of the goods on account of freight and insurance in the light of the above observations may, therefore, be extended to the appellants.

HEADNOTE: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 - Valuation of Goods for Customs - ITC - OGL - Import permissible if firm contract covered by period of currency of OGL - Contract revised after OGL withdrawn is not valid - Valuation - Undervaluation charge cannot hold without evidence and specially when price declared is fair - Cus. Act: section 14

FACT: The appellants imported a second-hand offset printing machine and claimed clearance under OGL (Import Policy 1982-83), declaring an assessable value of Rs. 4,96,306. The goods arrived during import policy period 1983-84 when they ceased to be covered by OGL. The appellants claimed benefit of condition 7 of Appx. 10 of Policy Book for AM 1982-83, according to which, if an importer had entered into a firm contract before 28.2.1983 but the goods could not be shipped before 31.3.1983 on account of the longer delivery period involved, the shipment may be allowed up to 31.3.1984. The Additional Collector of Customs denied them this benefit on the ground that although the original contract was dated 14.10.1982 and a letter of credit was opened on 9.12.1982, there had been a change of contract subsequently reducing the price of the machine and the latter contract, which is a firm contract, was entered into only in the 1983-84 policy period when the machine was withdrawn from the OGL List, and therefore the import was unauthorised. He confiscated the machine, fixed its value at Rs. 5,62,984 on the basis of contemporary import of such a machine by some other party, and imposed a fine of Rs. 1,25,000 in lieu of confiscation.

HELD: The appellants are not entitled to the benefit of condition 7, Appx. 10 of Import Policy 1982-83 as the machine was not imported under the original contract dated 14.10.1982, but under a subsequent contract reducing the price of the machine, and this contract is to be treated as a "firm contract". The import is therefore unauthorised as it was effected during 1983-84 policy period when the subject goods were not covered by OGL. "Here, though one contract was entered into before 28.2.1983, the subject import is not the one made pursuant to that contract but was under a new contract entered into somewhere in January-February 1984 as is evident from the letter dated 3.2.1984 from the supplier as also by issuance of afresh invoice dated 29.3.1984. ...Even assuming that because the same machine is brought and the same is in relation to the contract entered into on 14.10.1982, then also the contract entered into at that time could not be taken as a firm contract, as subsequently, there has been an alteration in the most essential ingredient in a contract of sale, namely the purchase price and if that could be done, the contract initially entered into could not be taken as a firm contract. Here however is a clear case of substitution of the original contract by a new contract of purchase at the reduced price."

2. Valuation--Enhancement of assessable value not sustainable in the absence of clear data before the department and when there is evidence on record to show that the declared value is fair and reasonable. "With no clear date available before the department that the value as assessed is not proper, and when the other evidence on record indicates the value to be fair and reasonable the finding of the adjudicating authority that the subject goods have been under-valued, cannot be endorsed and as such, the said portion of the order of the authority below cannot be sustained and has to be set aside."

3. Redemption fine reduced to Rs. 1,00,000/-. "The appellants are the actual users of the machine, and they had intended and attempted to bring the same during the policy period 1982-83 but could not do so for the reasons given. In that view of the matter, and with the allegations of undervaluation as not proved, there appears some scope of showing some leniency in relation to quantum of redemption fine. In that view of the matter the fine in lieu of confiscation is reduced to Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One lac only)."

V S DATEY

Background

Corruption in any department of Government is nothing new. Customs department is no exception [Of course this does not mean that there is no corruption in private sector, but there public at large is not the sufferer]. Reference to corruption in customs department are found even in Kautilya's writings. Let us be honest and say that people have accepted corruption as way of life. It is treated as 'lubricant' in doing business.

However, presently, in customs, it is not only a 'lubricant' but is tending towards 'rape'. This really hurts common importers and exporters. [Uncommon businessmen have their own way of doing things. Let us not count them].

One such tool of harassment in customs is 'Special Valuation Branch' (SVB). Luckily, this has been realized by CBE&C and SVB has been cut to size. The revised provisions relating to SVB as contained in CBE&C Circular No. 5 /2016 -Cus dated 9-2-2016 are discussed in the Article.

Purpose of SVB is to examine related party transactions

Related party transactions are almost always treated with suspicion in all tax laws including income tax, excise and customs.

The 'Special Valuation Branch' (SVB) was created as an institution in customs in 1998, specializing in investigation of transactions involving special relationships between buyer - seller or those involving other special circumstances surrounding the sale of imported goods. Both of these have a bearing on the assessable value.

Detailed instructions were issued vide Circular Nos. 1/1998-Cus dated 1-1-1998 and 11/2001-Cus dated 23-2-2001 in respect of SVB. This resulted in continued uncertainty due to provisional assessments, increase in transaction costs and burdensome procedure of renewal of SVB orders [These are not my words. These are words of CBE&C itself].

In the meanwhile, WCO (World Customs Organisation) has issued Guide to Customs Valuation and Transfer Pricing in June 2015. Hence, provisions relating to SVB have been revamped vide CBE&C Circular No. 5 /2016 -Cus dated 9-2-2016.

SVB will be under supervisory control of jurisdictional customs officers

Since 1-1-2013, functional control over SVBs was with the Director General of Valuation (DGOV). Now, SVB will be under supervisory control of jurisdictional Chief Commissioner/Principal Commissioner/Commissioner.

DGoV shall now only support the SVBs by issuing advisories on legal issues & guidance notes. DGoV shall also continue to qualitatively monitor investigation orders issued by SVBs.

The system of renewal of SVB orders has been discontinued with immediate effect.

Jurisdiction of SVB is where corporate office of importer is situated

The SVBs are presently functioning at the Customs Houses at Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata, Delhi and Mumbai. Jurisdiction of the SVBs will be based upon the principle of location of the corporate office of the importer. As andwhen imports requiring investigation by SVBs are noticed at any customs formation, the concerned Commissionerate shall transfer all relevant records to the jurisdictional SVB for investigations. However, where the import takes place through CHs of Mumbai / Delhi / Chennai / Kolkata / Bangalore, the importer will be free to select the SVB of the Customs House of import or the Customs House most proximate to the corporate office, as convenient to him.

Abolition of Extra Duty Deposit of 1%

At present, during investigation by SVB, 'Extra Duty Deposit' (EDD) @ 1% of declared assessable value is obtained from the importer for a period of 4 months during which time he is required to submit required documents and information to the SVB. However, in practice, the 1% EDD continues till completion of investigation. Obtaining refund is very cumbersome.

Hence, now, in case of cases referred to SVB, the assessment will be provisional on basis of Provisional Duty (PD) bond, but EDD will not be required.

However, if the importer fails to provide documents and information required for SVB inquiries, within 60 days of such requisition, security deposit at a rate of 5% of the declared assessable value shall be imposed by the Commissioner for a period not exceeding the next three months. Simultaneously, the importer shall be granted a further period of 60 days to comply with the requisition for information & documents. If the importer fails to submit documents within this extended period, the Commissioner in charge of SVB may consider the use of other provisions of the Customs Act for obtaining documents / information from an importer for conducting investigations.

In no case shall the imposition of Security Deposit exceed the period of three months specified above.

HEADNOTE: Rule 8 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 - Computed value - ITC Policy 85-88 - Project export--Valuation--assessment without notice to party is violation of principles of Natural Justice--Remanded. Customs Valuation Rules: Rule 8

FACT: The appellants imported from Iraq three lots of 8-10 year old used machinery under ITC Policy 85-88, under the heading 'Project Export'. They declared value of these machinery on the basis of assessment by an independent Chartered Engineer from Iraq. The Asstt. Collr. rejected the certificate of valuation in respect of the third lot and assessed FOB value by allowing the usual 3 years depreciation from the estimated CIF value of new machinery. Hence the appeal.

HELD: Natural Justice:--Enhancement of assessable value to the prejudice of the appellants, without issuing a show cause notice to them is against the principles of natural justice and cannot be upheld. "While enhancing the assessable value to the prejudice of the appellants, by rejecting the declared price of the equipment and machinery which was followed in respect of previous imports, and the contract/agreement for freight and insurance, the Assistant Collector ought to have issued a show cause notice asking them why the declared price, freight & insurance ought not to be accepted. An illegible "Query memo" and reply thereto cannot be treated as a substitute to the "show cause notice" and personal hearing......The order of the Assistant Collector is in violation of principle of natural justice and is liable to be set aside."

Circular is in nature of administrative instruction

A plain perusal of impugned Circular would unequivocally demonstrate that it is in the form of administrative instructions issued by the Central Board of Excise and Customs, New Delhi obligating the concerned authorities to initiate recovery proceedings against the confirmed demands in the eventualities narrated therein fixing periods therefor.

Broadly, three situations have been contemplated -

(1)

where no appeal has been filed against a confirmatory order in original;

(2)

where an appeal has been filed without stay application against a confirmatory order in original; and

(3)

where an appeal has been filed with a stay application against such order.

The assessees were distressed and aggrieved only against third category of the cases where impugned Circular had provided for recovery after expiry of prescribed period irrespective of disposal of stay applications. [Para 9]

Assessee cannot be penalized without his fault

The scheme of the Act not only confers a statutory right on the assessee and concerned revenue authorities, as the case may be, to prefer an appeal before the different fora within the time prescribed, which is extendable to the extent as legislatively intended, but also equips the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal to dispense with the deposit of the duty demanded or penalty levied pending disposal of such appeal on merits. Second proviso to section 35F of the Act, however, obligates the Commissioner (Appeals) to decide such application within 30 days from the date of its filing. [Para 11]

Thus, once appeals are filed and more importantly along therewith applications for dispensing with the deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied are submitted, it is incumbent on the appellate forums Commissioner (Appeals) or Tribunal, as the case may be, to entertain the same as expeditiously as possible and pass orders thereon. [Para 12]

Such a course, as is apparent from the legislatively designed scheme of the Act, is a statutory mandate and unless in a given fact situation, the assessee, in particular, is liable for the delay in this regard, he ought not to be penalized either for the failure of the Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal, as the case may be, to entertain and dispose of either the appeal or the interim request for dispensing with the deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied. [Para 11]

Circular had no legal sanction/backing

Though reference has been made to section 37(2)(ib) of the Act to salvage the impugned circular, the same being apparently not in exercise of the powers conferred by the Rules, it assuredly has no sanction thereof.

A plain perusal of section 37B of the Act does not even seemingly permit issuance of the impugned circular for the purpose conveyed by it.

Rule 31 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002 also does not validate the impugned circular as the same only confers powers on the Board or the Chief Commissioner or the Commissioner to issue written instructions providing for any incidental or supplemental matters consistent with the provisions of the Act and the Rules. [Para 13]

Circular was aimed at defeating right of appeal provided under Act, which can only be conditioned by Act itself

In the teeth of the framework of the Act outlined under Chapter VIA of the Act, the impugned circular is conspicuously dissentient thereto qua the eventualities where appeals with applications for interim relief by way of dispensation of deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied are filed but pending without any decision whatsoever sans any default on the part of the assessee and for that matter, the appellants.

Any view to the contrary would be repugnant to the statutory comprehensions and the underlying intendment of the Act providing the statutory remedies against the orders demanding duty and penalty as contemplated therein.

The right of appeal being statutory in nature, the incidental provision for exemption, in deserving cases, by way of interim relief, from making the otherwise mandatory deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied, can by no means be trivialized or annihilated by any administrative ukase. Such a conferment can permissibly be circumscribed only by and to the extent ordained by the statute. The extinction of such a statutorily conferred right by any administrative fiat without the sanction of the enactment endowing the same is impermissible. The remedy by way of appeal and interim absolution from the requirement of deposit of duty demanded or penalty levied being a legislative prescript, denial thereof by the ipse dixit of an authority even statutory de hors legal ratification would be unsustainable. In absence of any enabling power thererfor, express or implicit, by no means, can such an authority sans any valid empowerment vide instructions of administrative nature supplant statutory provisions of obverse over tones and thus, render the same otiose. [Para 13]

The ITAT does not agree with the revenue, because, in the assessee's case under consideration, the addition was made by the Assessing Officer, based on the information received from the state police department and not on the basis of enforcement agencies such as CBI/ED/DRI/SFIO/Directorate General of GST Intelligences (DGGI), which is mentioned in the modified said Circular No. No. 3/2018 (supra). The claim of the revenue, to recall the order of the Tribunal, and to hear on merit, is misconceived. As per Circular No. 967/01/ 2013, dated 1.1.2013, the recovery proceedings shall be initiated against a confirmed demand in the following order: As per the Circular, a confirmed demand remains an order in operation till it is stayed. Reliance on the Supreme Court decision

3. The Circular draws reference to the decision of the Apex Court in the case of Collector of Customs, Bombay v. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The Apex Court observed that "As is well known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a stay or suspension of the Order appealed against". It should be noted that this decision of the Apex Court was somewhat in a different context and was issued when the service tax was not even in force. In fact, the decision was passed by the Apex Court in favour of the assessee.

The appeal before the Apex Court was preferred by the Collector of Customs against the judgment of the Delhi Tribunal. The assessee, Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., imported machinery and classified as a 'Bevel Gear Generator'. The Customs authorities raised an objection and classified the machinery as 'Bevel Gear Planer', thereby confiscating the machinery.

The assessee was given an option to pay a redemption fine of Rs. 70,000/- and penalty of Rs. 10,000/- and clear the goods. Assessee filed an appeal before the Tribunal. The appeal was allowed by the Tribunal which agreed with the classification claimed by the assessee. The counsel for the assessee requested that the customs authorities may be directed to issue a detention certificate for the entire period during which the goods were detained till the date of issuance of the detention certificate.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal of the assessee by virtue of which the respondent was entitled to clear the machinery without payment of any duty. But the respondent required a detention certificate to clear the machinery. Evidently, in view of this problem, the Apex Court made the following interim order:

"Having heard Ld. Counsel for the Collector of Customs, Bombay and M/s. Krishna Sales (P) Ltd., we direct that the application made by the latter for a detention certificate should not be rejected on the ground that the Appeal is pending in this Court against the Order of the Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi."

However,when the assessee applied for issuance of a detention certificate, no such certificate was issued. The assessee submitted that the action of the authorities is relatable to and influenced by the public notice issued by the Collector of Customs, Bombay on July 25, 1985. So far as the detention certificate for a period exceeding six months is concerned, it can be issued only with the approval of and under the signature of the Collector. Para 4 of the public notice deals with issue of detention certificates to the parties succeeding in appeals and read as follows:

"Detention Certificate, as a rule, will be issued by the concerned competent Customs Authority to the Appellants succeeding in Appeals on receipt of the copies of such Orders which the latter making formal application for issue of Detention Certificates. However, in cases where the Customs House decides to go in second Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, the issue of Detention Certificate will be considered only after such second appeal is finally disposed of in favour of the parties."

The Apex Court held as follows:

"6. According to the above mentioned para 4, the goods will not be released even where the party succeeds in cases where the Customs Authorities decide to go in Appeal before the Tribunal or the Supreme Court. They will consider the issuance of such certificate only after the decision of the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. The Counsel for the assessee characterised the direction as arbitrary and contrary to law. We see the force in his submission. If the authorities are of the opinion that the goods ought not to be released pending the Appeal, the straight forward course for them is to obtain an Order of Stay or other appropriate direction from the Tribunal or the Supreme Court, as the case may be. Without obtaining such an Order they cannot refuse to implement the Order under Appeal. As is well-known, mere filing of an Appeal does not operate as a Stay or suspension of the Order appealed against. Moreover, such detention is likely to create several complications relating to the demurrage charges besides the possible deterioration of the machinery and goods. We hope and trust that the Collector of Custom Bombay shall appropriately revise the said public notice in the light of the observations made herein. If he does not do so, there is a likelihood of the Customs Authorities being themselves made liable for demurrage charges in appropriate cases.

5.5-9 Cost of Transport upto port should be added

Cost of transport, loading, unloading and handling charges as associated with the delivery of imported goods to the place of importation is to be added in 'Assessable Value'. [Rule 10(2)(a) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 as amended w.e.f. 26-9-2017]

Till 26-9-2017, the words were only 'cost of transportation'. The words in rule 10(2)(b) covered loading, uploading and handling charges associated with the delivery of the imported goods at the place of importation [This covered landing charges at the place of import].

Now, clause (a) covers loading, unloading and handling charge at the load port (i.e. from where goods were exported] are includible in the customs value. Landing charges at the port of import are not includible - para 4.2 of MF(DR) circular No. 39/2017-Cus dated 26-9-2017.

In other words, CIF value is the basis for valuation. If the goods are imported by air, the air freight will be very high. Hence, in case air freight is higher than 20% of FOB price of goods, only 20% of FOB price will be added for Customs Valuation purposes.

If cost of transport is not ascertainable, it will be taken as 20% of FOB value of goods. However, cost of transport within India is not to be considered.

6.2-6 Duel price in case of service parts and OE

It is standard universal practice to charge lower price when the component is supplied as OE (i.e. Original Equipment) part for manufacture of machine/equipment/vehicle to a co-manufacturer and charge higher price when same component is supplied as service part i.e. spare part. [The difference can be as high as two to five times].

CBI&C has confirmed, vide its circular No. MFCA(DR) No. 82-2002-Cus.V dated 3-12-2002, that such duel pricing is acceptable and both can be treated as 'transaction value' if other requirements of section 14 are fulfilled. Thus, price of OE component should be inclusive of factory cost, factory overheads, administration and commercial overheads and reasonable profit margin of original manufacturer. However, related party transactions should be closely looked into and aspect of 'transfer pricing' and 'tie-in sales' should be seen.

6.2-7 Related person under Customs Valuations Provisions

Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 define that persons shall be deemed to be 'related' only if one of the conditions is satisfied [same definition and same rule number prior to 10-10-2007]:

they are officers or directors of one other's businesses [rule 2(2)(i)]

they are legally recognised partners in business [rule 2(2)(ii)]

they are employer and employee [rule 2(2)(iii)]

Any person directly or indirectly owns, controls or holds 5% or more of shares of both of them [rule 2(2)(iv)]

one of them controls other directly or indirectly [rule 2(2)(v)]

both of them are controlled - directly or indirectly - by third person [rule 2(2)(vi)]

together they control a third person - directly or indirectly [rule 2(2)(vii)]

they are members of same family [rule 2(2)(viii)]. (what is "family" is not defined).

Person includes legal person i.e. Company, partnership firm, trust etc. [Explanation I to Rule 2(2)].

If a person is sole agent or sole distributor or sole concessionaire of other, he will be deemed to be 'related', if he falls within the criteria of rule 2(2) [Explanation II to Rule 2(2)]. Thus, sole selling agent or sole distributor or sole concessionaire will be 'related person' only if he falls within the criteria as specified in rule 2(2). A sole selling agent or sole distributor or sole concessionaire is not automatically deemed as 'related person' in all the cases.

Interpretative Note to rule 2 clarify that for purpose of rule 2(2)(v), one person is deemed to control other if he is legally or operationally in a position to exercise restraint or direction over the other. Thus, control need not be only legal - even operational control is enough.

Basis on which Circular was issued was arbitrary - Condition of recovery pending stay application read down - Recovery only if delay in disposition is due to fault of assessee : The Circular was purportedly issued in terms of judgment in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The said judgment lays down that mere filing of an appeal does not operate as stay or suspension of the order appealed against. But the Board over-looked the fact that the assessee is not seeking stay only on account of filing of an appeal, but for the reason that the assessee has sought dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied and has a right to demand decision on such application, the right which is created by the statute. Therefore, the very basis of the Circular is untenable, misconceived, wholly illegal and arbitrary. Therefore, the condition of recovery, if no stay is granted within 30 days, is illegal, arbitrary, unjustified and consequently set aside. [Para 44]

Right of consideration in appeal and on an application for waiver of pre-deposit, is a right conferred by the statute and such right cannot be defeated on the basis of Circular, which contemplates that the recovery can be effected, is stay is not granted within 30 days. Therefore, such condition in the Circular is not legal and is therefore set aside with the observation that till such time, the application for waiver of pre-deposit is decided in an appeal filed in terms of the statute, the revenue shall not proceed to recover the same provided that the assessee does not delay the hearing of the appeal directly or indirectly. In the event, the assessee is delaying the decision, the revenue shall be at liberty to move an application before the Commissioner (Appeals) to take the application for waiver of pre-deposit and seek orders thereon in accordance with law. If such an application is filed by the revenue, the Commissioner (Appeals) shall decide the same expeditiously. [Para 46]

Thus, direction to recover the duty demanded and penalty levied, if the stay was not granted within 30 days, contravenes the right of consideration of appeal and of an application for waiver of pre-deposit conferred under section 35F of the Act and is illegal. Such direction to the Administrative Officers to recover the amount pending consideration of application of waiver of pre-deposit is not justified and, thus, not enforceable in law. [Para 47]

Time-limit of 180 days in stay matters before Tribunal is not mandatory - Vacation of stay will take place only if Revenue claims before Tribunal that delay was attributable to assessee :

As per second proviso to section 35C(2A), if an order of stay is made in any proceedings relating to an appeal filed under sub-section (1) of section 35B, the Appellate Tribunal shall dispose of the appeal within a period of 180 days from the date of such order. The further proviso is if an appeal is not disposed of within the period specified in the first proviso, the stay order shall, on the expiry of that period, stand vacated. [Para 48]

Though the right of appeal is a creation of statute and it can be exercised only subject to the conditions specified therein, but the conditions specified have to be in relation to the assessee as something which is required to be complied with by the assessee. But where the assessee has no control over the functioning of the Tribunal, then the provision of vacation of stay cannot be sustained. [Para 51]

The assessee having preferred appeal and that Tribunal being satisfied that condition for dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied is made out, is compelled to pay the duty demanded and penalty levied, if the appeal is not decided within 180 days. The assessee has no control in respect of matters pending before the Tribunal; in the matter of availability of infrastructure; the members of the Tribunal and the workload. Therefore, for the reason that the Tribunal is not able to decide appeal within 180 days, the vacation of stay is a harsh and onerous and unreasonable condition. The condition of vacation of stay for the inability of the Tribunal to decide the appeal is burdening the assessee for no fault of his. Such a condition is onerous and renders the right of appeal as illusory. An order passed by a judicial forum is sought to be annulled for no fault of assessee. [Para 52]

Therefore, such condition of automatic vacation of stay on the expiry of 180 days, has to be read down to mean that after 180 days the revenue has a right to bring to the notice of the Tribunal the conduct of the assessee in delay or avoiding the decision of appeal, so as to warrant an order of vacation of stay. If the provision is not read down in the manner mentioned above, such condition suffers from illegality rendering the right of appeal as redundant. [Para 52]

5.5-11 Insurance cost should be added

Cost of insurance to the place of importation are to be added to customs value [Rule 10(2)(b) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 as amended w.e.f. 26-9-2017].

If these are not ascertainable, these will be calculated @ 1.125% of FOB Value of goods - third proviso to rule 10(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2017 as amended on 26-9-2017.

If FOB value and insurance cost is not ascertainable but FOB value plus cost of transport, loading, unloading of imported goods to place of importation is ascertainable, cost of insurance will be calculated @ 1.125% of such sum - fourth proviso to rule 10(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2017 as amended on 26-9-2017.

Relevant Date for Rate and Valuation of Import Duty

Section 15 of Customs Act prescribes that rate of duty and tariff valuation applicable to imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force at one of the following dates. (a) if the goods are entered for home consumption, the date on which bill of entry is presented (b) in case of warehoused goods, when Bill of Entry for home consumption is presented u/s 68 for clearance from warehouse and (c) in other cases, date of payment of duty.

Concept of Territorial Waters not relevant - It may be noted that concept of 'date of entering into territorial waters' is not relevant for purposes of determination of rate of customs duty.

11.6-1 Relevant Date of Bill of Entry for home consumption

As per section 46 of Customs Act, every importer of goods has to submit a 'Bill of Entry' giving details of goods being imported. The carrier of goods has to submit 'Arrival manifest or import manifest (words 'arrival manifest' inserted w.e.f. 29-3-2018)' or 'Import Report' giving details of all goods which are brought for unloading at the port. If shipping berth is available, 'Entry Inwards' is granted to the vessel.

If there is delay in submission of Bill of Entry, there will be delay in assessment and clearance of imported goods. Goods lying on docks will incur heavy demurrage. Hence, it is permitted to submit 'Bill of Entry' if the vessel or aircraft or vehicle in which goods have been shipped is expected to arrive at any time not exceeding 30 days prior to expected arrival of the aircraft or vessel if vehicle by which goods have been shipped for importation into India- second proviso to section 46(3) of Customs Act [first proviso re-numbered as second proviso w.e.f. 28-3-2021].

However, even if Bill of Entry is submitted earlier, relevant date for purpose of assessment (valuation and rate of customs duty) will be (a) date of grant of 'entry inward' to vessel or (b) date of submission of Bill of Entry whichever is later e.g. if Bill of Entry is presented on 5th January and 'Entry Inward' is granted on 10th January, relevant date will be 10th Jan., but if entry inward is on 10th January and Bill of Entry is presented on 13th January, then 13th January will be the relevant date - proviso to section 15 of the Customs Act.

In case of import by air or road, there is no procedure to grant 'Entry Inward'. Hence date of arrival of aircraft or the vehicle or submission of Bill of Entry, whichever is later, will be treated as relevant date for purpose of rate of customs duty and customs valuation - - proviso to section 15 of the Customs Act. [The words 'or the vehicle' has been inserted w.e.f. 6-8-2014].

It is a beneficial power given for proper administration of fiscal law so that undue hardship may not be caused to the assessee and the fiscal laws may be correctly applied [UCO Bank v. CIT [1999] 104 Taxman 547 (SC)]. Circulars are for public consumption - It cannot be said that instructions issued u/s 119 are not meant for public consumption. It is also provided in the above Rule 111B, that circulars necessary in the public interest shall be published in the Gazette. That means such circulars are for public consumption. If some document is relied on against an assessee to assess him to a high rate of tax, the document shall be disclosed to him. It cannot be withheld [Capricorn Shopping Complex v. ITO [1996] 218 ITR 721 (Ker.)].

Personal hearing - It cannot be laid down as a rule that the Board must give personal hearing to every assessee who makes an application seeking directions to the ITO, nor is it necessary that the Board should pass a reasoned order in every case. However, where the Board decides not to interfere in the matter, it must at least indicate, however briefly, as to why the powers were not exercised. The Board should then permit the petitioner to make a detailed representation and it would be open to the Board to consider whether any personal hearing should be given to the petitioner [Modern Chemical Works v. V. B. Kulkarni [1984] 17 Taxman 66 (Bom.)].

In case of individual assessee - The power u/s 119(2)(a) is a wider power and that power is not meant to be exercised on ground of undue hardship having been caused to an individual assessee. Further, the power u/s 119(2)(a) is to be exercised in respect of a clearly ascertainable class of income or class of cases. The decision to exercise or to refrain from exercising power u/s 119(2)(a) is that of the Board because it alone is required to consider necessity or expediency for exercise of power for purposes mentioned therein and it does not confer a right on any individual assessee to compel Board to exercise that power vested in it in favour of assessee [Precot Mills Ltd. v. CBDT [2004] 140 Taxman 662 (Mad.)].

Application of mind - The authority concerned has to apply his mind to the application before him and if he finds that not granting of the application would result in genuine hardship, then the application is to be allowed by condoning the delay. Vasco Sales & Marketing Corporation [2016] 66 taxmann.com 366 (Ker.).

'Genuine hardship', meaning of - A 'genuine hardship' would, inter alia, mean a genuine difficulty. That per se would not lead to a conclusion that a person having large assets would never be in difficulty as he can sell those assets and pay the amount of interest levied. The ingredients of genuine hardship must be determined keeping in view the dictionary meaning thereof and the legal conspectus attending thereto. For the said purpose, another well-known principle, namely, a person cannot take advantage of his own wrong, may also have to be borne in mind. Compulsion to pay any unjust dues per se would cause hardship. But a question, however, would further arise as to whether the default in payment of the amount was due to circumstances beyond the control of the assessee [B. M. Malani v. HELD: I. Old section 14 v. New section 14 amended from October 2007 : A reading of the unamended section 14 would show that the earlier/old principle was to find the valuation of goods 'by reference to their value'. It introduced a deeming/fictional provision by stipulating that the value of the goods would be the price at which such or like goods are 'ordinarily sold, or offered for sale'. Under the new provision, however, the valuation is based on the transaction price namely, the price 'actually paid or payable for the goods'. Even when the old provision provided the formula of the price at which the goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale, at that time also if the goods in question were sold for a particular price, that could be taken into consideration for arriving at the valuation of goods. The very expression 'ordinarily sold, or offered for sale' would indicate that the price at which these goods are actually sold would be the price at which they are ordinarily sold or offered for sale. Of course, under the old provision, under certain circumstances, the authorities could discard the price mentioned in the invoice. However, that is only when it is found that the price mentioned in the invoice is not the reflection of the price at which these are ordinarily sold or offered for sale. To put it otherwise, the reason for discarding the price mentioned in the invoice could be only when the said price appeared to be suppressed one. In such a case, the authorities could say that generally such goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale at a different price and take that price into consideration for the purpose of levying the duty. It could, however, be done only if there was evidence to show that ordinarily the price at which these goods are ordinarily sold or offered for sale is higher than the price mentioned in the invoice. In fact, this fundamental concept is retained even now while introducing the concept of 'transaction value' under the amended provision. More importantly, the rules viz. Valuation Rules, 1988 had incorporated this very principle of 'transaction value' even under the old provision. No doubt, as per this provision existing today generally the price mentioned is to be accepted as it is the transaction value. However, this very provision stipulates the circumstances under which that price can be discarded. In any case, having regard to the question with which we are concerned in the present appeals, such a change in the provision may not have much effect. [Para 21]

The underlying principle contained in amended sub-section (1) of section 14 is to consider transaction value of the goods imported or exported for the purpose of customs duty. Transaction value is stated to be a price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to India for delivery at the time and place of importation. Therefore, it is the price which is actually paid or payable for delivery at the time and place of importation, which is to be treated as transaction value. However, this sub-section (1) further makes it clear that the price actually paid or payable for the goods will not be treated as transaction value where the buyer and the seller are related with each other. In such cases, there can be a presumption that the actual price which is paid or payable for such goods is not the true reflection of the value of the goods. This section also provides that normal price would be the sole consideration for the sale. However, this may be subject to such other conditions which can be specified in the form of Rules made in this behalf. [Para 22]

As per the first proviso of the amended section 14(1), in the transaction value of the imported goods, certain charges are to be added which are in the form of amount paid or payable for costs and services including commissions and brokerage, engineering, design work, royalties and licence fees, costs of transportation to the place of importation, insurance, loading, unloading and handling charges to the extent and in the manner which can be prescribed in the Rules. Sub-section (2) of section 14, which remains the same, is an overriding provision which empowers the Board to fix tariff values for any class of imported goods or export goods under certain circumstances. [Para 23]

In contrast, in the unamended section 14, sub-section (1A) stipulated that the price referred to in sub-section (1) in respect of imported goods shall be determined in accordance with Rules made in this behalf. Therefore, Rules can be made in determining the price. However, these Rules have to be subject to the provisions of sub-section (1), the underline principle whereof, as stated above, is to taken into consideration actual price of the goods unless it is impermissible because of certain circumstances stipulated therein. [Para 24]

We have also noted that, in the case of Venus Enterprises also, there was repeated enhancement of assessable value in the sense canvassed by the ld. counsel and yet the proceedings initiated under Sec. 28 of the Act were held to be sustainable.

11. The next issue, which arises for consideration, is whether the enhancement of value in these cases is sustainable in law. We have noted that the importer in his statements clearly admitted that the supplier had agreed to show a lower price per piece in the invoices than what the importer was liable to pay. Even the amounts of extra payments made by the assessee to the supplier were also stated by the former. In the second statement, it was admitted that the price negotiated with the supplier was FOB price. The ld. counsel has made an endeavour to show that the first statement of the assessee was not voluntary and, therefore, anything contained therein is not reliable. We find that, in the second statement, Shri Patel never complained that his earlier statement was made under coercive circumstances. As a matter of fact, the second statement is seen to be clarificatory of certain aspects covered by the first statement. Additional particulars were also supplemented in the second statement. By and large, the two statements appeared to be consistent with each other and there is no significant conflict between the two. We find that a clear admission of undervaluation of the goods is reflected in the statements given by the importer under Sec. 108 of the Customs Act. It is also on record that certain payment was made voluntarily by them during the course of investigations. Therefore, we are not impressed with the plea made by the ld. counsel that the first statement was retracted by the importer.

12.
