Arguments that the earlier SVB order stops the department from opening up the issues in the second SVB order

14. The argument of the appellant is that in the first SVB order in 2011, their invoice values were accepted as not affecting the price in terms of Rule 3(3)(a). Therefore, in the second order passed in 2015 a different view could not have been taken. The Department's argument is that there is no promissory estoppel in taxation.

15. We have considered the matter. It is now well established that in Customs Act, each Bill of Entry is an assessment and can be appealed against. If excess duty is paid, the importer has to file an appeal against the assessment and can file a refund claim. Similarly, if there is short payment, a demand can be raised by the department by issuing a Show Cause Notice. Both the appeal against the assessment by the assessee and the demand by the department are subject to limitation of time after which neither can an appeal be filed by the assessee nor can the department raise a demand. Thus, insofar as the Bill of Entry is concerned, it reaches finality.

16. However, such assessment does not bind either the assessee or the department with respect to any future imports. If, for instance, excess duty was paid due to wrong classification of goods, erroneous computation of value or by not claiming an eligible exemption notification, etc. it does not mean that the assessee has to continue to pay excess duty in all his future imports. Conversely, if duty is short paid and the department failed to issue a notice within time, it does not mean that the department is estopped from making correct assessments of future Bills of Entry and collecting the correct amount of duty. Otherwise, it would lead to anomalous situation where the duty leviable will be based not on the correct legal position but on the past practices including erroneous ones. If the appellant's argument is accepted, for instance, if there are three Custom Houses and identical goods were correctly classified, valued and charged to duty at Custom House A, excess duty is erroneously charged in Custom House B and short duty is charged erroneously in Custom House C and appeals and demands were not raised within time to correct the mistakes, the errors in Custom House B and Custom House C would prevail over the law. Further, in the same custom house, for the same goods, if one importer is charged erroneously less and another is charged properly, there will be two different laws for them. Taxes and duties can never be assessed so. The principle of Res Judicata applies only to the extent of the assessment of the particular Bill of Entry at the particular level attaining finality. Thus, we find no force in the argument of the appellant that once a decision has been taken in the first SVB order, it binds the department in the subsequent SVB order.

17. Legally speaking nothing stops the officer from examining each import made by an importer from a related person to see if the relationship affected the price. As it will be rather cumbersome to do so, the investigation done once and an SVB order issued is normally applied for imports for a period of three years assuming that in all these years, the price is not affected by the relationship. Both the SVB orders issued in this case clearly indicate that they are subject to occasional review and also a final review after three years. Otherwise, an unscrupulous importer can import on invoices which are not influenced by the relationship until an order is passed by the SVB and then start importing on invoices with much lower prices from the related party. If this happens, nothing stops the department from examining the valuation in such cases. Therefore, we find no force in the argument of the appellant that since the first SVB order had found that their relationship with the foreign supplier had not affected the prices at that time, the department cannot examine if such is the case in all subsequent imports.

(1)

CONCEPT OF BENEFICIAL OWNER INTRODUCED

?

Definition of importer u/s 2(26) of Customs Act, 1962 ('CA, 1962') is proposed to be amended to include beneficial owner. Definition of 'beneficial owner' proposed to be included by inserting clause (3A) to Sec. 2 of CA, 1962 as under:

?

"Beneficial owner means any person on whose behalf the goods are being imported or exported or who exercises effective control over the goods being imported or exported".

?

The words 'effective control' is not defined under the CA, 1962. However Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and Rule 2(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Export Goods) Rules, 2007 defines that persons shall be deemed to be 'related' only if one of the conditions is satisfied. One of such condition under Rule 2(2)(v) is that one of them controls other directly or indirectly. Interpretative Note to Rule 2 clarify that for purpose of rule 2(2)(v), one person is deemed to control other if he is legally or operationally in a position to exercise restraint or direction over the other. Hence not just legal ownership but even operational control shall be sufficient to attract the provisions.

?

Applying said interpretation the words 'effective control' shall cover legal as well as operational control.

?

Said amendment has been proposed to cover those persons who use IEC of another to import goods and avoid the consequences because of some breach of law. One will also not be able to disown the goods on the ground of not being the owner.

?

As per current Sec. 46(3) a bill of entry may be presented at any time after the delivery of the import manifest or import report as the case may be.

?

It is proposed by substituting existing Sec. 46(3) to provide that the bill of entry must be presented before the end of the next day following the day (excluding holidays) on which the aircraft or vessel or vehicle carrying the goods arrives at a customs station at which such goods are to be cleared for home consumption or warehousing. Without sufficient cause, importer shall be liable for charges for late presentation. Hence CHA's shall have to ensure that bill of entry is presented in time otherwise importer shall have to pay the charges for late presentation.

It may be noted that as per Sec. 15 of CA, 1962 the date of presentation of bill of entry is relevant date for determination of duty. Similar decisions are also passed in other assessee's cases, viz., Lava International,Intex Technologies, Micromax India. Thus, a clear guideline has been issued by the Hon'ble Court stating that the customs department should not insist on reassessment and should not reject refund application in absence of appeals against assessment of bill of entry. Conclusion

5. Such a move, not adhering to direction of established judicial precedents by the executive, is a move of defiance of the judiciary. Also, such a stand of custom house is resulting in multiplicity of proceedings and wastage of time. Besides, it leads to additional financial burden to the mobile importers which is ultimately passed on to the ultimate consumers by way of higher price. Furthermore, the same is going against the policies and vision of the present government.

In the light of such contrary stands taken by the different customs houses, time has come to adhere to uniform practice by all customs houses for sanctioning refund and also to honor the judicial precedents.

Note to rule 10 In rule 10(1)(a)(i), the term "buying commissions" means fees paid by an importer to his agent for the service of representing him abroad in the purchase of the goods being valued.

Rule 10(1)(b)(ii)

1. There are two factors involved in the apportionment of the elements specified in rule 10(1)(b)(ii) to the imported goods - the value of the element itself and the way in which that value is to be apportioned to the imported goods. The apportionment of these elements should be made in a reasonable manner appropriate to the circumstances and in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles.

2. Concerning the value of the element, if the importer acquires the element from a seller not related to him at a given cost, the value of the element is that cost. If the element was produced by the importer or by a person related to him, its value would be the cost of producing it. If the element had been previously used by the importer, regardless of whether it had been acquired or produced by such importer, the original cost of acquisition or production would have to be adjusted downward to reflect its use in order to arrive at the value of the element.

3. Once a value has been determined for the element it is necessary to apportion that value to the imported goods. Various possibilities exist. For example, the value might be apportioned to the first shipment if the importer wishes to pay duty on the entire value at one time. As another example, the importer may request that the value be apportioned over the number of units produced up to the time of the first shipment. As a further example, he may request that the value be apportioned over the entire anticipated production where contracts or firm commitments exist for that production. The method of apportionment used will depend upon the documentation provided by the importer.

4. As an illustration of the above, an importer provides the producer with a mould to be used in the production of the imported goods and contracts with him to buy 10,000 units. By the time of arrival of the first shipment of 1,000 units, the producer has already produced 4,000 units. The importer may request the proper officer of customs to apportion the value of the mould over 1,000 units, 4,000 units or 10,000 units.

Rule 10(1)(b)(iv)

1. Additions for the elements specified in rule 10(1)(b)(iv) should be based on objective and quantifiable data. In order to minimise the burden for both the importer and proper officer of customs in determining the values to be added, data readily available in the buyer's commercial record system should be used in so far as possible.

2. For those elements supplied by the buyer which were purchased or leased by the buyer, the addition would be the cost of the purchase or the lease. No addition shall be made for those elements available in the public domain, other than the cost of obtaining copies of them.

3. The case with which it may be possible to calculate the values to be added will depend on a particular firm's structure and management practice, as well as its accounting methods.

4. For example, it is possible that a firm which imports a variety of products from several countries maintains the records of its design centre outside the country of importation in such a way as to show accurately the costs attributable to a given product. Likewise, clause (e) of sub-rule (1) of rule 9 which deals with other payments again uses the expression 'all other payments actually made or to be made as the condition of the sale of imported goods'. All these costs were to be included on actual basis. Only when such costs were not ascertainable, proviso got attracted which stipulated that such costs and charges shall be 25 per cent of the free on board value of such goods. Even when the aforesaid proviso was amended vide notification dated 19-12-1989, the spirit behind the unamended proviso was maintained and kept intact. Only difference was that instead of addition of 25 per cent of free on board value of goods in respect of all the three kinds of charges, under the amended proviso, this percentage fixed was different in respect of each of the aforesaid charges. As far as cost of transport is concerned, it was changed at 20 per cent of the free on board value of goods. Insofar as loading, unloading and handling charges are concerned, it was reduced to 1 per cent of the FOB value of goods and in case of insurance charges, the amended provision provided for such cost at 1.125 per cent free on board value of goods. However, as mentioned above, the spirit behind this proviso continued to be the same viz. the proviso was to made applicable only when the actual cost was indeterminable. [Para 30]

In contrast, however, the impugned amendment dated 5-7-1990 has changed the entire basis of inclusion of loading, unloading and handling charges associated with the delivery of the imported goods at the place of importation. Whereas fundamental principle or basis remains unaltered insofar as other two costs, viz., the cost of transportation and the cost of insurance stipulated in clauses (a) and (c) of sub-rule (2) are concerned. In respect of these two costs, provision is retained by specifying that they would be applicable only if the actual cost is not ascertainable. In contrast, there is a complete deviation and departure insofar as loading, unloading and handling charges are concerned. The proviso now stipulates 1% of the CIF value of the goods irrespective of the fact whether actual cost is ascertainable or not.

Having referred to the scheme of section 14 of the Rules in detail above, this cannot be countenanced. This proviso, introduces fiction as far as addition of cost of loading, unloading and handling charges is concerned even in those cases where actual cost paid on such an account is available and ascertainable. Obviously, it is contrary to the provisions of section 14 and would clearly be ultra vires this provision. When the actual charges paid are available and ascertainable, introducing a fiction for arriving at the purported cost of loading, unloading and handling charges is clearly arbitrary with no nexus with the objectives sought to be achieved. On the contrary, it goes against the objective behind section 14 namely to accept the actual cost paid or payable and even in the absence thereof to arrive at the cost which is most proximate to the actual cost. Addition of 1 per cent of the CIF value is thus, in the circumstance, clearly arbitrary and irrational and would be violative of article 14 of the Constitution. [Para 31]

No doubt, rule making authority has the power to make Rules but such power has to be exercised by making the rules which are consistent with the scheme of the Act and not repugnant to the main provisions of the statute itself. Such a provision would be valid and 1 per cent CIF value in determining handling charges etc. could be justified only in those cases where actual cost is not ascertainable. First amendment to the proviso to sub-rule (2) of rule 9 which was incorporated vide Notification dated 19-12-1989 would be justified. However, the impugned provision clearly fails the test. In the present case before us, the only justification for stipulating 1 per cent of the FOB value as the cost of loading, unloading and handling charges is that it would help customs authorities to apply the aforesaid rate uniformly. This can be a justification only if the loading, unloading and handling charges are not ascertainable. Where such charges are known and determinable, there is no reason to have such a yardstick. It cannot be ignored that this provision as well as Valuation Rules are enacted on the lines of GATT guidelines and the golden thread which runs through is the actual cost principle. Further, the loading, unloading and handling charges are fixed by International Airport Authority. [Para 34]

Procedure for cases where reference to SVB is not required

Where it is decided by the Commissioner of customs that a reference to SVB is not necessary, the Customs House shall issue a reference number to the importer and the Risk Management Division to indicate that the transaction has been examined from the point of view of need for SVB inquiries and it has been decided not to refer the same for SVB investigations.

Procedure in Special Valuation Branch Upon receipt of all related records from the referring customs formation, the SVB shall assign a case number and update the Central Registry Database (CRD) maintained by DGoV.

SVB shall commence inquiries. During the course of which the Deputy Commissioner / Asst. Commissioner (SVB) may call for further documents or information as required. The importer shall also be given suitable opportunity to submit evidence in support of the declared value.

The SVBs shall, as far as possible, complete the investigations and issue its findings within two months from the date of receipt of information. If not completed, extension may be obtained from Commissioner/Chief Commissioner.

Upon completing investigations, the SVB shall submit the findings before the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner. Upon approval by the Principal Commissioner / Commissioner, an Investigation Report (IR, for short) shall be prepared. A copy of the IR shall also be sent to the DGoV.

Finalisation of assessments

If SVB finds that the declared value is conforming to Rule 3 of the CVR, 2007, the provisional assessments shall be finalized without issuing any adjudication order,

However, when investigative findings of SVB are that the declared value has been influenced by the circumstances surrounding the sale, the proper officer shall issue a show cause notice to the importer within 15 days of the receipt of the IR, under intimation to the concerned SVB.

In cases where imports have been cleared through multiple customs locations, SVB shall take a proposal to CBEC recommending appointment of a common adjudicating authority.

The adjudicating authority shall, after following the principles of natural justice, pass an order quantifying the extent of influence on the declared transaction value.

Change in circumstances surrounding the sale

In any case where, the circumstances of sale or terms and conditions of the agreement between the buyer and related seller change, or any other payments of the kind referred under Rule 10 (1) (c), (d) & (e) of the CVR, 2007 become payable, the importers shall be required to declare the same at the place of import in the prescribed format.

The system of renewal of SVB orders has been discontinued with immediate effect.

Transitory provisions in respect of pending investigations

Transitory provisions in respect of pending investigations are contained in CBE&C circular No. 4/2016-Cus dated 9-2-2016.

A system of one-time declaration is being provided. Importers, in respect of whom SVB orders are pending renewal, shall submit to the jurisdictional SVB, a one-time declaration in the prescribed format by 31-3-2016.

In cases where the importer files declaration in Annexure 1, the process of renewal would be treated as dispensed with. The SVB shall immediately inform the Custom stations to immediately discontinue obtaining Extra Duty Deposit and finalize the related provisional assessments, before 30-6-2016.

In cases where a change in circumstances surrounding the sale has been stated in the declaration by importer, the SVB inquiry shall be initiated.

In cases, where EDD has been enhanced to 5%, due to the importer not having provided information or documents necessary for SVB inquiries, the Commissioner shall immediately take recourse to appropriate provisions under the Customs Act for obtaining the necessary documents for investigations and subsequently dispense with the EDD.

All existing cases should be disposed of latest by 31-10-2016.

Conclusion

If the instructions as contained in this circular are implemented in true spirit (which of course is doubtful), it will be a great step towards 'ease of doing business' in customs.

Provisions of 'self-assessment' have already been introduced in customs. However, these are followed more in breach. If these provisions are also implemented in customs in true spirit, corruption in customs department will become much more tolerable than what is today.

(1) Whether Section 145A overrides the provisions of Section 36(1)(iii)?

The proviso to section 36(1)(iii) incorporated in Part D of Chapter IV of the Act providing for the 'Method of Computation of Total Income', will override provisions of section 145A, which is incorporated in Chapter IV of the Act relating to 'procedure for assessment'. The words in the proviso to section 36(1) 'whether capitalised or not' will override the accounting practice followed in the books of account by the assessee. In the present case, the assessee has admittedly capitalised the interest paid on the borrowed capital. The assesse also did not claim that the land in question was put to use in the assessment years in question. Mere purchase of the land in the years in question out of the borrowed capital does not entitle the assessee to claim such interest paid on borrowed capital as a deductible expenditure in the present assessment years merely on the basis of method of accounting prescribed under section 145A which was brought in the statute to undo the effect of the decision of the Delhi High Court in Chamber of Tax Consultants v. Union of India [2017] 87 taxmann.com 92 [2018] 252 Taxman 77/400 ITR 178 (Delhi) which quashed the CBDT Notification No. 87 of 2016 dated 29.9.2016 finding it to be ultra vires. The method of accounting provided for the valuation of inventory under section 145A does not determine the allowability of the expenditure. The proviso to section 36(1)(iii), which says that such a claim of deduction will be allowed in the assessment years when it was put to use, will override the provisions contained in section 145A. [Mahindra World City Developers Ltd. v. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax, Company Circle-IV(1), Chennai [2019] 107 taxmann.com 16 (Madras)]

(2) Is it necessary to add customs duty (not yet paid) to the value of imported materials kept at customs bonded warehouse?

According to section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962, customs duty shall be levied on goods imported into or exported from India. Section 2(23) of the said Act defines 'import' as bringing into India from a place outside India. Section 2(27) of the said Act defines India as including the territorial waters of India. Therefore, the taxable event occurs when goods enter the territorial waters of India. Duty liability has arisen but is only deferred by deposit in the bonded warehouse. Deposit in the bonded warehouse does not extinguish the duty liability. Therefore, the duty element should be added for making the adjustments under section 145A. ["Issues on Tax Audit" by ICAI]

(3) Is a Deposit made with port trust in the nature of the tax, duty, cess or fee liable to be added under Section 145A to the cost of imports?

Deposit made with port trust will not fall under the category of tax, duty, cess or fee as mentioned in section 145A. The deposit made with the port trust is not includible in the computation made under section 145A, if it does not fall in the category of tax, duty, cess or fee levied under any law. Hence, the same shall be liable to be included in the adjustments made under section 145A only if it is shown that the payment was made under the authority of any law. Further, since the deposit so made is refundable to the assessee, then also the question of including the same under section 145A does not arise. [Mazagaon Dock Ltd. v. ITO [2017] 85 taxmann.com 213 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

On second appeal : HELD: There was no dispute about the applicability of section 41(1) in the instant case. The only dispute was when the liability to pay customs duty ceased. In other words, the issue was in which year the benefit in respect of customs duty liability by way of remission or cessation thereof accrued to the assessee and when the amount due to cessation of liability had been obtained by the assessee. The assessee company as well as other newspaper companies had filed writ petitions challenging the levy of customs duty by the Government. The Supreme Court vide order dated 6-12-1984 directed the Government of India to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and refix the rate of customs duty afresh, with effect from 1-3-1981. If on such reconsideration the Government decided that there should be any modification in the levy of customs duty or auxiliary duty with effect from 1-3-1981 it would take necessary steps to implement its decision. Until such redetermination of the liability, the Government was directed to recover only Rs. 550 per MT on imported newsprint towards customs duty and auxiliary duty and would not insist upon payment of duty in accordance with the impugned notifications. It was further stipulated in the Supreme Court’s order that even after such redetermination if it was found that any of the petitioners was liable to pay any deficit amount by way of duty, such deficit amount would be paid by such petitioner within four months from the date on which a notice of demand was served on such petitioner by the concerned authority. It was clear from the above order of the Supreme Court that the Government of India was directed to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on newsprint used for printing newspaper, periodicals, etc., with effect from 1-3-1981. Therefore, as on 6-12-1984 the liability of the assessee to pay customs duty, etc., had not ceased because the matter regarding payment of customs duty was to be considered by the Government. As a result of the directions of the Supreme Court, the Government of India had issued notification dated 19-12-1985 and the CBEC also issued a departmental circular on 10-2-1986 determining the customs duty in respect of imported newsprint. It was clear from the notification as well as circular that after examination of the question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on imported newsprint the Government had fixed the rate at Rs. 550 per MT. The notification as well as circular dates fell in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, i.e., 1987-88. Therefore, as a result of the notification and circular of the CBEC the assessee’s liability to pay customs duty had ceased in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88. The assessee thus obtained the benefit in respect of customs duty by way of remission or cessation thereof and the amount obtained by it and/or the value of benefit accrued to it had to be deemed as its profits and gains of business for the assessment year 1987-88. The customs authority by issuing the notice of demand had given effect to the notification dated 19-12-1985 issued by the Government of India and Circular dated 10-2-1986 of CBEC. A notice of demand did not have the effect of cessation or remission of liability of the assessee. The liability of an assessee ceased only under Notification dated 19-12-1985 of the Government of India read with circular of the customs authority dated 10-2-1986. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in confirming the addition made to the total income of the assessee for the assessment year 1987-88 after making necessary adjustments regarding claim, if any, disallowed under section 43B earlier while determining the amount assessable.

The benefit in respect of cessation of customs liability by way of remission or cessation thereof had to be taxed in the assessment year 1987-88 because the assessee obtained the benefit in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88 and if the assessee did not make entry in the relevant accounting year it would not effect operation of the provisions of section 41(1).

Introduction

1. This year whole emphasis of the budget is on two aspects, i.e., ease of doing business and to promote make in India. The tariff and non-tariff (legislative) changes are made keeping in view the above objectives in mind. In February, 2016 SVB procedure was revamped. This budget has further simplified the warehousing provisions under the Customs Act. Concept of warehousing stations itself has been removed, permitting the self-governance and promoting privatization of warehousing without any interference of customs/excise officers. It may further be noted that compliance of law is being promoted, however, at the same time duty evasion is being punished.

On tariff part, to promote make in India, exemptions on various finished goods are withdrawn and their raw materials are being exempted subject to actual user conditions. New baggage Rules would permit excess duty free imports. Customs (Import of Goods at Concessional Rate of Duty for Manufacture of Excisable Goods) Rules are introduced waving off various prior permission requirements. The new rules are mostly based upon self-declarations.

Details of changes made in customs laws, reasons and effect thereof are discussed hereunder:

Demand of customs duty can be raised in two years from date of import in non-suppression cases

2. Section 28 of the Customs Act providing for demand of customs duty has been amended to provide that demand of customs duty can be raised within period of two years from the date of import of goods. This provision would be applicable even for cases not involving collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts.

2.1 Earlier provision: Earlier the provision provided that customs department can raise demand of duty only within one year from date of import in cases of interpretation of provisions/exemption, etc. However, power to demand duty beyond one year of import was only available in case of suppression or mis-declaration by the assessee.

2.2 Reason of amendment: In cases where issue pertains to classification of imported goods or interpretation of the exemption notification, the assessee argues that there is no suppression on part of the assessee and customs was fully aware of details of goods. In those situations, customs duty could not be recovered for imports beyond one year's period from the date of imports.

From department's point of view, it was felt that due of paucity of time, i.e., one year's period, investigations could not be completed for various assessees and SCNs were not being issued within one year from date of import.

2.3 Effect of amendment: This amendment would give room of additional one year to customs for making detailed investigations and issue SCN.

From assessee's point of view, this would increase the uncertainty of duty demand till two years during which it can be raised even in cases of assessment with complete knowledge of customs officer. Further, in the era of stiff competition, even one SCN demanding duty after period of 20 months of import would have huge impact on assessee's financial planning.

The other class of importer traders would be deeply hit as their customers to whom imported goods are re-sold may not pay them the excess customs duty/differential duty demanded by department.

Thus, proposed amendment is, to some extent contrary to the principal of certainty, as assessee would be unsure of the duty demand, even though the assessment may have been done with the knowledge of the department.

Further, it is also not clear whether the said provision would be applicable even on past imports where one year's period from date of imports has expired and department also does not allege any suppression.

Date of publication in the official gazette

3. Section 25 of the Customs Act grants power to government to issue exemption notification. Section 25(4) of the Customs Act is amended to provide that every notification issued shall come into force on the date of its issue by the Central Government for publication in the Official Gazette. This is being amended so as to omit the requirement of publishing and offering for sale any notification issued by the Directorate of Publicity and Public Relations of CBEC.

The proposed amendment will nullify the effect of decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of Union of India v. Param Industries [2015] 59 taxmann.com 208/51 GST 702 wherein court had held that there are two mandatory conditions: (i) it should be duly published in the official gazette, (ii) it should be offered for sale on date of its issue by the Directorate of Publicity and Public Relations of Board, New Delhi.

By the present amendment second condition shall be removed.

Deferred payment of customs duty

Adverting to the method adopted by the lower authorities in arriving at assessable value we find that the lower authorities have taken into consideration the price of the goods at the time of manufacture and also that at the time of import and has allowed necessary depreciation after making adjustments in the price of the machines due to the general price rise in the value of the goods over the years. The depreciation allowed was 6-1/4%, the price rise was taken as 1/3rd of the total price rise between 1970 and 1980 of that in the case of prices of the new machines. No basis for the depreciation of 6-1/4% and for taking the appreciation in the value of the second-hand machines as one-third of that of the new machinery due to general price rise has been spelt out in the order of the lower authorities. However, we find the result of this exercise was that the price of the goods as worked out by the origins! authority came to £38,220.96 which was comparable with the value of similar machines imported and covered by invoice of February 1981. The Appellate Collector, however, allowed depreciation of 10% while upholding the methodology adopted for working out the assessable value. We find as a result of the modification as ordered by the Appellate Collector, the assessable value has been considerably reduced from the original value. The appellants were called upon to pay an additional duty of Rs. 27,619.39 over the duty chargeable based on the invoice value as against additional payment of Rs, 1,78,467.97 earlier demanded by the Assistant Collector in his order. We would like to observe that in the instant case, the value of comparable goods was available and the correct Rule that should have been applied by the lower authorities should have been Rule 3 of the Customs valuation Rules 1963 read with Rule 4 of the said Rules. We find that the value of comparable goods imported by the appellants was acceptable to the authorities and as such there was no need for the officers to traverse beyond these Rules to Rule 8 of the Valuation Rules. If this was done there was no need for doing an involved exercise for arriving at assessable value as. has been done and the area of dispute regarding fixation of the value would have been also reduced. In any case, we find that the appellants had not suffered any disadvantage on this account and probably the value fixed now in terms of the Appellate Collector's order is lower than what might have been fixed in case Rule 3 read with Rule 4 of the Customs Valuation Rules 1963 had been resorted to. We, therefore, find no reason to accede the appellants plea for accepting the invoice value for purpose of assessment.

The appellants second plea that no addition should have been made towards freight and insurance for arriving at assessable value in as much as their invoice price is cif price and the freight has been prepaid by the suppliers. We observe that since the price shown in the invoice has not been adopted as the basis of valuation under Section 14(1) but it is the export price of the new machines prevailing at the time of manufacture which has formed the basis for the purpose, the additions towards freight and insurance in the value as has been worked out is called for. The appellants have not shown as to how this addition in terms of the basis adopted by the lower authority for filing the value is not maintainable, in law. The conclusion of landing charges in the assessable value is maintainable in law seeing that the expenditure incurred for landing would become an integral component of their intrinsic value and accordingly "the price at which such or like goods are ordinarily sold for delivery at the time and place of importation" [Section 14(a) of the Act] or "the value at which such goods or comparable goods produced or manufactured by the. person who has produced or manufactured the goods to be assessed or ordinarily sold or offered for sale to other buyers in India" (R.3 of the Customs Valuation Rules, 1963). In view of this we find no reason to interfere with the impugned order. The appeal is, therefore, rejected.

Conclusion and parting remarks

While the issuance of said Circular is undoubtedly a step forward with the Board specifically taking cognizance and resolving the issues where payment is made vide TR-06 challan, the Circular has also parallelly opened a Pandora's box and aggravated the concerns of assessees in the aforementioned scenarios wherein no similar procedure has been prescribed to facilitate the availment of ITC legally accrued to such assessees. Such ambiguity continues to cause further confusion and unnecessary litigations among assessees. The additional issue of the jurisdictional customs officers refusing to amend the BOEs despite repeated requests of the importers so as to enable the flow of ITC also adds to the problem. Therefore, even the directions given in the present Circular for reassessment of the BOEs may not achieve the desired results. Additionally, the issue still remains open as to whether an assessee can get their BoEs re-assessed in respect of IGST already paid previously through TR-06 Challan in order to avail ITC.

To conclude, the industry expects the Board to further prescribe similar mechanism and procedure to enable the assessees to avail ITC which are legally accruing to them in the aforementioned scenarios, which is otherwise disallowed to them due to mere procedural ambiguities. Further, the industries may also file a suitable representation before the Government of India/Board, explaining such practical difficulties in the availment of ITC basis a standalone TR-06 Challan and how the absence of such mechanism/procedure as issued under the Circular continues to result in redundancy of efforts, increased ambiguities and the requirement to undertake undue compliances.

Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock [Inclusion of freight] - Assessment year 2007-08 - Assessee-company purchased material on CIF basis - However, in exceptional circumstances, where material was immediately consumed, transport charges were not included in purchase price, but were separately debited to profit and loss account as invoices of transporters were received after consumption of material - Whether, addition on account of non-inclusion of freight inward and import clearing expense to cost of closing inventory, in such cases was not justified, since revenue had accepted assessee's method of valuation of stock in past, especially when revenue failed to demonstrate that impugned method of accounting resulted in material underestimation of profits - Held, yes [Para 7.22] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in manufacturing and selling of two-wheelers in joint venture with a Japanese company. During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer referred the case to the Transfer Pricing Officer, as there were certain international transaction with its associated enterprises (AEs). It purchased material on CIF basis and ordinarily included freight and cost of delivery of goods in purchase price. However, in exceptional circumstances, where assessee has to immediately lift material, transport charges were not included in purchase price, but were separately debited to profit and loss account, since invoices of transporters were received after consumption of material.

The Assessing Officer added the amount of freight inward and import clearing expenses to cost of closing inventory. The assessee contended that the revenue had accepted its method of valuation in the past. It also contended that the transaction would be revenue neutral in the long run, as similar adjustment would also be required in the opening stock. However, the Dispute Resolution Panel confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On assessee's appeal:

HELD: Though, technically it can be argued that the value of closing inventory must include freight/ import clearing charges, the purchases in question were done under exceptional circumstances for immediate consumption. They were consumed immediately i.e. as soon as raw material entered the factory premises, hence, the question of such purchases being part of closing stock does not arise at all. In such a situation, when freight/import charges were directly debited to the profit and loss account along with the value of the purchases, the question of treating them as part of closing inventory does not arise. The assessee acted and accounted in a proper and acceptable method. Therefore, the relief should be granted on this count alone. [Para 7.14]

Alternatively, the undisputed fact remains that the assessee had been consistently following the said method of accounting in the last many years and the revenue had been accepting these facts and method of accounting without any demur.[Para 7.15]

The contention of the DRP that, the principle of res judicata does not apply in Income-tax proceedings and therefore, the Assessing officer is correct to come to independent conclusion and is not bound by past acceptance of a factual legal point by the department, is untenable. Technically, the principle of res judicata may not apply to the income-tax proceedings as each year is an independent year, yet there ought to be uniformity in treatment and consistency as propounded by the Supreme Court in the case of Radhasoami Satsang v. CIT [1992] 193 ITR 321/60 Taxman 248, where the facts and circumstances were identical. It is a judicially accepted principle that when the facts are same, a uniform view should be adopted for the subsequent years in the income-tax proceedings. Unless there is a material change in the facts, which is neither demonstrated by the Assessing Officer nor DRP, the view which is taken earlier, should not be changed, as held by various courts. [Para 7.16]

In the present case, the revenue rejected the method of accounting, which was consistently followed by the assessee, but it failed to demonstrate with facts and figures that the impugned method of accounting resulted in material underestimation of profits. On the contrary, the assessee demonstrated that the change in the method of accounting for year under appeal would result in loss to the revenue as the opening stock would also require similar adjustment and the cascading effect will be loss to revenue. In this case, the revenue unnecessarily disturbed the consistent method of accounting though it had been accepted in many years. Such tinkering with the method is unjustified when the exercise does not materially alter the profits. Such petty additions should be avoided on the ground of materiality, as AS-1, which talks about materiality, consistency, prudence etc., is part of the I.T. Act after it was notified under section 145(2). [Para 7.22]

In view of above discussion, this ground of the assessee is allowed. [Para 7.25]

FACT: Facts

Assessee's appeal along with stay application was pending before High Court.

Pending stay application, Department initiated recovery proceedings in pursuance of CESTAT order in favour of revenue.

Such action was taken in accordance with Circular No. 967/01/2013-CX, dated 1-1-2013.

Assessee argued that CBEC had no power to issue such Circular and, in any event, Sl. Nos. 3, 6, 9, 10 and 11 of para 2 of Circular were invalid.

Issue Involved

Whether recovery proceedings were valid in law ?

HELD: A. Board has power to instructions such as those issued in impugned Circular :

Power under Customs Act comes from section 151A : Insofar as section 151A of the Customs Act is concerned, it is worded widely and includes power of the Board to issue instructions, orders and directions for the purpose of uniformity in classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty thereon or for the implementation of any other provisions of the Act or any other law for the time being in force insofar as they relate to any prohibition, restriction or procedure for import or exports of goods. The power of the Board, therefore, to issue any orders, instructions, or directions for the implementation of the provisions of the Act if the Board considers it necessary and expedient to do so cannot be questioned. Recovery of customs duty with or without interest and penalty would certainly arise out of the provisions made in the Customs Act, 1962 and the Rules made thereunder. For example, section 142 of the Customs Act pertains to recovery of sums to the Government. The Customs (Attachment of Property of Defaulters for Recovery of Government Dues) Rules, 1995 provides for the procedure for such recoveries. In that view of the matter, power of the Board to issue such instructions for recovery of customs duty would flow from section 151A of the Customs Act, 1962. [Para 11]

Section 37B of Excise Act does not directly empower issuance of such Circular : Section 37B of the Central Excise Act, 1944, however, is not so widely worded. It empowers the Board, if it considers necessary and expedient to do so for the purpose of uniformity in classification of excisable goods or with respect to levy of duty of excise on such goods, to issue orders, instructions and directions to the Central Excise Officers as deemed fit. The powers of the Board, therefore, can be exercised for the purpose of uniformity in classification of goods or with respect to levy of duty of excise on such goods. When read in conjunction, both the elements touching the powers of the Board would have a bearing on the question of classification of the goods or with the levy of duty of excise on such goods. It is highly questionable whether recovery of excise duty along with interest and penalty can form part of matter of any instructions the Board may issue in exercise of powers under section 37B of the Central Excise Act. However, this issue was not examined in view of provisions of rule 31 of Central Excise Rules, 2002. [Para 12]

6.2-8 Burden of proof that transaction value is 'Value' Importer has to declare 'value' of goods. If the assessing officer has reason to doubt about truth or accuracy of the value declared by the importer, he can ask the importer to submit further information and evidence. If the customs officer still has reasonable doubt, he can reject the 'value' as declared by the importer. [rule 12(1) w.e.f. 10-10-2007 - earlier rule 10A(1) of Customs Valuation Rules added w.e.f. 19-2-1998]. If the importer requests, the assessing officer has to give reasons for doubting the truth or accuracy of value declared by importer. [rule 12(2) of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 - earlier rule 10A(2) of Customs Valuation Rules upto 10-10-2007]. Thus, burden is on the importer to prove that the 'value' declared by him is correct as per section 14 of Customs Act [This amendment was been made after agreement reached at WTO by all countries. - CBI&C circular No. 13/98-Cus dated 9-3-1998].

Mere having 'doubt' is enough. The assessing officer does not have to prove that the assessable value is not genuine. However, doubt has to be a 'reasonable doubt'. Thus, there should be some material or evidence to doubt the value declared. Mere hunch will not be sufficient.

Reason to doubt does not mean 'reason to suspect'. Mere suspicion upon the correctness of the invoice produced by an importer is not sufficient to reject it as evidence of the value of imported goods. The doubt has to be based on some material evidence and is not formed on a mere suspicion or speculation - CC v. Aggarwal Industries (2011) 272 ELT 641 (SC) = (2012) 1 SCC 186.

In Modi Rubber v. CC 2002(141) ELT 68 (CEGAT), it was held that marginal difference in prices within normal variation range by itself cannot be reasonable doubt about truth and accuracy of declared value.

Rule 12 is only mechanism to reject the declared value - As per explanation (1)(i) to rule 12, the Rule 12 does not provide any method for determination of value. It only provides mechanism to reject declared value, where there is reasonable doubt. If transaction value is rejected, valuation has to be done as per rules 4 to 9 [Explanation (1)(i) to rule 12 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007].

Assessing officer can raise doubts for reasons like (a) significantly higher value of identical or similar goods imported at about same time in comparable quantities (b) Abnormal discount or abnormal reduction from ordinary competitive price (c) Sale involves special discounts limited to exclusive agents (d) Mis-declaration of goods in parameters such as description, quality, quantity, country of origin, year of manufacture or production (e) Non-declaration of parameters such as brand, grade, specifications that have relevance to value (f) fraudulent or manipulated documents [Explanation (1)(iii) to rule 12 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007].

Declared value shall be accepted if assessing officer is satisfied about truth and accuracy of the declared value [Explanation (1)(ii) to rule 12 of Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007].

Rule 12 does not empower Assessing Officer to reject transaction value. It only provides mechanism for rejecting transaction value - PNP Polytex v. CC (2015) 318 ELT 649 (CESTAT).

Reasons for doubt have to be recorded by proper officer in writing and informed to importer - The proper officer must record reasons for having reasonable doubt on truthfulness of declared value. Simple doubt is not sufficient. The doubt must be reasonable i.e. degree of objectivity and basis/foundation for suspicion must be based on 'certain reasons' and not a simple doubt. These doubts must arise after preliminary enquiry from importer has been conducted and his explanation not accepted. The recording of reasons has to be read in rule 12. If his explanation is not accepted, specific grounds of rejection have to be informed to importer in writing - Century Metal Recycling P Ltd. v. UOI (2019) 367 ELT 3 (SC 3 member bench).

1.1-5 Common aspects of Customs and CGST

There are some common or similar provisions in Customs and CGST.

Both are Central Acts and derive power of levy from Constitution.

Both are under administrative control of one Board (Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs) (CBI&C) under Ministry of Finance.

Departmental organizational hierarchy is same from top upto Assistant Commissioner level.

Classification Tariffs of CGST and customs are based on HSN and principles of classification are identical.

Principles of deciding 'Assessable Value' are similar i.e. both are principally based on 'transaction value'.

Concept of 'related person' for valuation purposes appears in Customs as well as CGST. Principle of 'piercing of corporate veil' can apply in both cases.

Provisions of refund, including principle of 'unjust enrichment' are similar. Provisions for interest for delayed payment are also similar.

Provisions of raising demand for short levy, non-levy or erroneous refund are similar. Provisions in respect of recovery, mandatory penalty etc. are also similar.

Provisions for granting exemptions from duty - partial or full - conditional or unconditional are similar.

Powers of search and seizure are quite similar.

CGST and customs law make provisions of arrests and prosecution of offences.

Provisions in respect of Authority for Advance Ruling are similar.

Appeal provisions are similar in some aspects.

63. Need for clarity on the treatment of post-sales discounts and incentives

The ambiguity around post-sales discounts and incentives has been there since the inception of the GST law. Section 15(3)(b) of the CGST Act, 2017 allows for the exclusion of post-sales discounts from the taxable value, provided certain conditions are met. These conditions include:

The discount being agreed upon before or at the time of supply.

The discount being linked to a specific invoice.

The recipient of the supply reversing the input tax credit (ITC) attributable to the discount.

Thus, if any of the above conditions are not met, the GST law does not allow the deduction of discounts from the value of supply. The basic issue revolves around whether secondary or post-sales discounts can be deducted from the value of supply. There have been conflicting interpretations of these provisions. Some rulings consider post-sales discounts as a reduction in the original supply value, excluding them from GST, whereas others do not allow any deduction.

However, the debate does not end here. The CBIC had earlier clarified by way of circular14 that such an additional discount would represent the consideration flowing from the supplier of goods to the dealer for the supply made by the dealer to the customer. This additional discount would be liable to be added to the consideration payable by the customer for the purpose of arriving at the value of the supply made by the dealer. However, in view of the industry apprehensions, the given clarification was later withdrawn15 by the CBIC. However, the GST authorities are still following the given view and treating such additional discounts as a form of 'consideration' for a separate supply, attracting GST. In some cases, the authorities treat volume/additional discounts as subsidies and add them to the value of supply in terms of Section 15(2)(e) of the CGST Act, 2017.

This lack of consistency creates a challenging environment for businesses. To address this confusion, the Government needs to make necessary amendments or issue clear guidelines on how to treat various types of post-sales discounts and incentives across different industries.

64. Sale of Repossessed Goods under GST: Complexities for the Banking and NBFC Sectors

Under GST law, tax is levied on the supply of goods, services or both, and the value of such supply is determined in terms of Section 15 of the CGST Act, 2017 read with the CGST Rules, 2017.

For suppliers dealing in buying and selling second-hand goods, Rule 32(5) of the CGST Rules, 2017 provides a specific method for calculating the value of supply. This involves calculating the difference between the selling price and the purchase price, with negative values ignored. Thus, the value is determined based on the margin of the sale made by the supplier rather than the transaction value as per Section 15 of the CGST Act, 2017.

The proviso to Rule 32(5) provides a specific provision for determining the purchase value of repossessed goods from a defaulting borrower who is unregistered under the GST law in the case of recovery of a loan or debt. In such cases, the purchase price is deemed to be the purchase price of such goods by the defaulting borrower reduced by 5 percentage points for every quarter or part thereof between the date of purchase and the date of disposal by the person making such repossession.

Additionally, notifications on CGST rates16 and Compensation Cess17 offer concessional rates for specified old and used vehicles, provided the supplier has not claimed input tax credit.

The High Court held that as the appellants realised the extra charges only from their out-station buyers, the extra charges were in principle excludible from the assessable value, and further, ordered the department of investigate the assertion of the facts made by the appellants. While the matter was under enquiry, the department received some information that the appellants were indulging in under-valuation of their goods. The Anti-Evasion staff of the department scrutinised the documents of the appellants and came to the conclusion that the appellants had highly inflated the costs of the extra items so as to camouflage the true assessable value of the goods. On this ground, show cause notices were issued demanding differential excise duty of Rs. 1,88,84,508.57 and also a penalty of Rs. 50 lakhs was imposed on the appellants for making false and mis-leading declarations. Confiscation of the plant and machinery of the appellants in lieu of a fine was also ordered. The appellants contended that the show-cause notices issued by the department were time-barred as they were issued beyond the normal time of six months. Further, the appellants pointed out that there has been a violation of principles of natural justice as their request to make further clarifications on the matter, was not honoured by the department. The question as to which of the items of extras should be held to be excludible for determining the assessable value of the goods was also taken up in the instant case.

HEADNOTE: Section  56,  read with sections  50C  and  263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income from other sources  -  Chargeable as  (Revision) - Assessment year  2016-17  - Assessee, an individual engaged in business of manufacturing, export and sales against Form-H of electrical wiring accessories, filed return processed under section 143(1) - Case was reopened under section 147 on ground that assessee purchased an immovable property for consideration significantly lower than circle rate - Assessee held 1/3rd share in property - On assessee’s request disputing circle rate vis-à-vis FMV, Assessing Officer referred matter to DVO, who determined FMV at ?5.16 crores; assessee’s 1/3rd share came to ?1.72 crores, leaving a difference of ?15.14 lakhs, being less than 10 per cent of consideration - Assessing Officer, after considering assessee’s response, applied amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 (treated as retrospective), and accepted that variation below 10 per cent between sale consideration and DVO-determined value was to be ignored, thereby accepting returned income - Principal Commissioner invoked section 263 (including Explanation 2) to revise assessment, holding that Circular No. 8/2018 applied prospectively and that difference between stamp duty value and sale consideration should have been added to assessee’s income - Whether since view of Principal Commissioner was not supported by any judicial authority, his action in treating assessment order as erroneous and prejudicial to interest of revenue was merely a change of opinion and unsustainable - Held, yes [Para 9.3] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, an individual engaged in the business of manufacturing, export and sales against Form-H of electrical wiring accessories, filed a return declaring income of about Rs. 33.64 lakhs for assessment year 2016-17, which was processed under section 143(1).

■

The case was reopened under section 147 on the ground that an immovable property was purchased for consideration significantly lower than the circle rate, thereby attracting the provision of section 56(2) (viib). The total consideration for the property was about Rs. 4.71 crores against circle rate of about Rs. 9.01 crores; the assessee held a 1/3rd share with consideration of about Rs. 1.57 crores (about Rs. 1.54 crores paid by cheque and about Rs. 2.92 lakhs as TDS). On the assessee’s request disputing circle rate vis-à-vis FMV, the Assessing Officer referred the matter to the DVO, who in his valuation report, ascertained the FMV of the said property at Rs. 5.16 crores, accounting for 1/3rd share of the assessee, the FMV was arrived at Rs. 1.72 crores.

■

The Assessing Officer issued notice calling for explanation on applicability of section 56(2)(viib) and considered the assessee’s response, applied the amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 (treated as retrospective), and accepted that a variation below 10 per cent between the sale consideration and the DVO-determined value should be ignored, thereby accepting the returned income. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer completed the assessment at total income of Rs. 33.64 lakhs as declared by the assessee.

■

The Principal Commissioner invoked section 263, holding that Circular No. 8/2018 applied prospectively from assessment year 2019-20, and thus the Assessing Officer erred in not adding the difference of Rs.15.14 lakh.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The Assessing Officer noted that the difference of the FMV as determined by the DVO and the amount paid by the assessee was Rs. 15.14 lakhs (Rs. 1.72 crores - Rs. 1.57 crores) and the said difference between the actual consideration and FMV as determined by the DVO was less than 10 per cent. The Assessing Officer thereafter, considering the amendment to section 50C and CBDT Circular No. 8/2018 in line with pronouncements of various Courts and Tribunals, which held that when the margin between the actual consideration and the value ascertained by Departmental valuer was less than 10 per cent, noted that the said difference is liable to be ignored, for the purpose of Assessment. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer accepted the total income as declared by the assessee. [Para 9]

■

The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture of air-compressors, garage equipment, hydraulic presses, etc., for which purpose it imported certain components and raw materials. Besides paying the invoice price, it incurred customs duty, freight and handling charges. The accounting year under appeal was the calender year ending on 31-12-1960. For the financial year ending on 31-12-1959, the value of the closing stock, which became opening stock on 1-1-1960 included an ad hoc amount for customs duty and other charges. However, the valuation of closing stock was made without adding customs duty, freight and handling charges for the year ending 31-12-1960. The ITO held such valuation to be defective and, accordingly, made an addition thereon. The ITO made another addition on coming into possession of a letter in which it was found that the foreign principals from whom the assessee purchased components and other material had given a credit in a statement of account sent by them to the assessee which had not been accounted for in the assessee’s books. On appeal, the AAC held that the customs duty, freight and handling charges paid ought to have been included in the value of the closing stock. The AAC also confirmed the addition on account of the credits on the ground that all the credits on account of the purchases had not been accounted for. On second appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the decision of the AAC in respect of the under-valuation of the closing stock observing that both the opening stock and the closing stock should be valued on the same principle, i.e., the market value or the cost, whichever was lower, and that the opening stock could not be valued in a manner different from the valuation of the closing stock. In respect of the addition on account of failure to account for the credit note, the Tribunal held that the question was as to whether the original account given by the foreign party was to be believed or the subsequent account given by it reversing the said entry was to be believed and that the ITO should have probed that matter a little more in detail instead of relying on the first letter, however, since the assessee had not satisfactory explained the credit note and there was failure to account for it in the account books, the addition was to be upheld.

Since, the statute has not provided for such consequence, the executive cannot order the recovery of the amount only for the reason, that the application for waiver of pre-deposit has not been decided by the Appellate Authorities. [Para 38] Under section 35F, the Appellate Authority has a power to waive or reduce the amount of pre-deposit, but such power is sought to be taken away only if the Commissioner (Appeals) is not able to decide the application for stay within 30 days. Such a condition is relevant and meaningful, if the Central Government is in a position to ensure that all appeals and/or the applications for dispensation of duty demanded and penalty levied can be decided within a period of 30 days. [Para 39]

If the Central Government has no power to control the working of the Appellate Authorities and also to ensure that all appeals are decided within the time frame, such condition is wholly unwarranted. The assessee has also no control over such Authorities. The Commissioner (Appeals), a quasi-judicial Tribunal, has a jurisdiction to waive the condition of pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied, but such judicial discretion vested in the Authority under the Act cannot be interfered with in any manner administratively. [Para 39]

Since the statute confers a right of appeal on the assessee and also right to make an application to dispense with deposit of the duty demanded and penalty levied in the manner which the Appellate Authority deems appropriate. Therefore, unless such jurisdiction is exercised by the Appellate Authority either way i.e., to grant benefit of waiver or impose such conditions as it may consider appropriate, the Board cannot direct the Administrative Officers to recover the demand raised against the assessee. The statutory right of appeal or of consideration of an application for pre-deposit cannot be frustrated administratively. [Para 40]

An aggrieved party such as an assessee could only file appeal along with an application for waiver of the pre-deposit. It is, thereafter, for the public functionary i.e., Commissioner (Appeals) or the Tribunal to pass an order on such appeal and/or application. The decision on appeal and on application is not within the power and control of the assessee, but depends upon the acts of public functionary. The provisions of a statute relate to performance of a public duty. The failure of the Appellate Authority to decide appeal and/or application would work serious general inconvenience or injustice to persons who have no control over those entrusted with the duty. [Para 41]

The Commissioner (Appeals) is discharging a public duty and that failure to decide an application for waiver of deposit would lead to serious injustice to the assessee, who has no control over the Commissioner (Appeals), who is entrusted with the duty to decide such application. Therefore, such provision is only directory. [Para 43]

Basis on which Circular was issued was arbitrary - Condition of recovery pending stay application read down - Recovery only if delay in disposition is due to fault of assessee :

The Circular was purportedly issued in terms of judgment in Collector of Customs v. Krishna Sales (P.) Ltd. 1994 (73) ELT 519 (SC). The said judgment lays down that mere filing of an appeal does not operate as stay or suspension of the order appealed against. But the Board over-looked the fact that the assessee is not seeking stay only on account of filing of an appeal, but for the reason that the assessee has sought dispensing with the pre-deposit of duty demanded and penalty levied and has a right to demand decision on such application, the right which is created by the statute. Therefore, the very basis of the Circular is untenable, misconceived, wholly illegal and arbitrary. Therefore, the condition of recovery, if no stay is granted within 30 days, is illegal, arbitrary, unjustified and consequently set aside. [Para 44]

Right of consideration in appeal and on an application for waiver of pre-deposit, is a right conferred by the statute and such right cannot be defeated on the basis of Circular, which contemplates that the recovery can be effected, is stay is not granted within 30 days. Therefore, such condition in the Circular is not legal and is therefore set aside with the observation that till such time, the application for waiver of pre-deposit is decided in an appeal filed in terms of the statute, the revenue shall not proceed to recover the same provided that the assessee does not delay the hearing of the appeal directly or indirectly. In the event, the assessee is delaying the decision, the revenue shall be at liberty to move an application before the Commissioner (Appeals) to take the application for waiver of pre-deposit and seek orders thereon in accordance with law. If such an application is filed by the revenue, the Commissioner (Appeals) shall decide the same expeditiously. [Para 46]

FACT: Under the provisions of he Customs Act 1962, the assessee was entitled to pay import duty at concessional rates on spare parts and tools if their value did not exceed 10 per cent of the total value of imported machinery, but if the value exceeded this percentage, he was required to pay duty at higher rates. Section 143 of the Customs Act, 1962, also permitted the assessee to execute a bond, agreeing to pay the difference in duty when demanded by the customs authorities. For the assessment years 1973-74 to 1976-77, the assessee had executed such a bond and imported goods on which only provisional assessments at concessional rates of duty had been made by the customs department and the assessee had also paid duty at such conces-sional rates only. However, since the value of the imported goods exceeded the specified percentage, the assessee made provision in its accounts towards additional customs duty payable, and claimed it as a deduction. The ITO disallowed the claim since no demand had been raised by the customs department. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the claim.

On second appeal:

HELD: In T.M. Abdul Rahim Sahib & Co. v. CIT [1963] 50 ITR 508 , the Madras High Court had held that there can be no liability either notional or legal unless and until a demand had been made by the appropriate authority.

In view of the provisions of section 143 of the Customs Act, the liability for the payment of additional duty arises only when final assessment has been made. The words used in section 143 are 'notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or such other law'. Irrespective of the other provisions in the Act or any other law or item 72A of the Indian Customs and Central Excise Tariff, once a bond is executed under section 143, it is the terms of that bond that would prevail and the other provisions of the Act or any other law or tariff would not be applicable. After the provisional assessment is made, additional liability will arises only when final assessment is made and final demand is raised. Till then there is no liability for additional duty.

Consequently, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in allowing the assessee's claim.

Other points in provisional assessment

6. The other points that may be considered in respect of provisional assessment under the Customs Act are as follows:

Whether the customs authorities are having discretion to make provisional assessment? Whether the provisional assessment can be claimed as a right?

The case of Sachin Bhupendra Desai v. Union of India 2009 (240) ELT 360 (Cal.) gives answers to the said questions. It was held that -

In the event the petitioner satisfied the Customs Authorities for exercise of their jurisdiction or power under Section 18 for the purpose of provisional assessment of duty, the Customs authorities should adjudicate the matter and decide the same in accordance with the law. The order cannot be construed to be a mandatory direction for release of goods upon making provisional assessment;

Various circumstances have been laid down in Section 18(1) of the Customs Act, and on satisfaction of any one of the said conditions, the Customs authorities have been vested with the discretion to make provisional assessment;

Thus, it is clear that-

The customs authorities have been vested with the discretion to make provisional assessment;

The assessee cannot claim the provisional assessment as right unless he fulfils the conditions for seeking provisional assessment.

Finalization of provisional assessment

7. The provisional assessments are expected to be finalized expeditiously, well within six months. However, in respect of cases involving machinery contracts or large project imports, where imports take place over long period, such finalization may take more time since action can be taken only after all the imports have been made. However, effort should be made to finalize the case within six months of the date of import of the last consignment covered by the contract.

In Sigma Power Productivity Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner of Customs 2014 (304) ELT 19 (Cal.) the customs authorities raised a reasonable doubt as to the transaction value shown in the Bill of Entry at the time of import. The petitioner prayed for a provisional release of the said goods. Since no steps were taken by the authorities, the petitioner approached the High Court. The High Court directed the Department to make a provisional assessment within the specified time and the petitioner was directed to deposit with the authorities the customs duty payable on the value declared by them and also to furnish a bank guarantee of the differential duty after the provisional assessment was made by the Customs authorities and in addition thereto would also submit the P.D. Bond.

The directions of the Court were complied with both by the Department and assessee. After that no steps were taken for the final assessment. The Court directed the department to activate themselves in determining the value under Rule 12 of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 and to make a final assessment, after adhering to the statutory procedures and the norms and to see that the principles of Natural Justice were not violated.

Procedure for final assessment

8. In Saurastra Cement Ltd. v. CCE, Hamnagar - 2013 (297) ELT 365 (Tri. - Ahd.) the finalization of assessment should have been done by the details of Bill of Entry such as-

Bill of Entry number;

Date of bill of Entry;

Duty provisionally assessed;

Duty finally assessed; and

The difference payable or refundable.

Section 18 is relevant which provides that when the duty leviable on such goods is assessed finally in accordance with the provisions of this Act, then in the case of goods cleared for home consumption or exportation, the amount paid shall be adjusted against the duty finally assessed and if the amount so paid falls short of or is in excess of the duty finally assessed, the importer or the exporter of the goods shall pay the deficiency or be entitled to the refund, as the case may be. The Assessing Officer has to indicate the amount paid and adjusted. In the absence of such details the letter issued cannot be considered as an order finalizing the assessment.

see sells their goods directly to the customers through sales depots spread throughout the country. The assessment was framed on a provisional basis including the cost of free PDI and ASS in the transaction value for levy of excise duty. The assessee filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) against the order which was allowed and the case was remanded back. The department filed an appeal against the order before the CESTAT which was also rejected. The matter went to the Apex Court for consideration. The Apex Court looked into the detailed history of litigations and provisions applicable prior to year 2000 and post 2000 when the new valuation rules were introduced. The Apex Court placed reliance on several decisions and in-particular the decision in the case of Philips India Ltd.v. Collector of Central Excise 1997 taxmann.com 1239 wherein deduction of the cost incurred towards advertisement expenses and free ASS during guarantee period provided by dealers to the product of Philips under agreement was allowed. The court also placed reliance on the judgment of this vary court in the case of Commissioner v.Telco Ltd. 2001 (130) ELT A260 (SC), wherein the Apex Court has affirmed the view of the Tribunal holding that when goods are sold to independent dealers at arm's length, payment directly made by the manufacturer for labour ASS to additional service centres arranged by the manufacturer and subsequent recovery of such expenses by the manufacturer from the dealer, is not a case of flow-back of additional consideration nor does such an arrangement make such dealer an agent of the assessee.

Placing reliance on the above judicial precedents, the Apex Court held that PDI and ASS charges would not be included in the assessable value under section 4 of the Act for the purposes of paying excise duty. The Apex Court observed that where manufacturer himself does the ASS and incurs any expenditure thereon, the same is not deductible from the price charged by him from his buyer. However, where the manufacturer has sold his goods to his dealer and wholesale dealer thereafter does ASS to the customer and incurs expenditure therefore, it cannot be added back to the sale price charged by the manufacturer from the dealer for computing the assessable value. This is more so, where the ASS is done by the dealer many weeks after the goods have been sold to him by the manufacturer. Such a post-sale activity undertaken by the dealer is not relevant for the purpose of excise since the goods have already been marketed to the dealer.

The Apex Court overruled the judgment of Larger Bench in Maruti Suzuki India Ltd.'s case (supra) and quashed the circulars which provided for inclusion of PDI and ASS charges in the assessable/transaction value for levy of excise duty.

Comments

5. The judgment of Apex Court has put to rest the long drawn ambiguity in the matter pertaining to inclusion of PDI and ASS in the transaction/assessable value. It is noteworthy that this ruling puts to rest the ambiguity that got erupted again in the backdrop of legislative developments made vide amendment in section 4 of CEA which defined 'transaction value' as price actually paid or payable by the buyer including additional amount that the buyer is liable to pay or on behalf of the assessee by reason of sale or in connection of sale whether payable at the time of sale or at any other time including the amount charged for or to make provision for certain items such as advertising, servicing etc.

Conclusion

6. In light of the recent Apex Court ruling restoring the old thought process with respect to non-inclusion of cost of PDI and ASS borne by the dealer in the transaction/assessable value for levy of excise duty, the automobile industry might just find a ray of hope at the end of the tunnel.

This judgment is certainly a push back to the department after the admission of their Special Leave Petition by Hon'ble Apex Court against the order of Bombay High Court in Tata Motors Ltd.'s case (supra). However, considering the history wherein we have seen the law being amended to nullify decisions of Apex Court to prevail department's view, it will be no surprise that the Government in the ensuing budget may make necessary amendments in section 4 of the CEA to bring back the taxability of PDI and ASS within the ambit of transaction value which may again start a new array of controversies in this matter.

As we know, India is on the verge of a change in indirect tax regime from present complex tax structure to more simplified Goods and Services Tax regime. At this juncture, it is important for Government to take note of such issues and have clear guidelines to avoid possible litigation on such aspects under the proposed GST regime.
