M.S. Prasad*

In Caprihans India Ltd. v. Prakash Chandra [2002] 122 Taxman 862 (Bom.), the company filed the return along with its accounts and audit report. It was mentioned in the notes on accounts that excise duty on finished goods manufactured, and customs duty on raw material imported, which were both lying in the bonded warehouse, were not claimed as liabilities and, therefore, not included in the value of the closing stock. Later, the assessment was reopened on the ground that the taxable event was the manufacture of an excisable article and so the excise and customs duty were includible in the valuation of the closing stock. The High Court held that the reassessment was bad. It held that when the method of accounting followed by the assessee had been accepted by the revenue for subsequent years and duty liability on the bonded goods crystallised only on the date of ex-bounding, it could not be said that there was any reason to believe that any income had escaped assessment. The author of this article discusses the question of valuation of inventories lying in bonded warehouse in the context of the above decision - EDITOR

HELD: It is a well settled legal proposition that where an alternative remedy is available, the High Court would ordinarily not exercise powers under article 226 of the Constitution of India. However, it is equally true that there is no absolute proposition of law that where an alternative remedy is available, the High Court would refuse to exercise powers under article 226 of the Constitution even if the facts so justify. Non-entertainment of petitions under writ jurisdiction by the High Court when an efficacious alternative remedy is available is a rule of self-imposed limitation. It is essentially a rule of policy, convenience and discretion rather than a rule of law. Undoubtedly, it is within the discretion of the High Court to grant relief under article 226 despite the existence of an alternative remedy. However, the High Court must not interfere if there is an adequate efficacious alternative remedy available to the assessee and he has approached the High Court without availing the same unless he has made out an exceptional case warranting such interference or there exist sufficient grounds to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction under article 226. Some exceptions to the rule of alternative remedy are where the statutory authority has not acted in accordance with the provisions of the enactment in question, or in defiance of the fundamental principles of judicial procedure, or has resorted to invoke the provisions which are repealed, or when an order has been passed in total violation of the principles of natural justice. [Para 10]

In the present case, it is the case of the assessee that the adjudicating authority has not acted in accordance with the provisions of the Customs Act and in defiance of the law laid down by the jurisdictional High Court. On the facts as emerging from the record, and for the reasons that follow, this Court is of the view that the availability of an alternative statutory remedy of appeal, would not preclude the Court from entertaining this writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. [Para 12]

This principle is not new, but it has seldom been expressed with such clarity and force. The CESTAT traced the issue back to the basic structure of tax law, relying on Justice G.P. Singh’s Principles of Statutory Interpretation, which explains that taxation ordinarily involves three distinct stages: first, the creation of a tax liability; second, the assessment of that liability to determine the amount payable; and third, the recovery of the assessed amount if it is not paid voluntarily. The mere occurrence of a taxable event does not, by itself, make a tax or duty immediately recoverable. In the context of customs law, the duty must first be assessed under the statutory procedure prescribed in Sections 17 and 18 of the Customs Act, 1962, or determined through adjudication proceedings. Only thereafter can it be recovered. Where Parliament intends tax to be collected before assessment, it expressly provides for such a mechanism, as seen in the case of advance tax and tax deducted at source (TDS) under the income-tax laws. The Customs Act contains no comparable provision.

As the CESTAT precisely observed, any amount obtained from an assessee before assessment or adjudication occupies a distinct legal character. Although the money is in the State’s possession, it is not customs duty in the eyes of law. It remains a deposit held by the State in trust until the liability is properly determined, with the State acting merely as a custodian rather than as the owner of the funds.

Deposit vs. Duty: A distinction with profound consequences

The CESTAT’s order places considerable emphasis on the distinction between a deposit and duty—and for good reasons. Although the difference may appear technical at first glance, it carries important legal and financial consequences.

The distinction between a deposit and duty has been repeatedly recognised by the courts. The Madras High Court in Global United Shipping India Pvt. Ltd.2 explained that a deposit is an amount paid pending the determination of liability to safeguard the Revenue’s interests, whereas duty arises only after a statutory assessment crystallises the liability. The Delhi High Court in EBIZ.COM Pvt. Ltd.3 reinforced this principle, holding that money deposited during an investigation retains its character as a deposit even if it is temporarily appropriated towards a demand that is later set aside. In such cases, the State merely holds the money as a custodian and does not acquire it as duty.

The CESTAT in EMD Locomotive Technologies (supra) carried this principle to its logical conclusion. It held that where an amount was not duty when it was paid—because no liability had yet been assessed—it cannot later be converted into duty by a mere change in the department’s characterisation. Neither the issuance of a show cause notice nor the passing of an adjudication order can retrospectively alter the true nature of the payment. This finding has significant practical consequences. It prevents the department from artificially splitting investigation-stage deposits into “pre-deposit” and “duty” components and then using that distinction to restrict or vary the assessee’s entitlement to interest.

The entire deposit must be treated as pre-deposit

The CESTAT held that where an amount deposited during investigation exceeds the mandatory pre-deposit requirement and remains with the Department, the entire amount must be treated as a pre-deposit. The Department cannot arbitrarily classify only 7.5% or 10% as a pre-deposit and treat the balance as duty, since it has no legal right to recover that amount as duty while the appeal is pending. The CESTAT also rejected the Department’s reliance on CBIC Circular No. 984/8/2014-CX dated 16.9.2014, holding that an administrative circular cannot override the statute or binding judicial precedents, and describing the circular’s contrary view as ‘misplaced and unsustainable in law’.

Although the CESTAT has not recorded any specific finding on the vires of the CBIC Circular No. 984/8/2014-CX dated 16.9.2014, it appears to have the effect of implicitly overruling the same. It is anticipated that subsequent judicial pronouncements may address the matter with greater clarity and specificity. In any event, it is well settled that departmental circulars are not binding on the CESTAT in the exercise of its adjudicatory functions.

Interest is not a concession: It is compensatory in nature

There is a broader constitutional and equitable basis for requiring the state to pay interest when it refunds the amount deposited by an assessee. The Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in RHL Profiles Ltd.4, relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in Tata Chemicals Ltd5, and held that the state cannot retain and use money to which it was never lawfully entitled without compensating the person deprived of it. The payment of interest is therefore not a matter of legislative generosity; it is an essential component of restoring the assessee to the position it would have occupied had the money not been wrongly retained.

The Supreme Court reinforced this principle in Pratibha Processors6, holding that interest is compensatory in nature and is intended to make good the loss suffered on account of delayed return of the money. Accordingly, when an assessee succeeds and a refund is eventually sanctioned, interest from the date of deposit is not a windfall but compensation for the period during which the assessee was deprived of its funds.

FACT: Facts

The assessee was engaged in the manufacture of pig iron.

During the period June 1998 to August 1998, the assessee imported Low Ash Metallurgical (LAM) Coke under seven Bills of Entry, against four advance licenses without payment of —

basic customs duty (BCD) levied under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962,

special customs duty (SCD) levied under section 68 of the Finance Act, 1996,

special additional duty (SAD) levied under section 3A of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975, and

anti-dumping duty (ADD) levied under section 9A of Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

The department sought to deny exemptions on failure to fulfil export obligation.

Pending final adjudication of notice by the Commissioner, the assessee duly paid the entire duty payable towards BCD, SAD and SCD after considering partial exports already made. The assessee did not make any payment towards ADD.

The department confirmed duty demands along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent as per bond.

Tribunal enhanced ADD as per revised notification but reduced interest to 15 per cent.

The assessee challenged Anti-dumping duty, interest and penalty and other computations.

Assessee's Arguments

Basic customs duty and the special customs duty as well as special additional duty was payable by the assessee.

However, anti-dumping duty was not payable at all, as assessee was exempt under Notification No. 69 of 2000.

Notification No. 30 of 1997 did not stipulate that in the event of default, interest would become payable; hence, interest was not payable.

Since assessment was provisional, there was no provision for collection of interest for the period in dispute as section 18 was amended to include such a provision only prospectively with effect from 2006.

In any case, Anti-dumping duty could not be added for purposes of computing customs duty, special customs duty and special additional duty.

Also no penalty is imposable inasmuch as nothing contumacious was done by the assessee and the export obligation could not be fulfilled only because of bona fide commercial impossibility.

Since appeal before Tribunal was filed by assessee, he could not be worse off in an appeal filed only by the assessee herein to CESTAT and that on the assumption that the assessee was liable to pay anti-dumping duty, they should only pay the said duty at the lower rate prescribed by the Commissioner as revenue had not appealed to the Tribunal against the Commissioner's order.

Revenue's Arguments

The exemption contained in Anti-dumping duty Notification 69 of 2000 was only prospective and, hence Anti-dumping duty had to be paid for the relevant period.

Interest was payable as Notification No. 30 of 1997 independently levied a charge of interest.

Order of Tribunal was correct in law.

4.1 Departmental clarification regarding 'place of removal' in case of exports – CBE&C, videcircular No. 999/6/2015-CX, dated 28-2-2015 has clarified as follows –

In case of goods cleared by manufacturer exporter, transfer of property takes place when goods are handed over to shipping line. In that case, port/ICD/CFS will be the place of removal.

In case of export through merchant exporter, normally, property in goods passes to merchant exporter at the factory gate. Hence, that will be normally place of removal. However, in isolated cases, the port/ICD/CFS can be place of removal depending on facts of the case.

4.2 Validity of case law and departmental circular, after decision of Supreme Court – Though issue has become litigation prone, it can be argued that Supreme Court has only held that place of buyer cannot be 'place of removal'. Port is not the place of buyer. It can also be argued that port is a place 'referable to manufacturer', as the manufacturer continues to be owner of goods till goods are loaded in ship.

It can also be argued that when two interpretations are possible, an interpretation which promotes exports and which is beneficial to assessee should be adopted.

In any case, whatever assessee decides, it is advisable to inform department.

It is to be understood that no cost or value of the elements referred to in this paragraph shall be counted twice in determining the computed value.

4. The "amount for profit and general expenses" referred to in clause (b) of rule 8 is to be determined on the basis of information supplied by or on behalf of the producer unless the producer's figures are inconsistent with those usually reflected in sales of goods of the same class or kind as the goods being valued which are made by producers in the country of exportation for export to India.

5. It should be noted in this context that the "amount for profit and general expenses" has to be taken as a whole. It follows that if, in any particular case, producer's profit figure is low and his general expenses are high, the producer's profit and general expenses taken together may nevertheless be consistent with that usually reflected in sales of goods of the same class or kind. Such a situation might occur, for example, if a product were being launched in India and the producer accepted a nil or low profit to offset high general expenses associated with the launch. Where the producer can demonstrate a low profit on his sales of the imported goods because of particular commercial circumstances, his actual profit figures should be taken into account provided that he has valid commercial reasons to justify them and his pricing policy reflects usual pricing policies in the branch of industry concerned. Such a situation might occur for example, where producers have been forced to lower prices temporarily because of an unforeseeable drop in demand, or where they sell goods to complement a range of goods being produced in India and accept a low profit to maintain competitivity. Where the producer's own figures for profit and general expenses are not consistent with those usually reflected in sales of goods of the same class or kind as the goods being valued which are made by producers in the country of exportation for export to India, the amount for profit and general expenses may be based upon relevant information other than that supplied by or on behalf of the producer of the goods.

6. The "general expenses" referred to in clause (b) of rule 8 covers the direct and indirect costs of producing and selling the goods for export which are not included under clause (a) of rule 8.

7. Whether certain goods are "of the same class or kind" as other goods must be determined on a case-by-case basis with reference to the circumstances involved. In determining the usual profits and general expenses under the provisions of rule 8, sales for export to India of the narrowest group or range of goods, which includes the goods being valued, for which the necessary information can be provided, should be examined. For the purposes of rule 8 "goods of the same class or kind" must be from the same country as the goods being valued.

Rule 3(3)

1. Rule 3(3)(a) and rule 3(3)(b) provide different means of establishing the acceptability of a transaction value. 2. Rule 3(3)(a) provides that where the buyer and the seller are related, the circumstances surrounding the sale shall be examined and the transaction value shall be accepted as the value of imported goods provided that the relationship did not influence the price. It is not intended that there should be an examination of the circumstances in all cases where the buyer and the seller are related. Such examination will only be required where there are doubts about the acceptability of the price. Where the proper officer of customs has no doubts about the acceptability of the price, it should be accepted without requesting further information from the importer. For example, the proper officer of customs may have previously examined the relationship, or he may already have detailed information concerning the buyer and the seller, and may already be satisfied from such examination or information that the relationship did not influence the price.

3. Where the proper officer of customs is unable to accept the transaction value without further inquiry, he should give the importer an opportunity to supply such further detailed information as may be necessary to enable him to examine the circumstances surrounding the sale. In this context, the proper officer of customs should be prepared to examine relevant aspects of the transaction, including the way in which the buyer and seller organize their commercial relations and the way in which the price in question was arrived at, in order to determine whether the relationship influenced the price. Where it can be shown that the buyer and seller, although related under the provisions of rule 2(2), buy from and sell to each other as if they were not related, this would demonstrate that the price had not been influenced by the relationship. As an example of this, if the price had been settled in a manner consistent with the normal pricing practices of the industry in question or with the way the seller settles prices for sales to buyers who are not related to him, this would demonstrate that the price had not been influenced by the relationship. As a further example, where it is shown that the price is adequate to ensure recovery of all costs plus a profit which is representative of the firm's overall profit realized over a representative period of time (e.g. on an annual basis) in sales of goods of the same class or kind, this would demonstrate that the price had not been influenced.

4. Rule 3(3)(b) provides an opportunity for the importer to demonstrate that the transaction value closely approximates to a "test" value previously accepted by the proper officer of customs and is therefore acceptable under the provisions of rule 3. Where a test under rule 3(3)(b) is met, it is not necessary to examine the question of influence under rule 3(3)(a). If the proper officer of customs has already sufficient information to be satisfied, without further detailed inquiries, that one of the tests provided in rule 3(3)(b) has been met, there is no reason for him to require the importer to demonstrate that the test can be met. In rule 3(3)(b) the term "unrelated buyers" means buyers who are not related to the seller in any particular case.

Rule 3(3)(b)

A number of factors must be taken into consideration in determining whether one value "closely approximates" to another value. These factors include the nature of the imported goods, the nature of the industry itself, the season in which the goods are imported, and whether the difference in values is commercially significant. Since these factors may vary from case to case, it would be impossible to apply a uniform standard such as a fixed percentage, in each case. For example, a small difference in value in a case involving one type of goods could be unacceptable while a large difference in a case involving another type of goods might be acceptable in determining whether the transaction value closely approximates to the "test" values set forth in rule 3(3)(b).

PROCEDURE

Law applicable - If during the pendency of appeal, law is amended retrospectively, the amended law is to be applied by the authority deciding the appeal/reference [CIT v. Straw Products Ltd. [1966] 60 ITR 156 (SC)].

Raising objection as to delay in filing appeal - If an appeal by an assessee is admitted without the fact of delay in its presentation having been noticed, it is open to the department to raise the objection at the time of hearing of the appeal [Mela Ram & Sons v. CIT [1956] 29 ITR 607 (SC)].

Reference to Valuation Officer - Where reference to Valuation Cell is made, Commissioner (Appeals) is not required to give an opportunity of hearing to Valuation Officer during appellate proceedings before accepting valuation of assets disclosed by assessee [CIT v. Dr. C. Ashokan Nambniar [2000] 111 Taxman 431 (Ker.)].

Speaking order - A speaking order on merits with reasons and findings is to be passed by CIT(A) on basis of ground raised in assessee's appeal; he cannot dispose assessee's appeal merely by holding that AO's order is a self-speaking order which requires no interference [Ajji Basha v. CIT [2019] 111 taxmann.com 348/267 Taxman 545 (Mad.)].

PRODUCTION OF ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE [RULE 46A]

Constitutional validity - Rule 46A does not affect power of CIT(A) conferred upon him by section 250 or section 251 and, therefore, Rule is not ultra vires sections 250 and 251 [Smt. Mohindar Kaur v. Central Government [1976] 104 ITR 120 (All.)].

Applicability - Rule 46A applies when there is additional evidence and not when there is affidavit reiterating submissions [CIT v. Central Mall [2011] 12 taxmann.com 414/202 Taxman 268 (P&H)].

Essential requisites - As per Rule 46A(1), (2) and (3), if additional evidence is permitted to be produced, then firstly there must be reasons to be recorded in writing and, secondly, reasonable opportunity has to be given to assessing authority to refute and reject such production. Rule 46A(4) does not permit to do away with procedural law prescribed under the foregoing rules, once additional evidence is produced. Where, before assessing authority, assessee failed to adduce any sort of evidence to prove sale proceeds of utensils received by him but at appellate stage, appellate authority, without recording any valid or plausible reason and without giving any opportunity of hearing to revenue, allowed assessee to produce xerox copy of sale proceeds as additional evidence, appellate authority acted in violation of Rule 46A [CIT v. Ranjit Kumar Choudhury [2007] 162 Taxman 257 (Gau.)].

CIT(A) is under statutory obligation to put any additional material/evidence taken on record by him to AO before making any decision adverse to him on basis of that material [CIT v. United Towers (I) (P.) Ltd. [2008] 172 Taxman 267 (Delhi)]. Also see, CIT v. E. D. Benny [2015] 62 taxmann.com 302/234 Taxman 802 (Ker.).

Rule 46A(3) is a mandatory provision and non-compliance of same would vitiate order itself. Where assessee had produced additional evidence before CIT(A) not on direction of CIT(A) but by itself and CIT(A), on being satisfied with assessee's explanation regarding non-production of that evidence before AO, had permitted assessee to lead evidence in terms of Rule 46A(3), he was bound to give an opportunity to AO to examine documents and to produce any evidence to contrary, if he so desired [CIT v. Shri Kangra Steel (P.) Ltd. [2010] 188 Taxman 392 (HP)].

Admission of additional evidence could not be stated to be in breach of requirement of Rule 46A particularly when interest of revenue was safeguarded by calling for remand report and permitting AO to comment on such additional evidence [CIT v. Kamlaben Sureshchandra Bhatti [2014] 44 taxmann.com 459 (Guj.)].

the 'cost of transportation'. It is observed that what is includible in the cost of transportation as transit insurance is the premium paid to an insurance company for the possible loss and not the payment made to the customers for breakages and losses which cannot tantamount to insurance. In the instant case the amount is collected from the buyers to compensate the loss due to breakages, in addition to the premium paid to the insurance companies, hence, ought to form part of the value. [Para 24] Analysing the sample invoices, placed before the Bench by the appellant, after conclusion of hearing, for the relevant period 1999 to 2005, reveal that the appellant has shown an amount as 'cost of transportation' separately, in their respective invoices. There is no mention about 7 per cent of the charge as per Agreement, but on scrutiny of the said transportation cost, it is observed that part amount of the freight charge was paid in advance by the appellants and balance amount was required to be paid by the buyer on reaching destination; remaining amount shown in the cost of transportation, which they claim as 7 per cent of the total value of the goods inclusive of cost of packing charge, freight charge etc. Thus, in it is immaterial whether the deduction is claimed by including the said 7 per cent charge in the total price, or the same is shown separately, without including it in the assessable value but on merit to be added to the assessable value. The question for consideration is, whether the amount collected, for compensating the customers towards breakage of glass, during the course of transit, to be added to the assessable value, or otherwise. The Supreme Court, in Surya Roshni Ltd.'s case (supra) while considering the deductibility of the insurance amount, collected other than the premium paid to the insurance company towards loss/breakage of glass during transit observed that it is only the premium amount to be excluded and not the amount collected for compensating the customers in the event the goods are damaged/lost during transit. [Para 26]

In the instant case, it is not the excess amount of insurance charges collected and retained by the appellant but the amount has been collected as compensation for breakages during the course of transit by way of issuing credit notes. [Para 28]

The next issue that needs to be considered is, whether the demand issued for the period from 1-2-1999 to 30-9-2004 is barred by limitation as the demand notice was issued on 26-2-2004. It is the contention of the appellant is that the issue of inclusion or otherwise the insurance charges at the rate of 8 per cent of the price was placed through the letter dated 28-5-1994. A show cause notice was issued to them proposing demand of duty on Special packing and transit insurance. Thereafter two notices were issued to the appellant. The notices were adjudicated on 30-8-1995 allowing deduction on transit insurance on actual basis after verification by the Range Superintendent. After introduction of the new valuation provision, the appellant, informed through letter dated 31-7-2000 the method of computation of transaction value. Further, he has submitted that through their letter dated 21-2-1997, 11-11-1998, 6-10-1999 and 20-2-2001 they have submitted to the Department showing the deductions towards freight, octroi, breakage insurance, which were supported by Chartered Accountant's certificate. [Para 29]

From the above facts it is clear that the appellant had initially claimed 8 per cent of the Price being insurance charges, not part of the assessable value, but the Assistant Commissioner restricted the claim to the extent of actual expenses, while finalizing the provisional assessment and confirming the demands for differential duty short paid. The said practice of assessment followed for subsequent years on the basis of statements filed by the appellant showing the difference between the amount shown on the invoices and the actual expenditure incurred towards transit insurance. It is the contention of the revenue that such statements were not filed during the relevant period, hence, the extended period of limitation is invokable. There is no merit in the contention of the revenue, inasmuch as they do not lack the authority in directing submission of such statements to the appellant even though the said statement was not submitted for four years. Once the facts are within the knowledge of the Department, being always in dispute, hence the allegation that they had suppressed the facts from the knowledge of the Department, cannot be acceptable. In view of above, demand in the show cause notice dated 26-2-2004 be restricted to the normal period of limitation. [Para 30]

when the respondent pays duty at the time of clearance of goods, the duty is paid on the correct assessable value and correct rate of duty and there is no question of any short payment of duty at the material time and since the respondents have no means and knowledge that price of goods will increase, the assessee could not be faulted for not paying the duty at the clearance of goods. Since there is no suppression of fact or fraud, the assessee cannot be held liable to pay the duty. But the Tribunal of Ahmedabad in the case of Inducto Casts (supra) has a contrary view and held that an assessee has to pay the interest either way he chooses, i.e., if he chooses rule 7 (Provisional assessment) he has to pay the interest under rule 7(4) at the time of finalizalion. In such a case, the interest becomes payable from the first day of month succeeding the month for which such amount is determined till the date of payment thereof. Or if he chooses to assess according to transaction value because the valuation in terms of section 4 shall be the transaction value at the time and place of removal and include in addition the amount charged as price, any amount which the buyer is liable to pay to the assessee in connection with the sale, whether payable at the time of sale or any other time. In this case, since there is a price escalation clause, the amount becomes payable at a later point of time and as such the amount payable to the appellant in terms of price escalation is includible as transaction value as defined in section 4(3)(d ). A similar view was taken by the Tribunal of Chennai in the case of Ennore Foundries Ltd. v. CCE Chennai10 wherein it was held that an assessee has to pay interest for the period between the payment of provisional duty and the payment of differential duty on finalisation of provisional assessment.

Recently, the same issue has been decided by the Division Bench of High Court in the case of CCE v. Rucha Engg. (P.) Ltd.11 where it affirmed the earlier order of the Tribunal and has observed as follows :—

"There is nothing to indicate that there was any time-gap between the date on which the revised rates applicable with retrospective effect were learnt by the assessee and the date on which differential duty was paid. Had that been the case, the levy of interest as under section 11AB could have been considered because of delayed payment of duty, but this is the case wherein the assessee upon learning that the rates of the goods cleared were revised/escalated and therefore, they are liable to pay more duty than already paid at the time of clearance of the goods, has voluntarily paid the duty. Thus, there is no delay."

But the Commissioner (Appeals) of Pune in the case of Spicer India Ltd., In re.12 has given a detailed order and has at least clarified two issues, which were wrongly appreciated by the Delhi Tribunal in the cases of Rajasthan Explosive & Chemicals Ltd. (supra) and D.K. Electrics (supra) and held that :—

(i)During the period 28-9-1996 to 10-5-2001, suppression of fact, etc., was prerequisite for invoking interest under section 11AB and also for imposing penalty under section 11AC. For invoking section 11AB or section 11AC, duty was required to be determined under section 11A(2). With effect from 11-5-2001, suppression of fact and, mis-statement was not necessary for invoking section 11AB; whereas they continued to be necessary for invoking penalty under section 11AC.

(ii)With effect from 11-5-2001, payment of duty under section 11A(2B) was also brought under the purview of section 11AB for interest recovery.

The Commissioner (Appeals) refused to follow the Rucha Engg. (P.) Ltd.’s case (supra) on the ground that it was observed by the Commissioner (Appeals) that there was no determination of duty under section 11A(2) and, therefore, provisions of section 11AB were not attracted. It was held that under section 11AB, as it stood prior to 11-5-2001, there was a reference to only section 11A(2); whereas in the section 11AB as it stands now with effect from 11-5-2001 there is a reference of both section 11A(2) and section 11A(2)(b). Therefore, it is clear that the above decisions will not be applicable for interest recovery under section 11AB with effect from 11-5-2001.

The Commissioner (Appeals) had also wrongly misunderstood the decision of the Tribunal that there is no case of any non-payment, short levy or short payment as envisaged under section 11A(1). But observation of the Tribunal of Delhi in the case of D. K. Electrics ( supra) is acceptable to the extent that amount escalation is unforeseen circumstance and beyond the control of the assessee, and if in these circumstances the assessee is not able to pay duty, it cannot be construed to mean that it failed to pay excise duty. Hence, interest cannot be demanded from the assessee under section 11AB of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

The appellants manufacture weighing machines which are sold from their depots in different regions at varying prices. On the appellants quoting the price at Calcutta as the assessable value, the Excise Dept. charged them with mis-declaration as the sale prices at various depots were higher. The Department also claimed that the duty had not been paid on some of the machines removed from the factory. On application under section 256(2) : HELD: There is no controversy about the principle that the opening stock cannot be valued in a manner different from the valuation of the closing stock. Both have to be valued on the basis of the same principle. The opening stock for the year under reference was loaded with the value of the proportionate costs of customs duty, freight and handling charges. The closing stock did not have such an addition made to it. In order to bring the two on the same level, it was necessary to disturb the valuation either of the opening stock or of the closing stock. The Tribunal preferred to disturb the closing stock by valuing it on the same principle according to which the opening stock was valued. The assessee suggested that the customs duty, freight and handling charges should have been deducted from the opening stock, to bring the principle of its valuation in accord with the principle which had been adopted for valuing the closing stock. The adoption of this procedure would have hardly brought about any change in the results and would not have adversely affected the interest of the revenue. It would, on the other hand, have given to the assessee the benefit of avoiding the inconvenience and difficulty of splitting up the charges in question and allocating the same in proper proportions to the numerous components and materials. This would have regularised the assessee's balance-sheets in all the subsequent years. The insistence of the department in disturbing the closing stock instead of the opening stock and the approval to this practice given by the Tribunal did give rise to question of law which could appropriately be referred to the High Court. However, that question did not arise from out of the order of the Tribunal, who never considered the merits or demerits of the alternative procedure of disturbing instead the opening stock on the same basis, on which the closing stock was valued. The suggestion made before the Tribunal by the assessee was to deduct the sum of custom duty, freight etc. from the purchases. There was no suggestion to make a suitable deduction from out of the value of the opening stock, as now suggested. The Tribunal had not applied its mind to the suggestion of a deduction from the opening stock and had said nothing about this in its order. Thus, the question as to whether the Tribunal was justified in law in holding that on no account the opening stock could be revalued to make it consistent with the system adopted for valuation of closing stock, could not be said to arise out of the order of the Tribunal.

Further, the assessee agreed that the opening stock included customs duty and incidental charges. There was, therefore, sufficient material for the Tribunal to hold that the closing stock might necessarily be valued likewise. Thus, the question as to whether there was any material on which the Tribunal could hold that the closing stock might necessarily include the customs duties and incidental charges was not a question which the Tribunal could refer to the High Court.

So far as question regarding credit note was concerned the Tribunal came to its conclusion after assessing the evidence before it. It was competent to determine the sufficiency of the evidence before it. The inference drawn by the Tribunal from the evidence on record was a finding of fact and its refusal to make a reference, as desired by the assessee, called for no interference.

Under those circumstances, there was no merit in the instant petition which, accordingly, was to be dismissed.

There was no dispute about the applicability of section 41(1) in the instant case. The only dispute was when the liability to pay customs duty ceased. In other words, the issue was in which year the benefit in respect of customs duty liability by way of remission or cessation thereof accrued to the assessee and when the amount due to cessation of liability had been obtained by the assessee. The assessee company as well as other newspaper companies had filed writ petitions challenging the levy of customs duty by the Government. The Supreme Court vide order dated 6-12-1984 directed the Government of India to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and refix the rate of customs duty afresh, with effect from 1-3-1981. If on such reconsideration the Government decided that there should be any modification in the levy of customs duty or auxiliary duty with effect from 1-3-1981 it would take necessary steps to implement its decision. Until such redetermination of the liability, the Government was directed to recover only Rs. 550 per MT on imported newsprint towards customs duty and auxiliary duty and would not insist upon payment of duty in accordance with the impugned notifications. It was further stipulated in the Supreme Court’s order that even after such redetermination if it was found that any of the petitioners was liable to pay any deficit amount by way of duty, such deficit amount would be paid by such petitioner within four months from the date on which a notice of demand was served on such petitioner by the concerned authority. It was clear from the above order of the Supreme Court that the Government of India was directed to reconsider within six months the entire question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on newsprint used for printing newspaper, periodicals, etc., with effect from 1-3-1981. Therefore, as on 6-12-1984 the liability of the assessee to pay customs duty, etc., had not ceased because the matter regarding payment of customs duty was to be considered by the Government. As a result of the directions of the Supreme Court, the Government of India had issued notification dated 19-12-1985 and the CBEC also issued a departmental circular on 10-2-1986 determining the customs duty in respect of imported newsprint. It was clear from the notification as well as circular that after examination of the question of levy of customs duty and auxiliary duty on imported newsprint the Government had fixed the rate at Rs. 550 per MT. The notification as well as circular dates fell in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year under consideration, i.e., 1987-88. Therefore, as a result of the notification and circular of the CBEC the assessee’s liability to pay customs duty had ceased in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88. The assessee thus obtained the benefit in respect of customs duty by way of remission or cessation thereof and the amount obtained by it and/or the value of benefit accrued to it had to be deemed as its profits and gains of business for the assessment year 1987-88. The customs authority by issuing the notice of demand had given effect to the notification dated 19-12-1985 issued by the Government of India and Circular dated 10-2-1986 of CBEC. A notice of demand did not have the effect of cessation or remission of liability of the assessee. The liability of an assessee ceased only under Notification dated 19-12-1985 of the Government of India read with circular of the customs authority dated 10-2-1986. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in confirming the addition made to the total income of the assessee for the assessment year 1987-88 after making necessary adjustments regarding claim, if any, disallowed under section 43B earlier while determining the amount assessable.

The benefit in respect of cessation of customs liability by way of remission or cessation thereof had to be taxed in the assessment year 1987-88 because the assessee obtained the benefit in the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1987-88 and if the assessee did not make entry in the relevant accounting year it would not effect operation of the provisions of section 41(1).

Thus, from the circular, it is quite clear that in a case where the sale is on FOB/CIF basis, the place of removal has to be the load port only.

FACT: Facts

The assessee is engaged in ship breaking activity at Alang Ship Breaking Yard. The assessee imported a vessel, namely, M.V. Olinda, for the purpose of breaking the same, and filed a Bill of Entry when the vessel was imported on 7-2-1992.

It declared in the said Bill of Entry that the Light Displacement Tonnage of the vessel was 7009 metric tons.

On 19-2-1992, the assessee was informed by the Superintendent of Customs and Central Excise Alang that the Light Displacement Tonnage of the ship is actually 8570 tons and that customs duty was to be levied on this tonnage.

On 3-3-1992, the assessee cleared the vessel on payment of customs duty on the basis of 7009 metric tons and executed a bank guarantee for Rs.19,90,275/- being the difference in customs duty on 1561 metric tons.

On 25-3-1992, the Collector of Customs, Rajkot, directed the Assistant Collector, Bhavnagar to encash the bank guarantee furnished by the assessee.

On 2-4-1992, the Superintendent of Customs and Central Excise sent a letter to the assessee communicating the decision of the Collector, as aforesaid. The bank guarantee was duly encashed on 3-4-1992.

Steel Corpn. 2003 taxmann.com 1543, the Supreme Court held that since order of Superintendent was passed in pursuance of a policy framed by Collector, it continued to be order of Superintendent and was appealable only before Collector (Appeals) and not Tribunal.

(a)

an information is being sought from an authority outside India through a legal process; or

(b)

an appeal in a similar matter of the same person or any other person is pending before the Appellate Tribunal or the High Court or the Supreme Court; or

Authorities cannot direct importer to forego his statutory right of provisional assessment - Provisional assessment is a statutory right. Authorities cannot direct importer to forego his statutory right of provisional assessment - Century Metal Recycling P Ltd. v. UOI (2019) 367 ELT 3 (SC 3 member bench).

In Tata Chemicals v. CC (2015) 320 ELT 45 (SC), it has been held that customs officer can order testing of samples under section 18(b) of Customs Act only if there are good reasons. Subjective satisfaction of officer is not sufficient. The power given to the officer is not arbitrary power. Further, samples have to be drawn as per specified procedure.

Bond and conditions for provisional assessment - Provisions relating to bond and security have been specified in CBI&C circular No. 38/2016-Cus dated 22-8-2016 amended vide MF(DR) circular No. 19/2021-Cus dated 16-8-2021.

In case relating to determination of origin under FTAs based on reasonable belief that the matter involves mis-declaration of origin, bond with 100% of differential duty as security is required. In other cases, Principal Commissioner/Commissioner may reduce the amount of security or remove it completely for provisional assessment. In case of import by AEO-T3, security is not required - CBI&C circular No. 38/2016-Cus dated 22-8-2016 amended vide MF(DR) circular No. 19/2021-Cus dated 16-8-2021.

The bond should be with security, to pay the difference between the duty that may be finally assessed or re-assessed and the provisional duty. The security can be either bank guarantee or cash deposit, as convenient to exporter. In some cases, no security is required, only bond is sufficient.

Then, the proper officer may assess the duty on the goods provisionally at an amount equal to the provisional duty.

The bond is called as 'P D Bond' (Provisional Duty Bond). The bond is with security. Bank guarantee can also be given as a security.

The PD bond should be 20% of provisional duty. Cash deposit upto 50% of differential duty can be asked - Indoworth India v. CC (2010) 258 ELT 262 (CESTAT).

Bond or surety to be asked is at discretion of customs officer, to ensure recovery. Bank guarantee is safest and best course open to customs officer - Mohammed Fariz v. CC (2012) 275 ELT 303 (Ker HC DB).

Entire differential duty cannot be demanded for provisional release of goods. The regulations postulate only 20% of provisional duty for provisional release of goods - Bhaiya Fibres v. Additional DGRI (2012) 281 ELT 396 (Del HC DB) * Bella Imports v. CC (2014) 310 ELT 651 (Ker HC) * J B Overseas v. UOI (2016) 340 ELT 507 (Del HC DB).

2. CENVAT CREDIT

2.1 Manner of Distribution of Credit by Input Service Distributor - It has been clarified by the CBEC's Circular that the amended rule 7(d) seeks to allow distribution of input service credit to 'all units' in the ratio of their turnover of the previous year, rather than units to which service relates to.

2.2 Place of removal- defined in Cenvat - Definition of 'place of removal', is same as that already given under section 4(3)(c) of the Central Excise Act, 1944. It has been introduced separately in CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004.

2.3 Time-Limit - Time-limit for taking credit on input and input services has been introduced. Credit can now be taken maximum within 6 months from date of issue of any of the documents specified in sub-rule (1) of rule 9.

2.4 Conditions for taking credit in respect of input service - In full reverse charge cases, earlier credit was allowed only after payment of service tax and value of input service (both). Now, credit is allowed after service tax is paid. Condition relating to payment of value of input service prior to taking credit has been removed.

2.5 Export proceeds realization - Cenvat credit already reversed owing to non-realization of export proceeds of services within the specified period can be re-taken on pro rata basis to the extent of payment realized on the basis of documentary evidence of realization, provided export proceeds are received within one year from the specified period.

2.6 Inter-Unit Transfer of credit by large taxpayers - The inter-unit transfer of credit by large taxpayers has been withdrawn, if credit is taken on or after 11-7-2014 by any registered premises. Credit taken on or before 10-7-2014 would continue to be available for inter-unit transfers by large taxpayers.

3. CENTRAL EXCISE

3.1 Rule 8 of Central Excise Rules, 2002 amended - If assessee fails to pay the duty payable by him shown in the return within a period of 1 month from the due date then the assessee is liable to pay the penalty @ 1% on such amount of the duty not paid for each month or part thereof calculated from the due date for the period during which such failure continues.

Earlier, for default beyond 30 days the monthly facility to pay duty and Cenvat facility was withdrawn. This has been done away with.

3.2 Excise duty- E-Payment - Earlier, e-payment was mandatory for persons who had paid duty exceeding Rs. 1 lakh during preceding F.Y. Now every assessee shall electronically pay duty through internet banking and the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Central Excise having jurisdiction may allow assessee payment of duty by any mode other than internet banking.

3.3 Section 4A - For MRP based valuation under section 4A of the Central Excise Act, 1944, Notification No. 49/2008-CE(NT) has been amended to cover 'Filtering or purifying machinery and apparatus for gases – Parts' falling under Tariff Item 8421 99 00. The notified abatement is 35%.

3.4 Pouches of different RSP on a single machine - It is provided that with retrospective effect where a manufacturer manufactures pouches of different RSPs on a single machine in a month, the duty liability for that month would be the duty applicable to the highest of the RSP so manufactured – (Rule 8 of the Pan Masala Packing Machines (Capacity Determination and Collection of Duty) Rules, 2008 is being amended).

3.5 Additional duty of excise - Additional duty of excise, which was being levied only on pan masala and certain tobacco products under section 85 of the Finance Act, 2005 has been extended to 'waters, including mineral waters and aerated waters' @ 5%.

3.6 Amendment to Form 2 in Pan Masala Packing Machines (Capacity Determination and Collection of Duty) Rules, 2008 - Form 2 stands amended to provide for revised break up of duty owing to change in rate of duty/structure on Pan Masala.

22.1-1 No interest if duty voluntarily paid on issue of CBI&C order

Section 151A of Customs Act authorises Board to issue an order, instruction or direction for purpose of uniformity in respect of classification of goods or with respect to levy of duties of customs on such goods. Such orders are binding on officers of customs, though not on assessee. However, assessee may agree to abide by the order of Board and pay duty voluntarily on his own.

If he pays full amount of duty within 45 days from such order, without reserving right of appeal against such payment at any subsequent stage, he is exempted from payment of interest even if the duty was due earlier. However, if he pays only part of amount or pays the amount but reserves to himself right of appeal (i.e. if he makes payment under protest), the interest is payable from the month following the month in which the duty ought to have been paid. [Section 28AA(3) of Customs Act].

It may be noted that this relaxation from payment of interest is applicable only when CBI&C had issued a general order under section 151A of Customs Act. This relaxation does not apply if assessee pays duty on receipt of a show cause notice to him or even otherwise pays duty on his own.

By virtue of a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the High Court, company 'S' amalgamated with the assessee-company. The said company paid customs duty and claimed deduction under section 43B while including the same in the purchase price and thereafter in the closing stock. The assessee added back the same in the return of income as disallowable under section 43B. When the matter reached the Tribunal, the assessee filed a cross-objection and took the additional ground that the customs duty included in the closing stock of the amalgamating company be excluded because it was not taxable income as per the Supreme Court's decision in Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. CIT [1990] 186 ITR 278/53 Taxman 92. The assessee filed application for condonation of delay in filing the cross-objection submitting that the cross-objection was filed on the basis of the decision of the Supreme Court which was delivered on 4-9-1990 as the said decision was not available when the assessee filed the return and when the appeal was filed or when the appeal was decided by the Commissioner (Appeals). The Tribunal rejected assessee's application on the ground that same was filed after delay of more than a year and no sufficient cause had been made out explaining the delay.

On reference :

Earlier in the course of hearing of the appeal the assessee was directed to explain the entries of customs duty payment in the profit and loss account and balance-sheet. In response to the same, the assessee filed a supplemen-tary paper-book on 21-2-2007 explaining the entries made regarding the closing stock to show that the customs duty had been included therein, and had also explained in details as to how the provisions of section 145A introduced with effect from 1-4-1999 would have no effect in view of the overriding provisions of section 43B. These submissions had been briefly adverted to in the order of the Tribunal. One of the paragraph of the order of the Tribunal showed that the contention of the assessee that since inception, that is, from the assessment year 1994-95 till the assessment year 2006-07 the assessee had been following the inclusive method of accounting for customs duty payment while valuing the stock and that was accepted by the Tribunal. Further, the Tribunal had even stated in this paragraph that this claim of the assessee was not contradicted even in the assessment order. In the same paragraph, the Tribunal had also made an observation that in the year under appeal, the customs duty formed part of the closing stock, though the duty was not debited to the profit and loss account and had also referred to the fact that the duty was separately claimed as deduction in the return of income. In one other paragraph, the Tribunal had accepted the assessee's claim in principle and had observed that it was supported by the Special Bench's order of the Tribunal in Indian Communication Network (P.) Ltd. v. IAC [1994] 49 ITD 56 (Delhi), which was approved by the Supreme Court in Berger Paints India Ltd. v. CIT [2004] 266 ITR 99/ 135 Taxman 586. However, the observations made in the said paragraph showed that the Tribunal had considered that the customs duty was not included in the valuation of the closing stock. This observation was at variance with and contradictory to its earlier finding to the effect that the duty had been included in the closing stock as per the consistent accounting practice adopted by the assessee which was accepted in the assessment. It was only in view of the latter contradictory finding that the Tribunal thought it necessary to restore the matter to the Assessing Officer with the direction to examine the applicability of section 145A to the assessee's case. Even if it was assumed for the sake of argument that the case would have had to be restored to the Assessing Officer to be processed with reference to section 145 A notwithstanding the earlier finding of the Tribunal that the customs duty was included in the valuation of the closing stock, the fact that the assessee's argument was based on the order of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra) was not considered by the Tribunal showed that there was a mistake apparent from the record in light of decision of Supreme Court in Honda Siel Power Products Ltd. v. CIT [2007] 165 Taxman 307. [Para 8]

In Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra), it was held that section 43B has overriding effect over section 145A. This decision was referred to by the Tribunal in its order while summarizing the contentions of the department but unfortu-nately it omitted to deal with this decision and considered its applicability while taking a decision to remit the matter to the Assessing Officer with a direction to examine the applicability of section 145A. This omission had caused prejudice to the assessee in the sense that it had given rise to further proceedings before the Assessing Officer involving further delay in finalising the assessment proceedings, when the legal position already stood con-cluded by the binding order of the Tribunal in Maruti Udyog Ltd. (supra). The other mistake committed by the Tribunal to the prejudice of the assessee was its omission to refer to the assessee's plea that in the subsequent years, the Assessing Officer had accepted the assessee's claim under section 43B and assessments had been completed accordingly. [Para 8]

CLARIFICATION ONE

Instructions were issued vide CBDT Circular No. 21/2015, dated 10-12-2015, to the effect that appeals/SLPs should not be filed in cases where tax effect does not exceed the monetary limits specified under para 3 of the said Circular. It was also clarified therein that an appeal should not be filed merely because the tax effect in a case exceeds the monetary limits prescribed in the said Circular.

2. In para 8 of the aforesaid Circular No. 21/2015, it has been unambiguously and expressly provided that adverse judgments relating to the following issues should be contested on merits notwithstanding that the tax effect entailed is less than the monetary limits specified in Circular or even if there is no tax effect:

a.

Where the Constitutional validity of the provisions of an Act or Rule are under challenge, or

b.

Where Board's order, Notification, Instruction or Circular has been held to be illegal or ultra vires, or

c.

Where Revenue Audit Objection in the case has been accepted by the Department

d.

Where the addition relates to undisclosed foreign assets/bank accounts.

The direction to 'contest on merits' negates the mechanical filing of appeals in these cases.

3. However, it has been noticed that para 8(c) of Circular No. 21/2015, regarding cases where addition made on account of Revenue Audit Objection is deleted, is being erroneously interpreted and appeals are being mechanically filed by the Department without proper examination of the case on merits. This is contrary to the instructions contained in Circular No. 21/2015 and Circular No. 8/2016. It is, therefore, clarified that the import and intent of para 8 of the Circular No. 21/2015 is that even on issues mentioned in the said para, appeals against the adverse judgment should only be filed on merits.

Issue and submission of Declaration Forms for import

30. (1) A registered dealer desirous of importing or receiving into State from any place outside the State goods notified under or referred to in sub-section (1) of section 48 in excess of the quantity, measure or value specified thereunder shall send to the selling dealer or consignor of the other State two copies of the declaration in Form XVI, obtained by him under sub-rule (4).

(2) The registered dealer shall apply to the Assessing Authority, having jurisdiction over his principal place of business, for the issue of blank declaration forms.

(3) No blank declaration forms shall be issued by the Assessing Authority except on payment of a fee of rupees five per form. The application shall be signed by one of the persons mentioned in sub-rule (1) of rule 7 or a person duly authorized under rule 50.

(4) If the Assessing Authority is satisfied that the demand of the dealer for blank declaration forms is genuine and reasonable, he may issue such number of forms as he deems fit. No declaration form shall be issued unless the dealer has rendered an account of all such forms obtained earlier.

(5) If the fee paid is more than fee payable for the forms issued, balance shall remain to the credit of the dealer to be adjusted against future issues of the forms to him.

(6) The registered dealer shall send the original and duplicate portions of the form to the selling dealer or consignor of other State after filling in all the required particulars and signing it. He shall retain the counterfoil himself.

(7) Every declaration form obtained under sub-rule (4) shall be kept by the registered dealer in safe custody. He shall be personally liable for the loss, destruction or theft of any such form and the loss of Government revenue, if any, resulting directly or indirectly from such loss, destruction or theft.

(8) No registered dealer to whom a declaration form has been issued shall transfer the same to another person except for the lawful purpose of sub-rule (1).

(9) Every registered dealer to whom a declaration form is issued under sub-rule (4) shall maintain in a register in Form XII a true and complete account of every such form. If any form is lost, destroyed or stolen, the dealer shall forthwith report the fact to the Assessing Authority, make appropriate entries in the aforesaid register and take steps to issue proper public notice of such loss, destruction or theft.

(10) The registered dealer shall forthwith surrender all unused declaration forms remaining in stock with him at the time of discontinuance of his business or on the cancellation or expiry of the period of validity of his registration certificate, as the case may be.

(11) Where a duly completed declaration form, issued by the purchasing dealer or consignee to the selling dealer or consignor, is lost in transit or by the selling dealer or consignor, the purchasing dealer or consignee shall, on demand by such selling dealer or consignor, issue duplicate declaration form to him in the same manner as the declaration form originally issued:

Provided that before issuing it, the purchasing dealer or consignee shall give the following declaration in red ink, duly signed by him, on each of the three portions of such duplicate declaration form:—

"I hereby declare that this is the duplicate of the declaration form No. ………… signed on ………… and issued to M/s. ………….. in respect of …………. (description of goods) valuing at Rs. ……………….

Signature ……………."

(12) The Commissioner of Commercial Tax shall from time to time circulate the particulars of the declaration forms in respect of which a report is received under sub-rule (9).

(13) The Commissioner of Commercial Tax may, by notification, declare that declaration forms of a particular series, design or colour shall be deemed obsolete and invalid, with effect from such date as may be specified in the notification, and may in their place substitute new forms of fresh series, design or colour.

(14) Where a notification is issued under sub-rule (13), all registered dealers shall surrender to the Assessing Authority all unused forms declared obsolete and invalid which may be in their possession and obtain in exchange such new forms as may be substituted in place thereof:

Provided that new forms shall not be issued to a dealer until he has rendered account of the forms previously issued to him and until he has returned the balance, if any, to the Assessing Authority.

(15) No registered dealer shall issue any declaration except in a declaration form obtained by him from the Assessing Authority having jurisdiction over his principal place of business and not declared obsolete or invalid under the provisions of sub-rule (13).

Suppression of facts

4. In self assessment system it is the responsibility of assessee to furnish full and complete information. For example, if the assessee's are availing of exemption which is subject to fulfilment of the conditions, they are expected to state clearly in their returns whether they were fulfilled or not. Simply mentioning in the returns about availment of some conditional exemption without mentioning anything about fulfilment of those conditions amounts to willful suppression of facts if, subsequently, it is found that the condition of exemption had not been fulfilled.

4.1 Relevant Case Laws :

4.1-1 In CCE v. Quantum Instruments & Electronics 2014 (302) ELT 113 (Tri. Delhi) it was held that while using the brand name of another person, the assessee's are required to disclose such use to the jurisdictional Central Excise Authorities either in their ER-1 return or by direct communication, otherwise it would amount to suppression of facts.

4.1-2 In CCE v. IPCA Laboratories Ltd. – 2014 (302) ELT 306 (Tri. Delhi) the assessee was receiving inputs and sent the same to their job worker either directly or through them. The job worker was paying duty on the final product, which was being cleared by them on behalf of the assessee by raising the invoice on their account. The job worker was being reimbursed by the assessee for the duty paid by the job worker. The assessee availed of credit on the inputs. The Revenue was of the view that the assessee was not entitled to the credit since they had not paid the duty themselves. The Revenue invoked the extended period of limitation on the ground of suppression of facts and confirmed the duty with interest and penalty. The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal on the ground of limitation. The Tribunal also upheld the order of Commissioner (Appeals). The High Court held that the entire credit had been taken by the assessee on statutory records which had been reflected in those records, no suppression could be attributed to them. Accordingly, the demand was raised beyond the normal period of limitation.

4.1-3 In CCE, C&ST v. Precision Pipes and Profiles Co. Ltd. [2014] 42 taxmann.com 318/43 GST 695 (All.) the assessee availed of CENVAT credit on the strength of 11 bills of entry in which the additional customs duty had not been paid in cash but had been adjusted against Duty Entitlement Pass Book. The Revenue invoked the extended period of limitation and confirmed the demand. The appellate authority confirmed the demand of adjudicating authority. The Tribunal reversed the findings of the lower authorities. The High Court found that the assessee did not disclose or reflect that the additional customs duty had been paid through DEPB adjustments, nor did the returns show that the bills of entry were submitted to the department. Moreover, it had been found that the payment of additional customs duty through adjustment was not incorporated in any of the returns and it was only in the course of audit that it was found that the additional customs duty had not been paid in cash. It was on this basis that the extended period of limitation was invoked. The Tribunal did not consider the same. The High Court set aside the order of the Tribunal and remanded the case for reconsideration.

While SVB investigations are essential for ensuring accurate customs valuation, there are certain instances where such investigations are unnecessary, particularly when the revenue implications are negligible. Key exemptions include:

Samples and Prototypes: Imports involving samples or prototypes from related suppliers, which hold minimal commercial value, are exempt from SVB investigations.

Imports with Full Duty Exemption: Where the imported goods are fully exempt from customs duties or the applicable duty rate is nil, SVB investigations are not required, as there is no revenue impact.

Low-Value Imports: Transactions below Rs. 1 lakh, provided the cumulative value of such transactions does not exceed Rs. 25 lakhs in a financial year, are exempt from SVB scrutiny, ensuring that small-scale imports are not unnecessarily delayed.

7. Jurisdictional Framework of SVBs:

Currently, SVBs operate out of five key customs locations across India:

Bengaluru

Chennai

Kolkata

Delhi

Mumbai

The jurisdiction of an SVB is typically determined by the location of the importer's corporate or registered office.

8. Reform of Extra Duty Deposit (EDD) Provisions:

The earlier SVB regime was heavily criticized for its imposition of EDD—1% of the declared assessable value—which could be escalated to 5% in cases of non-compliance with document submission timelines. This was widely regarded as an excessive burden on trade. In response to industry representations, the government eliminated the requirement for EDD in Circular No. 05/2016.

However, under the revised regime, if an importer fails to submit the requisite documentation within 60 days, the customs authorities may impose a security deposit of 5%, valid for an initial period of three months. This deposit can be furnished in the form of either a cash payment or a bank guarantee, providing flexibility to the importer while ensuring compliance with customs requirements.

9. Conclusion:

The SVB's investigatory powers are pivotal in safeguarding the integrity of the customs valuation process, particularly in complex related-party transactions where the declared value may be subject to manipulation. The intricate interplay between contractual terms, such as royalties, and the customs valuation process necessitates careful oversight by SVBs to prevent undervaluation. Importers, for their part, can mitigate the time and cost implications of SVB investigations by ensuring full compliance with documentation requirements and maintaining transparency in their transactional relationships.

◆ The Inventory Valuation requires adjustment in respect of Duty, etc., paid or incurred for bringing the goods to the place or location. To illustrate, if goods are sent from Bombay to a branch in Surat and goods have reached Surat, the value would include Excise Duty paid for clearing the goods, Transportation and Insurance Cost and Octroi, if any, levied by Surat Municipal Authority. If the goods are in-transit, it would include Excise Duty and Transport/Insurance Cost; but, cannot include any Octroi which is payable only when the goods reach Surat.

Now, when net realisable value is adopted as a basis, it would include the price which is realisable as also various levies. As such, no further adjustment may be required. However, having regard to the language of the provision, it would be necessary to demonstrate that in the net realisable value, Duty, etc., in relation thereto, have been included.

In other words, such disputed assessment of duty, etc., cannot be added to the stock or even to the value of sale or purchase.

◆ Effect of amendment vis a vis opening inventory - Section 145A requires adjustment in value of inventory. As explained above, the Notes on Clauses clarify that the method prescribed by section 145A should also be followed for valuing opening stock. Now, if an assessee who does not provide for excise duty, pending clearance of goods, as per method of accounting regularly followed and accordingly, does not include the same in value of inventory in assessment year 1988-89, can, however, include, as per the provisions, such un-provided excise duty in the value of opening stock, in computing income for assessment year 1999-2000, which would have the effect of reducing his profits for assessment year 1999-2000. In Sita Ram (supra), it was observed:

"43. Of course, procedure is within the Court's power, but where it pares down pre-judicially the very right, carving the kernel out, it violates the provision creating the right. Appeal is a remedial right and if the remedy is reduced to a husk by procedural excess, the right became a casualty. That cannot be."

Therefore, the rule that object of the Legislature has to be kept in view and a construction consistent with the object has to be placed on the words used if there be ambiguity, is also applicable in construing a taxing enactment.12 Every taxing statute has a fiscal philosophy - a feel of which is necessary to gather the intent and effect of its different clauses13.

Various indirect taxing statutes especially Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 mandates for filing of appeal on the deposit of 10% of the amount of tax in dispute and on deposit of the same the recovery proceedings in respect thereof shall be deemed to be stayed. What deserves to be noticed is that under the Act stay is the consequence of deposit of 10% of the amount of tax in dispute and no independent power expressly under the Act has been conferred on the Appellate Authorities to exercise the power of stay even if a prima facie case is made out or is forthcoming from the Order of the Adjudicating Authority on account of being ultra vires the Act or without jurisdiction or patently illegal etc.

Conclusion:

The emphasis is on deposit of certain percentage of amount of disputed demand. What is demand of duty/penalty in dispute has not been defined under the indirect taxing statutes. Deposits made during the pendency of the proceedings, or even after the order-in-original is passed, have to be taken into consideration for determining and deciding whether condition of pre-deposit of certain percentage of duty/penalty has been satisfied. Earlier deposits do not get obliterated and are not to be treated as inconsequential as rightly pointed out by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of Santani Sales Organisation (supra)in view of the Circular (supra) issued by the Central Board of Excise & Customs. A Circular provides extraneous aid to construction being contemporanea expositio for interpreting a statute with reference to the exposition it has received from contemporary authority i.e., Central Board of Excise & Customs14. The proceedings under indirect taxing statutes culminate in the passing of an Order determining the duty/penalty payable after the imposition of self-assessment of payment of duty/tax and therefore, the entire amount of duty and penalty levied thereon is open to challenge before the Appellate Authorities on the ground of jurisdictional and/or legal errors emanating therefrom. In most of such cases, on the basis of self-assessment of the assessee/dealer duty is declared and deposited along with the returns. If the aggrieved assessee/dealer is to deposit de novo certain percentage of the entire amount of disputed demand of duty/penalty in addition to the amount already declared and deposited with the returns the provisions of Article 265 of the Constitution of India would come into play, thereby making such a mandate of deposit along with the memorandum of appeal a negation of not only the right to violate free access to justice but the right of appeal itself illusory and delusive particularly in the absence of any power of stay of demand conferred on the Appellate Authorities under the various indirect taxing statutes. Though equity and taxation are often strangers, attempts should be made that they do not remain always so and if a construction results in equity rather than injustice, then such a construction should be preferred with promotes justice and fair play which are the facets of rule of law and a part and parcel of Article 14 of the Constitution of India15. Thus, the inevitable conclusion drawn by the Hon'ble High Court of Punjab & Haryana backed up by the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi is fundamentally a correct view.

The Tribunal held that delay could have been condoned, if reason for delay was found acceptable by the Commissioner (Appeals) and, therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly dismissed the appeal on ground of limitation. [Vijay Baburao Petkar v. CST [2007] 11 STT 429 (MUM. - CESTAT)]

Section 86 - Appeals to Appellate Tribunal - Condonation of delay

The Tribunal cannot condone delay, which has occurred in filing of appeal before lower appellate authority. [Vijay Baburao Petkar’s case (supra)]. If an appeal is not filed by a party within time-limit stipulated in appeal provision, a legal right is accrued to other side on the ground that because of non-filing of appeal, order passed in favour of other side would have been accepted and reached its finality, and therefore, aforesaid legal right cannot be simply brushed aside by filing an application for condonation of delay of 350 days on ground that similar issue is stated to be pending before the Supreme Court. [CSTv. Lumax Samlip Industries Ltd. [2007] 11 STT 449 (MAD.)]

Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 - Cenvat credit - Input service - Transport services

Assessee, a manufacturer of cotton yarn, paid service tax on ‘Goods transport agency’s service’ received in connection with inward movement of its inputs and in connection with outward movement of its final product. Assessee utilized credit of duty paid on inputs and capital goods as also credit of service tax paid on input service. This was objected to by the department and amount equivalent to credit found to have been ‘wrongly’ utilized, was demanded. The Tribunal held that in view of the decision in the case of R.R.D. Tex (P.) Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 10 STT 255 (Chennai-CESTAT), assessee could validly avail credit of duty paid and, therefore, order demanding tax was to be set aside. [Soundararaja Mills Ltd. v. CCE, [2007] 11 STT 345 (CHENNAI - CESTAT)] But on the other side the Tribunal has taken different approach also. In one case, assessee, a manufacturer of cotton yarn, paid service tax on Goods Transport Agency’s (GTA) Service received by them for inward transportation of their inputs and outward transportation of their final product. It availed CENVAT credit of the duty/service tax paid on inputs/capital goods or input service. This was objected to by the department. But the Tribunal held the objection of department as unsustainable. [Iswari Spg Mills Ltd. v. CCE, [2007] 11 STT 194 (CHENNAI - CESTAT])]. In another case, assessees, manufacturers of yarn, availed Goods Transport Agency’s (GTA) service for inward transportation of inputs and outward transportation of final products. They treated GTA service as an ‘output service’ within meaning of expression given under prevailing rule 2(p) and made payments of service tax therefor by way of debit in CENVAT account. Such utilisation of CENVAT credit was objected to by department and demands were raised. The Tribunal held that since there was no prima facie case for assessees, they were to be directed to pre-deposit 50 per cent of respective duty amounts. The Tribunal held: [Thiyagarajar Mills v. III. Conclusion

In our opinion, the proposed amendment is a welcome change from its earlier version and will provide much-needed relief to those cases which have been pending for several years. The amendment reflects a broader trend of India's fiscal policy aimed at enhancing trade facilitation, modernizing India's Customs framework, and restoring faith of the public in the system.

While on a broader level, the change appears promising allowing businesses to focus on innovation and expansion, however on a deeper analysis, it does pose various questions on what the future holds. As the businesses prepare to adapt to this new framework, clarity and guidance from the Custom authorities and Courts will be crucial in ensuring a smooth transition into this new era of provisional assessments.
